stories.Headline: LeBron James sues PlayVision over AI app Bron using his likeness and nickname
stories.Summary:
LeBron James sued the makers of an AI sports-betting app on Tuesday, saying they deliberately violated his publicity rights and trademarks by calling it "Bron" and using artificially generated images of him in their marketing. The lawsuit was filed in U.S. District Court in New York, according to the Associated Press. James is a Philadelphia 76ers star and NBA superstar. The app's developer is PlayVision Inc., which is based in California. The app is called "Bron."

The complaint asks the court to block the makers from using James' name, to give up any money they've already made and to award damages, including fair market value for the use of his name as well as punitive damages. James' lawyers sent a cease-and-desist letter on Nov. 5, after which the startup removed the ad from its X and Instagram accounts. The company took the ad down, but not before it had been reposted and viewed about 1 million times, the lawsuit said. The ad attracted about one million views on X within a day, according to the lawsuit. The marketing campaign this month featured an image of a person resembling James, down to his tattoos, voice and No. 23 jersey, sitting in a locker room and scrolling through the app.

James' attorneys called it "a willful, bad-faith tactic" to use the player's fame, likeness and nickname to promote "a new and unknown product." The lawsuit states that "Defendants did not care that they had engaged in illegal conduct to gain notoriety for their previously unknown app." It says they "intentionally created the false impression that Mr. James endorsed and was affiliated with their Bron App, in an effort to drive downloads and paid subscriptions." Gupta responded to the attorneys' demand on social media by writing that the app would get a new name, but no new name had been adopted by the time the lawsuit was filed. Gupta wrote on social media this week that the new name will be announced Wednesday.

Messages sent by The Associated Press through the app's website and to email addresses for its founders seeking comment were not immediately returned Tuesday. The lawsuit notes that James typically commands tens of millions of dollars for such endorsement deals and that he already has an exclusive deal with the prediction market platform Polymarket. It alleges that the app's marketing was especially harmful in part because it showed the AI-generated James scrolling through bets involving NBA players. The lawsuit said "The integrity of NBA competition -- and the public's confidence that players are not betting on the games they play -- is of paramount importance to the league, its players, and its fans." It added that "Any suggestion that an active NBA player is betting on NBA games is therefore far from a trivial matter, and it should not be used for clicks and views."

The app's developer, PlayVision Inc., was launched by chief executive Anish Gupta and chief technology officer Marc Zoghby in 2025, with backing from the startup accelerator Y Combinator, as a program that would use artificial intelligence to analyze game and practice footage for sports teams and fans. This year, the company released its "Bron" app, which it says does not take direct wagers but charges a subscription fee for services such as bet tracking and odds comparisons. Bron is described in Apple's App Store as a "sports analytics and betting research app with live odds comparisons, data-backed picks, player and team trends, a multi-leg Slip and bet tracking." The listing says it does not accept wagers. PlayVision participated in Y Combinator's fall 2025 batch.

James is seeking damages and a court order preventing the defendants from using his name, image, likeness, and voice, as well as the Bron name. The lawsuit claims the founders calculated that the publicity would outweigh any potential legal consequences, effectively treating the alleged violation of James' rights as a marketing expense. It argues that James' endorsements are "uniquely valuable," adding, "That is why defendants decided to steal it for themselves." However, the ad remained available through third-party reposts, and the company had not changed the app's name as of the lawsuit's filing. Gupta wrote on social media this week that the new name will be announced Wednesday.

stories.Headline: DataMEDS AI interim co-CEO Gerald Commissiong authors Q4 outlook letter on cutting healthcare costs
stories.Summary:
On November 16, 2026, the healthcare company DataMEDS AI released a corporate outlook for the fourth quarter of the year. Interim Co-CEO Gerald Commissiong authored the letter to detail the company's strategic vision and current operational goals. The company is listed on the NASDAQ exchange under the ticker symbol MEDS and is based in Tampa, Florida. This announcement follows a turnaround process that the company says began during the second quarter of the year. The letter outlines how the firm intends to integrate technology and physical infrastructure to improve American healthcare outcomes.

The company uses its EinsteinRx artificial intelligence platform and PharmacyChain blockchain smart contracts platform to manage health information and physical infrastructure. It integrates these tools into the Health Lives Here mobile application developed by Tollo Health, LLC, for consumer use. The firm owns the Corexa Health subsidiary for pharmacy dispensing and Helomics Corporation, a molecular diagnostics lab based in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. Helomics focuses on the ChemoFx Assay chemotherapy selection diagnostics test to help oncologists make better treatment decisions for patients. These assets allow the company to manage GLP-1 patient therapy and work with a Florida-based Health Maintenance Organization.

Interim Co-CEO Gerald Commissiong stated that the American healthcare system is broken and requires a focus on helping both insured and uninsured patients. He explained that the business model aims to cut out middlemen to ensure payors pay fair prices and receive beneficial outcomes. Commissiong believes that leveraging patient data is necessary to rein in overcompensated stakeholders who are currently gouging the healthcare industry. He noted that the company seeks to narrow the arbitrage between the cost of healthcare and the actual results received. The executive believes that creating synergies through research and development will eventually deliver measurable benefit outputs for the shareholders.

The company believes that most patients are willing to allow their de-identified data to be used to improve treatment paradigms. Institutional payors are identified as the target clients who may see value in this scalable model for managing health journeys. The company claims that using competitors' platforms to achieve these specific objectives would violate its own healthcare technology intellectual property. Patients are affected by the goal to improve regimen compliance and manage the titration of therapy to reduce expensive side effects. Physicians are also affected as the technology helps them monitor their patients more efficiently using proprietary intellectual property assets.

A report from Menlo Ventures titled 2026: The State of AI in Healthcare notes that healthcare is the largest AI vertical. Spending in this sector grew 2.5x to 3.7 billion dollars, which is more than double the spend in the legal vertical. AI for drug discovery saw spend jump from 30 million to 700 million dollars as pharmaceutical companies deploy AI at scale. Clinical copilots grew 5.5x to 550 million dollars, while patient engagement grew 4.5x to 450 million dollars in the market. Payer AI spend lags behind providers by 19x, and 43 percent of payers say provider AI coding increased costs.

DataMEDS has 5,724,857 common shares outstanding, with 2,745,900 shares deposited in the Depository Trust and Clearing Corporation for trading. Certain stockholders holding 1,333,930 shares are under lock-up agreements that prevent sales for at least ninety days from the release date. There are 80,826 cash warrants outstanding with a fixed exercise price of 35.00 dollars per share for free trading shares. The company plans to drive for scale in 2027 after generating proof-of-concept revenue and maintaining strict financial discipline. The articles leave open whether the company will successfully complete its turnaround or achieve its goals for profitability and liquidity.

stories.Headline: Cambridge Dictionary names human its 2026 word of the year amid AI fears
stories.Summary:
The Cambridge Dictionary selected the word human as its word of the year for 2026. This decision was made on November 18, 2026, in London, United Kingdom. The choice was inspired by widespread fears regarding the rise of artificial intelligence. This selection reflects a cultural zeitgeist and a backlash against blurring lines between people and machines. The dictionary looked back to the 15th century to find this specific term.

The word human is an adjective derived from the Latin word humanus and has been used since the 1450s. Cambridge defines it as having the qualities, faults, and feelings of people, unlike gods, animals, or machines. Other 2026 contenders included analogue, for non-digital experiences, and agent, for AI systems that operate without human control. This choice differs from typical selections, which are often novel words or mainstream slang. The selection highlights a shift in how society views the distinction between biological and artificial intelligence.

Lexicographer Colin McIntosh stated that artificial intelligence is changing the way people talk about being human. He noted that fears about outsourcing thinking have caused people to reconsider their reliance on AI technology. This reconsideration affects a wide range of professionals, from top mathematicians to teachers of young children. McIntosh believes the word reflects a debate over the blurred lines between machines and people. He suggests that the term serves as a response to the current technological era.

Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates commented that AI is making people think harder about what it means to be human. Gates has promoted the smart use of AI but believes its success should be measured by human improvement. The articles mention that various professionals, including teachers and mathematicians, are affected by the outsourcing of human thought. These groups are now questioning the extent to which they should rely on automated systems. The broader public is also affected by the ongoing debate over artificial intelligence.

Dictionaries have focused heavily on artificial intelligence when choosing words of the year in recent years. Collins Dictionary chose the term AI in 2023, while Cambridge picked the word hallucinate that same year. Merriam-Webster recently named slop as its word of the year to describe low-quality content produced by AI. Collins also selected vibe coding to describe a specific method of AI-assisted software development. These previous choices show a consistent trend of tracking the impact of AI on language.

The dictionary has now officially designated human as the word that best captures the current cultural moment. The articles do not state if this trend will continue into the next year of selections. It remains open whether the backlash against AI will lead to more traditional word choices. The text does not specify how the dictionary will track the usage of human in 2027. No further details are provided regarding future lexicographical changes or upcoming word of the year candidates.

stories.Headline: Google rolls out Gemini 4 Hydrogen to free and paid users in the Gemini app
stories.Summary:
Google DeepMind launched Gemini in December 2023, and the system has since gone through several model generations, including Gemini 4 Argon in October and Gemini 4 Hydrogen on Nov. 12. CNET published its explainer on Nov. 16, 2026, written by Barbara Pazur and edited by Corinne Reichert. The name now covers Google's family of AI models and its consumer AI assistant, which began as a large language model. The models can understand text, images, audio, video and code and answer questions about them. Gemini 4 Hydrogen is rolling out to free and paid users in the Gemini app, with access in Google Sheets starting with Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers.

Gemini 4 Argon is included in those subscriptions for more complex reasoning and analysis, and Gemini 4 Hydrogen is also available in Antigravity to Pro and Ultra subscribers. Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber is restricted to approved cybersecurity defenders through Google's Fairwind program, while Gemini 4 Carbon is rolling out to Google AI Ultra subscribers in Google Antigravity, the Gemini app and AI Mode in Google Search. Gemini can connect with Gmail, Calendar, Docs, Sheets and Drive, and it can link to more than 40 apps, including Adobe and Shopify, plus Instacart for groceries and OpenTable for reservations. Skills will replace Gems on Nov. 17 for personal accounts, and Gemini Live offers 10 new voice options. AI Overviews are available in more than 200 countries and territories and over 40 languages, with more than 2.5 billion monthly active users, while AI Mode has surpassed 1 billion monthly active users.

A Google spokesperson told CNET by email that Gemini is powerful but only as helpful as the information shared with it, and that brief or vague prompts produce generic answers. The spokesperson recommended uploading files, screenshots or links so output becomes more helpful with detailed context and instructions. The spokesperson called Tasks, previously called Spark, one of the most overlooked features and described it as a 24/7 personal AI agent. On privacy, the spokesperson said users are in control, that Personal Intelligence was built with privacy at the core, and that connecting apps is entirely off by default. The spokesperson added that Gemini never trains its foundational models on private emails, photos or files.

Google faced criticism over hallucinations and over how Gemini depicted historical figures and different races, including generating images of Black and Asian Nazi soldiers, and critics accused Google of trying too hard to show diversity. Google paused Gemini's image generation and promised to clean up the mess, and its current image models use the Nano Banana name. Google came under fire for bizarre advice AI Overviews gave during its 2024 US rollout, including suggesting people eat rocks daily or put glue in pizza recipes, and the company quickly made some fixes. Some people still do not like AI Overviews, and they cannot be disabled. Gemini is built into Pixel phones and serves as the primary Google AI assistant across many Android devices, and it also powers Google Home features that summarize camera or doorbell recordings.

Gemini is free as a personal AI assistant, and the free version uses an Auto setting to choose the model, though users can adjust the thinking level to low, medium or high. Deep Research is technically available across tiers, but free users face much stricter capacity and usage limits than paid subscribers. For personal accounts, Google may use Gemini activity to improve its services, including with help from human reviewers, when Keep Activity is turned on. Temporary chats do not appear in recent conversations and are not used to improve Google's AI with human reviewers, but Google retains them for up to 72 hours. A Memory summary under Settings/Personal intelligence is available in English to eligible US subscribers with Memory and Keep Activity turned on.

Google AI Studio, with Gemini 4 Carbon and Hydrogen, now lets developers build and ship full-stack Android applications and publish to the Play Store in minutes, according to Google's developer blog post of Nov. 17, 2026. The Build agent takes a single prompt to a production-ready Kotlin Android app with data persistence, user sign-in and AI features, and developers can test on their own device from the Play Store at no cost. The agent provisions a Cloud Firestore database with Security Rules and Google Sign-In, and it configures Firebase AI Logic and Firebase App Check using Google Fraud Defense, formerly reCAPTCHA Enterprise, so API keys stay protected server-side. Developers get a faster high-definition Android emulator with real-time audio output, one-click emulator screenshots sent to the coding agent, and custom fonts. Previously, Android apps generated in AI Studio were limited to local session storage.

stories.Headline: TigerConnect's Peter Stetson says organizational barriers stall hospital AI pilots before scale
stories.Summary:
Dr. Peter Stetson, chief medical informatics officer at the clinical communication vendor TigerConnect and previously chief health informatics officer at Memorial Sloan Kettering, where he oversaw nearly 100 AI models, explained in a November 18, 2026 Healthcare IT News article why many hospital AI pilots stall before reaching scale. Hospitals and health systems are investing heavily in artificial intelligence and launching pilots meant to improve patient care, streamline clinical workflows and reduce administrative burdens, yet many of these initiatives struggle to move beyond the experimental stage even when the technology shows promising results. Stetson said the biggest obstacles are usually organizational rather than technical, because a pilot can succeed with a motivated team, dedicated resources and a tightly defined use case, while scaling demands that the same system work across multiple departments, clinical environments and operational workflows. He described situations where the AI worked exactly as intended but no clear process existed for who should act on the information, when they should act, or how that action fit into the broader workflow.

Before launching a pilot, Stetson said, health systems should define the problem they are trying to solve and how success will be measured, along with baseline measurements, and should agree in advance on what success and failure look like. Every AI initiative should have executive sponsorship, clinical ownership, operational ownership and clearly defined performance metrics, and projects often fail when responsibility is diffuse and everyone assumes someone else is driving adoption. Organizations that scale successfully treat AI as a transformation initiative rather than a technology initiative, bringing together clinical, operational, IT, quality and change management leaders from the outset. Stetson said AI needs to be embedded within the systems and workflows clinicians already use and trust, because clinicians do not like leaving their normal workflow, and he warned that inserting AI into an existing process does not automatically improve that process. Clinical workflow redesign is often where organizations fall short, and without that work even highly accurate AI can become just another alert, notification or dashboard competing for attention.

Stetson said successful organizations recognize that EHR integration, workflow redesign and governance are interconnected elements of a broader strategy rather than separate initiatives, and that the goal is durable, real-world workflows that reduce cognitive burden on clinicians and improve patient care at scale. He said the organizations that scale have connected three capabilities: a system of record that captures information, a system of prediction that generates insight and a system of activation that turns those insights into coordinated action, and he called activation the next challenge for healthcare. When judging whether an application is ready for expansion, leaders should look beyond technical performance metrics to clinical outcomes, operational efficiency, workflow adoption, user satisfaction, response times, throughput and whether the system reduces cognitive and administrative burden on staff. If a system is delivering measurable clinical, operational or financial benefits and is being adopted by end users, it may be ready to scale, while a strong value proposition with lagging adoption may call for workflow redesign or additional change management. If the technology continues to struggle to produce meaningful outcomes despite refinement, Stetson concluded, organizations should be disciplined enough to move on.

stories.Headline: Rebecca Bradley says AI changes how law firms train junior lawyers to build judgment
stories.Summary:
Rebecca S. Bradley of Foley & Lardner LLP wrote an article published Tuesday, November 17, 2026, in The National Law Review about how artificial intelligence is changing how lawyers learn. She described the traditional path of becoming a lawyer as starting with fundamentals, learning by doing, receiving feedback from more experienced lawyers, and gradually taking on more complex work. She said AI is changing that progression because some tasks AI can now accelerate gave junior lawyers repetitions to absorb legal concepts, recognize patterns, learn what matters, and develop judgment. She asked how new lawyers will build the judgment clients rely on if they spend less time performing foundational work. She said AI creates an opportunity and a responsibility for law firms to become far more deliberate about how lawyers learn.

Bradley explored what that could look like as a panelist for the Building The Law Firm of the Future: How Tech, Business, and Talent Decisions Collide program during Harvey Forum Chicago 2026. She was joined on the panel by Seth Gottlieb, Partner and Global Vice Chair of the Technology Industry Group at Latham & Watkins, and William H. J. Hubbard, Clifton R. Musser Professor of Law and Economics at The University of Chicago Law School. The conversation was moderated by Keith Enright, Chief Strategy Officer at Harvey. Bradley wrote that the apprenticeship model is not disappearing for lawyers beginning their careers but is evolving. She said AI creates capacity in a profession where time is always at a premium, and the challenge for firms is what they do with it.

Bradley said that if AI saves an hour on an assignment and that hour disappears into the next task, the firm gains efficiency but may lose a developmental opportunity. She said deliberately reinvesting some of that time in feedback, client exposure, and discussion of strategy and judgment can make the apprenticeship experience richer. She said learning takes time, repetition, experimentation, and sometimes struggle, and requires opportunities to decide, test reasoning, receive feedback, and try again. She said this investment can include simulated exercises and repetitions, such as privilege-review exercises, mock objections, and advocacy exercises for litigators. She said it can include more feedback from experienced lawyers who explain the why behind the work and earlier client exposure to understand context first-hand.

Bradley said honesty about the past is required because not every junior associate's struggle in the pre-AI era built judgment, and time saved on those tasks can be redirected toward experiences that do. She said AI can make simulations easier to create, personalize, and repeat, generating a fresh set of documents with planted privilege issues or playing opposing counsel or an arbitrator in a practice argument. She said supervising lawyers increasingly need to understand not only the finished product but also the process by which it was created. She said a supervising lawyer may address whether AI use is appropriate, where it might add value, client restrictions or expectations, and the level of verification required when an assignment is made. She said a partner who asks a first-year associate what they asked the tool to do and how they checked the citations learns far more about the associate's judgment than one who only reads the memo.

Bradley said the core capabilities lawyers need to develop, including judgment, ethical decision-making, writing and communication, and understanding client objectives, have not changed. She described judgment as the instinct that makes a first-year pause over a clause that looks routine or question a case citation that seems a little too perfect. She said one of the most important forms of judgment young lawyers will develop in an AI-enabled profession is knowing where AI belongs in the workflow, not simply knowing how to use it. She said a law student's or junior lawyer's value will come from understanding the problem well enough to decide what the tool should do, recognizing when its output is incomplete or wrong, and knowing how to improve it. She said AI makes the distinctly human parts of excellent lawyering, such as asking the right question, exercising skepticism, and understanding what matters to the client, even more important.

A separate press release dated November 17, 2026, announced that GALEX AI, an artificial intelligence platform specializing in forensic clinical auditing and medical record analysis, is expanding its international operations across the United States, Colombia, Mexico, and Spain. The release, issued from Bogotá, D.C., Colombia, said the company is also announcing an initiative to offer free pilot programs to public hospitals of lower complexity in Colombia. It said the initiative aims to make advanced artificial intelligence technology accessible to public healthcare institutions, supporting medical teams in reviewing clinical cases, identifying potential gaps in medical documentation, and strengthening clinical quality assessment. It said GALEX AI combines Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Big Data, and Machine Learning technologies to analyze extensive medical records and compare documented clinical care against clinical practice guidelines, medical protocols, healthcare regulations, and specialized reference sources. It said the platform is designed to help identify potential deviations, omissions, inconsistencies, and documentation gaps throughout the patient care process.

The release said the platform's analysis may include medical history and previous clinical records, diagnosis and treatment decisions, medication orders and administration records, laboratory results and diagnostic imaging, surgical procedures and postoperative care, patient monitoring, follow-up, and clinical documentation, and informed consent and relevant medical records. It said the platform is designed as a decision-support and auditing tool that does not independently establish medical negligence, replace professional medical judgment, or determine legal liability, and its findings require review and interpretation by qualified professionals. It said GALEX AI will initially offer free pilot programs to public hospitals of lower complexity in Colombia to test the technology in practical institutional settings, including medical board meetings, clinical case reviews, and health facilities. Maikel Nisimblat, Founder of GALEX AI, said AI should not only transform healthcare technology but should help save lives and make better medical care accessible to everyone. The release included illustrative images of Nisimblat at a hospital reviewing medical imaging and presenting the technology to healthcare professionals at a medical conference.

stories.Headline: Microsoft unveils six specialized AI models at Ignite to rival OpenAI and Anthropic on cost
stories.Summary:
Microsoft unveiled six specialized AI models at its Ignite conference in San Francisco on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, according to GeekWire. The models were released by Microsoft AI to compete with OpenAI and Anthropic at a fraction of the price. CEO Satya Nadella announced on the same stage that OpenAI's GPT-6.2, released that morning, is now available in Microsoft Foundry. Microsoft also introduced MAI Code 2, available in GitHub Copilot starting Tuesday. Microsoft introduced MAI Cyber 2 as part of the lineup.

Microsoft says MAI Code 2 delivers 96% of the coding performance of Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the price, on benchmarks Microsoft chose. Jacob Andreou, Microsoft's executive vice president of Copilot, presented a chart of estimated monthly costs per business user, including subscription and usage fees. The chart put Copilot at $30 for an "everyday" AI user, compared with $81 for ChatGPT and $205 for Claude. For "advanced" users of each company's agent tools, it showed $96 for Copilot, $149 for ChatGPT and $299 for Claude. Most of the Claude figure is estimated usage charges on top of Anthropic's $20 enterprise seat.

Judson Althoff, CEO of Microsoft's commercial business, said during the opening keynote that anything you can do in Claude or ChatGPT, you can do better with Copilot and for less. Andreou said Anthropic and OpenAI have embraced documents, slides and spreadsheets, but their simplified viewers and editors force compromise on power and collaboration. Andreou said the full versions of Word, Excel and PowerPoint inside Copilot are included in the subscription. He said Copilot is the only way to draft a PowerPoint presentation without spinning a meter. The numbers come from research Microsoft commissioned and paid for from GigaOm, based on testing Microsoft ran in October on modeled workloads.

The figures reflect enterprise pricing, which adds usage charges to a per-seat fee, not the flat monthly subscriptions that individuals pay for ChatGPT and Claude. Anthropic last week introduced new Claude-based tools for spreadsheets and whiteboards that compete more directly with Office. Anthropic is expected to make its IPO this week, putting new scrutiny on its financials and long-term growth prospects. Anthropic's Claude for Microsoft 365 lets people use Claude inside Office apps for tasks such as sorting email and creating slide decks. The product has less than a tenth as many weekly users as the paid version of Copilot in Office, The Information reported Monday, citing internal Microsoft data.

Microsoft is a partner and investor in both OpenAI and Anthropic, and it sells their AI models to its own customers. Andreou is one of the executives who see the user gap as a sign Microsoft can keep customers from switching, the report said. A separate Microsoft report highlighted both the investment and potential rewards of adopting AI for small businesses. A Microsoft spokesperson said AI is not just a technological trend but a transformative tool that, if adopted wisely, can yield significant returns. The spokesperson said seeing AI as a long-term investment rather than a short-term solution can shift the narrative around its costs.

The report said AI can reduce labor costs through automation, optimize decision-making processes and enhance customer engagement. It said AI chatbots help ease the workload on customer service teams by handling routine inquiries, freeing up human staff to address more complex issues. It said implementation often comes with upfront expenses, from software licensing fees to the need for new hardware. It said personnel may need training to effectively utilize new systems, leading to additional costs. It said ongoing maintenance and updates required for AI systems to function optimally can add to the total cost of ownership.

The report said compatibility is a significant challenge, particularly for small businesses with limited technological infrastructure. It said integrating AI solutions into existing systems may demand custom setups, increasing complexity during rollout. It said many small business owners might feel apprehensive about AI due to data privacy concerns. It said small business owners should clearly define goals, set a realistic budget that accounts for initial and recurring costs, and remain adaptable. The articles do not say when the remaining MAI models will be available or how the six models will be priced.

stories.Headline: Nvidia warns chip buyers of legal risks regarding remote access to AI chips in China
stories.Summary:
Nvidia warned chip buyers in recent months that a proposed remote access law could expose them to legal action, according to CNBC reports. The chipmaker sent these messages because Chinese companies were renting its processors through cloud services hosted in other countries. This warning came just before the company released its fiscal third quarter results on Tuesday, November 17, 2026. The report followed the resignation of chief executive Jensen Huang, who stepped down from his role last week. Two people with direct knowledge of the matter provided these details regarding the warnings sent to the buyers.

The Remote Access Security Act, or RASA, passed the House in January but has not yet passed the Senate. This bill would let the US government control cloud services the same way it controls physical hardware in various places. Nvidia will not sell chips to customers that rent more than 50 percent of their GPUs to Chinese companies. The company told data center clients to direct at least 51 percent of their services to non Chinese customers. The Bureau of Industry and Security issued an interim final rule on Monday to stop remote access to AI chips.

Nvidia stated in an August securities filing that it seeks to strictly comply with all existing US export control laws. The company noted it lacks physical control of products after sale and relies on the compliance programs of its partners. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called for a dramatic shakeup at Nvidia and suggested that other executives should face scrutiny. Bessent questioned if the company culture pressed illicit sales to goose revenues and earnings during an interview with Fox News. The Bureau of Industry and Security did not respond to requests for comment regarding the new remote access rule.

Megaspeed International, a Singapore based company with facilities in Malaysia, is suspected of selling remote access to chips to Chinese firms. Megaspeed stated it conducts lawful business and has retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation into matters. Representative Yvette Clarke of New York said facts must be investigated under oath to prevent this type of compromise from happening. The new rule affects adversarial governments that could access American technology through overseas data centers, which threatens US national security. The Bureau of Industry and Security stated the US is committed to promoting American technology for legitimate commercial purposes.

Since October 2022, companies needed a BIS export license to sell advanced computing chips to China, Hong Kong, and Macau. President Trump signed an executive order in September referring to artificial intelligence as super intelligence to reflect its advanced capabilities. The Biden administration wrote a framework on January 15, 2025, to control the worldwide distribution of advanced AI chips. In May 2025, the Trump Commerce Department called that framework ill conceived and counterproductive and intended to rescind the rule. Intelligence officials first briefed President Trump in October 2025 about Jensen Huang's affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence operative.

Jensen Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick are both expected to testify before Congress this month and next month. Huang has been asked to testify specifically before the Senate Banking Committee on December 3 regarding these recent events. Democrats may conduct further investigations into what Trump knew about the affair when they take control of Congress in January 2027. It remains unknown if Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive, influenced Jensen Huang's lobbying to loosen chip sales restrictions to China. The articles leave open whether the Senate will eventually pass the Remote Access Security Act to control cloud services.

stories.Headline: US imposes AI chip export rules on five countries causing Singapore data centre stocks to slide
stories.Summary:
The United States imposed new rules on AI chip exports on November 16, causing Singapore data centre REITs and related stocks to slide on November 17. These measures followed the disclosure of an extramarital affair between Nvidia founder Jensen Huang and Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive. Alice Huang is a Chinese businesswoman whom the US suspects of being a spy, while Megaspeed is a Singapore based cloud provider. Jensen Huang stepped down as the chief executive of Nvidia on November 12, and Alice Huang is believed to be in China. The new rules aim to stop people from using remote computing arrangements in third countries to circumvent sensitive technology restrictions.

The rules add Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, and Brazil to a list of countries subject to export restrictions with a 90 day compliance window. Companies must now obtain licences from the US Commerce Department to ship chips to these five designated countries to prevent transshipment to China. The measure creates a two tier environment where local and non US operators face strict licensing, but US hyperscalers like Google, Microsoft, and Amazon receive exemptions. Cloud providers must implement real time monitoring and know your customer protocols to ensure high performance hardware is not used for unauthorized AI development. The Bureau of Industry and Security identified these countries because their demand for high end AI compute exceeded their domestic development needs.

The Ministry of Digital Development and Information and the Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry said they are studying the measure and engaging companies. A Singtel spokesperson stated the impact should be minimal because their sovereign AI platform serves only Singapore, primarily public sector and research agencies. Singtel noted that 4MW of its 6MW RE:AI platform capacity is installed, and the remaining 2MW is already contracted for sovereign cloud services. Singtel also mentioned that an insignificant amount of Nxera data centre capacity is contracted to neoclouds, which is not a material part of revenue. An ST Engineering spokesman said existing operations are not impacted because their data centres already have the required computing infrastructure.

Saxo strategist Charu Chanana said the sector is not facing a demand collapse, but the next growth phase may become more complicated for operators. Chanana noted that the biggest risks are for firms dependent on Chinese AI customers, as licensing uncertainty could affect financing, expansion, and utilisation. OCBC analyst Andy Wong said the direct business impact is likely contained for landlords, though share prices may suffer from weak sentiment. Ritesh Ganeriwal of Syfe said structural demand for AI and cloud computing remains solid and runs deeper than any one group of customers. Ben Chong of Phillip Securities cautioned against treating the restrictions as a uniform reduction in demand due to exemptions for US headquartered users.

The US previously targeted direct exports to China, but the focus has shifted toward blocking remote access workarounds and third party transshipment of chips. Earlier rules already targeted the transshipment of H200 chips through Southeast Asia, which began to reshape how institutions handle their procurement practices. The new regime treats access to computational power as a strategic asset, similar to how the US controls stealth technologies or high end radar. This shift places the burden of enforcement on those who provide AI infrastructure, requiring them to monitor the actual usage of the chips. Research institutions must now audit procurement and screen international collaborators to ensure their computational environments do not violate these new export controls.

Institutions must align their collaboration screening and procurement processes with the new guidance before the compliance deadline arrives in early 2027. The Commerce Department may issue further operational guidance or clarifications for universities regarding academic research collaboratories and potential academic exemptions during this period. Research offices are currently reviewing data sharing agreements and updating security policies to manage the institutional risk of losing future federal research funding. The articles leave open whether the US government will expand these restrictions to other regions if transshipment patterns continue to evolve over time. It remains unclear how many operators will successfully capture the next wave of AI investment based on regulatory compliance and customer quality.

stories.Headline: Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang says he would return if the board asks
stories.Summary:
Former Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang said on November 17 that he would return if the board asked him to. The board dismissed Huang because of an extramarital affair with a woman suspected of spying for China. This statement was his first public message since his resignation on November 12. Huang had previously called himself a piece of shit before he quit the company. He stepped down under a cloud following a series of affair allegations.

Returning to the role requires the board to judge it as the best option for shareholders, employees, the company, and the United States. The board is not discussing a return, according to reports from the Wall Street Journal and other outlets. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News that Nvidia should hire a CEO from outside the company. Bessent pressed the board for an answer within 10 days regarding chips smuggled to China through a Singapore shell company. Alice Huang is the woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.

Huang stated in a statement that he received numerous requests to return from investors, business partners, customers, and Nvidia employees. He said he would gladly accept a request to come back as CEO if the board decided it was best. The board says it is not discussing his return at all. The Financial Times reported that Huang discussed return options with close associates. A war room of Silicon Valley executives is reportedly being assembled.

Elon Musk, the chief executive of Tesla and SpaceX, signed an online petition demanding the return of Jensen Huang. This petition has drawn more than 180,000 signatures from people in Silicon Valley and inside Nvidia. President Donald Trump told reporters at the White House that he would not mind if Huang returned. Trump said no one had proven Alice Huang is a spy and she might not be one. Scott Bessent said the company needs a sweeping overhaul.

Nvidia has maintained a no-layoff principle since 1996 while Meta cut 8,000 jobs and Microsoft cut 4,800 jobs. Huang drove a culture where engineers earning 500,000 dollars annually should spend 250,000 dollars on AI tokens. The company grants restricted stock units broadly to new hires and senior staff. This policy has left many mid-level engineers holding stock worth millions of dollars. Staff loyalty is high and colleagues do not speak ill of the chief executive.

The board continues to deny that any discussions about bringing Jensen Huang back as chief executive are currently taking place. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent continues to insist that the board look outside for a new leader. The articles leave open whether the board will answer Bessent regarding the Singapore shell company. It remains unclear if the pressure from the online petition will change the board's current position. The future of the company's leadership remains undecided.

stories.Headline: Donald Trump plans to name Nvidia as a national champion despite the resignation of CEO Jensen Huang
stories.Summary:
Donald Trump is preparing to give Nvidia a major government boost in November 2026. This follows the resignation of billionaire chief executive Jensen Huang after a sex scandal. Huang quit after revelations about three extramarital relationships, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. The 63 year old former boss denied knowing about any foreign espionage operation. He apologized for being unfaithful to his wife and children in a memo.

The White House scheme will name over two dozen tech firms as national champions. This includes Nvidia, Amazon, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Anthropic under a 2025 export strategy. These firms may get faster export permits, overseas customer help, and government backed money. Trump previously approved Nvidia deals for China that required a 25 percent government charge. The plan aims to help American AI companies outpace their competitors in China.

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, 65, is expected to unveil the national champion selections soon. Lutnick previously boasted on the All In podcast about giving Huang easy access to Trump. He is now facing criticism for his relationship with Huang and his chip restrictions. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent confronted Lutnick during a heated White House confrontation over security. Lutnick is due to join Trump on another trip to China this week.

Analysts say the scandal shows key man risk because Huang has no clear successor. Bernstein analyst Stacy Rasgon said the situation calls the architect of AI trajectory into account. Investors fear wider damage to the industry, and Nvidia shares slid 4.3 percent. This drop erased nearly 200 billion US dollars from the company's total market valuation. Google announced a broader array of AI chips to capitalize on this turmoil.

Huang had affairs with executive Kimberly Powell, an unidentified employee, and Alice Huang of Megaspeed. Megaspeed is a Singapore based company that may have diverted technology to Chinese businesses. Trump reportedly received warnings about Alice Huang before letting Jensen Huang fly on Air Force One. The president denies this claim, but photos show the pair embracing in June 2024. Nvidia's board says no company secrets were exposed or national security put at risk.

Lutnick's department is preparing new rules to stop restricted American technology from reaching Chinese companies. An independent board committee and outside counsel are investigating if Huang was targeted for intelligence. The articles leave open whether the government will change the national champion list. It remains unclear if the probe will find that Nvidia technology breached US restrictions. The White House and Nvidia have not yet provided comments to the Daily Beast.

stories.Headline: Paris Hilton urges House to pass DEFIANCE Act on AI deepfakes
stories.Summary:
Paris Hilton went to Capitol Hill and urged the US House of Representatives to pass the bipartisan DEFIANCE Act, which has already cleared the Senate unanimously but remains stalled in the lower chamber, CBS News reported. She joined Representatives Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Laurel Lee to press House leaders to bring the bill to the floor for a vote. Hilton said more than 50 million people had been affected by sexually explicit deepfakes. She also disclosed that more than 100,000 AI-generated explicit images and videos depicting her were circulating online. Hilton, who was 19 when an intimate video of her was leaked by a former boyfriend, spoke about the lasting impact of having private images circulated without consent.

The DEFIANCE Act would create a federal civil remedy for victims of non-consensual sexually explicit digital imagery, allowing them to sue the people who create or distribute such material. Under the proposed legislation, victims could seek damages and recover profits generated from the images. It would also establish a 10-year statute of limitations, beginning when the victim discovers the violation or turns 18, whichever comes later. The US Senate passed the legislation by unanimous consent in January, and Ocasio-Cortez said it had passed unanimously not once but twice, in 2024 as well as earlier this year. The bill builds on the Take It Down Act, championed by US First Lady Melania Trump, which made it a federal crime to publish authentic or AI-generated intimate images of a person without consent.

Hilton said outside the Capitol that ten months ago she stood there and told the world what it feels like to have your body exposed without your consent, and asked Congress to do something about it. She said the laws aren't protecting us, and that if this can happen to someone with her resources and platform, imagine how powerless a young girl might be feeling facing this completely alone. She cited research into the targeting of women lawmakers, saying 83 of the 156 women serving in the 119th Congress had been depicted in sexually explicit deepfakes online. She described the findings as shocking but hardly surprising. Hilton directly appealed to House Speaker Mike Johnson, Majority Leader Steve Scalise and House Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan to allow a vote.

Representative Laurel Lee said once these images are shared, the damage can be devastating, and that victims can face harassment, threats and lasting harm. Lee said their relationships, educational opportunities and even careers can be affected by fake images that were created entirely without their consent. Ocasio-Cortez questioned why the legislation had not been taken up despite bipartisan backing in the Senate, saying that for 10 months this critical legislation has sat untouched in the House, just waiting to be put on the floor. She said advocates had also been engaging with the White House and expressed optimism about the Trump administration's willingness to consider the legislation. Johnson's office did not respond to a CBS News request for comment on why the bill had not advanced.

Hilton had previously visited Capitol Hill to lobby lawmakers, and a week after the Senate passed the legislation she urged House lawmakers to approve it, but the bill has remained stalled in the lower chamber since then. Ahead of her meetings on Capitol Hill, Hilton said her team had researched the prevalence of sexually explicit deepfake images involving women members of Congress. Supporters of the DEFIANCE Act argue that existing protections are insufficient to address the scale of the problem, amid growing concerns over the use of artificial intelligence to produce and circulate fabricated sexual images. The Take It Down Act also requires social media platforms and other websites to remove such content within 48 hours of receiving a victim's request. Hilton's latest appeal comes as the bill awaits action in the House.

The articles do not say when the House might vote on the DEFIANCE Act or whether Johnson, Scalise or Jordan will allow it to reach the floor. They do not say what response, if any, the White House gave to advocates engaging with it. They do not say what damages or profit recovery amounts victims could expect under the proposed remedy. They do not say how the 50 million figure was calculated or what research produced the finding on the 83 women in the 119th Congress. They do not say what further steps Hilton or the bill's supporters plan if the House does not act.

stories.Headline: Mullin suggests AI may have caused the flight outage and corrects a reporter to call it SI
stories.Summary:
DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin suggested on November 17, 2026, that artificial intelligence could be behind the chaotic outages that recently hit airlines and banks, according to a report from the New York Post. The remark tied the disruptive failures at major carriers and financial institutions to possible AI involvement, though the article gives no further detail on which outages he meant or what evidence he cited. The same day, United Airlines was reported to have taken a firm stand against AI by blocking unauthorized artificial intelligence agents from its reservation systems. United announced on November 11, 2026, that it was restricting those third-party agents from accessing its digital platforms.

United's updated policies ban unauthorized AI agents from its booking platforms and allow the airline to cancel tickets purchased or modified by autonomous assistants without prior notice to the passenger. The restrictions reach beyond United.com and its mobile app to travel agencies and booking aggregators that distribute the airline's flights, and they cover booking, ticketing and distribution policies. The rules target personal AI assistants that act autonomously or semi-autonomously for travelers, including tools that access accounts, search for flights, make purchases or modify existing reservations. United cited risks such as customers exposing sensitive account credentials, triggering unintended purchases, changing reservations or letting assistants spend MileagePlus miles without understanding the consequences, along with aviation safety requirements.

United argued that automated check-in could bypass the required human acknowledgment that a passenger's checked baggage does not contain prohibited substances such as explosives. The airline's updated Digital Trust Center guidance provides additional details about the restrictions, and its updated Contract of Carriage identifies reservations made, modified or serviced by AI agents as bookings it may cancel without notice. Bookings made by AI agents before November 11, 2026, will not be canceled under the new policy, though United recommends checking that those reservations were properly booked and ticketed. Assistive technology used by customers with disabilities is not affected, and the airline says it does not currently work with any third-party AI agents.

Passengers can still use AI for general travel research or planning as long as the tool does not access United.com or the United app, and unauthorized agents cannot retrieve information from those platforms, search fares or manage reservations on a customer's behalf. Travel agencies and booking platforms cannot supply United's travel information to third-party personal AI agents for searching, booking, ticketing or servicing reservations without authorization, and travel agencies seeking to use their own AI systems must obtain specific permission from United. United's decision comes as airlines explore how automated assistants could influence the booking process, and its competitors have not adopted the same blanket restrictions.

stories.Headline: Gan Kim Yong unveils three national AI missions for finance at Singapore FinTech Festival
stories.Summary:
Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong announced three national artificial intelligence missions on 18 November during the Singapore FinTech Festival. These missions aim to strengthen financial crime prevention, improve access to financing, and enable AI-driven transactions. The government will bring together researchers, public agencies, technology companies, and financial institutions to develop these solutions. This initiative follows the establishment of the National AI Council, which is chaired by Prime Minister Lawrence Wong. The government intends to test promising solutions against global standards before moving toward wider deployment.

The first mission uses a trial with five banks to pool transaction data and identify suspicious patterns across multiple institutions. The Monetary Authority of Singapore will begin a design study in early 2027 to develop an industry-wide scam detection system. The second mission invites AI technology companies to use realistic synthetic data to improve financing for startups and SMEs. The third mission tests AI agents in controlled environments to handle automatic payments and purchases for businesses and individuals. These trials will examine accountability, authorisation, identity verification, and compatibility between different systems to ensure safe agentic transactions.

Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong stated that the government will build shared capabilities to achieve more than any institution could alone. He explained that scams are not confined to one bank, as stolen funds can pass through several institutions within minutes. Gan noted that traditional lending approaches may not fully capture the future potential of newer startups with limited assets. He emphasized that AI agents must operate within defined limits, while institutions remain accountable for transactions conducted on their behalf. Gan also warned that Singapore will act against any companies that flout laws to bypass foreign regulations.

Small and medium enterprises with limited financial records or assets are affected by the new AI financing initiatives. These businesses will be consulted to assess whether the new AI solutions actually address their specific financing needs. Companies affected by new US Department of Commerce rules regarding advanced semiconductor export licences are also currently being assessed. The government is engaging US officials to facilitate access to computing capacity despite these new chip export restrictions. These restrictions require licences to export, re-export, or provide remote access to semiconductors for five countries, including Singapore.

The government first announced these AI missions during Budget 2026 to drive transformation in key sectors like financial services. The National AI Council was created to lead this effort and coordinate the various national artificial intelligence missions. The Monetary Authority of Singapore and the industry have already worked together to broaden AI adoption and deepen capabilities. Current lending practices largely assess businesses based on repayment history, personal guarantees, and collateral rather than future potential. The government is now focusing on connecting information across the financial system to intervene faster against financial crimes.

The Future of Finance Institute will coordinate industry partnerships and develop guidelines and standards to support the three missions. This institute will also test the AI solutions for wider use across the entire financial sector in Singapore. The design study for the scam detection utility will initially focus on accounts and data located within Singapore. The articles leave open whether there will be future opportunities for cross-border cooperation regarding the scam detection system. It remains unclear how the US chip restrictions will ultimately impact the computing capacity needed for these AI ambitions.

stories.Headline: US stocks decline as AI companies face volatility and regulatory concerns
stories.Summary:
The United States stock market declined on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, as artificial intelligence companies experienced significant volatility. The S&P 500 sank 0.9 percent, while the Nasdaq composite dropped 1.2 percent and the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 541 points, or 1.1 percent. Nvidia saw its shares drop 2.9 percent, and other industry players like Advanced Micro Devices and CoreWeave also shifted from early gains to losses. These movements followed a previous day of selling and occurred while investors awaited a critical earnings report.

The situation requires Nvidia to demonstrate that its growth can persist after the sudden resignation of former leader Jensen Huang. To address these challenges, the company is establishing a new board committee to manage global trade compliance and national security. This action follows reports that Huang had an extramarital affair with a person alleged to be a spy for China. Interim CEO Colette Kress is now responsible for addressing Wall Street, marking her first time speaking to investors since taking over the role.

Market instability stems from a series of concerns, including whether AI stock prices became too high and if high interest rates would limit growth funding. Investors are also worried that Democratic victories in the recent midterm elections might lead to stricter regulations for AI data centers. Other factors affecting the market included a 1.8 percent drop for Home Depot and a 2.3 percent loss for United Airlines. The broader economic environment remains pressured by high inflation, expensive mortgage rates, and uncertainty regarding the war with Iran.

stories.Headline: Florida House Speaker Sam Garrison creates committee to examine AI risks and opportunities
stories.Summary:
Florida’s newly elected lawmakers were sworn in on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, and new chamber leadership took the reins in Tallahassee. The Florida House unanimously elected Clay County Republican Sam Garrison as House Speaker, and the Florida Senate unanimously elected Manatee County Republican Jim Boyd as Senate President. Governor-elect Byron Donalds attended the swearing-in ceremony ahead of his inauguration in January. The organizational session coincided with the Elections Canvassing Commission certifying the general election outcomes. The new leaders said affordability is a top priority over the next two years.

Amendment 3, approved by nearly 62 percent of Florida voters, will increase the state’s non-school homestead exemption to $150,000 next year and to $250,000 in 2028. Garrison said the measure presents an estimated $12 billion loss to local governments as the homestead exemption rises from $50,000 to $150,000 in 2027 and to $250,000 in 2028. Certified results confirmed victories for Donalds in the governor’s race, Republicans in every state Cabinet race, and Ashley Moody in the U.S. Senate race. Republicans maintained a 20-to-8 majority in Florida’s congressional delegation, a 25-member majority in the state Senate, and a 70-to-50 majority in the state House. Lawmakers will return to Tallahassee when the regular legislative session begins on March 2.

Boyd, a Republican and an insurance executive from Bradenton, said it is imperative that lawmakers tackle affordability. Garrison, an attorney from Fleming Island, said his priorities are a strong economy, safe streets and quality schools. Garrison said he created a committee to explore artificial intelligence’s risks and opportunities. Boyd said lawmakers will continue to pursue every opportunity that can offer more choices and lower rates to Floridians on property insurance. Garrison said he created a new Advanced Technology and Digital Security Committee and reinstated the House Public Integrity Committee.

Garrison said Amendment 3 is the single most transformative property tax reform in the history of the state and the biggest fiscal challenge the state has faced in a generation. He cautioned about budget adjustments required to offset lost local and state revenue across diverse counties from Dixie to Duval and Miami-Dade. He said the laws of economics remain undefeated and there is still no such thing as a free lunch. He said failure is not an option. He told the House it is his responsibility to help make Donalds the most successful governor in the United States of America.

Gov. Ron DeSantis has said he wants a special session to help implement the constitutional amendment before the end of the year. Boyd said he believes there is time later on during the regular session to talk about this and give it the time and attention it needs. DeSantis said he wanted to limit governments doing an end run around the amendment and taxing residents in other ways, like through a Taxpayer Bill of Rights. Boyd and Garrison did not commit to that. Garrison said he does not think lawmakers necessarily know the answer to how the same rules will apply to different counties yet.

Garrison said he was in a meeting earlier this year when someone made an offhand comment that the coming years will likely see disruption on a par with the Industrial Revolution, only compressed from a century’s time to two or three years, if not less. He said AI technology that improves itself so quickly that humans will lose the ability to understand or control it is not science fiction but a sober reality that many in the tech community predict will arrive as early this year or next. He asked whether we are AI’s tool or it is ours. Florida has been at the forefront of AI skepticism, led by DeSantis, who urged lawmakers to pass an AI Bill of Rights to protect consumers. Garrison’s predecessor as Speaker, Daniel Perez, preferred to let the federal government and President Donald Trump take the lead on regulating the new technology, so the measure did not advance in the House this year.

stories.Headline: Suzanne Nossel urges AI companies to adopt UN human rights frameworks over internal rules
stories.Summary:
Suzanne Nossel wrote about the human rights blind spot in artificial intelligence safety debates on November 17, 2026, for Foreign Policy magazine. She argues that the AI industry should adopt an existing human rights framework instead of writing its own internal corporate rules. AI companies and their executives have released many essays, white papers, and proposals to pledge their diligent self-control and good intentions. These efforts aim to address public fears regarding the impact of uncontrollable technologies on democracy, personal agency, and even human survival. The author suggests that the current approach to AI governance fails to incorporate established global precepts for corporate human rights responsibilities.

The proposed framework is the U.N. Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights, which the Human Rights Council unanimously endorsed in 2011. This system requires a protect pillar for states, a respect pillar for companies, and a remedy pillar for people who are harmed. It introduces human rights due diligence to identify risks, prevent harms, monitor results, and report on them across all global industries. France, Germany, and Norway passed laws requiring companies to address human rights risks, and the European Union adopted a directive in 2024. The principles cover globally recognized rights including equality, labor rights, freedom of expression, and privacy for all people affected by AI.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang championed a laissez-faire approach, arguing that companies developing these technologies are perfectly incentivized to do the right thing. He believes that further regulation is superfluous because the industry can manage its own ethics and safety without outside government constraints. In late September, the White House imposed no new constraints and praised what President Donald Trump called a tremendous self-policing aspect. OpenAI updated its Model Spec last month to serve human purposes, be truthful, minimize harm, and respect the freedom of people. Anthropic filed a form S-1 in October that details its specific vows regarding safety and its public-benefit commitments.

A September Quinnipiac University poll found that 74 percent of respondents held little or no trust in the leaders of AI companies. An Anthropic study published in June found that only 15 percent of Americans trust AI companies to make development decisions. Some key AI personnel have resigned in alarm, suggesting that the current pledges do not reassure those inside the industry. Regulators fear that the wrong constraints could hamper economic prosperity and global competitiveness, which limits their own competence in this area. The framework focuses on the rights of people who may be harmed rather than the intentions of companies or chatbots.

The modern human rights movement began after governments subordinated individual lives to national ambitions, ideological supremacy, and other grand designs. The U.N. Charter, signed in June 1945, affirmed the dignity and worth of the human person as a foundational global principle. In 2005, U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan appointed Harvard professor John Ruggie to define the human rights responsibilities of multinational businesses. This work addressed gaps in corporate responsibility caused by global supply chains and low-wage operations in places with weak legal protections. The resulting principles translate the commitment to human dignity into practical expectations for how all private enterprises should operate.

AI developers should examine if training data is obtained legitimately and how governments might use the technology for repression or discrimination. Companies must embed these findings into their budgets, product design, and commercial relationships while tracking if the safeguards actually work. They should exert leverage over partners to prevent abuses and terminate relationships when those efforts to stop the abuses fail. The articles leave open whether AI companies will actually adopt these U.N. principles or continue relying on voluntary self-policing pledges. It remains unclear if governments will move beyond the current laissez-faire approach to mandate these human rights standards for AI.

stories.Headline: South Korea inspects exam candidates glasses and blocks Wi-Fi to stop AI cheating
stories.Summary:
South Korea will inspect all glasses worn by students taking this week's national college entrance exam to prevent AI-assisted cheating. This action follows a confession on Sunday by a person who placed first in the 2026 tax accountant exam. The individual admitted to photographing questions with a microcamera and using an AI tool and smartphone to find answers. These events shook public confidence in the country's high-stakes testing system and caused panic before the college test. The government is now implementing strict security measures to protect the integrity of the upcoming national examinations.

The Education Ministry will inspect all glasses in every session of the College Scholastic Ability Test in Seoul and other centers. Smart devices were added to the banned items list in July, and public Wi-Fi will be blocked during the exams. Every exam room will have warning notices about criminal penalties, and each center will have one staff member monitoring devices. A hotline will link centers to local education offices and the ministry's control room to judge difficult cases on the spot. Prime Minister Han Seong-sook announced that emergency alerts will be sent before the exam to detect any hidden mobile phones.

Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin told a parliamentary hearing on November 16 that the ministry would inspect all eyewear worn by candidates. He stated that the ministry would work with parliament to lengthen the current one-year exam ban to three or ten years. Choi also noted that offenders may be reported to the police for obstructing official duties during the national testing process. Prime Minister Han Seong-sook said the government would form an emergency team to prepare measures to safeguard the college entrance exam. She urged officials to develop AI-based detection technology and called for strengthened penalties for those who cheat using technology.

Some people called for the university entrance exam to be postponed to ensure fairness, but the Education Ministry ruled out delays. The Suneung exam is seen as a ticket to well-paid jobs and better marriage prospects in a hyper-competitive society. Students are affected by these changes, as anyone caught using smart devices will have their results invalidated for the current year. They will also be barred from sitting the exam the following year under the current rules and potential new penalties. The national exam is so intense that much of South Korea will stand still on Thursday to minimize student distractions.

The scandal began when the top tax accountant candidate confessed on November 15 to using a microcamera and AI for cheating. Smart glasses are a global concern because they can record confidential material or people without their knowledge or any consent. Grepp, a company with a 90 percent market share in online proctoring, uses a service called Monito for recruitment exams. This technology is already used by major corporations like Samsung Electronics, LG Electronics, and SK hynix for their own hiring processes. Grepp recorded 13.5 billion won in revenue last year and is now expanding into physical test center AI solutions.

The ministry will consult specialists on radio-signal detectors and may introduce this technology for the 2027 test to stop AI cheating. Grepp CEO Lim Sung-soo is discussing a pilot deployment of Monito at Prometric test centers in the United States next year. The company plans to seek accreditation as a private operator of nationally recognized qualification assessments and pursue an IPO in 2028. Articles leave open whether thermal imaging cameras or radio-frequency detectors will be used, as they face legal and technical challenges. It remains unclear if the government will successfully implement these high-tech tools due to interference with nearby wireless communications.

stories.Headline: HHS finalizes HIPAA rule to speed patient access and ease care coordination
stories.Summary:
The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services' Office for Civil Rights released a 363-page final rule on HIPAA privacy changes late Monday, November 16, 2026. The rule is titled HIPAA Privacy Rule: Changes to Support Coordinated Care and Individual Engagement and Reduce Regulatory Burdens. It is slated for publication Thursday in the Federal Register. HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. announced the final rule in a statement. The rule aims to give patients faster and easier access to health records, including through third-party applications, and to reduce obstacles to information sharing for care coordination.

The rule becomes effective 60 days after publication, on Jan. 18, 2027. HIPAA-regulated organizations must comply with applicable provisions 180 days after the effective date, or July 17, 2027. Additional time is allowed for certain modifications to written business associate agreements. The rule cuts the time for healthcare organizations to respond to patient access requests from 30 calendar days to 15 days, with a one-time extension of up to 30 additional days under specific circumstances. HHS OCR issued the proposed modifications in January 2021, during the final days of President Donald Trump's first term.

Kennedy said Americans should never have to fight for access to their own health records. He said the rule modernizes HIPAA to serve patients and help providers spend more time delivering care and less time navigating bureaucracy. Privacy attorney Adam Greene of Davis Wright Tremaine said he appreciated the deletion of the requirement to obtain acknowledgments of receipt of the notice of privacy practices. Greene said that requirement was founded on good intentions but led to administrative burden and confusion with minimal corresponding benefit. Privacy attorney Kirk Nahra of WilmerHale said he would have liked an additional stage to obtain new comments on issues that changed significantly since the proposal was first issued five years ago.

Nahra said HHS chose coordination over individual privacy and that the rule essentially allows disclosure over the objection or lack of permission from the consumer. He said companies should remain cautious about these disclosures even if they are permitted. Greene said he was pleased HHS OCR considered public comments and dropped several provisions from the 2021 proposal. Privacy attorney Iliana Peters of Polsinelli said her biggest concerns involve the administrative burdens HIPAA-covered organizations will face in implementing several changes. The signatories of a letter to HHS last week, including the College of Healthcare Information Management Executives, did not immediately respond to ISMG's request for comment on the final rule.

The final rule retains several key patient-access and care-coordination provisions proposed in 2021 but abandons or scales back others that raised privacy concerns or would have increased administrative burdens. HHS OCR dropped a proposal that would have relaxed HIPAA's minimum necessary standard for certain disclosures of sensitive health information. The rule clarifies patients' rights to obtain electronic health information through personal health applications, including consumer apps not subject to HIPAA. Healthcare organizations generally can't refuse to transmit records to patients' chosen personal health apps solely because they believe the applications lack adequate privacy or security protections, such as encryption at rest. The rule prohibits covered organizations from imposing unreasonable identity verification measures that create barriers to patient access.

HHS said healthcare organizations participating in the federal Trusted Exchange Framework and Common Agreement generally should not refuse access requests submitted through personal health apps when specified digital identity verification conditions are satisfied. Those conditions include a cryptographically signed token issued by a credential service provider certified to perform identity verification consistent with NIST Identity Assurance Level 2, or IAL2, and Authentication Assurance Level 2, or AAL2. Another condition involves verifying that demographic information associated with the token matches the patient's information in the covered entity's designated record set. Healthcare organizations also may warn patients about privacy and security risks associated with particular apps. The final regulation clarifies that health plans may use and disclose PHI for individual-level care coordination and case management.

The rule expressly permits covered entities to disclose PHI to social services agencies, community-based organizations and similar third parties for care coordination and case management. HHS retained the minimum necessary standard for applicable healthcare operations disclosures rather than adopting a proposed exception for certain care-coordination activities. The final rule eliminates the requirement for covered healthcare providers to make a good-faith effort to obtain patients' written acknowledgment of receiving a Notice of Privacy Practices. The agency abandoned a requirement that would have obligated covered organizations to exercise individuals' right of access on their behalf by requesting designated record sets from other covered entities. Greene said that proposal would have led to a substantial unfunded mandate that would tax covered entities' already limited resources.
