stories.Headline: Google reports that cyberattackers use AI frameworks to automate vulnerability discovery and exploitation
stories.Summary:
The Google Threat Intelligence Group reported that state-sponsored and cybercrime groups are increasingly using generative AI to weaponise flaws. These threat actors used multi-agent offensive frameworks to automate vulnerability discovery and exploitation without any human intervention. This shift allows intrusions to occur at machine speed, which represents a paradigm shift in how attacks are executed. The reports were published in November 2026, following an analysis of attacks over a specific three-month period. These automated systems can chain complex attack paths to scale operations significantly and increase the velocity of intrusions.

The exploit_agent framework, found on an exposed staging server, compares patched and unpatched web application code to develop exploits. Attackers use Artex, Cairn, CyberStrikeAI, and PentAGI, while some experiment with HexStrike AI and the open source Agent Zero. Artex is most common among Chinese-speaking groups, while Cairn targeted the US aerospace sector and PentAGI scanned Asia. Between August and October, hackers used a customized PentAGI platform, and some used ZeroHollow for exploit development and routing. These tools allow actors to reverse engineer patches at machine speed to rapidly weaponise n-day vulnerabilities.

The Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant stated that AI adoption leads to reduced human involvement and increased stealth. They noted that the lower barrier to entry has fueled a wave of LLM-generated exploits that often fail. GTIG observed a Chinese group building its own automated attack framework, which is likely intended for espionage operations. They also found that LLMs improve the output quality of influence campaigns and help IPM networks scale political clickbait. The group assesses with high confidence that cybercrime actors will incorporate autonomous tools to increase their campaign reach.

Matt Hartman, the Merlin chief strategy officer, said that US critical infrastructure faces danger from attacks occurring at machine speed. He noted that water utilities, hospitals, and regional electric utilities cannot win this race if they struggle to patch monthly. Hartman stated that AI dramatically lowers the cost and expertise needed, putting powerful capabilities within reach of smaller groups. State-sponsored groups, including Iran-linked APT42 and multiple Chinese APTs, have already adopted these large language models. Phishing-as-a-Service operators, such as the Jieyou phishing service, are using LLMs to configure their chatbots.

The articles explain that attackers still use compromised credentials and target unpatched systems, but the speed of exploitation has increased. Google first noted an increase in LLMJacking in November, where hackers hijack AI systems to resell usage tokens. Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42 also found a Chinese-speaking actor using the Cairn framework against over a dozen organizations. Currently, unrestricted autonomous execution generates forensic traffic and leaves behind distinct code-level traces that defenders can potentially identify. However, the reports indicate that the trend toward automation has now reached a critical inflection point for cyberattacks.

Google anticipates that intrusions will become nearly fully agentic as large language models and agentic frameworks continue to advance. Defenders must nail cybersecurity fundamentals today while accelerating the shift toward automated defenses that respond at machine speed. The articles leave open whether attackers will maintain their current noise levels or become stealthier as tools improve. It remains unclear how many more organizations in Asia and the US will be targeted by these specific frameworks. Future reports will likely track if the success rates of autonomous campaigns compensate for any decreases in stealth.

stories.Headline: Marian Kamenistak builds a 123-automation AI executive assistant that saves an estimated 361 hours a month
stories.Summary:
Marian Kamenistak, VP of Engineering at Mews, published on hackernoon.com on 18 November 2026 an account of the AI executive assistant he built. He made an inventory of his automations on 25 October 2026 and found one job that had reported success for 48 days while its access key was being rejected. Another job sent LinkedIn messages on a Sunday because its schedule was off by one day, and a group of other jobs succeeded about 60% of the time and never alerted him. In late October 2026 he saw about 70% of his jobs failing on a dashboard he had built that weekend. He dropped meetings that were not critical and started fixing things, and found the root cause was that most jobs ran from his local PC, which was not plugged in.

The assistant is 123 scheduled automations, a set of AI skills and one dashboard he calls the Control Room, with 1,506 steps and 948 connections between them as captured on 15 November 2026. It saves an estimated 361 hours of work a month, about 4,330 hours a year, equal to 2.3 extra people at 160 hours a person a month. People cost avoided is €14,428 a month and €173,141 a year, or 352,415 and 4,228,980 Czech crowns, while the cost of running the automations is €464 a month and €5,569 a year, or 11,335 and 136,020 crowns, leaving €13,964 a month and €167,573 a year saved after costs. Euros are converted at the Czech National Bank fixing of 13 November 2026, 24.425 CZK per EUR, and 176 of the 361 hours are work he would otherwise have hired for, an SDR or a virtual assistant, about 1.1 people. With the tools he would pay for anyway the bill is about €811 a month, every subscription he pays is about €1,204, and none of the three totals includes his build time, which was one weekend for the dashboard and another 3 weeks to a month for the full monthly cycle.

He kept his personal human EA, Lucie, and calls it the best decision he could do, because she keeps him accountable and resolves everything on the spot. He says she was very persistent about making sure he invested his time into the right decisions and urges him to pay attention to non-business things, which go into relationships with his teammates. In invoicing the AI reads the bank lines and matches each one to a document, and Lucie finds the documents the AI can't, in Drive first, then Gmail, then the supplier portals. From July to October 2026, 79 of 248 bank lines were waiting for a document. He says the AI does the recurring work and Lucie does the part where somebody has to go and find the thing and decide on the spot.

ChatGPT, Perplexity and Gemini all answer "hybrid" when asked whether to replace an executive assistant with AI, and he agrees with hybrid and pays for it every month. Perplexity, asked on 15 November 2026, put an assistant stack at $20 to $200 a month and its upkeep at 2 to 8 hours a month, and ChatGPT leaned on vendor price pages such as Lindy's and cited a Forrester study commissioned by Microsoft for Copilot Studio where one customer says an agent saved 4 hours per user a month. He says those numbers are fair for one tool on one desk, while his bill is for a whole back office. The assistant serves five business streams: the Engineering Leaders Community, the ELC Conference, the Academy, hiring through Marian's List, and his mentoring at marian.coach. Tereza is Head of Community, and they have two recurring meetings, weekly preparation for the next week and checking the Control Room on the web, and monthly review of past KPIs and setting KPIs for the next month.

He spent 20+ years in software development and was VP of Engineering at Mews, where engineering grew from 8 to 80 teams, which is why he could build it himself. The plumbing needed an engineer, but writing down his niche, his ideal customer and his KPIs didn't, and that is the part that made the AI useful. The automations ran before the AI knew what business it was working for, and the fix was setting the niche, ICP and KPIs so the AI knows the context. Every stream must have a niche and a mission, one sentence each, max 160 characters, and concrete as to who, what and which geography, and his mentoring niche starts with one-to-one leadership mentoring for engineering and product leaders in Czechia and Central Europe. The ICP has 1 to 4 segments with consumers and companies kept separate, each saying who they are, what they buy and where that comes from, and one thing the company segment of his mentoring stream buys is a Mentor in Residence.

A watchdog now runs every hour in the cloud, off the Mac, and expects a heartbeat from each job, so a job silent past its schedule counts as failed and an unplugged computer can't hide. The AI may not fix outreach senders, finance and logins on its own, because a wrong fix on a sender goes out to real people, and there is a limit of at most 5 fixes a day and 1 per job per 7 days. A test on 15 November went from approved to fixed in 2 minutes, and he refurbished his 7-year-old MacBook Pro to run the local jobs. On 15 November 2026 the coverage page showed 140 jobs OK, 4 failing and 30 stale, the home page read "4 of 5 goals on track" with 1 goal behind, qualified mentoring leads, and 9 things wait for a person and 136 of 167 automations working. The 123 in the post is the count in the savings model of 14 November 2026, each page counts a different set of jobs and the set changes daily, and the system refuses to publish a stream missing its niche, ICP or KPIs, showing a target without a source as unsourced.

stories.Headline: Effingham County students pitch school projects for OpenAI funded grants
stories.Summary:
Three Effingham County residents sued OpenAI, local officials and others in November, alleging that plans for Project Camellia were kept secret until key decisions had been made, and the allegations have not been proven in court. OpenAI is the artificial intelligence company behind the ChatGPT platform. Project Camellia is OpenAI’s proposed $20 billion artificial intelligence data center campus at the Savannah Gateway Industrial Hub near Rincon. The proposal has drawn opposition from residents who raised concerns about transparency, electricity demand, water use, traffic and noise. County commissioners postponed a decision on the project’s preliminary site plan on Nov. 3 and were expected to revisit it Tuesday.

The District Innovation Challenge provides up to $15,000 for each of the Effingham County School District’s 17 schools, backed by $255,000 from OpenAI. Students and educators will work together on proposals that could address technology, STEM, artificial intelligence literacy, sustainability or other school and community needs. Following Tuesday’s districtwide kickoff, students and staff will develop project ideas, itemized budgets and presentations, and the district’s curriculum and technology departments will host presentations and question-and-answer sessions. In January, each school will review proposals and select a group of projects totaling up to $15,000 to represent it at the district level. Finalist student teams will present their ideas to a district panel in February.

Superintendent Yancy Ford said public education thrives when students are given real ownership over their learning and the resources to bring bold ideas to life. Ford said that through this partnership with OpenAI, students are not just learning about the future but are actively designing it for their classrooms, their schools and the Effingham County community. The panel will include Ford, school board representatives, district curriculum and technology leaders, and representatives from the data center and AI industries. Rather than serving as a high-stakes elimination contest, the panel will offer feedback and formally award funding to participating projects, the district said. OpenAI said it would continue working with county officials to address outstanding questions.

Supporters point to potential tax revenue and opportunities for local businesses from Project Camellia. OpenAI has pledged at least $80 million for community priorities tied to Project Camellia. The company also provided a $4.8 million grant to cover Effingham County students’ school breakfast and lunch costs for the 2026-27 school year. In October, OpenAI announced a $2 million grant for the first phase of Atlas Park, a planned recreation area at a former sand mine.

Students across Effingham County will have a chance to turn their ideas for improving their schools into reality through the new grant program. The Pike County Board of Commissioners will hold a special meeting on Wednesday, Nov. 18, to discuss and potentially approve a non-binding term sheet from SoftBank Energy and OpenAI for the PORTS-Pike data center project in Piketon. The special meeting will occur at 10:30 a.m. at the Pike County Administration Building, located at 230 Waverly Plaza in Waverly.

The county said the purpose is to consider, discuss and possibly act on the proposed non-binding term sheet, with possible actions including a resolution approving the term sheet and authorizing its execution and any related matters. The notice said the elected county board could also enter into a private executive session to discuss matters related to the data center deal. An agenda with more details has not yet been published for the special AI data center meeting. Japan’s SoftBank and OpenAI want to redevelop the U.S. Department of Energy Portsmouth Gaseous Diffusion Plant into a new data center.

The 3,700-acre U.S. government plant previously enriched uranium for nuclear weapons and later for nuclear energy plants, and it operated from 1957 to 2001. The plant property is owned by the U.S. Department of Energy, and adjacent privately owned properties have also been acquired as part of the planned AI data center development. At full buildout, there could be as many as 18 data center buildings at the southeastern Ohio site, and the AI development is projected to create 35,000 construction jobs and 2,500 permanent, operational jobs, according to the companies. AI chipmaker NVIDIA will provide the AI infrastructure at the data center, and the development also entails significant electricity infrastructure investments and upgrades.

stories.Headline: Maxine Dexter introduces bill to ban AI data centers on federal public lands
stories.Summary:
On November 11, Oregon Representative Maxine Dexter introduced a bill to ban AI data centers on national forests and Interior-managed lands. This legislation, called the Protecting Our Public Lands from Data Centers Act, was backed by thirteen Democratic cosponsors in the House. On October 5, 2026, Assembly members Cody Miller, Marisa Sweeney, and Joe Danielsen introduced New Jersey Assembly Bill A5607. This New Jersey bill aims to classify AI chatbots as consumer products to make providers more liable for user harm. Both legislative efforts seek to regulate the rapid growth of artificial intelligence technology within their respective federal and state jurisdictions.

The federal bill prohibits data centers on national forests and lands managed by the U.S. Department of the Interior. It requires federal land sold or transferred to return to government ownership if used for data centers without congressional authorization. New Jersey Bill A5607 imposes a two-year limit on chat log retention and restricts their use for advertising or profiling. This state bill also establishes civil penalties of 5,000 dollars per violation and allows users to sue for actual damages. New Jersey Bill A5090, introduced in May 2026, would impose civil penalties of 20,000 dollars per violation for specific harmful conduct.

Representative Maxine Dexter stated that public lands belong in public hands and Oregonians must have a say in their management. She argued that her bill keeps treasured lands safe for hunting, fishing, hiking, grazing, and protecting critical watersheds for future generations. Kara Williams of EPIC testified that the New Jersey bill would limit the ability of providers to exploit users' personal data. The Consumer Federation of America stated that the model bill provides a straightforward approach to address harms caused by tech companies. Ross Barnes of Galahad said that treating chatbots as consumer products is the right instinct for determining who is responsible.

Randi Spivak of the Center for Biological Diversity called data centers water-guzzling, pollution-spewing facilities that turn wildlife lands into corporate industrial sites. EPIC warned that unregulated chatbots cause devastating harms, including suicide, self-harm, violence, sexual exploitation, financial scams, and various mental health injuries. The legislation affects chatbot users, including those using OpenAI's ChatGPT and Anthropic's Claude, as well as businesses that distribute these tools. A Pew Research report found that 54 percent of Americans believe data centers are bad for the environment since January. A Rutgers study found that 74 percent of New Jersey residents used AI tools, while 59 percent favored strict regulation.

The Trump Administration sought to build data centers on public lands throughout 2026, with the BLM reviewing fifteen data center applications. The Interior Department published a strategic plan for fiscal years 2026 through 2030 to sell federal land to states and tribes. In July, the BLM approved an 86-acre AI data center near Lake Mead National Recreation Area, though an appeals board paused it. Meta built a 2.4-million-square-foot data center in Eagle Mountain, Utah, while 14 other proposed centers sit within ten miles of national parks. California's SB 243 and New York's AI Companion Models Law previously focused on chatbots designed for social or emotional relationships.

The federal bill was referred to the House Natural Resources and Agriculture committees, but it currently has no Republican cosponsors. Senator Ron Wyden introduced a similar measure in September, but Republican Senator Rand Paul blocked that specific legislative effort from moving forward. New Jersey Bill A5607 was referred to the Assembly Appropriations Committee on October 19 after a five to one and one vote. If passed by both chambers, Governor Mikie Sherrill will decide whether to sign or veto the New Jersey chatbot legislation. The articles leave open whether the House will pass the federal ban or if the New Jersey bill will be amended.

stories.Headline: Nigeria's electoral commission removes 1.6 million AI generated profiles from voter register
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence has recently begun to interfere with election discourse, creating new risks for future outcomes. The Independent National Electoral Commission discovered that AI was used to manipulate its voter register. This discovery occurred around November 2026, as reported by journalist Zinab Suleiman Okino. The agency removed 1.6 million AI generated profiles from the database. Staff members who were indicted for these irregularities also faced sanctions.

The commission noticed voter numbers inflated from 93 million to 103 million in the register. Only 268 irregularities were flagged before the removal of 1.6 million entries in Nigeria. This leaves 8 million AI generated profiles still potentially present in the system. The Senate repealed the Electoral Act of 2022 in February 2026 to reject real time uploads. Physical Form EC8A is now the primary source for collation instead of the IReV portal.

Professor Joash Amupitan, the INEC Chairman, stated that elections can be undermined before any ballots are cast. He attended a national summit on AI and electoral integrity with his commissioners and top staff. Amupitan noted that the commission cannot police the truth alone during these sensitive national assignments. He called for institutionalised fact checking channels and clear inter agency escalation procedures for information crises. The summit included partners like the European Union, IPC, CEMESO, and DAI.

Social media users and opposition members flagged duplicate profiles and inflated numbers in the preliminary register. Journalists raised alarms about the data breach, while Nigerians demanded a transparent forensic audit of databases. Politicians are accused of taking no responsibility and using AI to their own advantage. The public remains suspicious that disruptors will become more sophisticated before the 2027 elections. Many fear that AI could be used by scammers and fraudsters to cause upsets.

The 2015 elections saw controversy with Smart Card Readers, leading to the Rivers State governorship annulment. The Supreme Court later ruled that the card reader supplemented rather than supplanted the voter register. This ruling led to the legal introduction of BVAS and IReV for the 2023 presidential election. However, a technical glitch during that election broke public trust in the democratic institution. These events created a complicated history of moving from manual to technology aided voting processes.

INEC must now continue to clean its database and deploy tools against various electoral malpractices. The commission needs to bridge the credibility gap by improving digital literacy for the general public. Nigeria should strengthen digital infrastructure and seek partnerships with TikTok, X, Facebook, and Instagram. The articles leave open whether the remaining 8 million fake profiles will be successfully removed. It remains uncertain if the 2027 elections can be won fair and square without AI interference.

stories.Headline: Kiran Mazumdar-Shaw says AI can cut drug development from five to seven years to one or two
stories.Summary:
Biocon Executive Chairperson Kiran Mazumdar-Shaw said on Tuesday that Artificial Intelligence has the potential to drastically cut the time required to take a drug molecule from the lab to patients. She spoke on the role of AI in life sciences on the first day of the Bengaluru Tech Summit 2026. She said AI could compress the current five-to-seven-year timeline into just one or two years. She noted that accelerating this journey from lab to clinic will unlock major opportunities in precision and personalised medicine. The three-day Bengaluru Tech Summit started on Tuesday, with global leaders, innovators, founders, entrepreneurs, investors and thinkers from different industries participating.

Shaw said drug development does not end in the labs and has to be validated in clinical trials, including picking the right patients and generating early readouts. She asked whether the five-to-seven years to get a molecule from lab to patients can be compressed into a year or two. She said this would be the most fascinating outcome and impact. She said the change is not about making incremental change but about reimagining how to do discovery, development and drug innovation. She said that is the real opportunity AI gives and it should not be lost.

Shaw said autonomous wet labs are already conducting high-throughput screening and real-time analytics using AI. She said science and biology are currently done one target at a time, which is not going to move the needle. She said that when you understand where a target functions and how it functions using AI, you will be able to develop next generation drugs, next generation diagnostics and next generation technologies. She stressed that regulations must keep pace with accelerated discovery and development. She noted that discussions are underway on how to create a regulatory sandbox to validate proof of concepts much faster, and said Karnataka can take a lead in this space.

Shaw described biology as the most important frontier for AI to be deployed. She said AI will help simplify complex biological systems and allow scientists to connect the dots rather than studying one target at a time. According to Shaw, converging genomics, chemical pathways and neural networks through AI will enable next-generation drugs and next-generation diagnostics, such as detecting the first cancer cell to overcome late-stage diagnosis, as well as advancements in agriculture and bioenergy. She said AI is about accelerating intelligence and is the greatest assistant, embedded in daily life and business, helping people prioritise tasks, improve efficiency and get back time. The articles give no further background beyond the summit and her remarks.

The articles do not say what specific steps follow the discussions on the regulatory sandbox or when any such sandbox might be created. They do not give a date for when AI-compressed drug development might be achieved or which drugs or trials would be affected. They do not name the other participants at the Bengaluru Tech Summit or give details of any sessions beyond Shaw's remarks. They do not say what Biocon itself plans to do with AI or whether it has adopted any of the approaches she described. They leave open how regulators would validate AI-based discoveries and how the one-to-two-year timeline would be measured.

stories.Headline: DistroKid gives UMG and Sony data on AI music in Suno lawsuit
stories.Summary:
DistroKid provided data about AI-generated music on its platform to Universal Music Group and Sony Music after initially refusing, according to a Monday November 16 court filing obtained by Billboard. The data came in response to a third-party subpoena served by UMG and Sony as part of their copyright infringement lawsuit against AI music service Suno. The subpoena sought numbers on how much of the music passing through the leading DIY digital distributor is thought to be made with Suno and other AI generators. DistroKid initially refused to provide the AI data, leading the labels to initiate a legal action last month seeking to force compliance with the subpoena. The distributor has since changed its tune and produced responsive documents, and Monday's filing withdrew the subpoena petition.

UMG and Sony say the data is key to proving that Suno-generated music is eating into their market share and royalty distributions. Competition between AI songs and human music is a key part of the fair use inquiry, the test a judge will use to decide whether Suno infringed the majors' copyrights by training on millions of unlicensed tracks. DistroKid is not a party to the Suno suit. UMG still has an ongoing lawsuit alleging DistroKid is to blame for a surge in AI music on streaming services like Spotify, filed in September. That case alleges the distributor engaged in deceptive business practices and violated copyright law by flooding streamers with what it called mass AI-generated, SEO-optimized, and copyright-infringing slop.

Reps for DistroKid and Sony declined to comment on the matter on Tuesday November 17, and reps for UMG did not return a request for comment. In a statement when UMG's lawsuit was filed, a DistroKid rep said the company takes copyright protection, fraud prevention and the integrity of the music ecosystem seriously and works closely with digital streaming platforms, rightsholders and other industry partners. The spokesperson said DistroKid strongly disagrees with UMG's allegations and is disappointed that UMG chose litigation rather than established industry processes. The spokesperson added that DistroKid is confident in its practices and intends to defend DistroKid vigorously. Suno asked Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV on October 30 to pause the labels' second case until he rules on summary judgment in the first lawsuit.

In papers filed in Boston federal court last Friday November 13, the labels argued that a full pause could keep the case frozen into 2028. Under Suno's plan, they claim, its 2025 and 2026 models and business conduct, including v6, the model suite it launched in September, would be examined nowhere until at least 2028. The labels agree that the fair use ruling will shape the second case, and have offered to postpone the work of proving they own the more than 60,000 recordings at issue until Saylor rules. The second lawsuit, filed on September 18, accuses Suno of copying 60,202 of the labels' recordings without a license to train its AI models. US copyright law caps statutory damages for willful infringement at USD $150,000 per work, which gives those recordings a theoretical maximum of just over USD $9 billion.

The dispute began in June 2024, when Universal, Sony and Warner Music Group sued Suno. Warner settled and struck a licensing deal with Suno in November 2025, and the case now covers 560 of Universal and Sony's recordings. In May this year, Universal and Sony asked to add 61,026 more recordings to the original case after tracing them inside Suno's training data, and the second suit asserts slightly fewer, 60,202. Saylor refused on August 18, saying that adding them will have obvious consequences of complexity and delay, and steered the labels toward a separate lawsuit instead. In that ruling, Saylor wrote that evidence-gathering in any new case could proceed on a different schedule, or indeed be stayed pending resolution of the fair use issue. Suno says that means the court has already contemplated a stay, while the labels counter that a stay was only one of several options Saylor listed.

In the first case, fact discovery on the labels' infringement claims has largely closed, while discovery on their stream-ripping claim runs until this Friday November 20, and summary judgment motions are due by June 22, 2027. Suno launched its v6 models on September 9, nine days before the second suit was filed, saying they were built in partnership with Warner, BMG and Believe. The labels say Suno's document handover in the first case largely stops at February 2025, and no witness has been put forward to explain how v6 was trained. The labels warn that by the time discovery into v6 could begin under Suno's proposal, the engineers who built the models may have moved on and their recollections will have faded. The labels say they recently learned that the engineer responsible for Suno's data scraping and training data acquisition has left the company.

stories.Headline: Chinese entities use output from US AI models to train domestic rivals amid chip curbs
stories.Summary:
Chinese entities are using output from leading American artificial intelligence models to train domestic rivals. This practice has expanded into mainstream industrial use to offset tightening US chip curbs. A Reuters review of over 300 documents revealed this trend in late 2026. Beijing is encouraging this method to make AI easier to deploy in manufacturing. Washington announced further restrictions on chips from companies like Nvidia on November 16.

Distillation involves a teacher model generating answers to train a smaller student system. In November 2024, Shanghai Jiao Tong University used 5,000 OpenAI o1 answers for Alibaba's Qwen2.5-72B. Alibaba researchers used GPT-4 and GPT-4o for non-Chinese training material in April 2025. In February 2026, Meituan and Shanghai Jiao Tong University used GPT-4o for programming tasks. These efforts occur amid a November 18 to 19 APEC summit in Shenzhen.

US Commerce Department officials raised intellectual property theft concerns in Chengdu in July. They believe industrial distillation is why Chinese models narrowed the gap with American rivals. Chinese officials defended the technique as standard and said they would act against theft. The US Commerce Department and China's Cyberspace Administration did not respond to comments. A former Alibaba engineer said distillation makes one expensive query do repeated work.

OpenAI and Anthropic terms restrict using their output to develop competing AI models. Some sources argue that engineering, algorithms, and data also helped Chinese AI progress. Researchers from Shanghai Jiao Tong University warned that distillation could stifle original innovation. Chinese AI developers have asked the industry regulator for guidance on legal boundaries. These developers are affected by constraints on computing power and US chip curbs.

Eight Chinese agencies published a national AI+Manufacturing policy package in January. This guidance supports model training, fine-tuning, and distillation for various industrial applications. Cities including Shanghai and Shenzhen have encouraged techniques that reduce computing requirements. US authorities publicly accused Chinese companies of aggressive industrial distillation in September. Beijing aims to deploy smaller, cheaper AI systems across the second-largest global economy.

President Donald Trump and Xi Jinping are expected to meet during the APEC summit. The US continues to restrict Chinese access to advanced chips from Nvidia. Chinese developers seek clarity on the line between ordinary use and organized collection. The Ministry of Industry and Information Technology did not respond to comment requests. It remains unclear if China will make concrete commitments to stop IP theft.

stories.Headline: US Commerce Department restricts remote AI chip access in five countries to block Chinese firms
stories.Summary:
The US Commerce Department announced a new rule on November 16 to stop China from remotely accessing AI chips. This measure targets data centres in South-east Asia that allow Chinese firms to bypass existing American technology export restrictions. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent pushed for this rule with support from National Security Adviser and Secretary of State Marco Rubio. The crackdown follows a scandal involving Nvidia founder Jensen Huang and a suspected Chinese spy named Alice Huang. These events led to Jensen Huang stepping down as the chief executive officer of Nvidia on November 12.

The rule takes effect 90 days after being gazetted in the Federal Register and adds five countries to restrictions. These nations are Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, and Brazil, where companies must now obtain Commerce Department licences for shipments. It targets advanced computing integrated circuits, computers, servers, and electronic assemblies, but exempts online retailers and social media firms. American cloud hyperscalers like Google, Microsoft, and Amazon Web Services receive exemptions, creating a two-tier operating environment for operators. Data centres must now audit clients to ensure they are not shell companies from China, Macau, Russia, or Iran.

The Bureau of Industry and Security stated the rule prevents circumventing sensitive technology restrictions through remote computing in third countries. Singapore's Ministry of Digital Development and Information and Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry said they are studying the details. These ministries stated that Singapore is a trusted hub and does not condone using its association to violate laws. President Donald Trump noted that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick hold opposing views on China. Trump stated that one official wants to be friendly with China while the other wants a blow-up.

Paul Triolo of DGA Group said the rule makes it difficult to service large Chinese firms developing generative artificial intelligence. He noted that removing these major consumers complicates the economics of data centre operation and critical debt servicing revenue. The rule affects companies like Megaspeed International, which bought billions of dollars in Nvidia chips for South-east Asian centres. Chinese tech giants including Alibaba, ByteDance, and Tencent previously used these centres for unrestricted cloud access to advanced American chips. Singapore's Ministry for Home Affairs said the FBI and Department of Justice provided little help with their own investigations.

The US is concerned that Chinese companies used remote access to bypass prohibitions on selling advanced chips directly to China. Megaspeed International and US server supplier Super Micro are under scrutiny for potential false declarations regarding the purchase of servers. Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive and suspected spy, is believed to be in China after a Singapore ban. The US wants to lock South-east Asia into an American AI stack of chips, cloud infrastructure, and governance standards. This effort follows a Democrat sweep of the midterm elections and the political fallout from the Nvidia affair.

President Donald Trump will visit Manila for the ASEAN summit from November 17 to 19 to meet South-east Asian leaders. He is also scheduled to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping while attending the APEC leaders' summit in Shenzhen, China. The US will monitor countries that tolerate evasion and may impose broader trade or import restrictions if compliance is weak. There is a 60-day comment period for industry feedback, though Paul Triolo believes the chance of rollback is low. The articles leave open whether compliance friction will drive regional players toward Chinese alternatives or sovereign third-stack solutions.

stories.Headline: House Democrats led by McGovern call for a national moratorium on new AI data centers
stories.Summary:
Leading and incoming U.S. House Democrats called for a national moratorium on new artificial intelligence data centers on Tuesday, November 18, 2026. They made the call at a press conference outside the U.S. Capitol hosted by the advocacy group Food & Water Watch. The push followed midterm elections in which Democrats delivered a landslide majority in the House and also secured control of the Senate. Data centers, critical to storing the infrastructure for AI, have sparked widespread backlash over their effect on the environment and energy costs. The issue marked a major issue in the midterm elections.

The Artificial Intelligence Data Center Moratorium Act is numbered S. 4214 in the Senate and H.R. 9442 in the House. Independent Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont introduced it in the Senate and New York progressive Democratic Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez introduced it in the House earlier this year. The moratorium would be imposed until legislation is enacted that safeguards the public from the dangers of artificial intelligence, per the text of the bill. It would pause large data center projects until the federal government puts safeguards in place against job losses, environmental degradation and rising energy costs. McGovern is one of nine co-sponsors of the House bill.

Rep. Jim McGovern of Massachusetts, an original cosponsor of the House version and the top Democrat on the House Rules Committee, said it is time for Americans from across the political spectrum to demand a nationwide moratorium on data centers. He called for an immediate change to the status quo and said the alarm bells are flashing while the president and the White House are asleep at the switch on AI. He said they want to put everything in the hands of a few selfish, greedy, powerful men while the rest of us fight for scraps, and he said what we say is hell no. He called President Donald Trump a megalomaniac who refuses to hold Big Tech accountable and said Congress has been idle for the past two years under what he called Mike Johnson's MAGA majority. He said the American people are done getting screwed over by unelected, unaccountable Big Tech oligarchs.

Rep. Chellie Pingree of Maine, the top Democrat on the House Appropriations subcommittee that oversees U.S. Interior Department funding and in line to chair it in the next Congress, said data centers are driving up costs even further, straining the grid, dirtying air and water and degrading health and quality of life. She said that when energy prices are already sky high in places like Maine and across America, Americans don't want data centers, and that Interior Secretary Doug Burgum is fast-tracking a plan to give away 17,000 acres of public land across six states for data center projects. Rep.-elect Adam Hamawy of New Jersey said data centers cover bills, the environment, communities and farmlands, and that the American people, not the mega-corporations, really have a say. Hamawy also said it is obvious why data centers are an AI tax where hardworking families foot the bill for Silicon Valley. Rep.-elect Will Lawrence of Michigan acknowledged AI is a marvelous technology capable of amazing things, but said under current incentives it will put people out of work, harm the environment, undermine democracy and put us all at terrible risk.

Lawrence said his district saw five hyperscale data center proposals in 15 months and that companies remain in an out of control arms race to capture market share even if it kills us all. Local moratoriums or bans on large data centers have been approved in 18 Massachusetts municipalities, including Northampton, Holyoke and Westfield, and Sutton residents are petitioning to ban data centers, potentially blocking a proposed $16 billion data center sponsored by two Kraft family companies. A major bipartisan bill making its way through the Senate would overhaul the federal process for permits to construct energy projects, including data centers, and it advanced Monday on an overwhelming 70-27 vote. Food & Water Watch policy director Jim Walsh said in a statement earlier in November that the bad bill would only encourage and permit greater buildout of data centers and the polluting fracked gas power plants and pipelines required to serve these enormous facilities. The electricity to power data centers can exceed the demand of midsize American cities, and these costs are redistributed across the entire system, ultimately increasing electricity rates, the legislators said.

Most of this energy comes from fossil fuels like coal and natural gas, and The New York Times reported that the largest U.S. data centers release an estimated 25.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide each year, which equates to Bolivia's entire output. The Trump administration has pushed for the expansion of these centers and is also considering public land offers for data center development. Alphabet, Google's parent company, invested $205 billion in the effort this fiscal year, while Meta has committed $600 billion for AI infrastructure and job development by 2028. McGovern and his colleagues contend that pausing construction across the country would give communities time to study their impact and decide if they should be allowed, ensuring the buildout and creation of artificial intelligence that benefits the public. Pingree said the lands are national treasures that belong to the American public and do not belong to tech billionaires.

McGovern and the other Democratic Congress members promised to keep fighting for the American people and urged other legislators to join them. Hamawy said House Democrats have an opportunity to prove to the American people that they meant it when they said they were going to fight for them. McGovern vowed to assert congressional power to protect the American people and pass the moratorium. The articles do not say when or whether the moratorium measure will receive a vote. The articles also leave open whether the Senate permitting bill will pass.

stories.Headline: Google raises Gemini chat retention to about two months even with history off
stories.Summary:
Google updated the Gemini privacy policy on Monday, November 17, 2026, raising the conversation retention period from 72 hours to around two months, as reported by Gizmodo, IBTimes and TechCrunch. The change was made by Google for its flagship AI tool Gemini, according to Gizmodo. Gizmodo reporter AJ Dellinger published his story on November 17, 2026 at 5:00 pm ET. The updated Gemini Apps Privacy Hub page carried a notice that future chats will still be saved for around 2 months even if Gemini History is turned off. An archived version of the Gemini Apps Privacy Hub had a last update date of October 13, 2026, according to Gizmodo.

The retention period rises from 72 hours to around two months, and Temporary Chats will also be kept for around two months, according to Google's updated privacy documentation cited by IBTimes. Gemini History defaults to 18 months and can be changed to three months, 36 months or indefinite, and saved chats can be deleted at any time, Gizmodo reported. The Gemini History option in user settings still describes the retention period as 72 hours, Gizmodo said. Google's new settings let users keep their Gemini chat history while opting out of generative AI model training, and the new training controls are off by default, according to IBTimes. Conversations reviewed by human reviewers and associated information can be retained for up to three years even if users later delete their history, and feedback can lead to a conversation, attachments and other relevant information being reviewed and retained for up to three years, IBTimes reported.

Google declined to provide a comment to Gizmodo and instead directed it to a blog post titled "We're updating controls in the Gemini app." In that post Google said it was giving users more control over when Gemini chat history is used to train generative AI models. Google said the longer retention period was intended to strengthen safety and security protections as AI systems become increasingly capable, according to IBTimes. Google said retained information may be used to respond to requests, process feedback and protect the company, its users and the public. Google's updated Gemini Apps Privacy Hub also cites potential system failures as a reason for retaining chats and says temporary conversations are not used to train AI models, TechCrunch reported.

OpenAI claims it holds onto temporary chats for up to 30 days, and Anthropic says conversations with Claude are held for 30 days by default, with both noting they may hold certain chat logs longer if necessary, according to Gizmodo. TechCrunch said OpenAI may keep temporary ChatGPT chats for up to 30 days and Anthropic retains incognito Claude chats for 30 days by default, though companies may keep some data longer for legal or safety reasons or to investigate policy violations. The Register reported Tuesday that archived versions of Google's privacy documentation confirmed the earlier three-day limit, IBTimes said. Under the updated policy, conversations may remain associated with a user's Google Account during the temporary retention period even though they do not appear in the user's visible Gemini History, according to IBTimes. Google says conversations sent to service providers for review are disconnected from users' accounts, IBTimes reported.

Until now, chat history and AI training were tied to a single "Keep Activity" setting, TechCrunch reported. Previously, retaining Gemini conversation history was more closely tied to allowing Google to use those interactions to improve its AI systems, according to IBTimes. Google's documentation states that future chat content will not be used to train generative AI models when the training setting is disabled, except in certain circumstances including when users voluntarily submit feedback, IBTimes said. Temporary Chats are also excluded from generative AI model training, although Google still retains them temporarily for operational and safety purposes, according to IBTimes. Google warns that deleting Gemini history does not necessarily remove information saved through connected Google services, which may follow their own privacy and retention policies, and advises users not to enter confidential information they would not want a reviewer to see, IBTimes reported.

The updates will begin rolling out globally over the coming weeks, according to IBTimes. Google did not answer TechCrunch's questions about what prompted the change and whether it would affect how conversations are accessed or reviewed. Gizmodo said the Gemini History option in user settings will presumably update when the change goes into effect. Users who want to review their choices can open Gemini, go to Settings and select History, and can also manage retention preferences through Gemini History, according to IBTimes. Individual users may see different options while the global rollout is underway, and for users who leave chat history enabled the default automatic deletion period remains 18 months, IBTimes reported.

stories.Headline: Baidu CEO Robin Li urges companies to monetize AI and overhaul organizational structures to avoid a bubble
stories.Summary:
Baidu CEO Robin Li spoke about the urgent need for artificial intelligence adoption during the APEC CEO Summit in Shenzhen on November 17, 2026. He explained that the actual spread of AI applications is moving more slowly than people expected despite the intense competition in the technology sector. Li argued that companies must prioritize the monetization of these tools to prevent the risk of a market bubble. He believes that the industry cannot sustain its current growth without finding clear ways to generate revenue.

The process of reaping the benefits of AI requires a complete overhaul of traditional organizational structures within a company. Robin Li stated that he has made radical attempts to break down the boundaries of traditional jobs at Baidu to better integrate these new technologies. This shift involves reorganizing how teams operate to ensure that AI is not just a tool but a core part of the business model. Such changes are necessary to keep pace with the rapid evolution of the global tech map.

As the leader of Baidu, Robin Li is responsible for guiding his company through this transition while advising other executives on the necessity of structural change. He suggested that the current way of organizing work is an obstacle to the full potential of artificial intelligence. By removing rigid job descriptions, he believes companies can become more agile and responsive to technological breakthroughs. He emphasized that those who fail to reorganize their internal systems will likely struggle to compete in the future.

Ifeoma Ajunwa, one of three Emory Law professors leading the concentration, was named among the Top 50 Legal Innovators in Academia for 2026. The National Law Review and Wickard recently announced that national honor, which recognizes those shaping the future of legal education, according to the article. Emory Law is one of five law schools in Georgia, and the article said it is emerging as one of the top institutions in the country for making sure the next batches of attorneys know how to handle the technology.

The concentration includes formal courses in AI and the law, and Emory Law began the formal specialization in the fall, the article said. Other law schools offer AI-related courses but not a formal specialization, and Georgia State University College of Law is among the schools that have taught the topic, according to the article. Ajunwa said 21 years ago, during her education, there was no component around AI, and she said students would grapple with how to think about the technology. The article cited a survey showing that 65% of the largest law firms have fully implemented generative AI, 82% of lawyers use it, 32% of firms have implemented it across multiple areas, and 11% of firms have no plans to use it. The article also cited figures of 5,700, 202, 150 and 34 in connection with AI use and law firm practices.

stories.Headline: Giga Energy signs $1 billion lease for 60MW Texas AI data center
stories.Summary:
Giga Energy, an AI data center developer based in the United States, announced on November 17, 2026 a $1 billion lease agreement with an undisclosed U.S.-based AI cloud provider for a 60MW GigaBase AI data center in Hunt County, Texas. The company broke ground on the project, called Project Clay, in July and will develop, own and operate the campus for the customer. The roughly 30-acre campus is scheduled to be ready for service in spring 2027 and will provide AI computing capacity for hyperscale and AI cloud customers. The project is designed to meet priorities that Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa has called for, including protecting local resources, investing in dedicated infrastructure and ensuring communities benefit from growth.

The development is expected to create about 300 construction jobs during the build phase and 24 permanent full-time positions with estimated annual salaries ranging from $116,000 to $180,000. It is also expected to generate millions in new recurring annual tax revenue for local schools, infrastructure, emergency services and other public needs. The project includes an investment in new electrical infrastructure that taps underutilized capacity on dedicated power infrastructure in the county, and it is designed so it does not draw on distribution capacity serving existing homes and businesses. Instead of open-loop evaporative cooling, Project Clay uses a fully closed-loop system that operates independently of local water supplies, with the only local water used for sinks and employee bathrooms, on par with the usage of two homes annually.

Giga says the project will finish in under eight months, less than half the time of traditional builds, using a factory-first construction model in which much of the facility is manufactured off-site before final assembly in the community. Brent Whitehead, president and co-founder at Giga Energy, said the company believes AI infrastructure should leave a community stronger than it found it, through high-paying jobs, an expanded local tax base and long-term investments that benefit residents for decades. He said Hunt County is gaining an economic engine that will support schools, public services and future growth for generations. Whitehead also said the project is exactly the kind of AI infrastructure Texas needs, and that communities should not have to choose between economic growth and protecting local resources.

Giga Energy describes itself as a U.S.-based developer, operator and manufacturer of AI data centers, with factories in Long Beach and Houston, and says it has delivered gigawatts of sites and critical infrastructure across the country. The project aligns with Texas' growing emphasis on water-efficient data center development in drought-prone regions, according to the announcement. Giga Energy leaders say that as demand for AI infrastructure continues to accelerate across the United States, the next generation of data centers must do more than power technology and must also earn the trust of the communities where they are built. With this project, Giga officially unveils its GigaBase system, which the company says is engineered to address lengthy construction timelines, heavy water consumption and pressure on local utilities.

stories.Headline: Max Roser finds every high-quality US survey shows more negative than positive views on AI
stories.Summary:
Just Capital released the third edition of its monthly National AI Monitor on November 18, 2026, asking Americans how they experience AI in daily life. The survey was conducted online by The Harris Poll for Just Capital from October 19 to 21, 2026, among 1,008 U.S. adults ages 18 and older. It found that Americans' experiences with AI have trended positive or stayed steady across every measure since the research began in August 2026. The results contrast with a popular narrative, the release said, and show clear divides across demographics and stakeholder categories. When asked about the years ahead, the differences became more pronounced.

Respondents answered seven questions, one on AI's overall effect to date, one for each of five stakeholder groups, and one forward-looking question on optimism. All questions used a five-point scale from very negative to very positive, with "I don't know" as an additional non-forced option. Overall scores were plus 42 in October, plus 37 in September and plus 35 in August, calculated as positive minus negative responses on a range of -100 to +100. Work scored plus 47, plus 44 and plus 48, customer experience plus 26, plus 25 and plus 21, and community engagement plus 15, plus 12 and plus 7. Investments scored plus 31, plus 24 and plus 21, environmental stewardship minus 9, minus 12 and minus 17, and the next few years plus 14, plus 12 and plus 15.

The sample data is accurate to within plus or minus 3.6 percentage points using a 95% confidence level, and that interval is wider among subsets. Month-to-month changes are not statistically significant, but changes between August and October are statistically significant for community engagement, investments and environmental stewardship. Full-time workers, college graduates and adults ages 35 to 44 maintain a positive outlook, while retirees, people not employed, those with some college but no degree, and Americans 65 and over turn net negative. Just Capital CEO Martin Whittaker said Americans feel more positively about AI when they see tangible opportunities for themselves in the AI-powered economy. Whittaker said the results indicate that experience is most pronounced among working, educated Americans, and that there are early signs people can feel good about AI in their own lives while worrying about society at large.

Whittaker said whether America successfully embraces AI economically, socially and politically rests on closing the gap between what ordinary working Americans expect and what they experience. He said decision makers in tech, business and government will ignore this at their peril. A 58-year-old man in Florida with an associate's degree, self-employed part-time and lower income, said AI tools automate routine administrative tasks and let him focus on strategy and growth. A 37-year-old woman in Texas who completed graduate school, employed full-time and upper income, said companies' use of AI makes customer experience faster and more convenient but she sometimes worries about data privacy, inaccurate information and less human interaction. A 33-year-old man in California who completed graduate school, employed full-time and middle income, said AI optimizes local traffic management to cut city gridlock.

A 73-year-old woman in Texas who completed some college but no degree, retired and lower income, questioned whether AI is needed so much in every application that it requires enormous facilities and land and water resources for data centers. A 32-year-old woman in Ohio, a college graduate, self-employed part-time and lower income, said she lost her job to AI while it makes her technology increasingly unusable. Our World in Data published an article by Max Roser on November 16, 2026, combining recent high-quality surveys after cautioning that answers can shift with question wording. In Pew's survey, 37% took a middle answer when one was offered, and only 9% chose a positive view in both Pew's and Gallup's surveys. Every survey found more Americans negative than positive on AI, and in Pew's survey 52% were more concerned than excited against 9% more excited than concerned, a ratio of more than five to one. When Pew first asked in 2021, the ratio was about two to one.

In the Ipsos survey, 17% said AI is an extremely bad thing for society and just 2% said extremely good. In a Quinnipiac poll in September 2026, 35% were somewhat concerned and 38% very concerned that future AI systems could threaten human survival, and 73% believed there is a risk to humanity's survival. In Pew's survey, 56% of Democrats and 49% of Republicans were more concerned than excited, and in both parties only around one in ten were more excited than concerned. Roser wrote that if the industry wants to earn the public's trust, it will have to take these widespread concerns much more seriously than it has so far. Pew's survey of 3,488 US adults on the American Trends Panel ran June 22 to 28, 2026, and its November 2021 data came from the same panel November 1 to 7, 2021. Gallup and Bentley University surveyed 3,270 US adults on the Gallup Panel May 4 to 11, 2026.

Quinnipiac's telephone survey of 1,397 US adults ran March 19 to 23, 2026, and its release was dated March 30, 2026. The Annenberg Public Policy Center surveyed 1,320 US adults June 16 to July 19, 2026, and Ipsos surveyed 2,545 US adults on its KnowledgePanel October 9 to 13, 2026. The September Quinnipiac survey of 1,202 US adults ran September 24 to 27, 2026, using random digit dialing with live interviewers on landlines and cell phones. In that poll, 14% were not so concerned, 11% not concerned at all and 1% did not know or did not answer. Roser included only surveys based on probability samples, and Quinnipiac called randomly generated landline and cell phone numbers. The other four surveyed members of online panels recruited at random, mostly by mail to randomly selected addresses, and all five weight results to match the US adult population and publish full question wording.

Roser excluded opt-in online panels, citing an opt-in poll that found 20% of Americans under 30 agreed the Holocaust is a myth, while Pew's probability-based panel found 3%. In 2021 Pew introduced its question with a short definition and referred to artificial intelligence computer programs rather than artificial intelligence (AI), with the same answer options, and Pew reports the results as one trend. In the same Ipsos survey, 50% said AI is a good thing for them personally and 49% a bad thing, while 15% said extremely bad and 3% extremely good. In Quinnipiac's March 2026 poll, 55% expected AI to do more harm than good in their day-to-day life against 34% who expected more good. A Quinnipiac release dated September 30, 2026, said 73% were concerned about a potential threat to human survival and 86% supported independent safety standards for AI companies. Just Capital's release said additional qualitative findings and drivers of experience are available in the National AI Monitor.

stories.Headline: Telus ends partnership with Westbank to build two AI data centres in Vancouver
stories.Summary:
Telus Corp. ended its partnership with Westbank Corp. to build two artificial intelligence data centres in Vancouver. This decision was reported over the weekend before Monday, November 17, 2026. The company decided to pull out of these specific urban projects. However, Telus will still expand an AI data centre in Kamloops. These three sites were intended to form a sovereign AI factory cluster.

The projects involved a new 10-storey building at 150 West Georgia St. in downtown Vancouver. A second property at 111 East 5th Ave. in Mount Pleasant required redevelopment. Quebecor made an unsolicited $31 billion cash and stock offer for Telus on Monday. This bid represents a 60 per cent premium over recent Telus share prices. The offer follows an initial bid made in June for the Vancouver company.

Telus has not given a reason for exiting the Vancouver projects but will share its AI strategy later. Westbank confirmed Telus is no longer a partner but will proceed with the projects as planned. Westbank intends to announce a new partnership in the coming months for the compute infrastructure. Rob Goehring said the Telus leadership team has been seeking cost-cutting measures and strategic alternatives. He believes a confluence of recent events likely made the company skittish.

Rob Goehring of the AI Network of B.C. noted that Vancouver's new mayor and council dislike AI centres. Mayor Pete Fry agreed that council might impose stricter requirements and fees on data centre owners. This would affect developers who must commission third-party assessments on noise, heat, water use, and impacts. Fry noted that AI data centres are not currently a defined land use under city bylaws. A motion regarding these public impact requirements was going before council this week.

Telus and Westbank originally announced the sustainable AI infrastructure partnership in May of the current year. The Mount Pleasant site had a rezoning application that was paused in July before October elections. Municipal elections took place on October 17, and the city requested further consultation in early December. Telus originally planned to acquire 60,000 graphics processing units from Nvidia for these B.C. data centres. The company also aimed to secure 150 megawatts of electricity for the sites by 2032.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang stepped down following a scandal involving extramarital affairs and an alleged Chinese spy. This left questions about who will lead the chip giant that supplies key AI hardware and software. Westbank will share more details on its sovereign net-positive compute infrastructure for Canada in the near future. The articles leave open whether the new Vancouver partnership will be announced soon. It remains unclear if Telus will accept the $31 billion takeover bid from Quebecor.

stories.Headline: South Korean stocks fall for a fourth day as AI concerns deepen
stories.Summary:
South Korean stocks sank for the fourth consecutive session on Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026, as lingering concerns over artificial intelligence dampened investor sentiment. The benchmark Korea Composite Stock Price Index lost 132.02 points, or 2.59 percent, to close at 4,968.48. The index fell below the 5,000-point mark to its lowest level in nine months. The Korean won weakened against the U.S. dollar. Trade volume was light at 183.09 million shares worth 14.19 trillion won, or $10.61 billion.

Decliners far outnumbered advancers 709 to 182. Foreigners sold a net 1.44 trillion won, while institutions and individuals bought a net 543.56 billion won and 421.79 billion won, respectively. Top market cap Samsung Electronics decreased 3.3 percent to 190,300 won, and chip giant SK hynix shed 1.96 percent to 1.1 million won. SK Square, the parent of SK hynix, retreated 1.31 percent to 679,000 won. Power equipment manufacturer Samsung Electro-Mechanics sank 3.95 percent to 754,000 won.

The Korean won was trading at 1,338.2 won against the U.S. dollar as of 3:30 p.m., down 1.7 won from the previous session's close. Bond prices, which move inversely to yields, closed higher. The yield on three-year Treasurys shed 1.8 basis points to 3.725, and the return on the benchmark five-year government bonds fell 0.5 basis point to 3.825. Kang Jin-hyuk, an analyst at Shinhan Securities, said the market came under pressure from continued fallout surrounding Nvidia. He also cited U.S. restrictions on remote access to Nvidia's AI chips and concerns over the sustainability of AI demand, which dampened investors' risk appetite.

On Wall Street, the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite dropped about 2.5 percent Monday, while AI chip giant Nvidia shares slid 4.1 percent. The Nvidia decline came amid continued uncertainty following the departure of its CEO, Jensen Huang, last week. Nvidia is scheduled to report its earnings Tuesday, with investors closely watching its outlook for AI chip demand and infrastructure spending. Investors are also keeping an eye on AI giant Anthropic's planned Nasdaq debut Thursday. The AI sector is also facing increased regulatory scrutiny after the U.S. government issued new rules Monday restricting remote access to advanced U.S. computing chips and servers.

stories.Headline: Google reports attackers use AI agentic workflows to automate vulnerability discovery and exploitation
stories.Summary:
Google Threat Intelligence Group reported on November 17, 2026, that threat actors are using AI-powered agentic workflows to automate vulnerability discovery and exploitation, according to TechGig. The group said this development accelerates cyberattacks to machine speed and reduces the time defenders have to patch their systems. GTIG highlighted the use of CAIRN, an open-source multi-agent penetration-testing framework, in an attack against the U.S. aerospace sector. Suspected North Korean hackers have also used Claude Code to deliver malware, the report said.

Researchers estimate that unsophisticated, fully autonomous attacks requiring little human interaction will emerge within the next three months, while sophisticated fully autonomous agentic attacks are likely to appear within six months. The FBI warned last week that multiple threat actors have weaponized the ARTEX AI pentesting framework since August, targeting organizations in financial, government, technology, defense, and healthcare sectors. Google states that attackers systematically abuse open-source pentesting suites including ARTEX, CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI, and HexStrike AI, which facilitate adaptive attacks against internet-exposed endpoints vulnerable to low-complexity flaws. GTIG's AI Threat Tracker report cites a multi-agent system called exploit_agent that fully automated vulnerability finding and exploitation against French media, entertainment, and education websites.

GTIG identified an exposed staging server hosting the exploit_agent framework, which integrates with multiple frontier and local LLMs and analyzes software updates on popular web apps to find flaws and automatically attempt exploitation. The deployment of such frameworks dramatically decreases the time defenders have to patch their systems and also produces false leads, as seen with PHP2Shell, where hundreds of purported AI-generated proof-of-concept exploits appeared quickly. Google also observed UNC6836 using modified Claude Code to deliver the SOMBERMEME backdoor against cryptocurrency firms. AI is also routinely used in influence operations by state-backed groups, commercial vendors, and political networks, and LLMjacking has become widespread, with attackers exploiting this new revenue stream at significant cost to affected organizations.

stories.Headline: Hive debuts five AI marketing assistants that draft live event campaigns for human approval
stories.Summary:
Hive, a live events marketing platform, announced on Wednesday, November 18, 2026, that it is debuting a suite of AI assistants to help festivals, venues and promoters develop and manage marketing campaigns, according to a report by J.R. Lind on news.pollstar.com. The assistants will prepare campaigns using upcoming shows, past campaigns and brand preferences, incorporating artist information, event dates, ticket status and relevant links, drawing on ticketing information and audience data. Final approval and distribution of every campaign remains with the human user, so marketers keep the last word before anything goes out. The assistants learn each organization's voice from its previous campaigns and ongoing feedback, using past sends to reflect established messaging, tone and brand preferences.

As marketers review, edit, approve or decline drafts, that feedback informs subsequent campaigns, helping the assistants become more aligned with each team's approach over time. At launch, there are five assistants: Just Announced, Onsale, Newsletter, Countdown and Post Show, and each develops campaigns tailored to a specific stage of an event. Other assistants are being developed to handle other parts of the event life cycle, though the article gives no dates for those. The announcement follows Hive's $27 million investment from Frontier Growth to accelerate AI and automation development, deepen integrations and support global expansion.

Ian Roberts, CEO and Co-Founder of Hive, said that live-event marketers know their audiences and their shows, and that what they often need is more time to get the work done. He said the Marketing Assistants bring together the event data and brand context already in Hive to prepare campaigns for their teams to review. He added that marketers stay in control, and that their feedback helps shape the next draft. The article does not say when the assistants become available beyond the launch announcement itself.

The context is that Hive is positioning the assistants as a time-saving tool for an industry whose marketers already understand their audiences and shows, with the $27 million from Frontier Growth funding faster AI and automation work. The article does not say what happens next beyond the note that other assistants are in development for other parts of the event life cycle. No pricing, availability dates or customer names appear in the report.
