stories.Headline: Mayer Brown says companies deploying AI agents face antitrust and product risks
stories.Summary:
A law firm advisory published on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, by Mayer Brown described how AI agents can execute transactions, change records and communicate with customers and suppliers without a person reviewing each step. The advisory offered a hypothetical in which an artificial intelligence purchasing agent tasked with finding the lowest price agrees with agents working for other buyers to pay suppliers no more than a set amount. That scenario could expose the company deploying the agent to antitrust scrutiny and leave it in a separate fight with its AI supplier over who should have prevented the agreement. The advisory also offered a retail example in which a sales agent could encourage New York shoppers to buy scooters that exceed the applicable speed threshold. The retailer could face enforcement action even if it argued that the vendor should have built a safeguard against prohibited sales.

Regulators are expected to look first to the company that deployed the agent, and whether that company can recover losses from its supplier may depend on what the contract assigns to each party and what the company can prove about how the agent acted. Before rollout, companies can use these scenarios to agree with suppliers on who runs each safeguard, and for a retail agent the agreement could specify who maintains jurisdiction-specific product restrictions, who tests that the agent blocks prohibited transactions and who can suspend it when a control fails. Procurement teams can set limits on whom their agents contact and decide which commitments require staff approval, and the contract can spell out who covers losses if an agreed safeguard fails and whether limits on payments apply. Companies should agree with vendors in advance on which records to keep and how quickly teams can get them, including instructions, configuration changes, approvals and transactions. Companies can set performance benchmarks before launch, test vendor updates and agree on when repeated failures justify ending the contract.

The advisory said companies may also have to explain an agent's decisions to a regulator, and it named audit rights, verification tools and logs that document decision steps as key safeguards. It said performance disputes may turn on what a vendor promised and how the contract measures it, and that an agent which repeatedly places the same order could prompt a gross negligence claim aimed at recovering more than a damages cap allows. It said a customer might seek early termination if a customer relationship management agent routinely misses meetings or spams contacts, and that a supplier update which reduces accuracy could lead to a dispute over good faith. It said third parties may sue over misleading statements to customers or disparaging claims about competitors, and that if an agent visits a site that bars automated access, the parties may dispute who should have blocked it. It said similar allocation disputes may follow a privacy or security incident if an agent discloses sensitive information, and the parties may disagree over whether supplier safeguards or the customer's deployment controls should have prevented it.

The advisory said intellectual property disputes can arise during an agent's acquisition of third-party material, ownership of new code it produces, or a supplier's alleged use of customer data to train a competing product. It said a customer may struggle to gather enough evidence of unauthorized training to bring a claim and may still have trouble identifying its data in a training set, and that contract terms on ownership and data use are stronger when paired with a way to verify compliance. It said the supplier might point to the retailer's sales instructions, its configuration of the agent or its control over which transactions require approval. It said operations and compliance teams should walk through a simulated incident with the supplier before launch, and that the exercise can show who can stop the agent, how quickly the company can reconstruct what happened and whether it has the records it would need to answer a regulator. It said these records could help establish whether the incident followed a supplier update, a change made by the customer or a failure of a control both parties expected to work.

A separate article published on November 16, 2026, said organizations have spent the past few years accelerating AI adoption across software development and now face AI systems that can act faster than the organizations responsible for them can understand or govern what is happening. It said organizations are thinking about compliance, data privacy, security and model reliability while boards are demanding policies and regulators are developing frameworks, and the challenge now is turning those levers into tangible controls that work at the pace of today's AI-driven software development without creating a bottleneck. It said AI has significantly lowered the barriers to generating code, with assistants suggesting individual functions and increasingly capable coding agents working across repositories, running tests, making changes and executing multi-step development tasks. It said agents can perform multi-step workflows, access tools, retrieve data, write code, trigger actions and coordinate tasks on behalf of users, and that governance becomes murkier when agents are not only generating code but testing it, deploying it, opening a pull request, modifying multiple files or interacting with other systems. It said the distance between decision and action becomes much shorter, which simultaneously means the ability for humans to retain enough access to understand and monitor each step becomes much harder.

The article said developers still need to understand the code, architecture and systems they are responsible for, but increasingly must also decide what work to delegate, what context an agent needs and how to verify the result. It said most organizations already have policies governing software security, access and compliance, but policies alone cannot govern AI agents operating across repositories, tools and development environments, and controls need to be built into the environment where development happens rather than applied after an agent has completed its work. It said the first control to consider is traceability, meaning tracking AI-generated changes and making them auditable so teams can still read, review and understand the output, and that if an agent makes changes across multiple files and runs tests, the team should be able to identify exactly what actions were taken, including what was changed, which instructions were received and which tests were run. It said AI might be permitted to generate code and run tests automatically while changes to production infrastructure or other critical systems must require explicit human review and approval, and that these boundaries should be defined in advance by organizations. It said an AI tool that can modify application code does not necessarily need access to production infrastructure, and a coding agent that can run tests does not necessarily need permission to change deployment configuration.

The article said "tokenmaxxing" has been one of the defining AI trends of 2026, yet there is growing realization among organizations that AI activity and AI value are not the same thing, and that measuring usage rates, prompts and token consumption does not necessarily tell them whether AI is delivering better outcomes or creating meaningful business value. It said agentic systems can perform long, multi-step workflows and consume significant resources without a developer manually initiating every individual step, which is starting to drive interest in what the industry is now calling a "software harness," a layer of software around AI models that can provide context and give organizations greater control over tasks and token costs. It said what works when one developer is directing one agent becomes harder when multiple agents are operating across repositories, teams and shared systems, and that without a shared foundation the same autonomy that makes agents useful can also create fragmentation, inconsistent practices and new risks. It said the most successful organizations will not be those that deploy the largest number of AI agents but the ones able to create the clearest lines of accountability around them, and that when an AI output fails, customers blame companies not agents, so responsibility will always land within engineering teams. It said developers are no longer simply responsible for the code they write but also for reviewing, governing and understanding the work of systems capable of generating far more software than any individual engineer could ever produce alone.

stories.Headline: Warsh says AI could speed growth and warns of job losses and market declines
stories.Summary:
Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh said Monday that artificial intelligence could accelerate innovation and usher in an era of faster economic growth, in remarks that also acknowledged risks from the technology. Warsh said the adoption of AI could also lead to widespread job loss or a steep drop in the stock market if the healthy returns expected from the huge investments in AI infrastructure don't materialize. Warsh's remarks kicked off a one-day conference on AI and productivity at the Fed's San Francisco branch. Warsh did not mention inflation, even though many of his colleagues blame the buildout of data centers for accelerating price increases. Warsh did not comment on what the Fed's next steps would be on interest rates, nor did he say anything about recent government data showing that inflation accelerated last month.

That data led many of Warsh's colleagues on the Fed's rate-setting committee to signal their support for additional interest rate hikes, including at the Fed's next meeting in December. The Fed refers to AI as "super intelligence" following an executive order issued by President Donald Trump requiring federal agencies to use the term. Warsh appointed five different task forces soon after taking the helm at the Fed, and the conference Monday was part of a task force Warsh set up to evaluate AI and its impact on the economy's efficiency. Fed staff has begun evaluating different scenarios for how AI's impact may play out, Warsh added. Warsh has long said, including before his nomination as Fed chair, that AI could significantly boost the economy's efficiency, which would enable it to grow without worsening inflation.

"What might set SI apart, as an economic influence, is that it could supercharge idea generation," Warsh said. "It appears to be changing the method ,  and, at least as important, the speed ,  of innovation. If idea generation broadens, growth could be sustained at a level substantially higher than the long-run average." "As policymakers, we have to be mindful that great opportunities rarely come risk free," Warsh said. "And the risks in this case, if overlooked, can be highly disruptive and economically costly." Warsh said that "after significant capital investment and stock market gains, expected returns could turn down and equity valuations could fall, leading to an economic slowdown and a more notable rise in unemployment."

Warsh spent more time in his remarks considering the downsides of AI than he has in previous speeches. Other Fed officials have increasingly voiced concern that AI is fanning inflation because the buildout of AI infrastructure has sharply raised demand for computer chips, electronic components, electricity and copper. Those increases, in turn, have lifted the cost of smartphones, computers and other consumer electronics. Smartphone prices rose last month at the fastest pace on record, the government said last week. Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson said Friday that if AI does accelerate economic growth, it could lead to higher interest rates over time, even if inflation declines.

"If the new technology leads to permanently higher levels of productivity growth, it may increase firms' desire to invest and, hence, their demand for funding, raising the level of interest rates," Jefferson said. Warsh's generally optimistic outlook on the new technology is a view at odds with many of his colleagues. Warsh has previously touted AI as a technology that could significantly boost the economy's efficiency, which would enable it to grow without worsening inflation. In turn, the Fed could potentially lower interest rates under that scenario. The conference Monday was part of a task force Warsh set up to evaluate AI and its impact on the economy's efficiency.

Warsh appointed five different task forces soon after taking the helm at the Fed. Fed staff has begun evaluating different scenarios for how AI's impact may play out, Warsh added. Warsh did not address AI's impact on inflation, a top concern of many of his Fed colleagues. Last week, several policymakers expressed concern that AI is fanning inflation because the buildout of AI infrastructure has sharply raised demand for computer chips, electronic components, electricity and copper. Smartphone prices rose last month at the fastest pace on record, the government said last week.

Warsh did not comment on what the Fed's next steps would be on interest rates. Many of Warsh's colleagues on the Fed's rate-setting committee signaled their support for additional interest rate hikes, including at the Fed's next meeting in December. Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson said Friday that if AI does accelerate economic growth, it could lead to higher interest rates over time, even if inflation declines. stories.Headline: AI infrastructure stocks plunge as investors reduce exposure before Nvidia reports results
stories.Summary:
AI infrastructure stocks faced a wave of selling on Monday, extending losses beyond chipmakers to companies supplying computing capacity and networking equipment. CoreWeave, Oracle, and Nebius all plunged as investors reduced their exposure to AI businesses before Nvidia reports quarterly results on Tuesday. CoreWeave and Nebius each lost 7 percent, while Oracle dropped 4 percent during the morning trading session on that Monday. Other affected companies included Iren and Applied Digital, which also traded lower as the broader AI sector experienced significant market weakness. This decline follows a period of turmoil for neoclouds fearing that debt fueled data center expansion could backfire if demand slows.

Nebius reported third quarter revenue of 980.8 million dollars, including 325.1 million dollars in non recurring strategic partnership payments that raised questions. The company disclosed a 40 billion dollar capital spending plan for 2027, which rattled investors sensitive to the pace of infrastructure buildout. Applied Digital maintains a 36.2 billion dollar lease book, with CoreWeave holding 11 billion dollars and a hyperscaler holding 20.2 billion dollars. Iren has a 3.4 billion dollar customer relationship with Nvidia, while CoreWeave bonds currently yield above 17 percent in the market. Marvell proposed an all stock purchase of Lumentum valued at approximately 115 billion dollars, though analysts question if the deal proceeds.

CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator told Reuters that greater scrutiny could slow data center construction, but he does not expect significantly altered plans. He stated there will be no impact to planned capacity additions over the next year and the company will avoid unsecured debt. Dan Sheehan of Telos Wealth Advisors said CoreWeave earnings addressed the fear that had driven the previous selloff in AI stocks. Bernstein analysts led by Madison Rezaei noted that CoreWeave delivered a great quarter and addressed funding concerns with strategic moves. Interim Nvidia CEO Colette Kress is scheduled to hold a meeting with employees on Wednesday following the departure of Jensen Huang.

Bank of America flagged that Nebius guidance implies a sequential revenue decline in the fourth quarter due to third party data center delays. SoftBank took a 3.7 billion dollar writedown on non refundable equipment payments, contributing to a second quarter net loss of 7 billion dollars. Republican Senator Kevin Cramer from the Senate Banking Committee called for Jensen Huang to step down as CEO amid a company crisis. Applied Digital CEO Wes Cummins stated the company must still finance approximately 800 MW of capacity over the coming 12 months. Investors in Nebius, Iren, Oracle, and Applied Digital previously cheered gains between 6 and 14 percent after CoreWeave reported strong growth.

Jensen Huang resigned as CEO following allegations of a relationship with a Chinese businesswoman who was alleged to be a spy for Beijing. This controversy escalated with allegations that the relationship aided multi billion dollar Nvidia chip shipments to China, causing the AI industry to reel. Democratic midterm sweep candidates campaigned for tighter regulation and moratoriums on new data center construction, specifically in the crucial market of Texas. Most AI infrastructure stocks lost 32 to 48 percent this year, although Nebius surged 60 percent before the recent market decline. U.S. producer prices rose 6.5 percent annually in October, marking the largest yearly increase in four years for the United States.

Nvidia is expected to pull back on AI investments and credit guarantees following the exit of Jensen Huang as the company CEO. Nebius was due to report results before the opening bell on Thursday, while Applied Digital reports fiscal second quarter earnings in January. The market is pricing in risks for Applied Digital, which trades under 5x forward sales compared to an 11x average multiple. Analysts warn that CoreWeave will be among the first and hardest hit when the crunch in AI computing capacity eventually eases. The articles leave open whether the Marvell purchase of Lumentum will proceed and how the Nvidia leadership transition will impact investments.

stories.Headline: Baidu head Robin Li warns that artificial intelligence could be a bubble
stories.Summary:
Robin Li, the chief executive of Baidu, warned that artificial intelligence could be a bubble on Tuesday, November 17, 2026. He spoke during a panel discussion with business leaders in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen. This event took place ahead of talks between the world's top two economies regarding the sensitive technology sector. The warning came while Shenzhen hosted the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meeting during that same week. Li expressed concern that the current global landscape for this technology has become an urgent situation.

Chinese President Xi Jinping is due to hold talks with U.S. counterpart Donald Trump on Thursday, November 19. These leaders are expected to discuss the risks posed by AI during the APEC meeting in Shenzhen. The situation involves Nvidia, a U.S. chip titan reporting quarterly results after former CEO Jensen Huang quit. Huang resigned last week following an affair scandal involving a suspected Chinese spy, which increased scrutiny of export rules. Nvidia has since rejected an offer from Jensen Huang to return as the chief executive of the company.

Robin Li stated that AI adoption is not boosting profits for most companies and has fallen short of expectations. He questioned if companies are seeing higher revenues or increased profits after adopting the technology at the foundational level. Li warned that the concern about an AI bubble could become a reality if these issues are not addressed. He acknowledged that Baidu faces headwinds in online marketing despite seeing tangible results in the company's AI strategy. The Beijing-based search engine provider posted a sixth straight drop in quarterly revenue on Monday, November 16, 2026.

IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva told AFP in October that losing confidence in AI returns could lead to worldwide financial stability risks. She noted that tanking stock market valuations could occur if investors lose faith in the future of these investments. The scandal involving Jensen Huang has heightened market jitters over the boom and how Chinese companies access powerful chips. These chips are used to train and run AI systems despite the existing export rules set by the U.S. government. Many business leaders are affected by the intense competition and the lack of profit growth in the application layer.

Baidu, which is sometimes called China's Google, has made an aggressive push into artificial intelligence in recent years. However, the company's challenges have grown as a domestic consumer slump drags on cash flows generated by advertising. The U.S. and China are currently pushing for AI safety steps despite their fierce rivalry in the field. There are growing calls for cooperation between the two tech powerhouses to manage the risks of the technology. The global investment boom is now under question as companies struggle to turn AI adoption into actual profit.

President Xi Jinping and Donald Trump will meet on Thursday to discuss the risks and cooperation regarding artificial intelligence. The world awaits the quarterly results from Nvidia to see the health of the global AI investment boom. The articles leave open whether the two leaders will reach an agreement on AI safety and cooperation. It remains unclear if other companies will find ways to increase revenues through the application of AI technology. The reports do not state if the domestic consumer slump in China will continue to affect Baidu's cash flows.

stories.Headline: Alibaba Cloud expands global data center network to meet AI demand
stories.Summary:
Alibaba Cloud plans to expand its global data center network over the next year to meet growing AI computing power demand. This expansion was outlined by Yuan Zhiming during the company's Hong Kong summit held on Tuesday, November 18, 2026. Meanwhile, Amazon withdrew plans for four data center buildings on its Ashburn campus following an agreement reached on October 20. Loudoun County supervisors will vote on November 17 to pause new legislative data center applications for up to twelve months. These separate corporate moves reflect the intense global competition and local regulatory challenges surrounding the rapid growth of AI infrastructure.

The Alibaba expansion prioritizes Hong Kong because its three leased data centers there can no longer meet the current market demand. Amazon's withdrawn Ashburn project involved over 800,000 square feet on a 122-acre campus purchased for around 427.3 million dollars. Under Project Potomac Promise, Amazon will convey 25 acres to the county and seek to rezone the rest for housing. Loudoun County hosts about 233 data center buildings, which generated 1.2 billion dollars in tax revenue for fiscal 2026. This revenue accounted for 39 percent of the budget, with fiscal 2027 projections estimating 1.3 billion dollars or 40 percent.

Yuan Zhiming, the vice president of international business, stated that financial firms are adopting AI into their core business workflows. Amazon's Josh Weissman said the company took pointed community concerns seriously and chose a shared vision over costly litigation. Board Chair Phyllis Randall noted that the Ashburn campus was the wrong location due to resident opposition and needed infrastructure. AWS CEO Matt Garman cautioned that over 100 data center moratoriums are currently being considered across the United States. Amazon CEO Andy Jassy stated that capacity constraints continue to yield unserved demand despite adding 3.9 gigawatts of power.

Residents and Loudoun County supervisors opposed the Ashburn development, leading Amazon to abandon the Bridgefield Tech Center site plan. Governor Abigail Spanberger believes the decision to approve or block data center projects should rest with the community, not the state. State Senator Russet Perry has drafted a three-year statewide moratorium on data center approvals to address these growing local concerns. Dominion Energy requires new data centers to post 1.5 million dollars per megawatt in collateral to protect residential customers. Oracle is also affected, having issued a force majeure notice regarding its 2.45 gigawatt Project Jupiter in New Mexico.

Loudoun County previously used a 2000 zoning ruling that allowed data centers to be built by right as office buildings. Since March 2025, new data centers have required a special exception approved by a board vote rather than administrative processes. Amazon purchased the Ashburn campus in March 2026 and filed its site plan for the tech center in July. AWS reported 46 billion dollars in third quarter sales and a backlog totaling 578 billion dollars in the same period. Amazon's leases not yet commenced rose to 164.9 billion dollars in the third quarter, up from 137.2 billion dollars.

Amazon plans to spend meaningfully more in 2027 than the roughly 220 billion dollars it has planned for 2026. AWS and Nvidia plan to deploy over 2 million more GPUs on AWS during 2027 and 2028 to increase capacity. The county's final vote on November 17 will determine if new rezoning requests are delayed for up to one year. It remains open whether the 17 grandfathered applications totaling 11 million square feet will proceed without any further legislative delays. The articles leave open the final outcome of the air-permit decision regarding Oracle's Project Jupiter in Doña Ana County.

stories.Headline: ECB vice president Boris Vujčić warns rapid AI expansion threatens EU financial stability
stories.Summary:
European Central Bank Vice President Boris Vujčić warned on Monday, November 16, 2026, that rapid artificial intelligence expansion could threaten financial stability. He spoke at Euro Finance Week in Frankfurt about how stretched stock market valuations for AI increase the risk of a repricing. Vujčić noted that a correction following America's mid-term elections serves as a reminder for the region to remain cautious. The bank also published research on November 18 regarding the stability implications of AI adoption in the real economy. This research found that reliance on a small number of AI providers could amplify risks across the entire financial system.

The research paper suggests that banks and asset managers use AI for portfolio management, fraud detection, and credit scoring. Eurostat data shows about 20 percent of European Union enterprises used AI in 2025, an increase of 6.5 percentage points. Adoption was higher in northern European countries than in the south and east, and higher in finance than in manufacturing. Anthropic's index on Claude.ai showed automation rose from 27 percent in January 2025 to 39 percent in August 2025. The ECB now requires better data on AI use, stronger oversight of providers, and changes to supervisory capabilities and safeguards.

Boris Vujčić stated that system-wide stability risks now stem from quickening AI adoption, concentration of exposures, and potential cyberattacks. He said that external funding is expanding from equity to debt markets, which adds to the current financial stability risks. Vujčić argued that it is critical to have a resilient banking sector while maintaining supervision over non-banks and private credit. He noted that private credit warrants close monitoring due to limited transparency, liquidity mismatches, and growing interconnectedness with insurers. The official believes that geopolitical headwinds further elevate the risks that the European Central Bank must currently manage.

The International Monetary Fund reported that AI can accelerate vulnerability discovery and exploitation across shared technologies to create correlated disruptions. This report suggests that AI cyber risk is now an enterprise governance issue for merchants, FinTechs, banks, and critical infrastructure operators. The IMF noted that the main question is how much autonomy systems should receive and if organizations can contain them. Other affected parties include companies in information technology and finance, which the ECB found have high exposure to AI risks. These institutions are vulnerable through their reliance on a concentrated group of cloud service providers and AI model providers.

The ECB research drew on emerging research, evidence from investment funds, and recent surveys of banks and various industries. The authors examined how financial firms are exposed to changes at other businesses that are adopting new AI technologies. US survey data indicated that professional services, finance, and information technology used AI more than the manufacturing sector did. The authors admitted that survey results were not directly comparable because the populations, questions, and definitions differed across sources. The research focused on how AI helps asset managers process information and how banks assess borrowers and detect activity.

The European Central Bank will continue monitoring the rapid growth of private credit and the concentration of AI model providers. Future efforts will focus on improving market safeguards to address emerging risks and increasing the oversight of critical AI providers. The articles leave open how exactly the ECB will implement these new supervisory capabilities to manage the identified systemic risks. They do not specify the exact timeline for the requested changes to data collection regarding AI use across the union. It remains unclear how the bank will balance AI autonomy with the need to contain systems when things fail.

stories.Headline: US Commerce Department restricts AI chip exports to data centers serving Chinese firms
stories.Summary:
The Bureau of Industry and Security issued new rules on November 16, 2026, to tighten controls on advanced semiconductors. These regulations restrict the export of AI chips and servers to Malaysia and limit large-scale cloud services to China. The U.S. Department of Commerce aims to close routes that Chinese companies used to obtain computing power through overseas data centers. This interim rule requires licenses for shipments of advanced AI chips to data centers anywhere in the world. Such licenses are necessary if the facilities provide large amounts of computing power to companies headquartered in China or restricted jurisdictions.

The new rules affect data center customers in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil who must now receive special licenses. One specific Malaysian project known as A201 expects to open next year with hundreds of millions of dollars in Nvidia servers. This facility was designed to provide computing power to a Chinese technology giant despite existing U.S. restrictions on direct exports. Cantor Fitzgerald served as a financing or placement agent for companies including Bitdeer Technologies Group and Gorilla Technology Group in Asia. These specific Asian data center operations could be affected by the tighter American export controls issued by the Commerce Department.

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick resisted efforts by other senior administration officials to strengthen restrictions on Nvidia chip shipments to Asia. The Commerce Department defended its enforcement record and denied directing officials to avoid investigating particular companies regarding chip exports. Officials maintained that Lutnick fully divested his financial interests in Cantor and had no discussions with the firm concerning Nvidia. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent publicly criticized the failure to blacklist Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company suspected of helping China. Bessent argued the administration already has the tools to limit sales to China and should focus on enforcement.

Democratic Senators Elizabeth Warren and Ron Wyden demanded information about a loan from Tether to a trust benefiting Lutnick's children. This loan was reportedly secured by assets including more than half of the equity in the firm Cantor Fitzgerald. Republican lawmakers also questioned whether U.S. technology is reaching Chinese interests, while Democrats demanded stronger enforcement of chip rules. Companies in China and other countries are affected because they can no longer easily evade restrictions through long-standing loopholes. The White House has expressed confidence in Lutnick despite the mounting questions over the decisions made by his department.

Lutnick led Cantor Fitzgerald for more than three decades before joining the administration of President Donald Trump as Commerce Secretary. His sons, Brandon and Kyle, now lead the investment firm that worked with companies developing data centers in Southeast Asia. In July 2025, reports indicated Cantor offered to purchase potential tariff-refund claims for 20 to 30 percent of their value. This occurred while Lutnick was one of the most outspoken advocates for tariffs within the current U.S. administration. Additionally, the Commerce Department approved Nvidia export licenses involving Chinese companies with links to military contractors or sanctioned entities.

Lawmakers are intensifying scrutiny of how the Commerce Department handles chip exports amid the controversy involving former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. The department faced questions over recent months about why the Entity List had not been updated for over a year. Future actions remain open regarding whether the government will blacklist more companies like Megaspeed to prevent technology diversion. It is unclear if the new licensing requirements will successfully stop Chinese firms from accessing advanced computing power abroad. The articles leave open whether the conflict of interest allegations will lead to further official investigations into Howard Lutnick.

stories.Headline: Bharat Semi raises $24 million to develop AI enabled image sensors
stories.Summary:
Delhi-based semiconductor startup Bharat Semi has raised $24 million, or ₹215 crore, in seed funding to develop AI-enabled image sensors. The all-equity round was led by Info Edge Group, South Park Commons and Indus Bridge Ventures. Valour Capital, Micromax, Gaingels and individual investors also participated in the round. The company announced the funding on 16 November 2026, with the story published by Analytics India Magazine and Inc42. Bharat Semi plans to use the capital to expand its engineering team and prepare its sensors for commercial production.

The funding will support product development and expansion as the company targets customers in the US and other global markets. Bharat Semi expects to begin initial commercial production in 2027. The startup has secured design wins with US defence technology company General Atomics and India's Kaynes Semicon, a subsidiary of US-based Kaynes Technology. Its image sensors remain under development. The company currently employs around 75 people across India and the US, including engineering and business development teams in Santa Clara, California.

Co-founder Vrinda Kapoor told TechCrunch the architecture could reduce system costs by at least 70% compared with conventional systems. Bharat Semi is developing programmable image sensors that combine image capture, processing and AI capabilities on one chip, eliminating the need for separate processing components. Kapoor said the company's separate semiconductor fabrication project in India, announced in 2024 with a technology partnership with the US Space Force, remains under development. She said the latest funding will not finance the proposed fabrication facility. The company plans to follow a fabless model for its image-sensor business, outsourcing chip manufacturing while focusing on semiconductor design and software.

According to the startup, its programmable smart sensors reduce data movement between components by up to 99% and lower system costs by up to 10X compared with conventional multi-chip modules. The technology is designed to enable machines to interpret information and respond to their surroundings in real time without relying entirely on remote computing infrastructure. Bharat Semi is initially targeting the consumer electronics and surveillance markets, where cost, power consumption and latency are key considerations. Over the longer term, it plans to extend its technology to robotics, automotive, aerospace and defence applications. The startup is yet to commercialise its technology.

Expected use cases include controlling ceiling fan movement based on visual capture of a sleeping subject and sharing alerts from door cameras when a person or parcel has arrived. The technology could also signal to drones about obstructions in their flight path in real time without sending data elsewhere. Bharat Semi is eyeing a share of the global image sensor market, expected to reach $49.8 billion by 2030, growing at a CAGR of 7.7%. The global AI sensor market is expected to grow at a CAGR of 48.8% to reach $139.4 billion by 2033, according to Grand View Research. Bharat Semi will take on established players such as Japan's Sony Semiconductor Solutions and US-based OmniVision, alongside emerging startups such as Oculi and France-based Prophesee.

Bharat Semi was founded in 2021 by Vrinda Kapoor and Vinayak Dalmia. The company's first-generation sensors are already in prototyping, while its second-generation sensors will incorporate more advanced AI capabilities. Bharat Semi expects these prototypes to reach development milestones by mid-2027 and plans to get the newer sensors to customers by the end of 2027. The company plans to increase its US workforce to around 20 employees by mid-2027 and has started hiring engineers in Europe. The funding comes amid India's efforts to establish a domestic semiconductor industry, following the launch of the India Semiconductor Mission 2.0 earlier this year with a budget outlay of ₹1,27,500 crore.

stories.Headline: BBVA researchers train transformer models on app navigation data to personalize banking
stories.Summary:
BBVA's AI researchers developed a model that interprets how customers interact with the bank's mobile app, providing a deeper understanding of their needs and paving the way for more personalized and proactive banking. The research was presented at ICAIF, a leading conference on AI applied to finance. The paper was presented on November 15 in Milan at the ACM International Conference on AI in Finance. Asier González-Rodríguez is one of the paper's authors. The paper was presented at a pioneering event held as part of the conference, dedicated to research into foundation and multimodal models for the banking sector.

The research analyzed approximately 1.6 billion navigation sessions from eight million customers, covering one year of activity, using anonymized data. Of these, 90 million sessions were selected to train the new models. BBVA began exploring the use of embeddings in 2018. In 2023, this research focused on navigation data from the bank's app, transforming sequences of screens visited by customers into anonymized vector representations. The approach used until now was based on Word2Vec.

Researchers explored the use of Transformers, a deep learning architecture that makes it possible to analyze sequences and identify relationships between their elements, and which underpins large language models. Each screen visited in the app is treated as a token, the basic unit of data that AI models read and generate, while the sequence of screens viewed during a session functions much like a sentence. Through self-supervised learning, the model learns to recognize navigation patterns directly from activity logs, without the need to manually label each sequence. Researchers developed a hierarchical tokenization system that groups related screens and makes it possible to interpret new features based on existing categories, avoiding the need to rebuild the system whenever the app changes. A decoder architecture was ultimately selected, which learns to predict the next screens in a sequence and combines contextual information from the entire navigation journey to generate a compact, reusable representation.

The AUC metric increased by 2.7% in relative terms compared with the baseline model, also outperforming the result achieved with Word2Vec. The solution is integrated into a process that serves approximately eight million active users and processes four million sessions per day. BBVA is already taking the first steps towards developing a multi-source foundation model capable of integrating different dimensions and providing a foundation for building multiple AI applications. The models developed so far focus on one specific dimension of customer behavior: digital navigation. Much of a person's relationship with their bank is also reflected in other sources of information, ranging from transactions and account activity to interactions with relationship managers, phone calls and branch visits.

Physicist Nathaniel Craig, a visiting scientist at OpenAI, worked with GPT-6 Astra on a candidate lattice definition of the Standard Model. Craig leads the particle theory group at the University of California, Santa Barbara, and is a permanent member of its Kavli Institute for Theoretical Physics. In an October preprint prepared with the aid of GPT-6 Astra, Craig proposed a candidate definition on a lattice, a grid representing spacetime. Astra helped turn Craig's strategy into a construction and took the lead in developing the detailed proof. The Standard Model describes the known elementary particles and three of the four fundamental forces, the strong force, the weak force, and electromagnetism.

The success of the theory rests on outstanding agreement between theoretical calculations and experiments across eighteen orders of magnitude, from the low energies of hydrogen's 21-centimeter radio emission to the high energies of collisions at the Large Hadron Collider. For the full Standard Model in continuous spacetime, we don't have a nonperturbative definition, or even an understanding of whether the interacting theory is mathematically well defined. Lattice field theory has led to remarkable progress in our understanding of the strong force over the last few decades, including a quantitative understanding of the mass of the proton from first principles. The weak force treats left- and right-handed fermions differently, and so does not look the same under mirror reflections that exchange left and right. If we try to put a left-handed fermion on the lattice, the most natural rules give you a right-handed partner you never asked for.

The research presented at ICAIF represents another step towards realizing BBVA's ambition of a multi-source foundation model. The goal is to move towards an intelligent, comprehensive and unified understanding of customers, providing a foundation for deploying AI models and agents across different use cases. BBVA is building a foundation for a new generation of AI models that can contribute to a deeper understanding of customers' needs and expectations. Craig's October preprint proposed a candidate lattice definition of the Standard Model. The articles leave open what comes next for both the foundation model and the lattice definition.

stories.Headline: Altimeter Capital aims to invest 5 billion dollars in Anthropic's upcoming IPO
stories.Summary:
Anthropic is planning to go public on the Nasdaq index this coming Thursday, November 19, in a major industry event. Brad Gerstner of Altimeter Capital told CNBC on Monday that his firm aims to invest 5 billion dollars. This specific investment is five times larger than any amount Gerstner has ever put into an initial public offering. Anthropic will be the first major artificial intelligence lab to go public, beating OpenAI's target for next year. The company is offering 825 million shares at a total valuation of about 1.4 trillion dollars.

The indicative price range for the shares is currently expected to be between 70 and 78 dollars per share. Leading chipmakers and cloud providers are collectively investing 26 billion dollars, including Google, Microsoft, Nvidia, and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. Other investing firms include Advanced Micro Devices, Broadcom, and Micron, many of which already count on Anthropic as a customer. The final price for the shares will be set after the market closes on Wednesday, November 18, 2026. This milestone occurs during a downturn in semiconductors and a massive anti-AI swing in Washington.

Brad Gerstner said he is optimistic because the company is in an excellent position regarding its financials. He described the company as a cornerstone compounder for a long time and noted that this is where the trade is going. Gerstner expressed confidence in Colette Kress, who is currently serving as the CFO and interim CEO of the company. He sent a letter to the board of directors last week pushing for a full investigation into Jensen Huang. Gerstner noted that Huang had not discussed a potential comeback as CEO with him during their recent interactions.

Some experts believe a successful offering would reinforce confidence in the continuity of the artificial intelligence investment cycle. Other analysts warn that the real question is what kind of company the market is actually valuing. The situation affects Nvidia, where the board is not considering bringing back Jensen Huang as the company CEO. President Donald Trump said he would not mind if Huang was reinstated and questioned if Alice Huang was a spy. A petition for Huang's return has gained over 180,000 signatures, though the board remains focused on national security.

The background includes a scandal where Jensen Huang allegedly had an affair with a direct subordinate and alleged Chinese spy. This situation led to Huang stepping down, while the board now focuses on a national security investigation into him. Nvidia's revenue was driven by China for more than 20 percent of its total last year, adding further complexity. The market has seen turmoil, with Bitcoin holding near 65,000 dollars as the Nasdaq dropped 2.5 percent recently. Howard Lutnick's old fund reportedly cut its holdings of Nvidia by over 40 percent during the last quarter.

The company will officially list on the Nasdaq this Thursday to begin its life as a public entity. Investors will wait to see if the final share price stays within the 70 to 78 dollar range. The articles leave open whether the board will ever reconsider Jensen Huang for the role of CEO at Nvidia. It remains unclear if the national security investigation into Huang will lead to further legal actions or congressional testimony. The market is waiting to see if Anthropic's valuation of 1.4 trillion dollars will be sustained after the IPO.

stories.Headline: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns amid investigations into alleged ties to a Chinese spy
stories.Summary:
Nvidia founder Jensen Huang was forced to resign as CEO during a huge week for the company. The board began probing allegations that Huang had a relationship with a Chinese businesswoman suspected of spying. U.S. intelligence officials and Congress are also investigating these claims regarding the former chief executive. Nvidia will report its fiscal 2027 third-quarter earnings after the market closes on November 17. Interim CEO Colette Kress, the chief financial officer for over a decade, will lead the report.

The report will address revenue, sales acceleration, and guidance for the short and long term. Nvidia projected third-quarter revenue of 108 billion dollars, an 89 percent gain over 57.1 billion last year. Second-quarter revenue was 96.2 billion dollars, while the data center segment brought in 89 billion dollars. Investors want to know if demand for the next-generation Vera Rubin platform is progressing as expected. The outlook for the fourth quarter will determine if demand is accelerating or beginning to moderate.

Colette Kress and other executives will likely face questions about Jensen Huang and the company investigation. Analysts from The Motley Fool state that the current R&D phase is only the first act. They believe the second act, which is the global rollout, could be sixteen times bigger. The Motley Fool Stock Advisor team identified ten best stocks to buy, but Nvidia was not included. This team reports a total average return of 823 percent compared to 208 percent for the S&P 500.

Investors in AI power stocks are affected because these companies supply electricity and natural gas to data centers. Constellation Energy has a 690-megawatt deal with Amazon and an 890-megawatt deal with Alphabet for nuclear capacity. Bloom Energy reported third-quarter revenue of 1.24 billion dollars and raised full-year guidance to 4.4 to 4.6 billion. Energy Transfer recently announced agreements to transport natural gas to power plants currently under construction in Missouri. These energy companies could have good weeks if Nvidia demonstrates that AI spending remains at high levels.

Berkshire Hathaway ended September with roughly 377.4 billion dollars in cash and Treasury bills for future investments. CEO Greg Abel has expanded investments in Alphabet, signaling that some technology companies fit the portfolio criteria. ASML is the only commercial manufacturer of extreme ultraviolet lithography machines used by Intel, Samsung, and TSMC. ASML generated 11.7 billion euros in third-quarter revenue and 5 billion euros in net income. Management guided for full-year revenue between 44 billion and 45 billion euros with a 56 percent margin.

Markets reopen on November 18, which could be a huge day for AI power stocks if results are strong. Anthropic will hold its initial public offering on November 19, where investors will learn three key details. ASML has disclosed that some customers are already expressing interest in equipment deliveries for 2029 and 2030. The articles leave open whether Berkshire Hathaway will use its cash to buy ASML as its next stock. stories.Headline: Tax exam top scorer Han admits to using generative AI to cheat and turns himself in to Seoul police
stories.Summary:
The top scorer on South Korea's 2026 national tax accountant qualification exam turned himself in to police on Sunday and admitted to using generative AI to cheat, The Korea Herald and Korea JoongAng Daily reported. A 34-year-old man surnamed Han posted his results on Wednesday, boasting of a score of 397.5 out of 400 on the first stage of the exam. Han said in a YouTube video posted by his law firm on Sunday that he cheated on the first and second rounds using electronic devices and generative AI. He said he took photos of exam questions with a micro camera, sent them to AI and checked the answers on a smartphone. The Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency, which received Han's written confession, assigned the case to its public crime investigation team.

Han earned 97.5 in public finance on the first round and a perfect 100 in introduction to tax law, introduction to accounting and commercial law, missing just one of the 160 questions across the four subjects. In the tax law section, the 16,856 test takers averaged 30.18, and no one else broke 90. Article 314 of the Criminal Act states that anyone who obstructs another's business by deception or force faces up to five years in prison or a fine of up to 15 million won, or $11,300. The Human Resources Development Service of Korea, which administers the exam, said it decided to file a complaint against Han for obstruction of business and to proceed with revoking his score. The service added it would consider bringing in proctors dedicated to checking for AI devices and introducing radio frequency detectors.

Ha Joon-kyung, the presidential director of national policy, convened an emergency meeting on Sunday, where officials agreed to look into every case flagged so far. Ha said the Ministry of Education and other relevant agencies must closely examine every possibility to ensure that no cheating using AI takes place. Han said in his video that he cheated on the first and second rounds of the tax accountant exam using electronic devices and generative AI. His lawyer withheld details such as how the equipment was brought into the exam room and used, citing concerns that similar cheating could occur. The Korean Association of Certified Public Tax Accountants said it would launch a new evaluation system during practical training for apprentice tax accountants to screen out those who passed by cheating.

One tax accountant exam candidate said that since the fairness of the exam has collapsed, a retest should be held. A test taker in their 20s surnamed Lee, preparing for the grade-seven national civil service exam, said some cases were caught this time but asked how many more went undetected. A test taker in their 20s surnamed Park, preparing for the grade-five civil service exam, said national certification exams vouch for an individual's ability on their behalf, so failing to catch cheating is the responsibility of the organizing body. Park also said there may be even more people who use AI but adjust their accuracy rate appropriately and do not reveal themselves. An industry official said companies were already struggling with AI-related hacking threats, and tiny wearables like smart glasses add to their security worries.

Affiliates of Samsung, SK, Hyundai Motor and LG, along with shipbuilders and defense contractors, said that as of Tuesday they restrict smart glasses or require prior approval to bring them onto their premises. Samsung Electronics generally prohibits on-site photography with smart devices and requires camera-blocking stickers on smart glasses brought onto its premises. SK hynix bars smart glasses and reminded employees Monday to leave them in lockers before entering company buildings and to report anyone using similar devices inside. Hyundai Motor has required visitors to its Seoul headquarters to declare smart glasses and other AI wearables and get approval before bringing them in since June. LG Group bars unauthorized smart devices and requires cameras to be covered on smart glasses that cannot run its security software.

The National Police Agency's National Office of Investigation recorded 179 technology leak cases last year and apprehended 378 people, with semiconductors accounting for five overseas leak cases, the most of any sector. South Korea protects key semiconductor manufacturing processes under laws governing national core technologies and national advanced strategic technologies. Six cases of cheating with AI smart glasses were caught on national qualification exams held through October, including those for fire protection facilities engineers, information processing engineers, industrial electrical engineers and gas craftsmen. Cases were also caught on the financial investment analyst exam and the Legal Education Eligibility Test, and three Test of English for International Communication takers and one Test of English Proficiency developed by Seoul National University taker were caught using AI to cheat. The Education Ministry announced a plan last month to respond to cheating with smart glasses on the CSAT, listing AI smart glasses as banned items.

Test takers caught wearing them will have that year's exam voided and be barred from taking the test the following year. Radio frequency detectors, which pick up wireless signals from devices such as smart glasses, hidden cameras and earpieces, are not expected to be deployed at test sites until next year's CSAT. The Korea Radio Promotion Association is still developing the detectors, and they can be introduced only after field testing, while a revision to enforcement rules explicitly banning smart glasses is also expected to come next year. The Human Resources Development Service of Korea formed a task force in August to strengthen its response to AI-assisted cheating and created AI inspectors to detect smart glasses at test sites, but only 327 inspectors were deployed across two exams. Samsung Electronics said its upcoming glasses will feature an external LED that lights up when in photo or video mode and the camera will be disabled if the light is blocked or malfunctions, and Meta said its models sold in South Korea rely on spoken commands and audible replies, making them unlikely to be used for cheating.

stories.Headline: FIOR completes NCSC-assessed cyber resilience evaluation of its AI Gateway version 26.2
stories.Summary:
FIOR, a UK-based AI security company, completed an independent cyber resilience assessment of its AI Gateway, a product that identifies AI agents, controls their permissions and blocks unauthorized actions before they execute. NCC Group evaluated 72 security claims under the UK National Cyber Security Centre's Principles Based Assurance methodology, according to FIOR. The published report identifies no unmet claims and one area of doubt concerning accessibility. The assessment, announced Nov. 16, covers AI Gateway version 26.2 and gives enterprise and government buyers an independent reference point for judging the security of a product built to govern autonomous agents. FIOR's CEO and CTO both said it is the first AI identity and enforcement platform to publicly complete an NCSC CRTF assessment.

The report, dated Nov. 9, records no unmet claims and no assumptions, and its single doubt concerns accessibility, with assessors not satisfied that FIOR had shown people with disabilities can securely install, use and maintain the product. Assessors recommend completing accessibility testing against the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG). The findings apply only to version 26.2, and later releases require reassessment. Version 26.2, released Nov. 12, adds expanded discovery, model and tool catalogs, threat intelligence and identity integrations. The assessment report documents outbound HTTPS connections to a FIOR-hosted control plane but does not specify what data those connections transmit.

Founder and CEO David Williams said the company had already made its first commercial deployments and sought the assessment to give government and enterprise customers an objective basis for evaluating the product, a process he said took under six months. Williams said many companies have told FIOR they cannot exploit the benefits of AI until they are confident that the controls governing those agents are based on an identity that is secure. FIOR argued that inventories, written policies and after-the-fact monitoring cannot stop an unauthorized action in real time. FIOR positions the gateway as an independent enforcement layer between agents and the enterprise systems they access, checking identity and authorization before anything executes. FIOR said all processing happens inside the enterprise boundary, no information leaves the enterprise and no data is sent to an identity provider.

The assessment comes two weeks after the NCSC warned that UK critical national infrastructure should prepare for a ransomware attack using AI-powered malware by 2028. In its State of the Cyber Nation report, released Nov. 3, the agency said hostile actors' use of AI is highly likely to increase the scale and efficiency of ransomware, social engineering and vulnerability exploitation within two years. NCSC CEO Richard Horne said the rise in incidents is not because AI has invented new attacks, but because weaknesses organizations have tolerated for years can now be found and exploited at scale. In August, the NCSC issued interim guidance on agentic AI after several incidents in which AI systems carried out unsanctioned or unintended actions. Joint guidance the NCSC issued in May with cybersecurity agencies from the U.S., Australia, Canada and New Zealand called for continuous runtime authentication with a central policy decision point for every agent action.

The NCSC's Cyber Resilience Testing program helps buyers judge how well connected products protect themselves against common cyberattacks, and its Principles Based Assurance methodology examines how a product is designed, built, deployed and maintained. Assessments are run by NCSC-assured Cyber Resilience Test Facilities (CRTFs), not by the NCSC itself, and NCC Group is one of them. A CRTF assessment is not a certification, and products that complete one may carry the label "NCSC CRTF ,  Cyber Resilience Assessed." The process tests whether a product can protect itself, not whether every advertised security function works as intended or stops every form of malicious agent behavior. FIOR's assessment spanned secure development, the build environment, distribution and vulnerability management, support and maintenance, and usability, data protection and logging.

At a Nov. 11 World Bank webinar, ITU-T Study Group 17 Chair Arnaud Taddei said agents already act with no verifiable identity and no proof of authority. In July, SG17 launched the Focus Group on Trust and Identity for Humans and Agentic AI (FG-TIDA), backed by 54 governments and 48 companies. The group meets next in Paris November 30 to December 1, with registration closing November 20, and participation is free and needs only an ITU account, not membership. World Bank senior digital specialist Marie Eichholtzer said confirming that a specific action falls within an agent's authority remains "to be built." The government's Digital Standards Strategy 2026, 2030 aims to strengthen UK influence in global standards bodies while identity, biometric and AI frameworks are still being set.

stories.Headline: Fractal Analytics talks to 20 to 25 AI startups about acquisitions, CEO says
stories.Summary:
Fractal Analytics, an enterprise AI firm, is actively talking to 20 to 25 startups to potentially acquire them, its group CEO Srikanth Velamakanni told Reuters, as reported on November 16, 2026. The company is India's first publicly listed pure-play AI company and helps clients including Citibank and Nestle make business decisions using data analytics and AI. Fractal reported profit of 812 million rupees, or $8.63 million, and revenue of 9.57 billion rupees for the quarter ended September 30. Earlier in November, it acquired Geneva-based analytics firm PricingOne via a subsidiary, Asper, for 1.32 million Swiss francs, or $1.57 million. Velamakanni described that transaction as an acqui-hire, which would also give Asper.ai a foothold in Europe.

The company does not have a target but is open to acquisitions of up to 10 billion rupees, or up to ₹1,000 Cr, Velamakanni said. There is no lower floor for acquisitions, and Velamakanni said the sweet spot is between $50 million and $100 million for what the firm would spend. Fractal evaluated about 800 targets over the last 12 months and reported cash and cash equivalents of ₹1,728 Cr as of September 30, 2026. The firm is evaluating startups in healthcare, as well as agentic AI and AI engineering companies, to access good engineering talent and harness relationships that the target startups have with large cloud computing firms and frontier labs. Fractal is evaluating businesses with deep AI engineering talent, strong local presence across geographies and specialised expertise in industrial verticals.

Velamakanni said acquisitions and partnerships are a major vehicle of growth for Fractal. He said AI is getting better at doing longer-horizon tasks and solving more complex problems, and the cost of using it is continuously dropping, spurring greater demand for enterprise AI solutions. He said the cost of what he termed "fixed intelligence" has declined 48% quarter-on-quarter, and at that rate the cost of intelligence from a foundation model could fall 93% over a year. He said the upcoming IPO of frontier AI model company Anthropic will be a major tailwind for AI companies, including Fractal, if it succeeds, but warned that there were structural risks with the level of debt that US companies have taken on to build out AI infrastructure. He said the structural risk the US economy has is that it is very much driven by AI growth today, but that does not mean the need for AI will come down or that companies are not going to spend on AI.

Nearly half of all M&A deals in the last two fiscal years among Indian IT and tech companies involved AI and allied technologies, with most acquisitions being used to find specialised talent and access clients faster, according to research from Indian ratings agency Crisil Ratings. Velamakanni said acquisitions would not be treated merely as a growth lever and must improve Fractal's "right to win" by materially increasing its chances of securing future business. He said the company is looking for deals that can create a multiplier effect on its growth potential rather than simply adding the acquired business to its existing operations. He said Fractal has a healthy M&A pipeline and that its board is keen to explore the opportunity, and he added that the company has sufficient cash to pursue deals and expects to announce more transactions soon. He expects enterprise AI to scale significantly over the next year as foundation models become more capable and cheaper to run, with the impact becoming meaningful as early as FY28, and he added that this shift should also reflect in metrics such as Fractal's revenue per employee.

Founded in 2000, Fractal provides AI and advanced analytics solutions to enterprises including Google, Citibank, Nestlé and Wells Fargo, and it also earns revenue through licensing and subscriptions for its AI platforms including Cogentiq, Iqigai and Kalaido.ai. In April, the company reorganised its business around three pillars: AI-led Transformation, AI Foundations, and AI Work & Workforce, and its agentic AI platform Cogentiq is positioned as the common technology layer across the three divisions. As part of the restructuring, Fractal announced a leadership reshuffle in May, appointing Kunal Jain as head of AI workforce transformation and Suraj Amonkar as chief AI research officer, while Matthew Gennone was given additional responsibility as chief commercial officer and CEO of Cogentiq. Fractal reported record revenue from operations of ₹956.5 Cr in Q2 FY27, up nearly 20% from ₹798.5 Cr in the year-ago quarter, and revenue also grew 4.8% sequentially from ₹912.5 Cr in Q1 FY27. Its net profit more than doubled 139% YoY to ₹79.2 Cr, compared with ₹33.2 Cr in Q2 FY26, though profit declined sequentially from ₹115.8 Cr in Q1 FY27.

Adjusted EBITDA rose 30% YoY to ₹154.9 Cr during the quarter, while the adjusted EBITDA margin improved 123 basis points to 16.2%, which the company attributed to operating leverage while noting that investments in AI engineering talent had a short-term impact on gross margins. Among its business verticals, healthcare and life sciences recorded the highest revenue growth of 79% YoY in Q2 FY27, revenue from banking, financial services and insurance grew 30%, and consumer packaged goods and retail, its largest vertical, reported 19% growth, while revenue from telecom, media and technology clients declined 18% during the quarter. The company made its stock market debut earlier this year, listing at ₹876 on the NSE, a 2.7% discount to its IPO price of ₹900, and on the BSE its shares listed at the issue price of ₹900. Shares of Fractal ended today's trading session 3.41% lower at ₹802.80 apiece on the BSE. Inc42 said it has reached out to the company and that the story will be updated on receiving a response.

stories.Headline: Portland council president Jamie Dunphy proposes temporary moratorium on city AI procurement
stories.Summary:
On November 17, 2026, Council President Jamie Dunphy proposed a temporary moratorium on the City government's procurement and implementation of artificial intelligence. The proposal would pause new contracts and limit the expansion of AI use in City operations. Portland City Council will hear the proposal on December 2, according to Portland.gov. KOIN reported that Dunphy proposed the moratorium on Tuesday, November 17, 2026. The proposal asks for a pause on new contracts and AI expansion so the city can properly evaluate the technology.

The ordinance adds a new Chapter 34.20 to Portland City Code. The City may not procure or implement AI-enabled technologies by any means, including trades or giveaways. Existing software uses are limited to minimal-risk uses only, and AI contracts already in effect may continue through their current term but may not be renewed, extended, or amended to add AI functionality without a Council exemption by ordinance. New AI pilot projects must meet strict criteria for safety and public benefit, and the City must produce a citywide inventory of AI in use, approved or pending approval as a pilot, or under contract within 60 days of adoption, kept updated.

Dunphy said emergent AI technology carries substantial risks to both the public and the City, so the City cannot go full steam ahead without proper policy guardrails in City Code. He said his goal is to protect public privacy, security, and civil rights while the administration makes the City's Data and Privacy Office fully operable and adopts comprehensive legislative guidelines. He said government is not beholden to profit-driven shareholders and must move more intentionally to serve the public interest. He said considering impacts on real people is not being slow but taking time for critical thinking. He said his staff spent the last calendar year trying to get more information on the structural thinking behind the current internal process and found the guardrails and access to those guidelines unsatisfactory given the stakes and community members' vulnerability to data leaks.

Megan Notarte, co-founder of AI Portland, told KOIN 6 News that Seattle has a responsible AI use policy and that she would look at what Seattle is doing for a more educated view. She said there are probably ways of moving forward that maybe are not a moratorium for the year. The City's 7,500 employees include 800 represented by the City of Portland Professional Workers, who began a strike Nov. 9. Portland is a Sanctuary City. Cybersecurity and essential City functions are not impacted, and exceptions protect necessary software with embedded AI, like spellcheck and mail sorting, leaving staff free to defend City systems against cybersecurity threats.

The City established a Data and Privacy Office, led by a Citywide Data Officer, through Ordinance 192143 on March 7, 2026, and that office is not yet operable and cannot review technology contracts. Dunphy cited several cases where the City piloted risky AI models without first establishing rigorous safety testing or clear accuracy metrics. A recent WIRED article quotes Yoshua Bengio, a computer science professor at the Université de Montréal considered a godfather of modern AI, saying pauses are our best bets to avoid the most catastrophic things and that it takes time for democracy to adapt. Governor Kotek signed Executive Order 26-26, Establishing Responsible Artificial Intelligence Procurement Standards for State Government, and Dunphy said the City's pause aligns with the Governor's leadership. Dunphy said AI is increasingly embedded in software and services sold to the government, including tools that generate content, analyze personal data, and support or automate decisions affecting the public.

The ordinance will be heard at the City Council meeting on Thursday, December 3, 2026, and Dunphy encourages public feedback and engagement before the meeting. The full text of the ordinance is available on the Council website, where people can also sign up to submit written or verbal testimony. Portland residents can submit written or verbal testimony regarding the City's approach to AI on their website. Contact is Madeline West, Chief of Staff, Councilor Dunphy, at Madeline.West@portlandoregon.gov. The articles do not say what the Council will decide or when the moratorium would end.

stories.Headline: Banned Nvidia AI chips appear at a Shanghai data center linked to Alice Huang
stories.Summary:
Banned Nvidia AI chips were installed at a Shanghai data center linked to Alice Huang, according to reports from Bloomberg News on Friday. These restricted servers were placed in a facility connected to Megaspeed, a Singapore Nvidia cloud partner where Alice Huang previously worked. Documents filed with Chinese authorities show that a subsidiary of Shanghai Longteng pledged these servers as loan collateral in January 2025. The hardware included 22 Dell servers with H800 chips and 52 Super Micro systems with H100 and H200 chips. These specific Nvidia chip models require US export licenses for sale in China, but the US barred H800 exports since 2023.

The pledged hardware consisted of 193 servers totaling 485 million yuan, or 73 million dollars, including 119 Gigabyte Technology servers with unidentified chips. Alice Huang founded Shanghai Longteng in 2015 but sold her shares in 2017 to Huang Yu, the majority owner through January 2026. The data center president is Kang Wei, a business associate of Alice Huang and senior executive at the funding firm Shanghai Hexi. Some servers were first sold to Aperia Cloud Services, a Singapore Nvidia Cloud Partner, before they reached the Shanghai company. Dell halted all sales and support to Aperia International in February 2025 due to concerns about the smuggling of chips.

Megaspeed denied illegally diverting Nvidia chips to China, while Aperia denied wrongdoing and did not answer questions about Alice Huang or hardware. Jensen Huang stated in May 2025 that there was no evidence of chip diversion, but he resigned as chief executive on November 12. Interim CEO Colette Kress now leads the company after the board stated no company secrets or US national security were compromised. Nvidia declined to comment on whether a change in its Singapore revenue reporting related to the addition of Megaspeed to a block list. Super Micro stated its servers were sold lawfully under US export control rules and that it is not affiliated with the facility.

US authorities suspect Alice Huang of having intelligence ties to Beijing, and Singapore prosecutors charged five people in the Aperia case. Aperia's chief executive was arrested in February 2025 on charges of cheating server suppliers, though he has pleaded not guilty to these. Companies linked to Alice Huang invested in the Chinese AI developer DeepSeek, and her network was tied to a Huawei Cloud center. The Information reported that Jensen Huang's ties to Alice Huang enabled more than 7 billion dollars of chip sales to China. Jensen Huang's disclosure of an extramarital affair with Alice Huang is what pushed him out of his role at Nvidia.

Nvidia reported 10.16 billion dollars of revenue billed to Singapore for the quarter ended July 27, 2025, which was 22 percent of total. This filing stated that over 99 percent of controlled data center compute revenue billed to Singapore came from orders by US based customers. For the quarter ended October 26, 2025, Nvidia stopped breaking out Singapore revenue and reported by the location of customers' headquarters instead. This change occurred around the time Nvidia added Megaspeed to an internal block list in mid 2025, according to The Wall Street Journal. Professor Shiva Rajgopal noted the timing of this reporting change is curious, though public information cannot show what drove the decision.

Megaspeed has hired a US law firm as the scandal broadens, according to a report from Politico on November 12, 2026. There has been no public finding that Jensen Huang broke export control laws during his time as the chief executive of Nvidia. It remains unestablished whether Alice Huang had a personal role in buying the servers since she sold her company shares in 2017.
