stories.Headline: Librarian Lacey Anderson tests ChatGPT as a gardening guide and finds harvest predictions off by weeks
stories.Summary:
Lacey Anderson, director of the East Grand Forks Campbell Library, tested whether ChatGPT could guide a novice gardener to harvest at the GRO.UND Learning Garden along Stanford Street in Grand Forks, North Dakota. She described the experiment in a session of UND’s AI Forum Series, reported by blogs.und.edu on November 17, 2026. Anderson picked 50 of the garden’s 90 planted varieties of flowers and produce to deliver harvestable roots, fruits and vegetables through summer and fall. She turned to ChatGPT to write a prompt, a process that took around five months of periodic iteration and refinement. The final prompt ran more than 900 words, and Anderson presented a shortened version during her talk.

The prompt asked for harvest dates for crops in a Grand Forks, N.D. garden, using specific crop harvest data based on planting dates, plus advice on readiness, harvesting and storing. Anderson gave ChatGPT very specific climate data for Grand Forks and historical crop data along with the kinds of crops used. She kept detailed records through the growing season even as many volunteers and groups came and went, between hurried notes on her phone and pen-and-paper observations. The predictions ranged from 69 days too early to 33 days late compared with the real-world garden. On average, crops were harvested around 17 days later than AI predicted.

Anderson said there was a significant difference between when AI said things would be ready and when they actually were able to harvest them. She said that when you think of how AI is used in a classroom, students will say here is a beautiful paper I wrote, and on the surface level you can fake a lot of stuff. She said it says the right words and can format beautifully, but when you translate that to a garden, you can’t fake whether an eggplant is ready to eat. She said AI doesn’t predict heavy smoke cover, a filter to certain light reaching plants that affects growth rates, unless you ask it to pay attention to it. She said if she had done this type of thing every week and told it the variables to pay attention to, she probably would have received much more nuanced and accurate information.

Anderson said the trouble with relying solely on AI as a novice in almost any field is that you don’t know what you don’t know. She said you rely on this technology to fill those gaps, and if you don’t have that background information, you’re not going to know whether it’s accurate or not. She said the prompt delivered useful tips on plants to grow alongside others but didn’t deliver proper advice on the distance to keep, say, a bug-trapping plant away from desirable berries. She showed a side-by-side eggplant example: the picture on the left, taken on the date ChatGPT provided, showed it barely budding, and the picture on the right showed it after harvest two weeks later with its trademark purple sheen. By just relying on AI, the gardener wouldn’t have had anything worth eating.

Anderson admitted she killed a lot of plants in her first year as a new gardener, and as a researcher and longtime teacher she had years of experience studying sociology, sustainability and learning, particularly related to climate change. Her early garden experience led her to consider the importance of generational knowledge, and her Ph.D. in Educational Foundations & Research from UND culminated her study of the natural world. The garden is led by professors Cheryl and Joshua Hunter in the College of Education & Human Development and annually serves as a living classroom for people of all ages through seasonal cycles, ecological stewardship and community collaboration. As UND Today reported at its establishment, the garden provides a gathering space to connect and learn about others as well as the whole process of growing our own food from seed to compost. In another recent UND Today report, the Learning Garden was awarded the 2026 Dr. Robert H. Boyd Healthy UND Champion Award for its contributions to the health and well-being of the campus community.

Given the environmental impact of using AI, Anderson said she is leaving gardening research behind, and now as a librarian she pointed out there are a lot of excellent volumes on gardening in your local library. She said the results drew her to advocate for intergenerational learning, talking to the neighbor or family member who gardens or volunteering at a community green space. The Minnesota Department of Education granted the East Grand Forks Campbell Library an award of $50,000 to host a learning garden of its own to promote experiential learning. The goal is to replicate what Anderson learned working with the GRO.UND initiative to host classes for the community, passing her experiences and knowledge to the next generations of aspiring gardeners. The next AI Forum Series session will take place on Tuesday, Dec. 8, featuring Anna Kinney, Sri Lalitha Nuthulapati and Richard Van Eck representing UND’s Co.AI Initiative.

stories.Headline: Northeastern University London researchers propose in-game AI companions for player mental health support
stories.Summary:
Researchers at Northeastern University London published a peer-reviewed paper suggesting that in-game AI companions could provide psychological support for video game players. This proposal comes as artificial intelligence already functions as a fundamental part of modern gaming by adapting gameplay based on player behavior. The paper, titled Serving the Player or Shaping Them?, argues that these embedded systems can shape a gamer's wellbeing over time. Melika Vafafar, a PhD researcher in computer science, is the corresponding author who believes AI should not be simple characters. This academic provocation explores whether generative AI can be repurposed to support the emotional health of people who play games.

The proposal requires generative AI companions to have sophisticated conversations and use language models to produce real-time responses for the human players. These systems could use sensors in controllers to detect sweaty palms or track brain signals, skin conductance, and eye movements. Vafafar notes that games like PUBG: Battlegrounds and Where Winds Meet already use generative AI for characters that offer helpful tips. Such AI could notice frustration in a voice and encourage a break during a long session or after a losing streak. This approach targets gamers who may play for hundreds of hours a month, creating opportunities to influence their cognition and behavior.

Melika Vafafar stated that adaptive and emotionally responsive AI companions could become systems capable of shaping the wellbeing of players over time. She argued that games could become a platform for emotional support that feels far more personal than any existing digital tools. Christiane Eichenberg, head of the Institute for Psychosomatics at Sigmund Freud Private University, said AI is no substitute for human help. Eichenberg noted that chatbots are non-judgemental and available round the clock, which makes it easier for many people to open up. She added that some scientifically evaluated AI mental health programmes show effects comparable to psychotherapy when used for several weeks.

Travis Gilly, executive director of the Real Safety AI Foundation in Illinois, argued that game studios lack the expertise for such research. He questioned whether studios want to support players or simply add features that make people get attached to the game characters. Amy Bussey from the U.K. charity Ygam said AI could complement support systems for young people facing barriers to help. Bussey warned that boundaries between entertainment and emotional support are blurring, raising concerns about privacy, age assurance, and inaccurate medical advice. These risks affect young people, who might develop emotional dependency or a skewed understanding of relationships through their AI companions.

The articles explain that people turn to chatbots like Gemini, Claude, or ChatGPT because they are accessible and avoid social stigma. In Germany, those seeking therapy must wait an average of 20 weeks, which increases the popularity of these automated conversation partners. Previous AI support has come from chatbots like Replika and Wysa, which can reduce loneliness and improve a user's mood. However, another Northeastern University London study found that AI chatbots can cause emotional dependence, exacerbate symptoms, and even lead to self-harm. General chatbots differ from specialized mental health applications that operate based on clinically validated treatment protocols to help users manage stress.

Future AI companions may use repeated interactions to positively influence the habits and emotions of gamers through personalized and adaptive support. Specialist therapeutic chatbots might be used to bridge waiting times for traditional therapy or provide real-time support during acute stressful situations. Kevin Hilbert, a professor at the Health and Medical University of Erfurt, suggests AI may be effective for mild distress. The articles leave open whether the positive effects of AI-based mental health programmes are stable or long-lasting for the users. It remains undecided how much responsibility should be entrusted to generative AI to benefit human lives and society as a whole.

stories.Headline: Economists Dynan, Elmendorf and Sheiner assess how fiscal policy could respond to artificial intelligence
stories.Summary:
Karen Dynan, Douglas Elmendorf and Louise Sheiner published a Brookings paper on November 17, 2026 that asks how fiscal policy might respond to the rise of artificial intelligence. The paper says artificial intelligence will probably generate major changes in the United States economy, although the nature, timing and magnitude of those changes are highly uncertain. The authors analyze a set of long-term scenarios that combine faster productivity growth, greater income inequality, job displacement and a higher capital share of income. The research is part of a series prepared for a conference at the University of Utah in June 2026 called The Forces Shaping America's Fiscal Future.

For each scenario the authors assess the implications for federal debt and for potential policy responses related to faster economic growth, the distribution of income, support for workers who are laid off, and taxation and ownership of capital. The paper argues that policies which are robust to different scenarios would be especially valuable, given the uncertainty surrounding the economic effects of artificial intelligence. Dynan is a professor of the practice of economics at Harvard University and a nonresident senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics. Elmendorf is a nonresident senior fellow in Economic Studies and at The Hutchins Center on Fiscal and Monetary Policy. Sheiner is the Robert S. Kerr Senior Fellow in Economic Studies and policy director of The Hutchins Center on Fiscal and Monetary Policy.

The authors state in their acknowledgements that Dynan and Elmendorf are affiliated with Harvard University and NBER, and that Sheiner is affiliated with the Brookings Institution. They note that the paper was written for the Brookings Institution and University of Utah conference held in June 2026, and that they are grateful for valuable comments by participants at the conference. The Brookings Institution says it is committed to quality, independence and impact, and that it is supported by a diverse array of funders. It also says that, in line with its values and policies, each Brookings publication represents the sole views of its authors.

stories.Headline: CSUN chemists use ELFNet AI model to predict bonding features 350 times faster
stories.Summary:
A team of chemists at California State University, Northridge has taken what the university describes as a big step forward by using a hardcore AI model to predict complex chemical bonding features 350 times faster than traditional physics simulations. Their model, called ELFNet, could cut the time and computational expense for researchers who use the electron localization function, or ELF, to map electron density distribution in metal lattices, a process the university calls critical in materials science. The findings appeared in the Journal of Materials Informatics under the title “Prediction of electron localization functions from superposed atomic densities for accelerated superhydride discovery,” and served as the featured cover story of the most recent printed publication. The paper’s authors include chemistry professor Maosheng Miao, who teaches in CSUN’s College of Science and Mathematics, Austin Ellis, who graduated with a master’s degree in chemistry from CSUN last May and is currently a researcher at Oak Ridge National Laboratory in Tennessee, and Samantha Ellis, currently a graduate student in chemistry at CSUN.

ELFNet is an image-to-image deep neural network that maps inexpensive superposed atomic densities to three-dimensional electron localization functions, and it is based on the quasi-atom and chemical template theories developed in the Miao Lab and their research on superhydrides, which are high-pressure compounds with exceedingly high hydrogen composition and the ability to conduct electricity without energy loss when cooled below a certain temperature. Instead of using real electron density, the input is a cheap superposed atomic density created by adding individual atomic densities together. The model uses a convolutional neural network, a type of deep-learning network widely used to recognize patterns in images, to transform a three-dimensional map of superposed atomic electron densities into an ELF map showing where electrons become localized. The network passes the input through a series of processing blocks that progressively refine the prediction, while attention mechanisms help it focus on useful patterns and regions, connections between layers carry earlier information forward, and the model preserves the original spatial resolution throughout the process.

Miao said the model predicts complex chemical bonding features 350 times faster than traditional physics simulations, which lets the lab discover new high-pressure materials at an unprecedented pace, and he called it a potential big step in furthering the field of materials science. He said Austin made a major contribution to the project, working with considerable independence to design and build the model’s convolutional neural network architecture. Miao said calculating the ELF for every metal lattice requires intensive, full quantum mechanics calculations, which is manageable for a single material but too slow when modern science requires screening millions of compounds, and he added that traditional methods are impractical for large-scale material discovery. He said ELFNet can reduce what could take months, if not years to calculate down to just days.

Miao’s lab focuses on computational chemistry and studies atoms and bonds and how they change under high pressure. Electronic-structure calculations of metal sublattices reveal bonding and localization patterns that calculations of the whole compound alone do not capture, and the ELF represents these patterns as chemically interpretable three-dimensional maps. ELF is widely used to identify chemically meaningful features such as bonding and lone-pair basins, atomic shell structure and interstitial electron localization in molecules and solids. Discovering new high-pressure hydrides is challenging because many metal frameworks, hydrogen arrangements, compositions and pressures must be evaluated before promising candidates can be identified, which takes expensive computer time. Miao said the project demonstrates how image-to-image machine learning can be a powerful tool.

stories.Headline: MIT scholars study how AI reshapes cognition, creativity and society through MITHIC projects
stories.Summary:
The MIT Human Insight Collaborative supported scholars exploring how AI affects the human experience and reshapes higher education, MIT News reported on November 18, 2026. Pawan Sinha, professor of brain and cognitive sciences, spoke at an “AI and the Brain” event at MIT in October, supported by MITHIC. Sinha co-leads a research project exploring how AI might reshape human intellect over time. Eric Klopfer, professor of comparative media studies/writing, presented at the October “AI and the Brain” event. Klopfer co-leads the MITHIC project exploring the impact of AI on human cognition.

MIT students are going to office hours less often and spending less time working through problem sets and with one another, findings of MIT’s recent report on artificial intelligence and education. MITHIC launched in 2024 as a strategic initiative bringing together scholars, artists, educators, and researchers to explore the human dimensions of defining challenges. Since its launch, MITHIC has supported 67 projects across 31 MIT units, offering a total of $5.5 million in funding. Roughly a third of those projects focus on AI, society, and humanity, a topic MITHIC faculty co-lead Heather Paxson says has become increasingly important. An AI and Society Forum took place on campus earlier this year, co-organized by MITHIC, SHASS, SERC, and the MIT Generative AI Impact Consortium (MGAIC), featuring presentations and panels on jobs, democracy, and AI.

Paxson, a professor of anthropology and associate dean of the School of Humanities, Arts, and Social Sciences, said that when they refer to AI and society they are not only speaking about individual ethical decision-making or how to retrain workers. Paxson said they are looking at how AI is reshaping sociality and how people relate to one another. Seth Mnookin, MITHIC faculty co-lead, a science writing professor and head of Comparative Media Studies Program/Writing, said the report was not saying AI is here and everyone needs to adapt. Mnookin said the report was saying we need to be asking more fundamental questions. Mnookin said that when the United States entered World War II in 1941, the Institute’s newly minted scientists and engineers helped shape that era through science and technology.

Mnookin said we are at a similarly consequential moment with AI, and the difference is that this time the questions that matter most cannot be answered by technologists alone. Mnookin said that is where the humanities, arts, and social sciences come in. The report on AI and education warned that AI is eroding the “creative friction” that has long defined an MIT education, students debating ideas and challenging one another, their professors, and their teaching assistants, in class and out of it. In the context of the 2026 U.S. midterm elections, political science professors Adam Berinsky and Charles Stewart III and MIT Sloan School of Management Assistant Professor Chara Podimata are studying how large language models have become intermediaries of democratic knowledge. The ongoing project demonstrated how voters in Alaska’s midterms who conducted their pre-election research using Anthropic’s AI model, Claude, may have received incomplete information about candidates and their views, and was recently featured in The New York Times.

Podimata told the Times that AI is becoming part of the way people encounter and make sense of political information, yet we know relatively little about what that information environment actually looks like. Podimata said we know relatively little about how it differs for different user demographics, political identities, and geographies. Klopfer and Sinha co-lead research measuring AI’s near- and long-term effects on cognition, meeting at the intersection of AI, education, and neuroscience. The professors are examining whether generative AI is increasing the human brain’s consumption of information but offloading cognitive function, or supporting an increase in cognitive function when used as part of the creative process. Anna Huang, a professor of music technology holding an MIT Schwarzman College of Computing shared position with the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, and Joe Paradiso, a professor at the MIT Media Lab, are examining how incorporating AI impacts the creative process and live performance experience.

Huang and Paradiso’s project, “Live Musician-AI Improvisation, Tuning the Social Aesthetics in Human-AI Partnerships,” explores what happens when human composers and contemporary machine learning systems improvise to make music together. A collective of MIT musicians, ethnomusicologists, and engineers meets for regular sessions to experiment with improvisation frameworks like stopping to discuss how technology impacts authorship and musical direction, ensemble dynamics, and other cornerstones of improvisation. Faculty will ultimately incorporate their takeaways into a future course or practicum on AI-improvisation. Graham Jones, professor of anthropology, and Arvind Satyanarayan, associate professor of computer science, used MITHIC’s SHASS+ Connectivity funding to help launch a course, 6.S061/21A.S02 (Humane User Experience Design). In the course, students examine how AI systems are designed and grapple with the consequences of AI agents entering into socio-cultural relationships with people through their ability to mimic human thought and speech.

Jones said at the inaugural MITHIC Annual Event that the crux of their collaboration is the term “humane,” a bit of a double-entendre meaning both human-serving or benevolent, and humanlike. Jones said what is interesting is that their students are discovering a fundamental tension between building a system that is good for people and one that seems human, because real people can develop dangerous dependencies. Another project, “Rebuilding Computing and Society at MIT,” is supported by MITHIC’s Education Impact Fund and led by Dwai Banerjee, associate professor of science, technology, and society. The initiative revitalized the Computing and Society concentration launched in 2019, a HASS concentration that had gone dormant, listing classes no longer being offered and with minimal student interest. The concentration now features current classes across 11 SHASS units in which students can explore computing through different humanistic and social science angles.

Banerjee, who serves as the concentration’s advisor, is also working with lecturer and research affiliate Mariel Garcia-Montes PhD ’26 to find ways to connect the concentration instructors and campus initiatives on computing and society. MIT senior Daniel Gonzalez is also part of the project, developing a research and outreach program that centers undergraduate voices in computing and society efforts across the Institute. Another MITHIC project funded by the EIF, “Review of Generative AI Assistive and Resistant Communication Assignments and Supporting Workshops,” is led by Michael Trice, a lecturer in MIT’s Writing, Rhetoric, and Professional Communication program. The project is responding to a consistent SHASS faculty request for additional training and skills needed “to fully address generative AI concerns in their classes.” Trice is creating a bank of faculty resources and facilitating workshops and visiting lectures on generative AI and writing, including a talk given earlier this fall by John Gallagher from the University of Illinois, who presented findings from a large-scale survey on AI-usage and writing conducted with undergraduates at his institution in 2026.

MIT leaders agree that MITHIC, now in its third year, is playing a central role in the Institute meeting the moment, as AI presents both extraordinary potential and disturbing risks. MIT President Sally Kornbluth recently said there has never been a more important time for constructive collaboration between science and technology and the human-centered disciplines. Kornbluth said that through MITHIC, MIT is giving faculty the support to reach out across disciplines and pursue their dreams. Agustín Rayo, dean of SHASS and co-chair of MITHIC, said MIT is uniquely placed to help us understand this extraordinary moment and to generate the values, tools, and policies we will need to shape AI so that it becomes a force for good. Rayo said it is essential that we deploy AI technology in a way that elevates human existence, rather than diminishing it.

At the recent SHASS 75th Anniversary Symposium, Provost Anantha Chandrakasan said given the rapid development of AI, an understanding of the ethical implications and societal impact of implementing new technologies is especially urgent. Chandrakasan, who also serves as MITHIC co-chair, said SHASS provides an essential perspective on questions concerning how technology can be developed thoughtfully and deployed responsibly, with the aim of improving human well-being. Looking ahead, MITHIC and SERC are developing a series of events that pair humanists or social scientists with colleagues in a single field, starting with mathematics, to examine what AI is changing about how that field produces knowledge. The articles do not state what the events will conclude or when the series will begin. The articles do not state further outcomes of the projects described.

stories.Headline: Mary Nichols says California lacks data on AI data centers carbon emissions
stories.Summary:
California is trying to find out how much artificial intelligence is contributing to climate change, and UCLA School of Law's Mary Nichols spoke with Marketplace about the lack of data regarding carbon emissions from AI companies' data centers in the state. Nichols is the former chair of the California Air Resources Board, and she said that once regulators and the public gain a better understanding of what data centers are and their carbon footprint, pressure will build on companies to clean up. The discussion was highlighted by UCLA in its daily news archive on November 17, 2026, alongside other media coverage of university research. The article does not give specific figures for the emissions involved or name the companies whose data centers are concerned.

The account does not specify any new rule, reporting requirement or deadline that California has adopted, and it gives no numbers for energy use or emissions from the data centers. What it describes is a gap in information, since Nichols points to the absence of data on the carbon emissions of AI companies' data centers in California as the starting problem. The piece also does not say which state agency, if any, is conducting the inquiry or when any findings might be published. It frames better public and regulatory understanding as the step that would precede any pressure on companies.

Nichols, who formerly led the California Air Resources Board, is the person quoted on the issue, and her view as paraphrased is that clearer knowledge of what data centers are and what they emit will lead to demands that companies reduce their impact. The article does not attribute any statement to the companies involved or to current state officials. It also does not say what steps, if any, firms have taken in response to concerns about AI's energy use. No further comments from Nichols beyond that assessment appear in the piece.

The item appeared among UCLA's media highlights for November 17, 2026, which also covered a study in Psychoneuroendocrinology linking inflammation and anhedonia, a KTTV-TV interview with UCLA's Anne Rimoin on measles no longer being considered eliminated in the United States, and New York Times comments from David Jewitt on light photons pushing bodies in space. The articles do not say what happens next in California's effort beyond Nichols's expectation that pressure on companies will grow as understanding improves. They give no timeline for further action or additional data. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Penn's John Lapinski leads a new Chief AI Officer Initiative to connect government AI leaders and students
stories.Summary:
The University of Pennsylvania's School of Arts & Sciences has launched a new Chief AI Officer Initiative, which was announced on November 17, 2026, as the newest facet of the AI & Data Across SAS Collaborative under the SAS Horizons strategic framework. The program aims to fill the current networking vacuum for Chief AI Officers, a leadership role that has emerged in government as artificial intelligence expands into new fields, and to partner with a few such professionals to create experiential learning opportunities for Penn students. Leading the initiative is John Lapinski, the Robert A. Fox Leadership Professor of Political Science, who is one of three SAS AI Advisory Group members and also serves as Faculty Director of the Robert A. Fox Leadership Program and Fels Institute of Government. Mark Trodden, Dean of the School of Arts & Sciences and Thomas S. Gates, Jr. Professor of Physics & Astronomy, said it is a vital moment for this kind of work and that some of the best and brightest minds in SAS are thinking critically about the new technology.

As a first step, Lapinski began working with key faculty at Penn to build out a team, and this academic year their focus is on starting discussions about AI's role in government through workshops and an inaugural conference. Lapinski also hopes to begin collaborating with AI leaders in governments from Philadelphia to Seattle and Washington, D.C., working closely with Penn San Francisco and Penn Washington to start building relationships. Down the line, the plan is to help public officials navigate AI use more broadly and to foster expanded curricular opportunities for students in data-related minors in the College of Arts & Sciences. Overall, Lapinski sees the initiative as a way to bring together theory and practice, to learn from and engage with colleagues about AI, and to foster dialogue about the right mix of how this technology gets used and taught.

Trodden noted that the Chief AI Officer Initiative will foster collaboration with AI leaders at many levels of government and drive important conversations in this space. Lapinski said the initiative will not solve all the challenges but that he would like the group to be convening the table, and that they are well-positioned to do so. The program is the newest facet of the AI & Data Across SAS Collaborative under the strategic framework SAS Horizons: Pathways for a Changing World. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the planned workshops, the inaugural conference and the hoped-for collaboration with government AI leaders.

stories.Headline: Stanford awards $3.5 million to seven teams for human-centered AI research
stories.Summary:
Seven interdisciplinary research teams at Stanford University recently won a total of $3.5 million to pursue human-centered approaches to artificial intelligence across medicine, science, law and education. The Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI awards the Hoffman-Yee grants to groups of scholars who aim to solve the toughest scientific, technical and societal challenges in the field. Each winning team for 2026 received $500,000 in support of its proposed research, and every proposal had to show a commitment to the institute's three research priorities. Those priorities are understanding the human and societal impact of AI, augmenting human capabilities, and developing AI technologies inspired by human intelligence.

Philanthropists Reid Hoffman and Michelle Yee gifted funding for the program in 2018, and in 2026 Google.org also supported it. A new cohort of grant recipients has been named every two years, with additional funding available to select teams in the second year of their research. To date, the program has allocated a total of $31 million to 25 teams. One winning team of legal AI scholars at Stanford will develop technologies to augment the capabilities of human lawyers and policymakers in high-stakes legal settings such as housing policy, benefits adjudication and policy formulation. After initial development, the team plans to pilot its novel AI systems with several government agencies and public institutions.

James Landay, the Denning Director of Stanford HAI, said this year's grant winners are reimagining what AI can do for humans and society. He said that across medicine, science, law and education they are building novel systems to work alongside human expertise instead of replacing it. Daniel E. Ho, a professor of law, political science and computer science by courtesy and a senior fellow at Stanford HAI and the Stanford Institute for Economic Policy Research, described his team's goal. He said the aim is to develop, assess and evaluate AI systems that are not only powerful but also legally rigorous, transparent and aligned with democratic values.

The legal team notes that the U.S. legal system is vast and complex, consisting of 50 million words in the U.S. Code and another 200 million words in the Code of Federal Regulations. The article says AI can help reform and simplify this legal and policy language, but only if it is deployed responsibly. It adds that legal AI must prove it can reason in environments of disagreement and uncertainty created by shifting human values and hierarchies of authority if it is to be trusted. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the planned pilots with government agencies and public institutions.

stories.Headline: Dartmouth panelists debate how AI reshapes creativity and learning as students report mostly using it to learn
stories.Summary:
The Dartmouth Political Union hosted a panel discussion on November 11, 2026, to debate how artificial intelligence reshapes creativity and learning. This event took place at the Nelson A. Rockefeller Center for Public Policy and was opened by events director Josh Montvelisky. More than 75 people, who were mostly students, attended the roundtable to discuss authorship and originality. The panel featured Paul Cherian, Eli Moyse, computer science professor Nikhil Singh, and professor Russell Muirhead. Nika Bigelow served as the moderator for the session.

The discussion addressed whether AI companies should pay for using copyrighted material, noting a five billion dollar settlement involving Anthropic. Russell Muirhead expects compensation from that company for internalizing his books. The panel also examined how AI affects academic assessments at Dartmouth. Paul Cherian noted that his history class looks different than it did a year ago. Some professors are replacing multipage essays with shorter in-class writing and exams.

Nikhil Singh stated that while AI might produce original thoughts, humans should not outsource the enriching process of creating art. Russell Muirhead argued that AI is a massive disruption but could eventually lead to beneficial pedagogical reform. He expressed concern that AI threatens the sense of possession people feel toward their own words. Singh suggested that government bodies should regulate AI to minimize risks while maintaining progress. Muirhead disagreed, stating that the regulatory process is too slow for evolving technology.

Eli Moyse warned that people could become de-skilled in thinking over the next ten to twenty years. He feared a world where a small group of people influence the models that shape perceptions of reality. Paul Cherian and Eli Moyse noted that AI is already altering how professors assess student achievement. Students are affected by the shift toward in-class testing to prevent the outsourcing of essays.

Moyse argued that this change could make it harder to master longform writing based on research. The panel followed a conference called AI at 70: What Must Remain Human? which released a survey on college students. This survey found that students mostly use AI for learning rather than cutting corners.

About 17 percent of Dartmouth undergraduates reported using AI to draft essays. This figure is lower than the 23 percent reported across the United States. However, these students believe that 63 percent of their peers use AI for drafting. The panelists ended the session with an optimistic note regarding the promise of AI to improve human life.

They discussed the likelihood of AI bringing about the end of humanity during a final lightning round. The articles do not state the specific percentage likelihoods the panelists provided for this outcome. They also leave open exactly what a government regulating body for AI would look like. The text does not specify the final conclusions reached regarding the regulation of AI.

stories.Headline: DDN opens flagship Manhattan office and creates 233 jobs with state tax credits
stories.Summary:
DataDirect Networks, a California-based AI data intelligence company known as DDN, is establishing a new flagship office at 452 Fifth Avenue in Midtown Manhattan, Empire State Development announced on November 17, 2026. The company has signed a lease for approximately 30,000 square feet of office space, moving from its existing coworking location to a dedicated facility that will support its growing New York operations. The expansion will create 233 new full-time jobs and builds on DDN's existing workforce of 45 employees in New York State. DDN is investing more than $5 million in the project, including renovations, new equipment and improvements meant to accommodate the company's continued growth.

Empire State Development is supporting the project with up to $3.5 million in performance-based Excelsior Jobs Program tax credits, which are tied to the company's job creation commitments. Most of the new positions will focus on bringing DDN's technology to customers, including roles in sales, marketing, sales engineering and product marketing. The company also plans to hire across legal, finance, people and culture, data and analytics, and information technology. Founded in 1998, DDN builds an AI data intelligence platform used by thousands of organizations, including strategic AI companies, major cloud providers, research institutions and governments, after decades of powering scientific research and supercomputers.

ESD President, CEO and Commissioner Hope Knight said New York is increasingly becoming a destination for companies developing the technologies that power artificial intelligence. She said that under Governor Hochul's leadership the state is attracting leading technology companies from across the country that recognize the value of its talented workforce and growing AI ecosystem. Knight said DDN's decision to establish a flagship office in Manhattan and create hundreds of new jobs shows New York competing for and winning investments that will shape the future of the industry. DDN Chief Financial and Operating Officer Guido Torrini said New York is home to some of the best talent in the world, which is exactly why the company chose to build a flagship office there, and that the team it hires will help bring the next generation of AI to life.

The expansion builds on Governor Hochul's efforts to strengthen New York's position as a center for artificial intelligence and emerging technologies. The announcement cites New York City's deep talent pool, leading research institutions and growing network of technology companies as the resources and connections businesses need to develop new technologies and expand their operations. By supporting companies developing the infrastructure behind AI, the state says it is helping grow an interconnected technology ecosystem spanning software development, advanced computing and data management while creating new economic opportunities for New Yorkers. Empire State Development is New York's chief economic development agency, promoting business growth, job creation and greater economic opportunity throughout the state through offices in each of its 10 regions.

stories.Headline: Quad leaders launch business forum and cybersecurity cooperation at Manila summit
stories.Summary:
On November 17, 2026, President Donald J. Trump of the United States, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese of Australia, Prime Minister Narendra Modi of India, and Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae of Japan met for a Quad Leaders' Summit in Manila. The year marks nearly a decade since the Quad was revived and the tenth anniversary of the vision of a Free and Open Indo-Pacific first articulated by the late Prime Minister Abe Shinzo of Japan in 2016. The four leaders said that a decade on, that vision is stronger than ever, and that together they have shown the Quad is a force for good and a partnership of action committed to peace, stability, and prosperity. They strongly opposed any destabilizing or unilateral actions that seek to change the status quo, including by force or coercion, which they said escalate tensions and undermine regional peace and stability.

They expressed grave concerns about economic coercion, including through arbitrary export restrictions. The leaders said they are securing critical supply chains, protecting freedom of navigation and overflight, driving growth through technologies of the future including investments in and deployment of trusted Super Intelligence, and responding to disasters with life-saving assistance. They committed to work together to ensure open, safe, and resilient maritime transit corridors in the Indo-Pacific, and said they are working with regional partners to tackle shared challenges and deliver tangible benefits to the region. They announced the inaugural Quad Business Leaders' Forum, scheduled to be held in early 2027, bringing together business leaders, government officials, and policy experts from Quad countries to foster greater business ties across private sectors, including promotion of commercial deals and partnerships critical to the prosperity of the Indo-Pacific.

They affirmed the importance of the Super Intelligence Accelerator, announced by their Foreign Ministers in Atlanta, which is intended to coordinate and fund efforts to support trusted Super Intelligence access, deployment, and technical assistance across the Indo-Pacific. A footnote in the release states that in Australia, India, and Japan, "Super Intelligence" refers to "artificial intelligence." The leaders welcomed the Indo-Pacific Maritime Surveillance Collaboration, a new initiative to enhance information sharing and maritime domain awareness, and said that in 2027 their respective P-8 and P-3C patrol aircraft are scheduled to fly in a maritime exercise for the first time in a Quad context, making the seas safer. They noted progress under the Quad Partnership for Cable Connectivity and Resilience, which has expanded access to secure and trusted communications infrastructure across the Indo-Pacific, and welcomed an expansion of Australia's contribution to the Partnership to focus on electricity cables, strengthening regional energy security and connectivity.

They also welcomed upcoming undersea cable projects in the Indian Ocean intended to strengthen regional connectivity. The leaders acknowledged the rapid increase in the number and scale of cyber incidents in the region and announced enhanced Quad Cybersecurity Cooperation, through which they plan to work together to achieve an open and secure cyberspace. They unequivocally condemned terrorism and violent extremism in all its forms and manifestations, including cross-border terrorism, and committed to strengthening the Quad's ongoing cooperation on counterterrorism. They reaffirmed their unwavering support for ASEAN centrality and unity, and said that together they are committed to upholding a free and open Indo-Pacific.

stories.Headline: Oakland City Council unanimously extends AI data center moratorium until October 2027
stories.Summary:
The Oakland City Council voted unanimously this week to extend the city's moratorium on AI data centers for 10 months, giving the city time to produce a policy protecting residents from public health and safety dangers posed by data center proliferation. The extension passed at Tuesday's council meeting. It keeps the existing 45-day moratorium in place until Oct. 5, 2027. Councilmember Carroll Fife is leading the City Council's efforts to pass the moratorium. Protesters rallied against data centers outside Oakland city hall in September.

The original 45-day moratorium passed on Oct. 6 and was set to expire on Nov. 20. Mayor Barbara Lee backed the original moratorium in her recent State of the City address. Other California cities that already have passed data center moratoriums include San Francisco, Hayward, Oakley, Richmond, Monterey Park, Gilroy, South El Monte, Montebello, and Calexico. Thirty-five public speakers signed up to talk about the moratorium extension, and almost all of them supported it. A speaker for Care for Community Action said her organization surveyed more than 400 residents and found that 73% favor a permanent ban on all data centers being built in Oakland.

Fife said two of the giants in the tech industry have leased space in West Oakland, and another has shown interest in a downtown location. She said she felt it was imperative to take immediate action to protect Oakland residents from what has been seen in other parts of the country. She said the move is not a rejection of technology or economic growth but guardrails against an industry that has steamrolled individuals throughout the entire globe. She said it is important that staff have the ability to do the appropriate study and outreach so the community has a voice in anything that will impact their lives. Lee said residents need to weigh in on any industry that is trying to come to Oakland.

Bill Gilchrist, director of the city's Planning and Building Department, said the city is committed to looking at areas that might be most severely impacted by land use and residential proximity. He said the city will make sure to engage members of the community who may historically have not been able to participate or be invited to participate in this kind of discussion. He said the idea is to do no harm. Laney College professor Peter Brown said not to cast votes based on the illusion of the old economy, where corporate investment in Oakland meant thousands of lasting, good-paying jobs and property, business, and income taxes flowing into city coffers.

Nyah Tisdell, an East Oakland community organizer with Communities for a Better Environment, said community members say no to data centers that will go straight to East Oakland, which already has so much industry and pollution. Rev. Leslie Bowling-Dyer said data centers are part of the necessary infrastructure for the rise of an economically and politically untouchable class. He said people are not being lunatics displaying an irrational fear of technology.

He said technological innovation is not equivalent to social progress. He said technological advance is not the problem in itself, but the people who control it are. Some of the speakers urged the council to consider a permanent ban on data center development in the city. The articles do not state what specific policy the city will produce during the 10 months.

The articles do not state when the council will take up the matter again. The articles do not state the names of the tech companies that leased space in West Oakland or showed interest downtown. The articles do not state what action, if any, the council took on the calls for a permanent ban. The articles do not state whether the mayor signed the extension.

stories.Headline: Hugging Face integrates OpenRouter to route language model requests through its Inference Providers service
stories.Summary:
Hugging Face announced on November 16, 2026, that its Inference Providers service now uses OpenRouter to route supported language model requests. This migration changes how the system handles chat, vision language, and agent requests by routing them through OpenRouter. Existing Hugging Face tokens and application code are intended to keep working for users during this backend transition. However, provider keys previously configured for server side routing no longer work through that specific route. Image, video, and audio generation tasks continue to use the existing Hugging Face provider infrastructure.

The new system routes requests from applications to the Hugging Face router, then OpenRouter, and finally to an eligible provider. OpenRouter serves over 600 models from 80 plus providers to more than 10 million users every month. The catalog includes 160 models from 38 labs, though one API check observed 164 entries. Users can choose routing policies like fastest, cheapest, or balanced, or pin a specific provider using a model suffix. This change does not affect dedicated Inference Endpoints or models that users run locally.

Hugging Face stated that the account and billing experience will remain on their side for the users. They explained that the router now picks the best provider based on live price, speed, and reliability. The company noted that failed requests are now retried on another provider instead of returning an error. They advised users to check their model availability, credit balances, and actual bills for Hugging Face managed billing. They also suggested that teams identify workloads relying on custom provider keys and decide where billing should live.

Users with custom provider keys are affected because their specific contracts, credits, or capacity may no longer be active. OpenRouter reported that open weight models grew 60 fold in weekly volume between October 2025 and September 2026. These models cost an average of 0.28 dollars per million input tokens, which is four times less than closed models. On the Intelligence Index, the open weight Kimi K3.1 Pro scored 46 compared to 65 for Claude Fable 5.2. This cost trade off is considered worth it for many different types of workloads.

OpenRouter previously conducted a routing experiment with 24 million requests and 103 billion input tokens over one week. That study showed a 6 percent increase in cost per request but improved throughput and time to first token. OpenRouter also found that its new routing method cut capacity errors by 46 percent and improved throughput by 16.3 percent. Open weight models represented 71.7 percent of tokens served by OpenRouter at the end of September 2026. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 was the most used model this week with 59.2 trillion tokens.

Users should now verify model identifiers and eligible providers using the OpenAI compatible model catalog at the Hugging Face router. They must test their largest prompts, tool calls, and schema requirements to ensure the new routing works. The articles leave open the exact cutover hour, the specific rollout cohorts, and the available grace period. Future work mentioned by Hugging Face includes the implementation of account linking for the users. It remains unclear if a stream that has already emitted text can be restarted without duplicating output.

stories.Headline: Joe Gerstl of Velotic speaks at a webinar on data foundations for AI-powered manufacturing on November 19
stories.Summary:
Representative Im Munyeong sponsored a bill in the National Assembly on November 17, 2026, to support small and medium manufacturers. This legislation aims to expand support beyond smart factory construction to include the collection and use of manufacturing data. The bill focuses on helping these smaller companies adopt artificial intelligence technologies to improve their overall production capabilities. It seeks to bridge a digital gap created by the discontinuation of certain government programs for basic factories. Fifteen lawmakers, including Park Haecheol and Kim Seongbeom, co-sponsored this amendment to the Smart Manufacturing Innovation Act.

The bill targets the Partial Amendment to the Act on the Promotion of Smart Manufacturing Innovation by Small and Medium Enterprises. It requires infrastructure to collect and manage data from production equipment and supports AI training for small and medium manufacturers. Provisions include adding sensors and communications modules to old equipment through retrofit methods in Gwangju Gwangsan-eul and other areas. The law establishes a legal basis for young AI specialists to collaborate with experienced workers at various production sites. Other co-sponsors include Jeong Ilyoung, Oh Sehee, Kim Junhwan, Jang Jongtae, Moon Geumju, Hwang Myeongseon, Kwon Hyangyeop, Lee Gwanghee, Shin Jeonghoon, Park Jiwon, Lee Geontae, and Park Yonggap.

Representative Im Munyeong stated that the Yoon Suk Yeol administration created a digital transformation gap by abolishing basic smart factory programs. He explained that this loss of support weakened the foundation for manufacturing AI transformation and reduced productivity opportunities. Im noted that some companies struggle because they lack automated equipment or have not received adequate follow-up maintenance services. He believes the amendment will build basic capabilities and connect site expertise to AI competitiveness to protect the industry. The lawmaker intends to preserve the skills of experienced workers in design, processing, and quality control as data.

The Ministry of SMEs and Startups reported that only about 20 percent of small and medium manufacturers have built smart factories. These companies are affected because they lack the capacity to collect and analyze data generated during their production processes. Even when industry leading AI models are developed, these firms cannot apply them without the ability to refine data. Experts like Joe Gerstl from Velotic suggest that trusted, contextualized operational data is the critical foundation for successful AI.

CPG manufacturers are encouraged to use manufacturing execution systems to connect equipment, process, quality, and production data. The articles state that budgets for AI and smart factory upgrades have increased since last year to help these companies. However, the Yoon Suk Yeol administration discontinued the program that provided basic-level smart factories and initial equipment construction support. This policy change led to a decline in opportunities for companies to establish infrastructure for managing their manufacturing data.

Many manufacturers still rely heavily on the knowledge of experienced workers who may retire or close their businesses. This reliance creates a risk that accumulated expertise in quality control and processing will disappear over time. The proposed amendment will provide support for assessing data-use capabilities and designing systems to refine, process, and analyze production data. It will also fund the creation of data specifically for AI training to help small and medium sized manufacturers.

A webinar on November 19 at 2 p.m. Eastern will further explore building data foundations for AI-powered manufacturing. The Converters Expo South will take place on February 25, 2027, at the Charlotte Convention Center to discuss production challenges. The articles leave open whether the National Assembly will officially pass the bill or how the funding will be allocated.

stories.Summary:
The AI developer Anthropic launched its initial public offering on Thursday of this week. This float is expected to value the company at 1.4 trillion dollars. The event will likely turn more than 4,000 staff members into millionaires. These employees will gain wealth as their stock options vest. This financial surge is expected to boost London's high-end property market.

The IPO may generate a minimum value of 20 million dollars for each staff member. Anthropic employs 5,000 people worldwide, including more than 200 employees based in the UK. The company plans a new London office capable of accommodating up to 800 people. In 2024, it spent 24.1 million pounds employing an average of 43 staff. Research engineers have seen base salary listings of up to 630,000 pounds.

Buying agent Jo Eccles says tech buyers have budgets ranging from 2 million to 40 million pounds. Jeremy Gee of Beauchamp Estates says AI buyers are younger and move quickly. He notes that these buyers prioritize location and quality and will pay a premium. Shona Baijal of Coutts says young entrepreneurs often feel overwhelmed by their wealth. She advises these new clients not to rush into making any decisions.

Igor Babuschkin of xAI reportedly bought a 57 million pound penthouse overlooking Hyde Park in February. Suneil Setiya of Quadrature Capital reportedly paid 270 million pounds for Providence House in Chelsea. Aidan Devane says the success of his firm is partly due to nearby AI labs. OpenAI staff in London earned 2.3 million pounds on average last year. This pay is 58 times the median UK full-time employee earnings.

Anthropic was founded in San Francisco in 2021 and now works in King's Cross. Demis Hassabis co-founded DeepMind in 2010 and sold it to Google for 400 million pounds. Other firms like Meta and OpenAI also cluster in the King's Cross knowledge quarter. In San Francisco, one-bedroom rentals now average 4,400 dollars, up over 25 percent. The UK economy grew 0.7 percent in the third quarter due to IT services.

stories.Headline: HSF Kramer hires legal engineering team to strengthen its AI capabilities
stories.Summary:
Herbert Smith Freehills Kramer, known as HSF Kramer, tapped a legal engineering team to fuel its AI capabilities, according to Above the Law on November 16, 2026. The firm moved to build out legal engineering as a hot new job at the intersection of law and AI. The hire was reported by Above the Law in a piece published at 20:15 on that date. The move places HSF Kramer among law firms building internal teams for AI work. The article frames legal engineering as a role spanning law and artificial intelligence.

In October 2026, Harvey and Legora each launched a product called Intake, built to help corporate legal departments receive, sort and route incoming legal requests with AI. The two announcements arrived roughly 24 hours apart, and Wordsmith had already released its own Intake earlier in the year. Goodwin unveiled Regina OS, its proprietary AI operating system, on August 14, and days later Davis Wright Tremaine announced a firmwide expansion of Harvey and Microsoft AI tools. Kenny Gary, CEO of the communications firm LIMELIGHT, documented that overlap in a three-part series for JD Supra Perspectives. Over 85% of surveyed Association of Corporate Counsel members say they have embedded AI in their own legal departments, and ACC has roughly 48,000 members.

Jason Brown, president and CEO of the Association of Corporate Counsel, said on Infodash's Legal Innovation Spotlight podcast that over 85% of surveyed ACC members report they have embedded AI and actively use it. By his account, that share rose sharply over roughly two years. He said the overwhelming majority of members tell ACC they are not seeing efficiency or cost gains from their law firms. He expects that gap to push more work in-house if it persists. General counsel, he said, want the gains to show up as a visible drop in outside counsel spend, alongside more work done at a faster rate.

Lynn Tellefsen Stehle, writing November 11 in JD Supra Perspectives, put the advantage inside the firm, as change management treated as a permanent skill with its own people and accountability. She said many firm leaders she has worked with know their firms need to change but have no team to lead it. Brie Leung, founder and principal of Red Bird Strategy and a former chief strategy officer, said rolling out a new tool can threaten someone's competence, confidence, autonomy, status or professional identity. Catherine Alman MacDonagh, CEO and founder of the Legal Lean Sigma Institute and author of Lean Six Sigma for Law Firms, compresses her method to three words in a fixed order: people, process, platform.

Jen Leonard, founder of Creative Lawyers and former chief innovation officer at the University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School, said organizations do not change, people do. Gary is careful to say there is no reason to think any of these companies knew a rival's plans. He concedes that some convergence is inevitable, because companies hear the same customers and face the same pressures, and simultaneous launches can signal a maturing market. He points to Thompson Hine's AI-enabled SmartPaTH Plus, which rests on more than a decade of investment in its SmartPaTH delivery model.

Leung learned her point training legal secretaries to move from WordPerfect to Word, people colleagues called when a document broke. MacDonagh's idea for Legal Lean Sigma came from reviewing outside counsel bills as an in-house lawyer. Gary's third installment, promised on positioning, timing and strategic alignment, is the next marker in this conversation. The articles leave open whether ACC members will begin reporting that law firm AI investments show up as lower or more predictable outside counsel spend.

They leave open which firms would then be named. They leave open how HSF Kramer's legal engineering team will be staffed and measured. They leave open whether the gap Brown describes will push more work in-house. They leave open what Gary's third installment will say.

stories.Headline: Lansing residents oppose a data center ban vote as TeraWulf subsidiary sues the town
stories.Summary:
On Tuesday night, Nov. 17, 2026, residents of Lansing, a town in Tompkins County, packed the Lansing Central School District Middle School Auditorium to oppose a proposed data center. They spoke at a special Lansing Town Board meeting held for public comment on a proposed local law. The law would amend the town code to define “cryptocurrency,” “cryptocurrency data mine,” “data center” and “general processing.” The meeting came as officials weigh a possible outright ban on data centers. The company behind the project, TeraWulf, argues in a lawsuit that lawmakers are working behind-the-scenes to stop the potential undertaking.

The law, if approved, would include “cryptocurrency data mine” or “data center” as uses within the Schedule of Land Uses or Activities. That would establish that cryptocurrency data mines and data centers are disallowed uses for the town’s zoning code, according to the local law proposal. This would essentially ban data centers within the town. TeraWulf, a company that started in bitcoin mining and is expanding into data centers, previously proposed a facility at the former Cayuga Generating Station along Cayuga Lake’s eastern shore. The town board is set to vote on the proposed ban during a regular meeting starting at 6:30 p.m. Wednesday at the middle school auditorium.

Pace Ralli, vice president of product development for TeraWulf, took to the podium to defend the proposal. He said it was an opportunity to put an unused industrial property back into productive use, create jobs and rethink what exists on the lakeside waterfront when the coal power plant is taken down. He also asserted the undertaking could bring significant private investment and new tax revenue to the community, helping support schools, public services and local infrastructure. Lake Hawkeye, a limited liability company and subsidiary of TeraWulf, filed a suit against the Town of Lansing, the Lansing Town Clerk’s Office and town supervisor Ruth Groff. Town supervisor Ruth Groff, who is named in the suit, declined to comment.

One member of the public said loons are often heard in the distance because sound really travels over the water, and contrasted that with a data center emitting over 50 decibels of noise 24/7 at the lake’s edge. Another speaker argued that going against the ban “doesn’t mean automatic support of a data center,” and said it means individual projects should be thoughtfully reviewed as they come along. Many attendees showed their support for the ban by wearing red, and a person in red said that with the same supply of electricity and more demand from data centers, everyone’s costs go up. Lake Hawkeye, which operates at the site of the former Cayuga power plant, is seeking an order directing the Town of Lansing “to conduct a legally sufficient search and produce responsive documents in response” to the LLC’s two state Freedom of Information Law requests.

The suit said the Town has not complied with FOIL and appears to have concealed documents responsive to the requests. It said Lake Hawkeye filed the FOIL requests to obtain information about back-channel discussions among Lansing Town officials seeking to thwart the construction of a data center on the site. The document claimed that to avoid detection or produce communications under FOIL, town board members took to a private Google Group managed by Ms. Karen Edelstein, the spouse of Town Board member Joe Wetmore, to discuss strategies to block the Data Center. It said access to the group was strictly limited by Ms. Karen Edelstein, ensuring that town residents who supported the data center and the jobs it would bring could not join. It said the petitioner sought admission to the private group and was explicitly denied, so it was not able to participate in these discussions of public concern to the Town.

The suit contends that the alleged use of a private, exclusionary forum by a quorum of Board members to discuss and formulate official policy on the Data Center Project violates the New York Open Meetings Law, which states all of a public body’s meetings must be open to the general public. The town board is set to vote on the proposed data center ban during a regular meeting, which starts at 6:30 p.m. Wednesday at the middle school auditorium. People argued for and against the data center ban at the meeting. The articles do not say what the board decided at that Wednesday vote. The articles also do not say how the town will respond to the lawsuit.

stories.Headline: New York City Council bans surveillance pricing under bill sponsored by Speaker Julie Menin
stories.Summary:
The New York City Council approved legislation banning surveillance pricing across the city’s five boroughs, sponsored by Speaker Julie Menin, as reported on November 16, 2026. The bill prevents companies from using New Yorkers’ personal data and algorithms to sell goods and services at different prices to different consumers. The council described the measure as among the strongest surveillance pricing bans in the country. The op-ed, published November 17, 2026, was written by State Sen. Rachel May and Assembly Member Emerita Torres. May represents the 48th Senate District covering Syracuse and parts of Onondaga and Cayuga Counties, and Torres represents the 85th Assembly District covering southern and southeastern Bronx.

The One Fair Price Act passed both houses of the New York State Legislature with strong support and bans companies from using personal data to determine how much consumers pay. It preserves legitimate discounts including loyalty programs and senior discounts. New York is the second city and fifth jurisdiction in the United States to ban the practice, after Maryland, Connecticut, New Jersey and Seattle. The state legislature passed the One Fair Price Act this past June, and Gov. Kathy Hochul has until the end of the year to act on it. The articles cite data including geolocation, browsing history, ZIP code, gender and when a paycheck hits a bank account.

Menin said the City Council is putting consumers first by ending the deceptive and insidious practice of surveillance pricing. She said charging different people different prices for the same products is unethical and worsens the affordability crisis. She said the council takes consumer protection extremely seriously and will continue fighting to lower prices and stop predatory corporate tactics. May and Torres wrote that Governor Hochul has an opportunity to lead and urged her to sign the One Fair Price Act. They wrote that it is time to stop letting algorithms rig the economy against consumers.

UFCW International VP Ademola Oyefeso cautioned that New Yorkers not buying airline tickets or ordering groceries online, especially those with lower or fixed incomes, remain vulnerable as long as the council allows electronic shelf labels in grocery stores. He said AI-powered systems let retailers change prices throughout the day based on various factors even without a shopper’s personal data. He said consumers need a blanket protection against price manipulation, achievable by removing ESL capabilities from brick-and-mortar stores. The UFCW represents 1.2 million workers across North America, including grocery store associates. The NGA said ESLs are price tags enabling grocers to update prices and discounts quickly and accurately, not to change prices based on who is in the aisle.

The articles state that many consumers believe the economy is rigged, with wages largely stagnant and prices rising. They describe surveillance pricing as exploiting consumers and driving the affordability crisis by basing prices on willingness to pay rather than supply and demand. They give examples of parents charged higher prices for medicine and families shown higher airfares when attending a funeral. They state that when ZipRecruiter incorporated data about location, industry and employer benefits into its products, it dramatically increased prices, leading to an 84% increase in profits. Over 40 legislatures have introduced legislation to ban surveillance pricing, and several pieces of federal legislation have been introduced.

In June 2026 the state legislature passed the One Fair Price Act, and Governor Hochul has until the end of the year to act. The U.S. Senate Judiciary subcommittee Chair, Missouri Republican Josh Hawley, called surveillance pricing one of the biggest scams in American history. The Stop Price Gouging in Grocery Stores Act, led by Sen. Ben Ray Luján, D-N.M., and Sen. Jeff Merkley, D-Ore., was introduced this past February with a House companion led by Rep. Rashida Tlaib, D-Mich., and Rep. Val Hoyle, D-Ore. The UFCW introduced the Affordable Groceries and Good Jobs Campaign this year to ban surveillance pricing and ESLs in grocery stores. The articles leave open whether Governor Hochul will sign the One Fair Price Act.

stories.Headline: Proof launches x401 in ChatGPT so users approve AI agent actions with biometrics
stories.Summary:
Proof released the first version of the Proof MCP, its Model Context Protocol server for AI assistants, in ChatGPT on Nov. 18, 2026, from Boston. The first flow featured in the MCP is x401, so anyone using ChatGPT can add the Proof app and carry their verified identity into its work. When ChatGPT reaches a website or service that asks who authorized a request, the person reviews the details and approves with a biometric. The business then verifies the signature for itself, according to the GlobeNewswire release carried by The Manila Times. The release follows Proof's Oct. 15 launch of x401, the open protocol that lets any website or API ask an AI agent for evidence of the person behind it.

The Proof MCP is built to be the one install that brings Proof into a person's AI environment, and Proof will add more offerings to the same MCP over time. At launch, x401 was announced live in production with support for dots, and developers could connect Proof's MCP server to ChatGPT through a manual setup. By extending HTTP 401, the web's standard unauthorized response, x401 lets a site state exactly what evidence an agent must provide before proceeding. A hardware-protected key binds a person's verified legal identity to the exact terms, and the business can verify the result itself offline. Change one term and the signature fails, and the Proof MCP makes that exchange available to every ChatGPT conversation without requiring the business to integrate with ChatGPT.

Pat Kinsel, founder and CEO of Proof, said that when x401 launched last month the company said the hard part isn't getting agents to act but trusting that a real person authorized them. He said ChatGPT is where hundreds of millions of people will first ask an agent to do something that matters, such as pay a bill, sign a form or move money. He said that with the first release of Proof's MCP, the agent can show up with evidence of who sent it and what they agreed to, and the business on the other end can check it for itself. He said that is how AI gets to do more for you while you stay in charge. Proof calls the problem the Agent Evidentiary Gap, and it is why services from retailers to banks have been blocking agents rather than admitting them.

People add the Proof app from ChatGPT's app directory and sign in once, and every consequential action then comes to them for approval. Businesses that speak x401 can now expect ChatGPT users to arrive with a verifiable answer to who sent them and whether they said yes. Developers keep the same protocol, specification and MCP server released on Oct. 15, and nothing they built changes. The Proof MCP is available now as a connector in ChatGPT's app directory, consumers can set up their Proof credential at proof.com/digital-credential, and developers can add x401 to any site or API using the specification, identity scheme and reference implementation at proof.com/x401. Organizations that need higher assurance, signed authorization evidence or credential issuance can reach Proof at proof.com/contact-x401.

Proof created the online notarization category and has secured more than $1 trillion in transactions for more than 8,000 businesses, helping change more than 40 state laws along the way. Proof operates a WebTrust-audited certificate authority and issues verified digital credentials after Kantara-certified NIST IAL2 identity proofing. In 2026, Proof launched x401, the open protocol that lets any business verify who an AI agent is acting for and what that person approved. The Proof MCP is the latest step in a sequence that began with x401's production launch on Oct. 15 and has since brought the protocol to payment rails and edge infrastructure, including demonstrations and integrations announced during Money20/20. x401 applies to real money, legal rights and consequential decisions, and it is not a requirement to identify oneself to browse or to chat.

Sites choose when to ask and people choose whether to approve, and the Proof MCP is available now as a connector in ChatGPT's app directory. AI Rudder, the Singapore-headquartered voice specialist that already powers over 80 billion automated calls, has rolled out CALL-E, which lets agents inside ChatGPT, personal assistants such as Muse, OpenClaw and Hermes Agent, and coding platforms like Claude Code, Codex and Cursor place real phone calls on a user's behalf. Meta's Muse clocked five million US downloads in its first three weeks, while Grok Bot, from Elon Musk's SpaceX, drew 400,000 weekly users in its opening month. Your agent passes over the errand, CALL-E dials the number, handles the chat and brings back a receipt of what was settled. Teng Ren, chief executive officer of AI Rudder, said the smartest AI model in the world can still fail a phone call, and all it takes is one mm-hmm.
