stories.Headline: Tencent updates LightVela AI Agent to function as a personal assistant with long term memory
stories.Summary:
Tencent recently updated its cloud based AI Agent product called LightVela to evolve into a personal assistant. The company launched the public beta in April and opened the service to all users in late September. This new version allows users to create multiple AI assistants with independent personas and long term memory. It also includes a cloud computer that provides the Agent with an independent desktop environment. These upgrades aim to integrate AI more deeply into the daily work and life of users.

The product supports interaction via web pages and software including WeChat, Feishu, DingTalk and QQ. New users receive one month of free experience and 4500 AI points. The connector includes six applications named Tencent Meeting, Feishu, DingTalk, Tencent Docs, Tencent Securities and ima. Users can customize Bots using recommended templates or a persona test. The interface is divided into Daily and Explore sections to manage skills and settings.

Lei Tech conducted a real world test to evaluate the performance of the new LightVela version. The tester noted that the product is more convenient than deploying the open source Hermes Agent manually. However, the tester found that the interactive design for delivering files is not intuitive enough. The researcher Bot failed to provide a requested screenshot due to a display service conflict. The tester also experienced failures when trying to launch a personal display website.

The tester reported that the AI cited international site documents that were not applicable to domestic users. This suggests that users must still verify if sources actually support the statements made by the AI. The "My Workbench Beta" feature provides templates for data dashboards and personal display benches. These tools require technical stacks such as React, TypeScript and Tailwind to function. The tester found that the actual access to launched pages sometimes showed the page did not exist.

LightVela originally migrated the open source Hermes Agent to the cloud to save users from deployment and maintenance. It now positions itself as a cloud personal assistant for development, business operation and financial management. The product uses SkillHub to share existing AI skills and offers collectible persona cards. It includes a Diagnosis Center to help users reset the working environment. The design logic requires creating an assistant before deciding its materials and interaction methods.

The product remains far from perfect compared to other mature designs like WorkBuddy and Muse. Users must still understand environment failures and technical requirements to use the system effectively. The articles leave open whether ordinary users can smoothly find the functions they need. It is unclear if the cloud computer can operate software independently without user takeover. The final analysis suggests that the product details are not yet sufficiently polished.

stories.Headline: Remanence raises $30M seed led by EQT Ventures and FirstMark to help firms train open-weight AI models

Paris-based Remanence, a startup that helps companies train and fine-tune open-weight AI models, raised $30 million in seed funding, CEO Pierre-Louis Cedoz told Axios Pro exclusively. The round was led by EQT Ventures and FirstMark, according to the report published by Lucinda Shen on November 17, 2026. The company works with open-weight players so that businesses can train their own AI models rather than relying on outside providers. Axios reported the funding as an exclusive.

The report says the funding could wean companies off more costly closed-source models, as open-weight technology catches up with the alternatives. Remanence's business is built around helping companies train and fine-tune open-weight AI models, which the article describes as its core work. The $30 million seed round is the only figure the article gives for the raise, and EQT Ventures and FirstMark are named as the two leads. The article does not say how the money will be spent or give any other terms of the deal.

Cedoz is named as the company's CEO and is the person who confirmed the funding to Axios Pro. The article quotes him only briefly, and the report does not include further comment from him or from either of the lead investors. No statement from EQT Ventures or FirstMark appears in the article. The report also gives no details on Remanence's other backers, its customers or its plans.

The context the article offers is that open-weight technology is catching up, which it says could let companies move away from more costly closed-source models. The report does not say what happens next for Remanence beyond the funding itself. It gives no timeline for new products, hiring or expansion, and it does not say when the round closed.

stories.Headline: TaxDome report finds 74% of AI-using clients fact-check or would fact-check their accountant
stories.Summary:
A new report from the practice management platform TaxDome says that 74% of clients who use artificial intelligence have either fact-checked or would consider fact-checking their accountant's work with AI, based on a survey of 1,000 clients who use an accountant or tax professional. The 2026 Accounting Client Satisfaction Report found that AI is now increasingly part of the client relationship, that more clients are willing to pay for faster service, and that clients care more about quick response times than quick work delivery. Sixty-eight percent of clients say they have at least tried AI for their taxes or finances, and 39% have used it, mostly to ask a tax question or understand something. Very few hand it the real work, since only 3% have used AI on an actual return.

One in five clients have already used AI to review work their accountant completed, and among clients who have used or explored AI that rises to 29%, while another 45% have not done it yet but say they would consider it. For some, checking is already routine, since 24% of the clients who have checked their accountant's work with AI do it regularly, and top-paying business owners are checking their accountant's work with AI at 2.4 times the rate of all clients. The clients using AI to check their accountant's work are among the most willing to pay for more, with 78% saying they would pay for structured advisory check-ins compared with 55% of all clients, and 57% wanting a quarterly check-in on their finances compared with 45% of all clients. Across all clients who have tried AI, 61% would pay for structured advisory check-ins, compared with 43% of clients who have never tried it.

Ilya Radzinsky, co-founder and chief product officer of TaxDome, said in a statement on Nov. 18 that in the age of AI the firms that win will be the ones closest to their clients. He said the research shows what that looks like, with quick answers, a heads-up before clients have to ask, and advice they can act on. He said the firms that get it right will earn the trust, and the continued business, that AI cannot. The report says many clients also look closely at what an accountant adds, and it describes clients as not waiting for their accountant to bring AI into the relationship, since most have already started.

stories.Headline: Darren Jones calls for a multinational superintelligence safety treaty as a scholar urges UK-led AI assurance culture
stories.Summary:
Darren Jones MP, the former chief secretary to the prime minister under Keir Starmer, recently called for a new multinational treaty governing the safe development and use of superintelligence, where AI substantially surpasses humans across most cognitive tasks, and argued that Britain's growing reputation for AI safety and trustworthiness made it a good conduit for such collaboration. The article's author, a business scholar, concurs with those calls and with a leading role for the UK, and frames the underlying question as a management and organisational one: whether systems of governance can keep pace with AI development while ensuring it is safe. The piece notes that global tech leaders and some of their employees believe there is a greater than 10% chance that AI could kill all humans within the next decade, while cautioning that this prediction must be distinguished from current risks and from what might happen as AI systems become able to independently improve themselves and move towards superintelligence. It draws on normal accident theory, associated with the US sociologist Charles Perrow, and high reliability theory, associated with the American political scientist Todd LaPorte, as a framework for thinking about AI safety and regulation.

Normal accident theory holds that in complex, interdependent systems such as nuclear power plants or spacecraft built to carry humans, accidents are not necessarily the consequence of individual incompetence, negligence or bad design, but can emerge from the interaction of multiple components in ways that are difficult to anticipate. Events happen rapidly in such systems, leaving little time to intervene between one potential failure and the next, which can lead to a cascading error with the potential to cause a catastrophe; the article's example is the partial meltdown at the Three Mile Island nuclear plant in Pennsylvania, US, in 1978, which occurred because of a combination of mechanical malfunction, instrument faults and human factors. Risks increase when AI agents, systems that carry out tasks in response to instructions, are added to such a complex system, and an individual component might meet acceptable quality thresholds while the difficulty lies in the interactions between components and our understanding of them. Recent reports have described AI agents behaving in ways their developers did not expect, and the UK government has highlighted risks associated with increasingly capable AI agents and stressed the importance of testing frontier AI models and developing a scientific understanding of their capabilities. If AI systems become more autonomous, more interconnected and faster moving, the conventional idea of a human in the loop to correct major errors could become increasingly challenging.

High reliability theory offers a counterpoint, having emerged from research into organisations operating technologies where failure could have catastrophic consequences, such as nuclear power plants, aircraft carriers and air traffic control, and its central insight is that organisations can develop practices and cultures allowing them to operate extraordinarily complex technologies with very low failure rates, as seen with the electricity system, space travel and bioengineering. These organisations achieve high reliability because their baseline assumption is that they are not safe: they remain attentive to hints of bigger problems, do not automatically dismiss anomalies, learn from near misses and failures and build redundancy, for example backing up offline systems and providing kill switches. They routinely rehearse failure, establish operational processes, adhere to regulation for safety and assurance, comply with professional standards and certification schemes, have independent oversight, give experts the authority to challenge decisions and continuously learn from their performance. The article argues this suggests asking what a high-reliability organisation would look like if AI was embedded throughout it, rather than simply how to regulate AI, and that AI safety cannot be reduced to a model passing a one-off technical test before deployment but must span different organisations and transcend international boundaries.

The article says the current political conversation about AI regulation risks being too narrow, because government cannot realistically sit permanently inside every AI company and inspect every model, nor can legislation anticipate every technical configuration AI will take, even though governments need to understand what frontier laboratories are developing. The UK government recognises it must cultivate trustworthiness in AI through assurance, which asks whether there is credible evidence that a system is behaving within defined boundaries, whether those boundaries are appropriate, whether risks are being monitored and whether someone is accountable when they are breached. The aircraft industry has engineering standards, certification regimes, professional qualifications, independent inspection, incident reporting and regulatory oversight, nuclear power operates within an elaborate ecosystem of safety engineering and regulatory assurance, and financial institutions and medicine both have sophisticated systems of assurance, yet AI's assurance infrastructure remains comparatively immature given the speed at which frontier systems are developing. The institutional challenge is not simply to produce more AI regulation but to create the professional safety culture that makes regulation meaningful, and a potential new multinational treaty on the safe and regulated development of superintelligence would frame AI safety as a rapidly evolving global challenge while potentially creating a once-in-a-generation opportunity for the UK to help shape the emerging architecture of AI governance.

stories.Headline: 16 Questions Law Firms Should Be Asking About SEO, AI Search and Online Visibility
stories.Summary:
The article, published on 17 November 2026 on the Social Media Butterfly blog, sets out 16 questions law firms should ask about SEO, AI search and online visibility. It was written by an author who says she has worked with law firms of all sizes. She says she has worked with firms whose attorneys have decades of experience, impressive client relationships and extensive publication histories. She says very little of that information appears on their websites. She calls that a missed opportunity as more people turn to AI tools to research legal issues and find lawyers.

The article says a smaller firm with 30 substantive, well-organized pages may perform better for its target searches than a firm with hundreds of generic articles. It names Chambers and Best Lawyers as organizations whose recognition firms should record. It cites New York Labor Law Sections 200, 240 and 241(6), contractual indemnification and risk transfer as topics a construction litigation firm may address on dedicated pages. It says a smaller firm may benefit from concentrating on three to five areas where it has a meaningful track record. It names Google Search Console and website analytics as tools for monitoring organic search impressions, keyword performance, traffic and inquiries.

The author says larger firms have extensive marketing resources and thousands of pages of content, while smaller firms may have only a handful of articles and relatively basic practice descriptions. She says the amount of content a firm publishes is only part of the equation. She says how well that content demonstrates expertise, answers relevant questions and connects to other credible information also matters. She says one of the biggest opportunities she sees is making better use of the experience and content firms already have. She says improving online visibility often starts with documenting accomplishments, strengthening existing pages and creating a more comprehensive picture of what the firm and its attorneys actually do.

The article says attorneys can often reference and link to articles they wrote at previous firms, but republishing the full content may require permission from the copyright owner. It says any description of prior work should accurately identify the attorney's experience and avoid suggesting that matters handled at another firm were handled by the current firm. It says recognition does not automatically improve search rankings or guarantee AI citations. It says different AI search tools use different methods for retrieving and citing information.

It says adding external links simply to increase their number is not an effective SEO strategy. The article says firms should review attorneys' historical articles, client alerts, CLE materials and conference presentations to identify content worth updating, summarizing or linking to. It says a CLE presentation can become an article, a series of FAQs and several LinkedIn posts. It says a webinar can generate a written recap, shorter practice-specific articles and updated content for attorney biographies.

It says an initial project might involve collecting attorneys' publications and credentials, expanding three priority practice pages, updating biographies and creating a centralized archive of news and recognition. It says outside marketing support can help coordinate the work without requiring a large internal team. The article says firms should monitor organic search impressions, relevant keyword performance, website traffic, engagement with priority practice pages and inquiries from prospective clients. It says firms can periodically test how AI-powered search tools describe their capabilities, whether they reference accurate information and which sources they cite.

The text of the article ends mid-sentence in the fifteenth question. The article does not give the sixteenth question. The article gives no figures on results achieved for any firm. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Urban Legend pays right-wing influencers to promote Nvidia chip sales to China and pro-AI articles
stories.Summary:
Urban Legend paid right-wing influencers to promote Nvidia chip sales to China and pro-AI articles. This activity occurred for more than a year and ended on November 10, 2026. Over 80 influencers on X and other platforms received payments for these endorsements. The marketing firm used a network of about 1,400 different campaigns. These efforts boosted the chipmaker and two dark-money groups in the AI industry.

The campaigns promoted Nvidia H200 chip sales to China and open-weights AI. Build American AI is linked to Greg Brockman, Marc Andreessen, and Ben Horowitz. Innovation Council Action is connected to Trump AI Advisor David Sacks and Jordan Schachtel. Lyceum launched on June 9, 2026, and published four tied policy editorials. Trending Politics marked four of five promoted articles as Sponsored or Sponsored Plus.

Urban Legend declined to comment on the investigation into its influencer marketing practices. One influencer, Kaya Jones, posted a referral link asking others to become paid influencers. Another creator, Ash Saves USA, stated she was helping drive traffic to articles. Lyceum claimed that its publication remains editorially independent despite the promoted content. Upward News did not respond to requests for comment regarding its native advertisements.

The campaigns targeted AI doomers and criticized Anthropic and OpenAI for being woke. These efforts aimed to align AI industry narratives with the Trump administration's goals. Influencers like Donald Trump Jr. and Kash Patel stopped posting these links in November 2024. Readers were affected by undisclosed ads that appeared as organic social media posts. Some promoted articles were written by humans while others were likely AI-generated.

Urban Legend used tracking domains like mycreator.studio, registered on May 29, 2021. The firm paid creators per click or action based on a 2023 agreement. Redirects through exc.to were identified by WIRED Magazine as early as 2021. The company recently registered bitlicustom.com after being questioned about its tracking methods. Most campaigns were unrelated to AI and covered a wide range of topics.

The firm continues to use new domains to track conversions for its clients. It remains unclear who specifically paid for the sponsored articles on Trending Politics. The articles do not reveal the total amount of money paid to influencers. It is unknown if other dark-money groups funded these specific AI campaigns. The full list of the 80 influencers has not been disclosed.

stories.Headline: Dell expands its AI Factory with Nvidia and AMD systems to move agentic AI into production
stories.Summary:
Dell announced new additions to its Dell AI Factory with NVIDIA on 16 November 2026, according to IT Brief Australia, extending a portfolio it says now includes more than 420 offerings and serves more than 6,500 customers. Dell Technologies also expanded its Dell AI Factory with new AMD-based infrastructure products spanning servers, modular platforms and rack-scale systems, IT Brief Asia reported on 17 November 2026. The Nvidia announcements focus on four areas: data preparation for AI, management software for AI infrastructure, partner-built validated solutions, and new storage options for large AI workloads. The AMD update includes the Dell PowerEdge M8825 server, new configurations for the Dell AI Platform with AMD, and the AMD Helios Rack-scale Solution from Dell. Dell says the changes are intended to help companies move agentic AI projects from pilot stages into production.

The PowerEdge M8825 is an air-cooled server based on AMD EPYC processors, offering up to 512 cores and 1,024 threads per node for agentic AI and other compute-intensive workloads. Dell expanded its Dell AI Platform with AMD by adding modular configurations built on the PowerEdge XE7745 and R7725 servers, which use AMD Instinct MI350P PCIe GPUs. The AMD Helios Rack-scale Solution can deliver up to 2.9 exaflops of performance with 72 AMD Instinct MI455X GPUs, paired with Dell PowerRack for networking and storage. Dell added Agentic Data Gateway, which in internal testing reduced token consumption by as much as 76% and increased answer accuracy from 60% to 94%. Dell introduced Dell OpenManage Rack Scale, which can manage up to 100,000 devices, up from 8,000 in the previous generation.

Arthur Lewis, President, Infrastructure Solutions Group, Dell Technologies, said AI outcomes do not come from models alone and take data with the right context, infrastructure that scales and solutions validated to work together. Lewis said the Dell AI Factory with NVIDIA is that full-stack foundation, one you own and control, with 6,500 customers already proving it works. Dell said Dell and AMD are giving customers more ways to deploy AI with confidence, whether they are starting small, scaling fast, or going all-in on frontier infrastructure. Dell describes the liquid-cooled storage platform as a 2OU platform supporting up to 32 NVMe drives and designed for file, block, object or parallel file storage. Dell says the 1U platform offers 67% higher drive density per rack unit than the previous generation.

Ashish Nadkarni, Group Vice President and General Manager, Global Domain Lead, Enterprise Infrastructure, IDC, said success increasingly depends on combining trusted data, scalable infrastructure, operational simplicity and ecosystem integration into a repeatable model for AI deployment. Nadkarni said vendors like Dell that help reduce complexity and accelerate time to value will be well positioned to support enterprise AI adoption. Dell says software-defined PowerScale on Dell Exascale has achieved NVIDIA-Certified Storage validation at the Foundation level. Dell says Dell Fabric Manager, in internal lab analysis, could cut Day-2 operational effort by up to 80% while maintaining a fully accurate device inventory. Partners in the latest wave include F5, JFrog, DataRobot, Dynatrace, Ipsotek, Iternal Technologies, Teradata, Aible, Atolio, Maven AGI, OpenAI and ClearML.

Dell is also adding hybrid data pipeline orchestration so pipelines can run where data already sits, including on-premises private clouds, Dell AI Factory with NVIDIA environments, non-Dell systems and public clouds. Other changes include Storage Intelligence and Data Intelligence tools to show data provenance, quality and usage across large file environments, along with a unified data access layer for tables, images, video and documents. Dell says the system can route vectors to existing databases without requiring migration, and cited indexing speeds of up to 12 times faster based on external benchmark data. The platform is also being linked with tools from LangChain, OpenAI, Codex and Unstructured.io. The Enterprise SONiC Distribution by Dell Technologies is being extended to support additional platforms, including the Z9964F-ON and NVIDIA Spectrum SN4700 switches.

The broader architecture also includes modular infrastructure built around Dell PowerStore, Dell PowerEdge XE9785 systems with NVIDIA HGX B300 GPUs, and Dell-supported NVIDIA AI Enterprise software. The expanded AMD platform will include validated support for AMD Enterprise AI Suite, Red Hat OpenShift Container Platform and Red Hat AI Enterprise. Dell says its AI Factory Engineers model brings together teams across platform design, workload delivery, data, governance and security, while its data centre services focus on power, cooling and space planning for AI deployments. Dell says the modular approach lets customers start with a single compute node and add GPUs, nodes, storage or networking as demand grows. Dell said the AMD package is backed by deployment and lifecycle services, giving customers a single supplier for integrated AI infrastructure.

stories.Headline: Ohio bill lets AI data center companies seize private land through eminent domain
stories.Summary:
A leaked bill in Ohio could allow AI data center companies to seize private land. This proposed legislation would use eminent domain law for these buildouts. The news of this potential law surfaced on 18 November 2026. It aims to expand the list of beneficiaries who can take land. This move follows a trend of resisting new data centers in Ohio.

The bill would classify data centers as public utilities to expand eminent domain. Current beneficiaries include municipal corporations, electric cooperatives, and agencies with Federal Energy Regulatory Commission certificates. The leak to WCPO Cincinnati adds agencies with power siting board certificates for transmission lines. This includes facilities for gas pipelines and associated electric transmission line infrastructure. Such changes would allow transmission developers to seize land for data centers.

Legal experts warned that power companies could seize land for data center facilities. The Ohio Business Roundtable trade group recommended these changes to lawmakers in June. They suggested extending possession authority to energy infrastructure projects once necessity is established. The government can delegate this land grabbing power to common carriers or private entities. Owners must receive appropriate compensation when the government takes land for public use.

Residents in Georgia were affected when a utility company removed 30 residential properties. These people claimed the grid upgrade was intended to power nearby AI data centers. In Nashville, the Metro Council used eminent domain to block a data center. They aimed to stop a 69,220 square foot facility next to a zoo. This action blocked a local developer from completing a 700 million dollar buildout.

A July 2026 report showed the government seized private land for transmission lines. These lines were needed to provide power for new AI data centers. Eminent domain allows the government to take land without the owner's consent. This power is granted as long as the land is for public use. The law allows the delegation of this power to utility companies.

The leaked bill must now progress through the legislative process to become law. It remains unclear if the Ohio government will officially adopt these specific changes. The articles do not state if the bill has a formal number. There is no information on when a final vote will occur. The text leaves the ultimate fate of the proposed legislation open.

stories.Headline: ERCOT audits large data centers and files grid reports with Texas regulators by December 10
stories.Summary:
The Electric Reliability Council of Texas will file reports on large data centers by December 10, 2026. This audit follows a directive from Governor Greg Abbott to verify projects waiting for grid connections. The process targets data centers and crypto mines to ensure they meet specific state requirements. The Public Utility Commission of Texas will then meet on December 17 to review these findings. This review occurs during a transition of power before a new governor takes office in January.

The Batch Zero process sorts projects of 75 MW or more into three distinct categories. On September 3, ERCOT placed 204 projects totaling 66.4 GW in the base load tier. It put 158 projects totaling 127.9 GW in the studied tier and excluded 373 projects totaling 302.2 GW. The audit examines water reuse, ownership, and whether projects provide their own power or pay their own way. It also includes a community impact review for facilities of 25 MW and above.

Governor Greg Abbott ordered the audit to ensure that failing projects are denied a grid connection. He also told the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality to stop processing permits on September 21. Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, a Democrat taking office January 19, 2027, said she would keep approvals frozen. She intends to maintain this moratorium until the Texas Legislature passes new protections for the state. ERCOT general counsel Chad Seely stated the study will miss its April 9, 2027, deadline.

Developers like Skybox Datacenters and Mesquite H2 filed complaints at the commission over their project classifications. Power producers such as NRG Energy and Vistra saw shares fall 14 percent after the recent election. Jefferies analysts noted that slower data center arrivals could lower wholesale power prices for Texas consumers. CoreWeave chief executive Michael Intrator wrote to Hinojosa asking for the responsible completion of permitted projects. These changes affect a pipeline of 474 GW, which is five times the record peak demand.

The Batch Zero process began in June 2026 through a planning guide rule change called PGRR 145. This system was created because data center power requests outran the ability of the operator to study them. Texas currently holds about 23 percent of all planned data center capacity in the United States. The current freeze affects 17 large loads that had completed stability studies and expected to come online. Some developers continue to file projects, including an 8 billion dollar building by Integra in Quanah.

The Public Utility Commission has not committed to acting on the reports during its December 17 meeting. It remains unclear when the Batch Zero process will officially restart or when the permit freeze ends. The Texas Legislature will convene in January 2027 to consider bills that could repeal industry sales tax exemptions. Lawmakers may also introduce requirements for data centers to obtain specific permits from the commission. ERCOT has not yet proposed a new date to complete the delayed Batch Zero study.

stories.Headline: Democratic majorities in Congress push for AI laws targeting data centers and model safety
stories.Summary:
The new Democratic majorities in Congress will likely press for various AI laws. These lawmakers seek to regulate data centers, frontier model safety, and cybersecurity. They also want to protect workers' welfare, civil rights, and national security. These efforts follow midterm elections where AI concerns played a seminal role. Some legislation may move during the lame-duck session to restrict chip exports.

Sen. Mark Warner introduced the Data Center Tax Accountability and Disclosure Act in July 2026. Rep. Greg Landsman introduced the No Harm Data Centers Act in April 2026. In September 2026, Sen. Shelley Moore Capito introduced the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act. The Senate voted 73 to 25 on November 9 to advance that act. Rep. Jay Obernolte introduced the FRONTIER Act in June 2026 for model safety.

Sen. Mark Warner proposed the SAFE AI Act and the AI AGENT Act. He also suggested the National Workforce Transition Fund and the PHD Talent Act. Rep. Jay Obernolte said developers must take specific steps to ensure model safety. Rep. Ayanna Pressley urged Democrats to prioritize the AI Civil Rights Act. The Congressional Black Caucus vowed to ensure civil rights protections in AI laws.

Voters are affected, as 56 percent cited AI as a major voting factor. Over 40 ballot measures to restrict data centers were passed by these voters. Rep.-elect William Lawrence campaigned on opposing local data center development and pausing AI. Rep.-elect Manny Rutinel campaigned on requiring notice before AI-driven layoffs at large employers. Rep.-elect Scott Wiener proposed reviving the U.S. Digital Service to advise federal agencies.

Public perception of data centers is negative regarding environmental and energy impacts. Recent AI agent-enabled cyber breaches have increased the focus on cybersecurity issues. Competition with China remains a high priority for national security and AI policy. Some lawmakers want to prevent the release of AI superintelligence and recursive self-improvement. Others seek to protect critical infrastructure from quantum computing and foreign national security adversaries.

Congress may include the AI Overwatch Act in the National Defense Authorization Act. This would require licenses for the export and transfer of certain integrated circuits. The Chip Security Act is another bill that may be included in that act. The articles leave the scope and timing of laws uncertain due to divided government. It remains to be seen which specific proposals can actually become federal law.

stories.Headline: Mullin says AI superintelligence may have caused Microsoft, bank and airline outages
stories.Summary:
Major technology disruptions hit Microsoft, several large banks, and the aviation industry throughout the week ending November 17, 2026. These outages affected core Microsoft 365 services including Teams, Outlook, Exchange Online, and Copilot across 74 different countries. On Friday, the Federal Aviation Administration grounded flights nationwide for over four hours due to instability in legacy equipment. Customers of Capital One, U.S. Bank, Wells Fargo, Bank of America, and Chase reported banking outages on Monday.

The situation requires an investigation into how rapidly advancing artificial intelligence might overwhelm older systems that cannot keep pace. Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin noted that a technology expert suggested superintelligence could be responsible for these events. He explained that AI programs capable of writing code might create a ripple effect when they attempt to self-fix. On November 14, officials from the FAA and the Transportation Department stated the aviation issues were not connected to the new SMART AI system.

Secretary Mullin told Fox News that he is 98 percent certain a cyberattack did not cause the disruptions. He argued that there are no footprints of an attack and no one has claimed responsibility for the events. Conversely, former national security adviser Michael Flynn suggested on social media that the patterns were suspicious and looked like a massive cyberattack. President Donald Trump dismissed the concerns on Tuesday, stating that such things happen when organizations are big and powerful.

stories.Headline: Toxicologist Thomas Hartung argues AI biological twins need agreed validation standards before regulators trust them
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is transforming biological digital twins across every level of biological organization, according to a theoretical analysis by toxicologist Thomas Hartung published in Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence and reported by bioengineer.org on November 18, 2026. The analysis examines how deep learning, transformer architectures, foundation models, and physics-informed neural networks have elevated biological simulation beyond static systems of differential equations. Biological digital twins maintain internal states coupled to physical counterparts through continuous data assimilation rather than functioning as generic classifiers or open-loop simulations. Across five nested scales, from single-cell multi-omics to the environmental exposures of entire populations, these architectures show capacity to model human biology without surrogate animal species. Hartung argues that technical ingenuity alone cannot secure regulatory trust without agreed credibility standards, independent prospective testing, and formal governance of self-updating algorithms.

The analysis establishes four foundational commitments that exclude conventional simulations, software dashboards, and static pattern predictors. A biological digital twin demands specificity, binding its computational state to a distinct biological instance such as a single patient or an individual organ-on-chip rather than an average population category. It requires continuous data assimilation, an iterative loop where telemetry, biosensor readings, or longitudinal omics samples update the model to track physical drift over time. The twin must encode mechanistic constraints from biological principles rather than statistical correlations alone, and it demands empirical testability with refutable predictions and quantified uncertainty. Representations lacking any criterion, including frozen neural networks, open-loop simulations, or decorative avatars, fail this definition and cannot serve as dependable regulatory instruments.

At the cellular level, representation learning and foundation models fuse multimodal single-cell measurements into dynamic latent manifolds. Single-cell foundation models such as Geneformer, scGPT, and scFoundation learn compressed representations across tens of millions of cellular profiles, separating technical batch artifacts from genuine biological signals. This manifold enables virtual perturbation experiments simulating cellular trajectory shifts under novel pharmacological compounds, gene knockouts, or environmental toxicants. In exploratory toxicology, virtual cells reorder experimental pipelines, nominating informative hypotheses for bench testing while reducing reliance on early rodent toxicity screens and primary animal cell cultures. General foundation models serve as shared infrastructure rather than digital twins until conditioned on specific cell populations and coupled to incoming experimental data.

At the in vitro level, computational twins model engineered cell cultures, microfluidic devices, and organoids, which Hartung identifies as the most technologically mature tier. The DigiLoCS liver-on-chip framework separates intracellular metabolism, passive permeability, and compartment partitioning, predicting clinical drug clearance distributions more accurately than conventional lumped single-compartment methods. Emerging organoid twins incorporate biophysical priors and active learning to forecast therapeutic responses and drug resistance in patient-derived cancer tissues, offering alternatives to patient-derived xenograft rodent models. Coupled with laboratory automation, closed-loop organoid systems can predict responses, execute robotic perturbations, and update internal states within hours. Mathematical unidentifiability, where multiple unmeasured parameter combinations yield identical observable outputs, remains a persistent challenge requiring targeted, standardized physical measurements rather than algorithmic expansion alone.

At the organ level, digital twins confront fluid dynamics, biomechanics, barrier transport, and electrical propagation across anatomical structures. Investigators deploy physics-informed neural networks to bypass the computational cost of traditional finite-element modeling without large-animal studies in dogs or pigs. By penalizing violations of physical conservation laws within loss functions, these networks act as rapid surrogate models executing organ-scale biomechanical simulations in near-real time while maintaining physical plausibility outside training domains. A three-organ microphysiological platform linking gut, liver, and placental tissues investigates maternal-fetal pharmacokinetics during pregnancy, addressing conditions where animal testing routinely misleads because reproductive toxicity and placental transfer diverge sharply between rodent models and humans. Derived from the Virtual Physiological Human tradition, these hybrid architectures integrate mechanistic physical principles with machine learning for auditable, trustworthy organ-scale safety assessments.

At the individual patient level, the Virtual Human Twin integrates multimodal health records, wearable telemetry, high-resolution imaging, and personal omics into an individualized clinical forecast. Personal twins enable clinicians to compare therapeutic regimens, evaluate dosing schedules, and anticipate adverse drug reactions in silico prior to clinical administration. In cardiology, personalized models calibrated to patient-specific electrophysiology and anatomical imaging have simulated arrhythmic activation pathways to guide catheter ablation procedures before surgery. In oncology, hybrid twins simulating tumor microenvironments assist clinicians in navigating heterogeneous malignancies without relying on animal xenografts.

The review cautions against hype surrounding all-encompassing digital human replicas claiming to forecast a patient's entire lifespan, noting that current clinical twins are narrow decision-support instruments that must contend with data harmonization challenges, physiological drift across aging, and algorithmic biases disadvantaging underrepresented demographic populations. At the population level, digital twins aggregate individual profiles to analyze community disease dynamics, conduct in silico clinical trials, and evaluate environmental hazards across the human exposome. While genetics reveals inherited susceptibility, the exposome maps the modifiable totality of environmental exposures including diet, occupational chemicals, and airborne pollutants. Exposome twins link external exposure monitoring, biokinetic internal dose modeling, molecular pathway alterations, and clinical endpoints to guide precision prevention strategies rather than producing unverified correlations.

Statistical mining and generative modeling of historical control databases enable virtual control groups for toxicity studies, curtailing the sacrifice of concurrent control animals, an application recognized in a March 2026 draft qualification opinion from the European Medicines Agency regarding non-Good Laboratory Practice rat dose-range-finding studies. In human trials, synthetic cohorts extend clinical evaluations into hard-to-enroll populations such as pregnant women or rare-disease patients, provided researchers apply rigorous counterfactual reasoning and target-trial emulation to prevent confounding and spurious certainty. Despite computational demonstrations across all five biological scales, the review stresses that independent scientific validation and regulatory credibility, not algorithmic novelty, represent the binding constraints on the discipline. Most published twin frameworks remain retrospective demonstrations conducted by original developers rather than prospectively verified methods evaluated across independent laboratories.

Because biological digital twins are inherently adaptive systems that continuously assimilate fresh data and update internal parameters, traditional validation frameworks treating assays as frozen, one-time tests are structurally inadequate. Hartung advocates next-generation validation, an iterative and risk-proportionate methodology evaluating methods across five dimensions: technical reliability, biological relevance, predictive performance, applicability domain, and data integrity. Twin credibility must be assessed against human-relevant biological mechanisms rather than concordance with historical animal tests, which themselves frequently suffer from poor reproducibility and limited predictive accuracy for human outcomes, and validation must operate as an ongoing, modular case-building process evaluating mechanistic backbones and adaptive learned components independently. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Tokenomics Foundation launches as Linux Foundation project to set open AI cost standards
stories.Summary:
The Tokenomics Foundation launched in August 2026 as a project of the Linux Foundation, working alongside the FinOps Foundation, which did the same job for cloud spending, according to a November 18, 2026 opinion piece by Raul Leite in InfoWorld. Its members include large AI buyers such as banks and retailers, plus cloud and model providers, and it does not sell a product or ship a cost-tracking tool. Instead it acts as a standards body whose working groups publish open, vendor-neutral definitions, so everyone means the same thing by input, output, reasoning and cached tokens, and standards for cost data that mainly extend FOCUS, the FinOps billing format, so AI providers report usage in the same way. The actual measuring is done by tools on the market, like AI gateways and observability platforms, and the Foundation's job is to make sure they all speak the same language.

The piece defines AI tokenomics as the practice of managing that economy and connecting the cost structure to business outcomes, noting that one token is roughly 4 characters, or 0.75 words, in English, and that the term has nothing to do with crypto, where it means the supply and incentives of a coin. Leite describes a stack mapping everything that shapes the cost of an AI answer, from energy and hardware at the bottom through infrastructure management, inference, model selection, and access and control, to demand at the top, and says its value is showing where to look before you start cutting. He also presents Big-T, an idea like Big-O notation in programming, describing how fast token use grows as more people use an app, including agent-multiplied growth where agents spawn other agents and calls pile up fast, and unbounded growth where a loop with no exit runs until someone pulls the plug. The key insight, he writes, is that the multiplier is usually invisible, since a user asks one question and the app makes five or 10 calls behind the scenes.

Leite, a principal solution architect at Red Hat who says the views are his own, writes that token prices keep falling but AI bills keep rising, because cheaper tokens lead teams to build bigger systems with longer conversations, more documents per question and agents calling agents. He says the big savings usually come from the middle and the top of the stack, using a smaller model for simple tasks, caching repeated work and sending less context, and he advises asking of every workflow how many model calls one user request really triggers. He sums up the Foundation's mission as moving AI from experimental spending to accountable operations, since most organizations cannot connect their AI spend to an outcome their CFO would accept, and says it wants to fix that by building open standards, benchmarks and a shared language. The goal, he writes, is not just about making AI cheaper but about making it worth it.

stories.Headline: Dental hygienists Dryer and Fisher write that AI enhances radiographs and charting but cannot replace clinical judgment
stories.Summary:
Marianne Dryer, MEd, RDH, and Andrea Fisher, MSML, RDH, wrote an article published by RDH on Nov. 17, 2026, about artificial intelligence in clinical dental hygiene practice. The article says AI can enhance radiographic interpretation and help hygienists identify periodontal changes more consistently. It says visual AI tools can make complex findings easier for patients to understand, supporting codiagnosis and treatment acceptance. It says voice-assisted charting and integrated AI can strengthen documentation, workflow efficiency, and longitudinal periodontal monitoring. The article says dental hygienists make hundreds of clinical decisions every day that influence patient outcomes.

The article says advanced imaging platforms can detect subtle changes in crestal bone height, quantify radiographic bone loss, and compare findings over time. It says accurate classification still depends on clinical attachment level, probing depths, bleeding on probing, recession, furcation involvement, mobility, medical history, and an understanding of disease activity. It says studies show less than 16% of periodontal charts are recorded to completion. It says bleeding on probing affecting 30% or more of the mouth is consistent with generalized moderate gingivitis. It says concerns about insurance coverage and reimbursement often limit use of the preventive CDT code 4346 for scaling in the presence of generalized moderate to severe gingival inflammation.

The article says the dental hygienist remains responsible for interpreting findings within the context of the patient's clinical presentation, risk factors, and overall health. It says AI should never be viewed as a substitute for comprehensive periodontal assessment. It says AI can identify patterns and highlight areas of concern but cannot independently determine etiology, classify disease, or establish an individualized treatment plan. It says comprehensive periodontal assessment, classification, patient education, treatment planning, and clinical judgment remain the responsibility of the dental hygienist. It says AI does not determine treatment or coding.

The article says AI bridges a communication gap by converting complex diagnostic information into clear, visual representations. It says color overlays, highlighted areas of bone loss, and side-by-side comparisons of previous radiographs transform abstract findings into meaningful conversations. It says patients are more likely to accept treatment when they understand what clinicians see. It says incomplete records may affect diagnostic consistency, treatment planning, communication among providers, and insurance reimbursement. It says AI-assisted radiographic interpretation, along with comprehensive depiction of CAL and disease activity, will support early coverage for D4341 and D4342, nonsurgical scaling and root planing.

The article says AI is far more than a technology trend and is an emerging clinical tool. It says AI's greatest value lies not in replacing clinical expertise but in enhancing it. It says some AI platforms function as standalone applications that analyze radiographs or identify patterns of disease. It says others are fully integrated into practice management and imaging systems, allowing clinicians to access AI-generated insights without disrupting their clinical workflow. It says one of the fastest-growing applications is voice-assisted AI.

The article says dental hygienists should consider how technology supports patient care, documentation, and communication rather than asking which AI platform is best. It says the most valuable systems integrate seamlessly into existing workflows, improve efficiency without increasing administrative burden, and enhance rather than replace clinical decision-making. It says AI should simplify the clinician's day while strengthening the patient experience. The article ends mid-sentence in the text provided, at voice-enabled periodontal charting. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Epic asks court to order Apple to produce 122,000 withheld documents and impose daily fines
stories.Summary:
Epic Games asked a federal judge on Nov. 13, 2026, to order Apple to hand over more than 122,000 internal documents that Epic says Apple is withholding as irrelevant, and to fine Apple for every day it fails to comply after Dec. 2, 2026, according to a motion filed in the US District Court for the Northern District of California. Epic says agreed search terms were run on the files of seven Apple custodians, four of them the executives Apple identified as decision makers on the fee (Tim Cook, Eddy Cue, Carson Oliver and chief financial officer Kevan Parekh) and three others (Nate Barton, Alex Roman and Phil Schiller). Apple produced 632 documents from those seven custodians, 157 of them from the four decision makers, and is withholding more than 122,000 on claims they are not responsive, which Epic says is roughly 99.14% of the documents directly hit by the search terms. The terms included case words such as "proffer," "contempt," "injunction" and "link-out," and Epic says Apple produced nearly 27,000 documents from the same custodians or their predecessors during the earlier contempt proceeding.

According to the filing, Apple's production contains no App Store profit-and-loss statements, no internal analysis of the financial impact of the proposed commissions, and no data supporting Apple's statement that its incremental link-out costs are "essentially zero." Epic says Apple told it in meet-and-confers that the terms mostly returned press releases, analyst reports and other irrelevant material, and that Apple maintains its relevance review was proper. Epic asks the court to order Apple to produce all non-privileged documents that hit the agreed terms by Dec. 2, 2026, one week after Apple's Nov. 25 deadline to substantially complete production, irrespective of any relevance or responsiveness assessment, so Epic can review them itself, though Apple could still withhold privileged material. Epic also asks for a daily monetary sanction for each day Apple fails to comply after Dec. 2, 2026, without proposing a figure.

A hearing on the motion had been set for Nov. 24 before Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers, but 9to5Mac reported that a new order, not yet public, refers the discovery dispute to a magistrate judge and terminates the related deadlines and hearings. Apple's response was not included in the filing or the 9to5Mac report. The documents relate to Apple's Aug. 13, 2026 proposal for the commission it may charge on linked-out purchases, which 9to5Mac reported ranges from 5% to 15%, and which the Ninth Circuit sent back to Judge Gonzalez Rogers to decide.

Judge Gonzalez Rogers ruled in 2021 that Apple's anti-steering rules violated California's Unfair Competition Law and barred it from stopping developers from linking to outside purchase options, and in 2025 she held Apple in civil contempt and barred any commission on linked-out purchases. The Ninth Circuit upheld the contempt finding but sent back the question of what commission, if any, Apple may charge. Epic has separately asked the Supreme Court to uphold the contempt ruling, and its filing cites the earlier proceeding, in which the court found Apple's privilege over-designation intentional and sanctioned it, as evidence that Apple cannot be trusted to fix the problem through its own re-review.

stories.Headline: Atturra forum speakers urge schools to set clear AI boundaries and limit data exposure
stories.Summary:
Atturra hosted an education forum in Sydney on the use of technology in schools, and speakers said schools need to adopt digital tools carefully as AI and cyber risks reshape teaching, administration and parent engagement. The forum focused on how schools are managing rising expectations from teachers, students and families while under pressure to improve efficiency and protect sensitive data. Discussion covered AI in classrooms, cybersecurity, administrative systems and the challenge of ensuring smaller schools can keep pace with change. Brett Auton, Director of Scholarion at Atturra, said schools were being forced to think more strategically about technology decisions across teaching, risk management and communication. The forum was reported by IT Brief Australia on 18 November 2026.

Speakers said institutions should not treat AI as a neutral tool and must set clear boundaries around its role in learning. Dr Joseph Sweeney, Adviser at IBRS, said some schools may increasingly consider replacing large external technology platforms with sovereign AI tools built for their own environments, although he suggested that option would be more realistic for better-resourced institutions. According to the Australian Education Technology Industry Association, K-12 schools spent an estimated AUD $3.2 billion on education technology products and services in 2025, up 28 per cent since 2023. Barrett said Microsoft's data shows more than 15,000 emails containing malicious QR codes are aimed at the education sector every day. Auton said schools needed to examine what information they hold, who can access it, how long it is retained, and their exposure to third-party providers.

Auton said school leaders need to understand the strategic implications, teachers need to understand how technology will support their work, and students and parents need confidence that information is being handled appropriately. Sweeney said schools must keep teachers firmly in charge rather than letting software act as a moral authority or companion, and must safeguard kids against manipulative, addictive algorithms. Sweeney said AI should prompt students to think rather than simply hand over answers, and that if ungoverned it has the potential to be even more damaging to children's cognitive development and learning than social media has been. Lee Barrett, AI Education and Advocacy Lead at Catholic Education Network, said teachers are entitled to ask for the evidence and parents are entitled to understand what their children are using and why.

Vivek Puthucode, General Manager of Microsoft Elevate Asia, said the question is no longer whether students should learn to use AI but how we equip them to use it wisely, safely and creatively. Barrett said schools are working incredibly hard but are up against a lot, and that education is consistently among the most targeted sectors. Puthucode said success in the age of AI won't be measured by how much technology we put into classrooms but by how much more time educators have to teach and how well we protect the trust that students, families and communities place in schools. Auton said knowing and limiting your exposure is becoming the main game in town, which means understanding what information you hold, reducing unnecessary duplication, reviewing who has access to it, challenging how long you retain it, and being much more deliberate about the systems and providers you use.

Auton said simplifying admissions, improving communication with families, removing duplicate data entry and making student information easier to access can deliver significant value across a school. Barrett said when a new staff member logs in on day one and everything they need is already connected, that is back-office technology doing its job well, and when a teacher in a remote school gets the same reliable network and tools as one in the city, that is equity. Auton said strong core platforms, reliable data, cybersecurity, integration capabilities and the skills needed to use technology effectively are the foundations that allow schools to take advantage of new capabilities as they emerge. Puthucode said the real value of AI in education isn't simply about saving time but about how we reinvest that time, and that by reducing administrative burdens we can help educators focus more of their energy on improving learning, supporting student wellbeing, and helping young people thrive.

Speakers warned that smaller schools may struggle to keep up with emerging technology because of cost and limited internal expertise. Sweeney said pooling resources lets schools access sovereign AI platforms, negotiate better vendor terms and share specialist teachers remotely across campuses so students don't miss out. Auton said schools shouldn't need to become technology companies to operate effectively, and that standardised platforms, cloud-based services, shared capabilities and repeatable implementation approaches can all help reduce the cost and complexity of adopting modern technology. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Bank chiefs and NSA tell Congress that AI-found patches cause outages
stories.Summary:
Wall Street executives and the National Security Agency told members of Congress that this week's widespread technology outages were caused by attempts to fix vulnerabilities that artificial intelligence had identified, according to three sources familiar with the private conversations. Over the last few days the country faced a series of startling tech failures, including a pause in all flights nationwide, customers being unable to access their bank accounts, and a highly classified communications network at the National Security Agency going down. While the disruptions do not appear to have been caused by a cyberattack, government and banking officials told lawmakers that they stem from efforts to fix cyber defense gaps found by AI models, and those fixes temporarily overwhelmed the systems. On Monday banks such as JP Morgan Chase blamed software-related bugs for the service issues, and on Tuesday the NSA said scheduled routine maintenance was responsible for the temporary degradation of some of its networks. The outages carried costs and raised questions the articles leave partly open.

The Federal Aviation Administration canceled more than 20,000 flights as a result of the nationwide ground stop, according to The Wall Street Journal, and Microsoft experienced a major outage of Outlook, which Microsoft blamed on a technical defect. It is also unclear what caused the FAA systems to go down. One congressional official briefed on the matter said the models are identifying massive vulnerabilities, which increases the urgency to patch right away, and that agencies are trying to push through a lot of patches all at once, more than the system was designed for. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin told CNBC on Tuesday that new technology is being pushed on top of really old computer systems and it just seems to overwhelm the system, and he predicted the country will see more of this as new technology rolls out. Nathan Calvin, the chief strategy officer at Encode, said there is some sense in which this is reassuring because it means there is not an attack, but it shows the extent to which safety critical infrastructure relies on software with large vulnerabilities on legacy systems.

He said updating those will be a rocky process and, as more advanced models arrive, this will not be a one and done thing because more vulnerabilities will continue to be found. The NSA did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Powerful companies and government agencies have increasingly trained the most powerful AI models on themselves to identify vulnerabilities that others may weaponize against them, and once gaps are found they face immense pressure to patch them quickly, knowing malicious actors have access to comparable AI tools or will soon. That urgency has driven a wide range of public and private actors to rush fixes faster than they normally would, the sources said, but even entities with large resources, such as the nation's top banks and the intelligence community, are finding it difficult to do so without accidentally causing outages. The sources spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe private conversations.

stories.Headline: FTC investigates ISS and Glass Lewis over proxy advice competition
stories.Summary:
The articles report that in November 2025 the FTC launched a formal antitrust investigation into ISS and Glass Lewis, focusing on their ESG-related recommendations and questioning whether the duopoly constitutes unfair competition. The following month President Trump signed Executive Order 14366, which directed the SEC to review its regulatory regime as applied to proxy advisors' recommendations. The order also directed the DOL to examine the ERISA fiduciary duty implications of proxy advisors advancing non-financial or political agendas. It further directed the FTC to investigate, in concert with the Department of Justice, potential federal antitrust violations or unfair methods of competition or deceptive practices. On July 1, 2025, the D.C. Circuit unanimously held in ISS v. SEC that proxy voting advice does not constitute a "solicitation" under Section 14(a) of the Exchange Act.

In April 2026 the DOL issued a technical release clarifying that proxy advisory firms whose advice reaches ERISA-covered plans may be ERISA fiduciaries. On August 5, 2026, the DOJ's Antitrust Division withdrew the 1987 Business Review Letter it had issued to ISS, concluding the Letter is not applicable to ISS's current business practices. The Antitrust Division pointed to the concentration of the proxy advisory market, with ISS and Glass Lewis together controlling more than 90% of the market, as a further competition concern. Texas led with Senate Bill 2337, effective September 1, 2025, requiring proxy advisors to disclose their reliance on "nonfinancial factors" and to deliver adverse recommendations to the subject company at the same time they are provided to clients. Kansas enacted the Proxy Advisor Transparency Act in April 2026 and Indiana enacted HB 1273 in March 2026, and Kentucky and Oklahoma enacted similar statutes later in 2026.

The Texas Attorney General investigated ISS in September 2025 under the state's deceptive trade practices and fiduciary duty theories. Florida sued ISS in November 2025, alleging that undisclosed ESG-driven recommendations misled clients and breached duties owed to them. Four states filed coordinated lawsuits in May 2026 advancing similar consumer protection and fiduciary claims alongside alleged violations of the new disclosure statutes. Several state attorneys general and legislators have characterized the proxy advisory duopoly as a "proxy advisory cartel" whose market power distorts governance and imposes politically motivated agendas on American businesses. On July 24, 2025, both ISS and Glass Lewis filed lawsuits in the Western District of Texas challenging SB 2337 on multiple constitutional grounds.

On August 29, 2025, a Western District court granted preliminary injunctions blocking enforcement against both firms. The firms subsequently obtained injunctions against the Kansas and Indiana statutes in June 2026 and against the Oklahoma statute on October 31, 2026. ISS declared that the Texas ruling "safeguard core First Amendment principles." The proxy advisory firms' arguments rest on three constitutional theories: that proxy voting recommendations are protected speech, that the statutes compel speech and discriminate based on viewpoint, and that the statutes burden interstate commerce in violation of the dormant Commerce Clause. Courts have found these theories persuasive enough to grant preliminary relief, and the viewpoint discrimination challenge has drawn the most attention and signals the statutes may be vulnerable on constitutional grounds.

For over three decades, Institutional Shareholder Services Inc. (ISS) and Glass, Lewis and Co., LLC (Glass Lewis) have occupied a singular position in American corporate governance through their advice to institutional investors on how to vote their shares in public companies. Their influence has extended to areas such as board composition, executive compensation, shareholder rights and anti-takeover defenses. The most viable federal path for regulation now runs through the Investment Advisers Act of 1940, where ISS is already registered and Glass Lewis is reportedly moving toward registration. The SEC's recent proposed rule amending the filer status framework would exempt Non-Accelerated Filers with a public float of less than USD2 billion from say-on-pay, say-on-frequency and say-on-golden-parachute votes. If the USD2bn cut-off is adopted, which the authors expect it will be, 81% of current public companies would be classified as NAFs, with all newly public companies retaining NAF status for at least five years post-IPO regardless of float size.

In November 2026 the SEC proposed rules to revise the executive compensation disclosure requirements, which if adopted will significantly reduce executive compensation-related disclosure. The articles state that AI may pose the greatest threat to the proxy advisors' business model, forcing the question of whether independent proxy advice remains necessary at all. The premise underlying the dominance of ISS and Glass Lewis has always been one of practical necessity, because institutional investors managing thousands of investments cannot independently research and formulate voting decisions. The articles leave open whether, when the dust settles, proxy advisors will remain influential or whether proxy advice will become more regulated, fragmented and technology-driven. The articles note that the injunctions are interim victories and the merits remain to be finally litigated.

stories.Headline: US governors implement diverse AI regulations and data center policies
stories.Summary:
Various US governors and governor-elects implemented diverse AI regulations and data center policies during the 2026 midterm election cycle. These leaders took varied approaches to the AI boom and the infrastructure needed to power it. Some officials viewed the technology as an economic opportunity, while others focused on safety and regulation. The debate included issues like deepfakes, environmental impacts, and the rapid expansion of data centers. Voters decided if these issues would play a role in the outcome of the elections.

California governor-elect Xavier Becerra proposed expanding AI literacy and using AI for government audit and transparency tasks. Outgoing California Governor Gavin Newsom and New York Governor Kathy Hochul explored an AI kill switch to disable advanced systems. In 2025, Alabama Governor Kay Ivey banned Chinese platforms DeepSeek and Manus from state devices and networks. Colorado's new bill on automated tools takes effect January 1, 2027, after Governor Jared Polis repealed Senate Bill 24-205. Delaware Governor Matt Meyer signed legislation in 2025 launching an AI regulatory sandbox for corporate and health technologies.

Governor Kay Ivey stated that generative AI is a monumental step for government service but requires careful study. Governor Sarah Huckabee Sanders wrote that Arkansas cannot afford to be left behind as AI changes how people work. Governor Matt Meyer described his regulatory sandbox as a way to combine innovation with transparency and public trust. Governor Ron DeSantis wrote that his AI Bill of Rights defends Florida families and children from potential harms. Governor Katie Hobbs described her goal as ensuring AI strengthens rather than undermines the state economy.

Local residents pushed back against data center projects over potential energy costs and environmental impacts. Goldman Sachs economists predict Democratic wins may lead to short-term moratoria affecting 45 percent of planned US capacity. Alaska governor-elect Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins supports a temporary moratorium until developers cover their own energy and infrastructure costs. Alabama governor-elect Tommy Tuberville also campaigned for developers to pay their own electricity, water, and infrastructure costs. Florida governor-elect Byron Donalds believes local governments should decide if data center facilities belong in their towns.

The AI boom has slowly become a flash point in US politics across the political spectrum. Governor Mike Dunleavy argued that Alaska has an arctic advantage that reduces cooling costs for server racks. Governor Sarah Huckabee Sanders joined RAISE US, an initiative launched by Eric Holcomb and Gina Raimondo. Governor Jared Polis previously signed a consumer-protection law in 2024 to stop AI-driven algorithmic discrimination. Governor Ned Lamont launched the third phase of the Tech Talent Accelerator in February to expand AI education.

Governor-elect Phil Weiser suggested that former coal towns could be potential areas for geothermal-powered data centers. Governor Katie Hobbs created an AI steering committee in 2025 and launched a government tool in 2026. Governor Ron DeSantis signed a bill to prevent residents from paying for hyperscale data centers through utility bills. Governor Sarah Huckabee Sanders urged Congress to remove the AI regulatory moratorium from the One, Big, Beautiful Bill. The articles leave open how federal action will evolve as states move ahead with their own rules.

stories.Headline: Florida House speaker urges quick action on AI as Senate president prioritizes affordability
stories.Summary:
Florida’s Legislature opened its new term with the House speaker urging lawmakers to move quickly on artificial intelligence, while the Senate president put affordability at the top of his agenda. Both leaders took office with a $12 billion question hanging over local budgets after voters approved a sweeping property tax cut. The Jacksonville Business Journal reported the opening on November 18, 2026, and noted that a new Florida House panel will focus on AI and digital security. The same report pointed to related action on Amendment 3, which state leaders had delayed in special session.

The property tax cut approved by voters leaves local governments facing a $12 billion gap, and the article ties that figure directly to the budgets the new term must address. The House speaker wants fast movement on AI, and a new House panel will focus on AI and digital security. The Senate president’s priority is affordability, which the article places at the top of his agenda. The report also lists related coverage on flying cars taking another step forward in Florida, without giving further detail.

Responsibility sits with the new House speaker and the Senate president, who each set a priority as the term began. The speaker urged lawmakers to move quickly on AI, and the Senate president put affordability first. The article does not name either leader or give direct quotations beyond those paraphrased positions. It also does not say what specific AI legislation the speaker wants or what affordability measures the Senate president supports.

The context is a term opening under the weight of the voter-approved property tax cut and its $12 billion effect on local budgets. The article notes that Florida leaders had delayed a special session on Amendment 3, and that Governor DeSantis had called a special session on the property tax cut. What happens next is not detailed beyond the speaker’s call for speed on AI and the Senate president’s affordability focus. The article gives no timeline for legislation, no vote counts and no further statements from either leader.

stories.Headline: Hong Kong Monetary Authority explores agentic AI to detect crypto financial crime
stories.Summary:
The Hong Kong Monetary Authority began exploring the use of agentic AI to monitor crypto asset transactions on Tuesday, November 18, 2026. Executive Director Raymond Chan announced this initiative during a speech at a workshop hosted by the central bank to combat money laundering. This new technology aims to analyze both onchain transfers and offchain customer transactions to identify anomalies. The system would specifically flag rapid fund layering that occurs when users switch between cryptocurrency and fiat money.

This approach requires integrating blockchain analytics, scam intelligence, and customer due diligence into a single on-chain AI agent. Such a system would allow for the monitoring of suspicious wallets and the rapid freezing of illicit funds. Raymond Chan noted that illicit addresses received over 150 billion dollars in 2025, with stablecoins making up 84 percent of those transactions. He also highlighted the Virtual Asset Intelligence Taskforce, which was established in November 2025 to strengthen these efforts.

Raymond Chan stated that the central bank wants to make financial crime monitoring more effective and efficient through AI. He explained that criminal networks use digital assets for human trafficking and fraud because of their global reach and pseudonymity. Chan admitted that no single tool provides complete protection, so the city must rely on multi-layered safeguards. He noted that the primary challenge is quickly linking digital wallet activities to real-world identities to stop funds from disappearing.

The Virtual Asset Intelligence Taskforce treats crypto crime as an ecosystem issue involving regulators, law enforcement, and trading platforms. This public-private group includes the Hong Kong police, the Customs and Excise Department, and the Securities and Futures Commission. By collaborating with licensed crypto trading platforms, the task force has already improved the quality of intelligence. These agencies continue to work together to strengthen the prevention and detection of crimes across the entire digital asset landscape.

stories.Headline: Chinese bottle-cap manufacturer challenges AI automation hype at Shanghai conference
stories.Summary:
Zhu Shihui, a manufacturer of bottle caps, presented a critical perspective on artificial intelligence during an AI Engineer conference in Shanghai in early November. The speaker challenged the prevailing hype by arguing that the final stage of implementation represents half of the total journey. Zhu criticized consultants who believe every industrial process can be easily automated regardless of the existing infrastructure. This presentation highlighted the practical difficulties of integrating advanced technology into traditional manufacturing environments. The speaker explained that many factories rely on pre-digital equipment and employ workers, averaging in their late 40s, who lack deep digital skills.

Furthermore, these companies often operate on margins so thin that they cannot afford a complete digital transformation. Instead of using an aggressive approach, Zhu suggested that the best method is to exercise humility. This requires seeking out the tacit knowledge of an organization to serve as the foundation for any technological change. Zhu argued that the current trend of ignoring human expertise in favor of automation is a mistake. The presentation served as a reminder that technical capabilities must be balanced with the reality of the workplace.

Other attendees, such as Ryo Lu, also questioned how self-worth is measured when code can be written by machines. Lu expressed a desire to build tools that increase human involvement rather than proving that people are needed less. The conference showcased a relaxed attitude toward artificial intelligence in China, where practitioners view it as a marketing tool rather than a global threat. Demos included a 35 billion-parameter model from AutoArk running on an iPhone 16 Pro and robot hardware from DYNA. The event also featured a significant number of women engineers, contrasting with the gender dynamics often seen at similar events in America or Australia.
