stories.Headline: Google and FBI warn agentic AI frameworks accelerate autonomous hacking attacks
stories.Summary:
Google and the FBI warned that agentic AI frameworks are accelerating autonomous hacking attacks during November 2026. These automated tools allow hackers to execute multi-stage intrusions at a much greater operational velocity than before. Google stated that the use of AI by adversaries has now reached a critical inflection point. The FBI released a FLASH report on November 13, 2026, regarding the ARTEX penetration testing framework. This framework was released on GitHub in July 2026 by a developer named Autumn-27.

The ARTEX platform requires external LLM providers like OpenAI GPT, Anthropic Claude, DeepSeek, GLM, Grok, or Kimi. It translates natural language goals into machine commands executed by specialized agents, requiring minimal human interaction. The FBI noted that some intrusions progressed from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours. The tool targeted sectors including financial services, government, technology, defense, semiconductor, energy, healthcare, manufacturing, telecommunications, and legal. It specifically targeted South Korean banks in October and ConnectWise Cloud Backup customers, affecting over 2,250 downstream tenants.

The FBI stated that ARTEX poses a serious threat because it reduces the time needed to chain attack techniques. Google researchers said adversary tradecraft has transitioned from manual prompting to deploying autonomous multi-agent offensive frameworks. Amazon's threat intelligence team observed an uptick in ARTEX use to steal AI model credentials and bypass identity verification. Cisco Talos researchers said these open-source frameworks are lowering the skill threshold for attackers and accelerating intrusions. They described these autonomous frameworks as the new reality for the current cybersecurity landscape.

The attacks affected approximately 67,000 individuals in South Korea through the exfiltration of their personal information. Microsoft attributed the ConnectWise supply chain compromise to a China-state aligned actor known as Storm-0940. Other affected targets included more than 200 organizations and various Japanese companies. The FBI identified that Chinese models, specifically the DeepSeek Flash family, are the most prevalent among attackers. These models are favored for their capabilities, low cost, and lack of observable guardrails during testing.

ARTEX was originally intended for authorized testing and gained 1,500 to 2,000 GitHub stars within ten weeks. The developer made the repository unavailable on October 8, 2026, after reports of abuse surfaced. However, the tool remains available through mirrors, community forks, archived copies, and a commercial version called ARTEX PRO. Researchers found over 1,600 publicly exposed ARTEX consoles in early November. Other frameworks being abused by hackers include CyberStrikeAI, HexStrike AI, and PentAGI.

The FBI recommends that organizations inventory and shrink their external attack surface to protect peripheral systems. Future evolution of these tools will likely include autonomous lateral movement followed by data identification and exfiltration. The FBI asks organizations to vet indicators of compromise before blocking them on their networks. The articles leave open how Democratic gains in the Tuesday election might reshape AI policy and data center growth. It remains unclear how companies will deploy technology under new scrutiny of AI policy.

stories.Headline: Cathie Wood's Ark buys Nvidia, CoreWeave and Archer Aviation and trims Palantir and Tempus AI
stories.Summary:
Cathie Wood's Ark Invest bought more Nvidia, CoreWeave and Archer Aviation and sold parts of its Tempus AI and Palantir holdings, Yahoo Finance reported on November 17, 2026. The Motley Fool's Marc Guberti wrote the article, published at 1:01 PM CST that day. Late last month Wood told a Bloomberg interviewer the AI trade is not in its first inning. She said the sector is "still in the parking lot before we entered the baseball game." She cited Palantir's 123% year-over-year U.S. revenue growth as evidence of the long-term opportunity in AI.

Most Ark Invest funds focus heavily on AI stocks, which have had a bumpy month but trended higher in recent years. Wood has put a lot of money behind her statement through Ark's exchange-traded funds. The article says AI demand will rise for chips, optical cables, liquid-cooling solutions and electricity. It says humanoid robots and self-driving vehicles are among the next big opportunities. Waymo leads the robotaxi space, and Tesla's Cybercabs are in limited production.

Wood is the founder of Ark Invest, and the article ties her bullish view to Palantir's 123% U.S. revenue growth. It says Palantir excels at agentic AI, which helps explain how the stock crushed the S&P 500 over five years. It says chipmakers keep reporting exceptional growth and enthusiasm for more AI growth in 2027 does not match recent stock performance. It says such setups create asymmetric risk opportunities but require accepting a lot of volatility. It says Wood's Ark Innovation ETF has had many downturns of 20% or more.

The article says the Ark Innovation ETF slumped more than 80% from its February 2021 peak to a December 2022 cyclical low. It says the fund is still down more than 50% from that peak despite promising periods in the intervening years. It says the fund has not recently had the upward momentum it enjoyed from the mid-2010s to 2021. It says the recent pullback in AI stocks has created a more compelling opportunity.

It says the Motley Fool holds positions in Palantir and Tesla and recommends both, and that Guberti has no position in any stock mentioned. The article says ChatGPT first had no connection to the live internet and could not take uploaded images, PDFs and other documents. It says Anthropic's Claude was similar early on but has become an autonomous digital coworker, and Claude Code can create entire apps and websites from a few prompts. It says new features will raise customer expectations, and in five to 10 years current versions of ChatGPT and Claude could look archaic.

It says Tesla's Optimus humanoid robots could become lucrative once AI robotics is ready for broad commercialization. It says 1990s investors underestimated the internet's impact, a pattern that may be taking shape with AI. The article says Stock Advisor's total average return is 802% against 205% for the S&P 500, as of November 17, 2026. It says $1,000 invested in Netflix on December 17, 2004 would be worth $327,620, and $1,000 in Nvidia on April 15, 2005 would be worth $959,410.

stories.Headline: Global leaders and educators call for collaboration to use AI to close learning and economic divides
stories.Summary:
John Lee Chi-kin chaired a high-level session on AI ethics and social responsibility in Hong Kong on October 27 and 28, 2026. This event occurred during the Global University Presidents and Leaders Summit 2026 to discuss high-tech innovation and the future of education. China also hosted APEC 2026, which focused on the three pillars of openness, innovation, and cooperation for the Asia-Pacific community. Participants at the 2026 Global South Modernization Forum in Cairo, Egypt, also called for the effective use of artificial intelligence. These leaders aim to use technology to close divides in learning, information, and economic opportunities across different global societies.

The mission requires collaboration between governments, academia, the technology sector, and the business community to dismantle barriers to accessibility. Hong Kong serves as a bridge to ASEAN and Belt and Road Initiative countries, supported by the Chinese mainland. The Education University of Hong Kong, or EdUHK, is ranked within the top seven globally in education by QS. Since 2017, EdUHK has served as a core consultant for World Bank education initiatives in Vietnam to foster digital transformation. The university also promotes policy dialogue and talent development in the United Arab Emirates, Kazakhstan, and various ASEAN countries.

John Lee Chi-kin and other leaders believe that education is central to harnessing AI for productivity and human development. Shannon Kane, an assistant clinical professor at the University of Maryland, says candidates must be prepared to judge AI outputs. Jennifer Kidd from Old Dominion University believes teachers must understand how AI works and its different impacts on learning. Justin Reich of MIT's Teaching Systems Lab argues that domain knowledge is necessary to tell if AI output is useless. Tracy Rock from the University of North Carolina at Charlotte says faculty should be critical rather than just AI cheerleaders.

Novice educators are affected by these changes, as over half of teachers now use AI for parts of their jobs. A 2023 ISTE report found that 56 percent of new teachers lack confidence in using technology in the classroom. K-12 school districts are affected by inconsistent policies, with some districts banning AI while others embrace the new technology. Students at George Mason University in Fairfax, Virginia, are now studying the benefits and drawbacks of AI in instruction. Many teacher candidates are also affected, though nearly a quarter of them do not want AI preparation in programs.

Teacher preparation has long struggled to effectively prepare aspiring teachers to integrate technology into their classroom instruction. An EdWeek Research Center survey of 268 teacher educators in August and September 2026 revealed various hurdles in AI integration. About 60 percent of faculty members decide individually whether to include an AI focus in their specific university courses. Many programs struggle to offer AI instruction because other priorities and national accreditation standards take precedence over new technology. Faculty professional development is limited, with only 14 percent of respondents reporting that they receive ongoing professional development.

Next, programs must navigate the rapid development of AI, which 57 percent of respondents cited as a major hurdle. Faculty at the University of North Carolina at Charlotte are using communities of practice to learn about tools like Gemini. Some instructors, like Jennifer Kidd, must revamp their course materials every single semester because the technology changes so quickly. The articles leave open whether K-12 school district leaders will actually prize AI skills when hiring new teacher candidates. It remains unclear if high-quality research will soon prove whether AI tools can actually improve student learning outcomes.

stories.Headline: Anthropic cuts high and critical vulnerability disclosure window to 30 days
stories.Summary:
Anthropic announced on November 16, 2026, that it had updated its coordinated vulnerability disclosure policy, cutting the window for high- and critical-severity issues from 90 days to 30 days and setting a 45-day window for all other vulnerabilities. The new timelines apply to vulnerabilities reported to vendors and maintainers on or after January 1, 2027, while reports already in progress on that date keep their existing deadlines. The company said the change responds to frontier AI models becoming much better at discovering vulnerabilities over the previous several months. Anthropic also said it had reported some high- and critical-severity vulnerabilities more than 90 days earlier that now exceed the deadline in its current policy and have not yet been disclosed publicly. It is notifying the maintainers of those projects that they are getting an additional 30 days, after which the reports will be published on Anthropic's dashboard in line with the updated policy starting January 1, 2027.

Beyond the shorter windows, Anthropic is making two related changes to how it handles reports. It will aim to escalate to an external vulnerability coordinator after 15 days instead of 30 if a maintainer does not respond to its initial vulnerability report, and it will wait 30 days instead of 45 after a patch is available before sharing full technical details. The rest of the policy remains the same, including the seven-day disclosure window for any vulnerability under active exploitation, which is unchanged. The update does not apply to AI-discovered findings that have not received human review, such as those found by OSS Scanner.

Anthropic said flaws in hard-to-deploy software, such as critical infrastructure, and flaws that require changes to a specification or RFC cannot always be resolved in 30 or 45 days, and in those cases it will work with the vendor on a remediation timeline. Anthropic said many coordinated disclosure norms, including those in its own policy, were developed well before AI could discover vulnerabilities and assumed that fixes moved at human speed and that independent rediscovery of the same bug was unlikely. It said neither assumption holds today, because models can now help develop fixes and a bug that one model can find is increasingly likely to be found by another, and it is seeing a higher rate of vulnerability rediscovery as these capabilities increase. A 90-day window made sense when a vulnerability could be expected to stay private for months, but the company no longer believes it can, and it said the changes are intended to keep pace with progress in AI capabilities and strike the right balance for defenders.

Anthropic acknowledged that shorter timelines may put more pressure on software maintainers and said it will continue to include actionable guidance with each report, along with a patch or mitigation where possible. To reduce the burden on maintainers, Anthropic said it will also continue to agree on a sustainable pace with maintainers before sending a large volume of findings to a single project. It pointed to three programs meant to help maintainers and defenders work at the new pace: OSS Scanner, a no-cost service that periodically scans the code of critical open-source projects with the company's strongest models and sends findings directly to maintainers; the Claude for Open Source Program, which offers eligible maintainers and contributors six months of Claude Ultra at no cost; and the Cyber Verification Program, which tailors Claude's safeguards to enable legitimate defensive work by security professionals, including open-source maintainers. The articles do not say what further steps follow beyond the January 1, 2027 start date and the additional 30 days given to maintainers of the older undisclosed reports.

stories.Headline: CrowdStrike ranks highest in growth among AI SOC vendors in Frost Radar report
stories.Summary:
CrowdStrike announced on November 16, 2026, that it had been named the Visionary Leader in the Frost Radar™: AI Security Operations Centers, 2026. The company issued the announcement from Austin, Texas, and its stock trades on NASDAQ under the ticker CRWD. CrowdStrike ranked highest in Growth among all vendors evaluated in that Frost Radar report. The company said the ranking underscores how it is leading the shift from manual security operations to the agentic SOC. The announcement said adversaries weaponize AI to attack at machine speed, and human-speed defense cannot keep pace.

The Frost Radar report on AI Security Operations Centers evaluated vendors and ranked CrowdStrike highest in Growth among all of them. The report states that of AI SOC vendors, the strongest providers do more, though the article text ends there. CrowdStrike's platform materials describe Next-Gen SIEM as the world's only AI-native SOC platform. They describe Agentic SOAR as orchestrating agents, workflows and automation across a security ecosystem. They describe Charlotte AI as accelerating outcomes with autonomous intelligence fueled by world-class expertise.

CrowdStrike President Michael Sentonas said organizations are accelerating efforts to get more outcomes from AI. He said the company sees every week that agents combine multiple actions and, when they hit obstacles, take actions that were not originally permitted. He said one control point is not enough to stop that, and agents, network and endpoint must be handled together. He said this makes security a driver of AI adoption rather than a barrier.

A separate announcement dated November 16, 2026, and translated from a release issued in the United States on November 3, 2026, covered Falcon Guardian innovations. CrowdStrike introduced a new AI Kill Switch in CrowdStrike Falcon® Guardian and multiple innovations to protect AI agents at every control point. CrowdStrike also announced a plan to acquire Fiddler AI, which leads in AI agent observability. CrowdStrike said that through the Falcon platform it will provide the industry's broadest AI agent security and safety capabilities. Falcon Guardian protects AI agents at runtime on the endpoints where they execute.

The new innovations add agent-facing and network-facing capabilities, with agent-level hooks controlling AI agents to act as instructed. Endpoint network inspection lets organizations see communications between AI agents and models and tools. CrowdStrike said it alone can integrate agent, network and endpoint together, so organizations can accelerate AI adoption while keeping control. Agent-level hooks can see prompts but not model responses and cannot capture every agent action. A network-only approach can monitor traffic but cannot block actions.

The articles leave open what the Frost Radar report says beyond its statement on the strongest providers. They leave open the terms of the planned Fiddler AI acquisition and when it will close. They leave open how the AI Kill Switch is configured and which customers will receive it. They leave open how the agent-level hooks and network inspection are priced and packaged. They leave open how the combined controls perform against the unauthorized agent actions Sentonas described.

stories.Headline: Congressional Research Service warns high costs may limit generative AI model development
stories.Summary:
A new report from the Congressional Research Service released by November 13, 2026, warns that extreme costs may limit the number of companies capable of building generative artificial intelligence models. This financial barrier creates an antitrust question for Congress, although the Department of Justice and the Federal Trade Commission had not filed any lawsuits for anticompetitive conduct by that date. Researchers estimated that training the Grok 4 model released by xAI in July 2025 cost approximately 390 million dollars, excluding labor and data acquisition. Meanwhile, DeepSeek claimed one of its models required 2.8 million graphics processing unit hours, though some analysts question if those cost estimates were comprehensive.

Addressing these barriers may require Congress to hold hearings, send letters to agencies, amend antitrust laws, or codify a federal research program. The National Science Foundation launched the National AI Research Resource pilot in January 2024 under Executive Order 14110, and later established an operations center on September 1 to manage long-term infrastructure. This program involved at least 26 private sector partners and 14 federal agencies before a January 23, 2025 executive order from the Trump administration revoked the original directive. While Congress could make this resource permanent, doing so might further entrench the incumbent firms that currently supply essential AI resources.

Antitrust enforcers from the European Commission, the UK Commission on Markets Authority, the Department of Justice, and the Federal Trade Commission expressed concerns in July 2024 regarding the concentrated control of key inputs. A January 2025 staff report from the Federal Trade Commission highlighted potential switching barriers and the ability of cloud providers to access sensitive information. Additionally, the Department of Justice inquired into Nvidia in June 2024, while the Federal Trade Commission looked into Microsoft and OpenAI during the same month. These agencies worry that large incumbent digital firms are entrenching their power through arrangements among key players.

The current market remains small but competitive, although some reports suggest that switching between different AI models can take several weeks. N. Ram, the director of The Hindu Publishing Group, noted that Chinese models like Kimi and DeepSeek demonstrate a path to high performance without the massive resources of tech giants. Legal experts note that exclusive contracts are generally lawful unless a company with market power uses them to block competition, which would violate Section 1 of the Sherman Act. Congress must now decide whether to legislate new protections or allow the current market dynamics to continue.

stories.Headline: Robert Izquierdo picks SoundHound AI over Rigetti Computing for 2027 on revenue growth and valuation
stories.Summary:
Robert Izquierdo of The Motley Fool published an updated comparison of Rigetti Computing and SoundHound AI on Nov 15, 2026 at 2:05PM EST. The article weighed Rigetti's superconducting quantum processors and cloud-based quantum services against SoundHound's conversational artificial intelligence platform. Rigetti sells access to its hardware to global enterprise and research clients, including partners like Amazon and Microsoft. SoundHound develops voice and agentic artificial intelligence software for automotive, retail, and hospitality industries. The piece concluded that SoundHound is the better investment going into 2027.

Rigetti's revenue for the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025 reached nearly $7.1 million, a decrease of 34.3% from the previous year. Nearly 90.2% of Rigetti's revenue last year came from U.S. government contracts, and its net loss was $216.2 million. Rigetti's December 2025 balance sheet showed a current ratio of 37.4x and a debt-to-equity ratio of zero, with free cash flow of negative $77.2 million. SoundHound's revenue for the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025 reached $168.9 million, an increase of 99.4%, with a net loss of $14.0 million. SoundHound's December 2025 balance sheet showed a current ratio of 4.6x and a debt-to-equity ratio of zero, with free cash flow of negative $103.1 million.

The author said he would invest in SoundHound for 2027, citing the current state of quantum technology versus AI as the most important factor. He said Rigetti management predicts quantum advantage is at least three years away, and that Rigetti's tech requires special cryogenic equipment colder than outer space. He said SoundHound announced in its third quarter report that it expects to reach adjusted EBITDA profitability by the second half of 2027. He said SoundHound's Q3 revenue was $62.4 million, a 49% year-over-year increase, and it anticipates sales of at least $250 million in 2026 and a minimum of $350 million in 2027. He said consistent revenue expansion, the move to profitability, and superior share price valuation make SoundHound the better investment.

The article said Rigetti faces hurdles as an early-stage hardware developer with a history of substantial operating losses and depends heavily on a small group of government customers. It said Rigetti competes against well-capitalized rivals such as IonQ and D-Wave Quantum in an industry where achieving quantum advantage is not guaranteed. It said SoundHound deals with a history of substantial net losses and negative cash flow from operations and operates in a crowded market where incumbents like Microsoft and Amazon have vast resources. It said SoundHound faces the complex task of integrating several major acquisitions while navigating evolving global regulations on artificial intelligence and data privacy. It said SoundHound appears more reasonably valued on a P/S ratio basis, at 6.8x versus 251.1x for Rigetti.

The article said Rigetti is a pioneer in quantum computing aiming to solve problems current computers cannot touch, and SoundHound focuses on voice-enabled artificial intelligence for situations such as in-car commands and restaurant drive-through ordering. It said Rigetti builds superconducting quantum computers and operates them through its proprietary Quantum Cloud Services platform. It said SoundHound, following its acquisition of LivePerson, has integrated digital messaging and automation tools to broaden its customer reach. It said Rigetti's rivals are producing quantum machines that can operate at room temperature, adding to Rigetti's competitive pressures. It said SoundHound has grown revenue consistently for years as it scales up customers, while Rigetti's sales are inconsistent due to the experimental nature of its technology.

The article said Rigetti's stock was $9.62, down 6.87% or $0.71, with a market cap of $3.3B and a 52-week range of $9.19 to $30.21. It said SoundHound's stock was $3.49, down 3.06% or $0.11, with a market cap of $1.6B and a 52-week range of $3.40 to $13.19. It listed Rigetti's gross margin at -5093.24%, P/E ratio at -26.86, and EPS (TTM) at -$0.36, and SoundHound's gross margin at 30.55%, P/E ratio at -7.80, and EPS (TTM) at -$0.45. It said forward P/E was n/a for both companies, and that valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep and may differ from other data providers. The article left open whether SoundHound will actually reach adjusted EBITDA profitability by the second half of 2027 and whether Rigetti will achieve quantum advantage.

This move comes as investors fear an AI bubble and financing costs rise. The company is pressing ahead despite a shaky market and political headwinds. This blockbuster sale could raise more than 60 billion dollars.

The offering uses the ticker name ANT and sets a price range of 70 to 78 dollars per share. At the top range, it could raise 64.4 billion dollars and value the company at 1.4 trillion dollars. Nvidia has agreed to buy an estimated 10 billion dollars of stock after the debut. Anthropic has 6.2 billion dollars in debt and plans to spend 70 billion dollars next year. Total computing and infrastructure spending will reach 900 billion dollars in the coming years.

CEO Dario Amodei told Jamie Dimon of JPMorgan Chase that the company is very paranoid about AI safety. Amodei stated that the firm focuses on enterprise customers and coding tools to remain synergistic with safety. He said he spends 40 to 50 percent of his time on talent and company culture. Amodei noted that the company avoids hiring jerks or people not oriented toward the public benefit. He believes cognition is exponential and will open new markets like scientific research.

Investors are jittery, and some fear that the AI bubble could burst soon. CoreWeave stock plunged 15.5 percent on October 14 before surging 25 percent and then dropping 7 percent. Newly elected Democrats in Texas and Georgia vow to stop new data center construction. These politicians and a Congressional effort seek a national moratorium on new data centers. This political environment threatens to slow the growth of the artificial intelligence industry.

Nvidia stock dropped 4 percent after CEO Jensen Huang resigned over affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. In 2021, nearly 400 companies went public, but only 71 did so the next year due to recession fears. President Donald Trump's Liberation Day tariffs in April 2025 caused StubHub and Klarna to postpone their offerings. Firmus, an Australian data center company, called off its IPO last month. Robert Shiller's measure shows stocks currently trade at 40 times their long term earnings.

Anthropic will beat rival OpenAI to the public market if the offering proceeds as expected. The company may fetch top dollars for shares before Democrats take office in January. The articles leave open whether the company will postpone the IPO at the last minute. It remains unclear if the company can find a clear path to profitability. stories.Headline: Artist Olivia Tai collects confessions about using AI to write personal messages
stories.Summary:
Olivia Tai, an artist who has repeated a project called the Confession box more than a dozen times in the Bay Area, New York and Denver, set up a purple box on a folding table in San Francisco’s Alamo Square that held dozens of secrets written by passersby. A sign on the box read “Confession box: Everyone has an AI secret,” and among the confessions about farming out too much work or using artificial intelligence to suggest a first-date spot were several admissions about using it to write deeply personal messages. The confessions included “I had AI write my breakup text,” “I had ChatGPT date my boyfriend. Every text,” and “I used AI to write my girlfriend’s grandmother’s 80th birthday letter.”

Tai said calling the project a confession suggested people were admitting that using AI made them feel at least a little guilty, but they used it anyway. The question the project raises is whether using a chatbot for personal messages crosses a line, and whether it is ever acceptable to use AI to write a holiday card, a birthday message, a love letter or wedding vows. Danielle Hass, a professor at Kennesaw State University in Georgia who conducted vignette-based experiments as part of research for a Ph.D. in consumer behavior, found that people who had used AI before felt just as guilty as those who had not. Hass said everyone felt guilty and that the driver of this relationship was dishonesty, with people feeling like they were manipulating others.

Scott Claessens, a senior researcher at the University of Bristol in the UK, said his research suggests that people who use AI are perceived as lazier, less competent and less trustworthy, even when they are honest about their AI use. Claessens noted that people often already supplement social tasks, such as using pre-written birthday cards or poems in love notes, but something about the effortless way that AI works turns people off. He said what people really want in social relationships is for others to put effort in, because it shows as a signal that you are invested in the relationship. Sarah Newman, who collaborated with Tai as director of art and education at Harvard University’s metaLAB, said AI adoption is happening so quickly that norms will likely emerge about when it is appropriate and when it is not.

Newman suggested using conflicted feelings as a guide, asking whether you would be comfortable telling your partner you used AI to write your wedding vows, and said personal messages do not need to be perfect because part of what makes them authentic and endearing is that they are imperfect. Tai and Claessens said some situations could warrant using AI in personal situations, such as people in relationships who use it to communicate better with a partner who does not share a native language, or people with learning disabilities such as dyslexia who could use it for help. Hass said she believes people are quickly accepting that AI can make them more efficient in some work contexts, but she said she is glad people feel guilty using it for personal messages. Hass said guilt’s purpose in this context is to show us our interpersonal wrongdoings and to show us where we are supposed to be human.

Toobit, the global cryptocurrency exchange based in George Town in the Cayman Islands, announced on November 18, 2026 that it is showcasing two trading analysis tools available through Toobit Futures. Both tools are designed to complement traders' existing analytical approaches rather than replace them.

SmartK features five proprietary indicators covering market signals, entry scoring, multi-timeframe positioning, volume-price relationships and momentum divergence. AI Trading Assistant offers AI crypto market analysis and AI trading opportunities, providing potential trade setups for scalp and swing trading. Its analysis includes directional signals, entry zones, take-profit targets, stop-loss levels and adjustable risk-to-reward ratios to support trade planning and risk assessment. Both offerings support independent trading decisions, allowing traders to incorporate technical analysis and AI-generated insights into their existing strategies while retaining control over their trades.

Toobit describes itself as an award-winning cryptocurrency derivatives exchange that provides zero-fee spot trading, AI trading tools and high leverage for both crypto and TradFi markets. The announcement cites eToro's September 2026 Retail Investor Beat, which surveyed 11,000 retail investors across 13 countries, finding that 56% already use or are open to using AI tools to select or adjust investments. Among those respondents, 41% believe AI can save time on research, which the announcement presents as reflecting interest in AI-assisted investment analysis.

The announcement was distributed through GlobeNewswire and carried by outlets including markets.businessinsider.com and the Manila Times, and it includes a contact named Davin C. along with the website www.toobit.com. stories.Headline: AI analysis of one echocardiogram clip plus H2FPEF score identifies 78% of hemodynamically confirmed HFpEF cases
stories.Summary:
Researchers applied an artificial intelligence model called EchoGo HF to resting echocardiograms from 280 outpatients who had been referred for suspected heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, and each patient also underwent exercise hemodynamic testing as the diagnostic gold standard, according to research published in the November 2026 issue of the Journal of Cardiac Failure. Adding the AI analysis of a single routine echocardiogram clip to the H₂FPEF clinical score identified 78% of patients with hemodynamically confirmed HFpEF, compared with 48% using the score alone. The AI model added the most value for patients with low or intermediate H₂FPEF scores, the group where diagnosis is hardest, so the authors tested a two-step strategy of calculating H₂FPEF first and then applying AI only when the score is inconclusive. An AI-detected HFpEF result also independently predicted elevated filling pressures and reduced exercise capacity, which suggests the model reflects disease severity as well as diagnosis.

The November issue, focused on artificial intelligence in heart failure, also includes a study in which investigators used clinical notes from 599 patients seen in cardiology clinics to optimize a large language model, OpenAI's o1, that classified the documented reason for non-prescription of SGLT2 inhibitors with 84.7% accuracy. Physician-attributed factors were the most common theme at 28.7% of notes, and the leading specific reasons were deferring the decision to a future visit at 15.4% and the physician judging the patient low-risk or unlikely to benefit at 7.4%. A review in the same issue maps current AI applications across the heart failure care continuum, including AI-enabled ECG and imaging for opportunistic detection of low ejection fraction, HFpEF and structural heart disease, risk stratification based on electronic health records, clinician decision support, remote medication titration and wearable monitoring. The review's authors conclude that the strongest evidence favors AI built into active clinical workflows that guide targeted testing, treatment optimization and follow-up, rather than AI used only to send passive alerts.

In their Editor's Page, guest editors Jonathan W. Cunningham of Mass General Brigham and Harvard Medical School, Elena Donald and Nir Uriel of Columbia University Irving Medical Center, and Ankeet S. Bhatt of Kaiser Permanente San Francisco Medical Center wrote that heart failure's population burden is growing and outcomes are worsening while the number of heart failure physicians is flat and training spots go unfilled, and that AI could help close that gap. They wrote that promise alone is insufficient and that AI, like any innovation intended to change clinical care, must be rigorously studied to understand where it adds value, where it does not and how it can be implemented safely and effectively. The editors called on the heart failure community to move past retrospective and in silico demonstrations of model performance and instead want prospective studies, including randomized trials where feasible, that test whether AI tools improve clinical decisions, treatment delivery, outcomes, equity and clinician workload. They wrote that AI researchers will continue to advance these tools but that clinicians and patients must lead their translation into care, and the complete November 2026 issue is available online now.

stories.Headline: Tencent reports slower revenue growth as AI demand boosts cloud business
stories.Summary:
Tencent Holdings reported an eight percent rise in third quarter revenue on Wednesday, November 18, in Beijing. The company saw slower growth than previous results and analyst expectations because gaming business growth cooled. Demand for artificial intelligence services helped the cloud business, which is a key focus for many investors. These investors want to know if heavy spending on AI is paying off or squeezing the company margins.

The company reported revenue of 207.3 billion yuan, or 31.1 billion dollars, for the three months ended September. This figure was slightly below the LSEG consensus estimate of 210.8 billion yuan, following eleven percent growth previously. Fintech and business services revenue rose nine percent to 63.7 billion yuan, while value added services rose three percent. Value added services reached 98.3 billion yuan, with domestic games growing eleven percent and international games sliding nine percent.

CEO Ma Huateng issued a statement saying the company is making substantial progress toward building a new, AI empowered Tencent. He noted this progress is happening in terms of intelligence, applications, and infrastructure for the tech giant. Net profit edged up zero point eight percent to 63.61 billion yuan, beating analyst expectations of 59.46 billion yuan. The company is spending heavily on AI to improve its services and infrastructure for its many global clients.

Investors are monitoring the company, and shares in Chinese cloud service providers, including Tencent, slid on Tuesday. This decline followed new Washington rules restricting remote access to advanced US AI chips through overseas data centres. Chinese tech giants have struggled to obtain advanced Nvidia chips because of these strict export restrictions from the US. These restrictions affect how companies rent computing power to external clients and manage their own internal AI chip usage.

Tencent said a year ago that chip shortages were constraining its cloud growth as it prioritised internal AI chip use. Capital expenditure in the September quarter was 81.4 billion yuan, compared with 52.8 billion yuan in the June quarter. The company spent 84.7 billion yuan in the first half of the year, exceeding its total 2025 spending. Total spending in 2025 was roughly 79 billion yuan, showing a significant increase in recent capital investment costs.

The company will continue to navigate US export restrictions while trying to expand its AI empowered infrastructure and services. Investors will watch if the increased capital expenditure leads to higher revenue growth in the coming financial quarters. The articles leave open whether the new Washington rules will further hinder the growth of Chinese cloud providers. It remains unclear if Tencent can overcome chip shortages to increase the rental of computing power to external clients.

stories.Headline: Diligent Institute finds only 15% of APAC boards very confident in overseeing major risks
stories.Summary:
Diligent Institute published its APAC Governance Outlook 2027 report on 18 November 2026, based on an online survey run during August and September of board members, C-suite leaders, general counsel, company secretaries and other governance leaders across Asia-Pacific, with Australian-headquartered organisations making up 63% of respondents. The report found that cybersecurity, data protection and privacy were the leading strategic priority for 69% of respondents, with AI deployment next at 54% and operational cost optimisation at 52%. Despite that focus, only 15% said they were very confident their board had the information, expertise and processes needed to oversee significant risks, and the most commonly cited barriers were insufficient time at 26% and a lack of relevant expertise at 17%. Respondents also described a broader risk backdrop, with 55% expecting economic downturns to disrupt their organisations over the next 12 months, 53% naming geopolitical events as a major threat and 48% identifying cyber and data privacy incidents as a likely source of disruption.

On AI, 29% of respondents said adoption was outpacing governance, 25% said governance was keeping pace and 8% said governance was ahead of adoption, while a quarter said they used approved AI tools for governance workflows, 17% reported informal use of general-purpose or consumer tools and another 25% had no foreseeable plans to use AI in those settings. Asked about the main opportunities from AI, 78% pointed to improved data analysis and reporting and 58% named workflow automation, while 66% cited security and privacy as their leading AI concern and half named hallucinations, misinformation or disinformation. Digital technology, including AI and data management, was the most frequently cited board skills gap at 62%, more than double the 29% who named cybersecurity, and 65% said more time for strategic planning or dedicated planning meetings would improve the boardroom while 26% said their board lacked time to discuss emerging risks. Nearly half called for more formal development, with 49% selecting mandatory director training or continuing education and 48% wanting greater access to outside parties or experts on specific issues and risks.

Dottie Schindlinger, executive director of Diligent Institute, said effective oversight is not about adding every emerging issue to an already full agenda but about understanding how risks intersect, identifying what matters most to the organisation's strategy and decisions, and ensuring management is taking action. She said boards can start by asking for clear, integrated reporting that connects emerging risks to business priorities, dedicating time to challenging assumptions, and gaining a clear understanding of where and how AI is being deployed, including in their own governance processes. The articles say the findings come as boards in Australia face regulatory scrutiny over operational resilience, cyber governance and executive accountability, and that the concentration of Australian respondents gives the results particular relevance for local boards as organisations deal with cyber threats, data governance questions and pressure to demonstrate clearer oversight of AI use. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the report's findings and recommendations.

stories.Headline: IBM study finds only 18% of chief AI officers control AI investment decisions
stories.Summary:
The IBM Institute for Business Value published a study on November 17, 2026, dated from Armonk, New York, finding that only 18% of surveyed Chief AI Officers have full control over AI investment decisions. The global study surveyed more than 1,600 Chief AI Officers and equivalent enterprise AI leaders. It was conducted in cooperation with Oxford Economics, which surveyed 1,667 senior executives responsible for enterprise AI strategy, governance, implementation, and value realization. Those surveyed included Chief AI Officers, Chief Data and AI Officers, Heads of AI, and equivalent AI leaders, whom the study refers to collectively as CAIOs. The survey ran from April to June 2026 across 33 geographies and 20 industries.

Just 29% of respondents say their organizations adjust decisions and resources quickly when AI performance insights identify opportunities to improve outcomes. Fewer than one-third of surveyed CAIOs say AI is reshaping the business model, including what the organization sells, how it prices, or how it captures value. While only 32% say AI is reshaping the business model, 35% say it primarily strengthens the existing model, and 26% expect it to reshape the model but have not made the necessary shifts. 48% of CAIOs say AI agents initiate and execute actions across workflows, yet 75% say governance, risk or compliance delays AI-driven action. While 73% of respondents have defined where human oversight is non-negotiable, only 61% say AI decision rights are clearly defined and consistently applied.

Joanne Wright, Senior Vice President, Transformation and Operations at IBM, writes in the study's foreword that few leaders have a broader view of how AI is creating value across the enterprise. She writes that the outcomes Chief AI Officers are accountable for often depend on decisions made by others. She says successful AI leadership requires more than technical expertise or operational oversight. She says it requires gathering evidence, influencing decisions, and measuring success. The study identifies a group of high-impact CAIOs whose organizations report stronger results.

High-impact CAIOs report that 63% of AI projects deliver measurable business outcomes, compared with 43% for all other CAIOs, and that 49% move from pilot to production, versus 33%. They scale successful initiatives enterprise-wide in eight months, compared with 13.5 months among all other CAIOs. High-impact CAIOs are nearly four times as likely to say they can quickly pause, adjust or redirect AI systems without disrupting operations, and 96% of them say AI-generated outputs can trigger actions autonomously, compared with 40% of all other CAIOs. Nearly all high-impact CAIOs say AI is embedded directly into workflows compared with 59% of all others, and 94% say they use business outcomes to determine which initiatives receive additional funding and talent and which do not. 96% of high-impact CAIOs say they stop or reduce investment in initiatives that fail to deliver, even when those initiatives have senior sponsorship, compared with 46% of others, and 95% say they reinvest AI-generated productivity gains in higher-value transformation, compared with 44% of other respondents.

Only 31% of all CAIOs say clear thresholds for stopping AI initiatives are critical to AI success, and 40% say decisions are discussed when performance insights reveal opportunities, but action is delayed. 71% of CAIOs believe their organizations risk falling behind competitors in AI transformation, and CAIOs rank workflows and business processes as the top priority for change. The findings link the stronger outcomes of high-impact CAIOs with differences in how their organizations manage AI autonomy and control, redesign business workflows, and make evidence-based investment decisions. Additional analysis examined organizational behaviors associated with stronger enterprise outcomes across governance, decision rights, workflow integration, operating-model design, value management, transformation execution, and business-model innovation. The IBM Institute for Business Value is IBM's thought leadership think tank, combining global research and performance data with expertise from industry thinkers and leading academics.

The full report is available at a link on IBM's website, and the media contact is Marisa Conway of IBM Corporate Communications. IBM describes itself as a leading provider of global hybrid cloud and AI and consulting expertise, helping clients in more than 175 countries. The articles do not say what organizations should do in response to the findings, beyond the report link. They do not give the names of any surveyed CAIOs or the identities of the high-impact group. They do not break the results down by geography or industry, though the survey covered 33 geographies and 20 industries.

stories.Headline: Microsoft and over 40 partners launch AI Transparency Initiative to set open standards for accountable AI
stories.Summary:
At Microsoft Ignite on Tuesday, Microsoft Chairman and CEO Satya Nadella announced the AI Transparency Initiative, a collaborative effort with customers and partners. The initiative is a common, open approach to security and governance across models and providers. Microsoft launched it with organizations across industries to strengthen enterprise trust in AI models and agents. The announcement came from Redmond, Wash., on Nov. 17, 2026. The initiative reflects a principle that greater AI autonomy requires greater transparency.

The initiative has three parts, the first being that Microsoft will expand its participation in the National Institute of Standards and Technology's SI Agent Standards Initiative and draw on its research. Second, Microsoft is collaborating with more than 40 organizations, including Accenture, Adobe, KPMG, Mastercard and Volvo Cars, to help develop open standards for AI systems that are accountable, independently verifiable and safe by design, regardless of the model or provider. Third, Microsoft will incorporate this work into Microsoft AI, Microsoft Foundry and Microsoft Copilot, enabling customers to use the resulting evidence with their security and compliance tools, whether from Microsoft or other providers. The initiative is designed to work across models and providers, including closed and open-weight models, so developer teams can change or update the models powering their agents without compromising IT and security teams' ability to govern them securely or compliance teams' ability to audit their actions. Organizations interested in helping shape the initiative or following its progress can learn more and sign up at aka.ms/learnmoreAItransparency.

Hayete Gallot, Executive Vice President, Microsoft Security, said every organization needs greater transparency into the model itself for security controls to be effective. Gallot said the work will bring more transparency to all models and called it a critical step in making containment smarter and stronger, allowing better accountability and traceability. Aanchal Gupta, Chief Security Officer, Adobe, said security teams need clear visibility into what agents are accessing, what actions they are taking and how those actions can be verified. Gupta said building a common approach to AI transparency across the industry is essential to strengthening trust and helping organizations innovate with confidence while maintaining security and accountability. John Israel, Global Chief Information Security Officer, KPMG International, said clients want to move faster with AI and should not have to choose between innovation and safety.

Israel said trust in AI requires transparency, explainability and responsible oversight, and that KPMG is proud to work with Microsoft on the initiative to help establish open, industrywide standards. Harpreet Sidhu, global cybersecurity lead, Accenture, said organizations taking the next step in their AI reinventions need a solid foundation of trust and confidence to build from. Sidhu said initiatives like this from Microsoft to take an open, industry-driven approach to AI transparency can help as Accenture secures AI models and fits them with controls and governance. Enterprises are connecting AI models to data, tools, credentials and infrastructure, enabling agents to take actions without human approval at every step. Agents with access to data, tools and credentials carry the risk profile of a privileged insider but operate at machine speed and scale, making independent oversight essential.

Existing controls can observe much of the activity around AI models, but they cannot see what happens within them or independently verify their accounts of their own behavior. This limits organizations' ability to understand the context behind an agent's actions, and that evidence gap creates security, compliance, audit and accountability risk. Security teams need a new trust architecture to address the growing insider risks posed by increasingly capable AI agents. Accountability stays with the organization, and when something consequential happens, leaders answer to customers, employees, boards, auditors and regulators.

Blaming the AI isn't an answer, and "trust the model" isn't a control. Microsoft believes every organization should be able to see what AI systems access and do, verify their actions independently and control what they are permitted to do. On seeing, organizations should know what the AI was asked and authorized to do, which model and runtime were used, what data and tools it accessed, and what actions it took, and monitor agent activity and risk signals continuously against policies and thresholds. On verifying, agents cannot be the sole source of truth about their own behavior, and frontier models cannot be trusted to govern themselves.

Evidence covering agent identity, delegated intent and actions should identify its source, the model, the runtime around it, or independent systems such as identity and policy, so model-reported signals can be checked against independently observed records. Organizations should be able to independently verify AI activity using their own security and compliance systems, without relying solely on the model provider's account of its behavior. On controlling, clear evidence of each workflow's purpose, owner, data and delegated authority helps organizations enforce their policies before consequential actions occur and reconstruct what happened during investigations, containment, recovery and audits. That evidence should stay with organizations when models and providers change, and organizations should retain control over what data their agents can access and how that access is governed, regardless of the model or provider.

Microsoft and industry leaders will share insights at Microsoft Ignite on how organizations can manage AI models and agents with confidence. More is available on the Microsoft Security blog, and press can contact Microsoft Media Relations, We. Communications for Microsoft, at (425) 638-7777. The articles leave open what the open standards will contain and when the work will reach Microsoft AI, Microsoft Foundry and Microsoft Copilot.

stories.Headline: Fluke study finds 78 percent of data center operators hit electrical disruption in past year
stories.Summary:
Fluke Corporation published a study on November 17, 2026, finding that 78 percent of data center operators experienced electrical or power-system issues contributing to disruption, delays, downtime or serious near-misses in the past year. The study was announced from Everett, Washington, and distributed by GlobeNewswire. Fluke said the global race to build and expand AI data centers could face a major setback. The research raised questions about whether the infrastructure behind the AI boom can deliver on the industry's ambitious growth plans. Operators are racing to secure additional grid capacity while weaknesses inside data centers threaten to delay new AI workloads and disrupt existing operations.

Only 33 percent of operators say their electrical infrastructure is fully ready for higher-density AI workloads. 34 percent say electrical skills shortages have delayed infrastructure upgrades or new capacity. 29 percent say power-quality issues have reduced their ability to deploy or operate AI/GPU workloads. 29 percent report that electrical problems are only identified after performance or equipment failure, or downtime, has occurred. Fewer than half of operators, 45 percent, report real-time visibility across critical electrical systems.

Parker Burke, President of Fluke Corporation, said the industry has spent years asking where the power will come from. He said the findings show the focus should also be on how effectively data centers can use the power they already have. He said the electrical infrastructure inside data centers is becoming a critical bottleneck as AI drives unprecedented demand for computing capacity. He said that without addressing this last-mile challenge, the industry risks having the power to expand but not the infrastructure to deliver. Burke also said grid constraints are largely outside an operator's control, while what is within their control is how effectively they monitor, maintain and manage the electrical infrastructure they already have.

Six in ten operators, 60 percent, say recruiting qualified electrical technicians has become more difficult. Three-quarters of operators, 76 percent, say access to sufficient power and grid capacity is moderately or severely limiting their ability to expand. Operators report an average 12-month wait to secure additional grid connection or power capacity for AI and GPU-related expansion. The study was commissioned by Fluke on behalf of Censuswide and surveyed 1,300 data-center industry operators and professionals across six countries: the US, UK, Germany, France, India and the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. Censuswide is an international market research consultancy headquartered in London, with offices in New York, Dubai, Bristol and Glasgow.

Fluke Corporation was founded in 1948 and describes itself as the world leader in compact, professional electronic test tools and software for measuring and condition monitoring. Fluke customers are technicians, engineers, electricians, maintenance managers and metrologists who install, troubleshoot and maintain industrial, electrical and electronic equipment and calibration processes. The study examined the power, infrastructure and workforce challenges facing the industry as AI demand accelerates. The findings suggest the challenge is no longer simply securing power from the grid but ensuring data centers have the infrastructure and expertise to turn that power into reliable computing capacity. Burke said greater visibility into electrical systems and a proactive approach to maintenance will be increasingly important as operators look to maximize existing capacity, reduce disruption and support growing AI demand.

Fluke said data center operators can improve electrical reliability through regular electrical testing, power-quality monitoring, thermal inspections and preventive maintenance. Fluke said poor power quality can cause equipment malfunctions, overheating, unexpected shutdowns and downtime, and that voltage fluctuations, harmonics and electrical disturbances can affect the reliability of critical data center systems. Fluke said operators can help reduce the impact of electrical skills shortages by investing in technician training, standardized testing procedures and diagnostic tools that make electrical troubleshooting more efficient. Fluke said it provides electrical testing and measurement tools, power-quality analyzers, thermal imaging cameras and condition-monitoring solutions for data center environments. The articles leave open which specific operators or countries accounted for the reported issues and near-misses.

stories.Headline: Africa Tech Festival opens in Cape Town to advance AI development across the continent
stories.Summary:
The Africa Tech Festival 2026 officially opened on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, in Cape Town, South Africa, to advance digital transformation. This event focuses on positioning the African continent to seize various opportunities that arise in the current age of artificial intelligence. Organizers brought together leaders from the technology and telecommunications industries, along with investors, policymakers, entrepreneurs, and innovators, to explore emerging technologies. These participants gathered to foster new partnerships and advance digital development across the continent during this influential and large technology event. The festival aims to help Africa move from being a consumer of foreign solutions to a developer of its own technologies.

The 29th edition of the festival runs through Thursday at the Cape Town International Convention Centre under the theme Powering Africa's Digital Transformation. More than 13,500 attendees and 2,000 companies from over 130 countries joined more than 450 speakers and 350 exhibitors at the venue. Six content pillars guide the event, including Data Centers, Artificial Intelligence, Cybersecurity, Startups, Digital Transformation, and Telecoms and Connectivity, for all participants. The schedule includes keynote speeches, panel discussions, technical masterclasses, investment forums, roundtables, networking opportunities, and specialist industry sessions for the attending guests. An exhibition also features various startups and providers of AI solutions from across the telecommunications and technology sectors for the attendees.

South African Deputy President Paul Mashatile delivered a virtual opening address where he urged African countries to shape the global AI landscape. He stated that the continent must become an exporter of emerging technologies instead of remaining a consumer of solutions developed elsewhere. Mashatile argued that digital transformation is fundamentally about human development and must be inclusive and people-centered to ensure a prosperous future. He called for active participation in developing and governing these technologies to ensure they advance the developmental goals of the continent. The Deputy President also urged African countries to build their own capabilities by drawing on local talent to solve regional challenges.

Mashatile warned that millions of people could be left behind due to infrastructure gaps, skills shortages, and high connectivity costs. He noted that inadequate broadband access remains a significant barrier that must be addressed to make digital transformation truly inclusive for all. The Deputy President highlighted the African Continental Free Trade Area as a key opportunity to establish a single digital market across Africa. He argued that closer regional integration would help drive inclusive growth, investment, and innovation through harmonized regulations and stronger cross-border collaboration. To realize this, he said the continent must enable interoperable payment systems and trusted data flows between the different African nations.

The articles describe the Africa Tech Festival as one of the largest and most influential technology events currently held on the continent. This event covers key areas ranging from entrepreneurship and digital infrastructure to the growth of the broader African digital economy. Mashatile outlined five priorities, including investing in human capital, building future-ready infrastructure, and strengthening the innovation ecosystems found across the continent. He also emphasized the need for responsible digital governance and cybersecurity to build trust while deepening regional integration and continental cooperation. These priorities are intended to translate the digital potential of the continent into broad-based prosperity for all of its people.

The festival will continue through Thursday with various sessions designed to turn high-level discussions into tangible progress for the African people. Mashatile called for bold investment, decisive action, and stronger partnerships to build a more connected, competitive, and inclusive future for generations. He believes Africa will compete in the age of AI by creating solutions with global relevance rather than through simple imitation. The articles leave open how specific countries will implement these five priorities or how the single digital market will be established. They do not state which specific companies are exhibiting or provide the exact outcomes of the various investment forums and roundtables.

stories.Headline: Marsh's Schnur links AI tools to a doubling of client cyber incidents
stories.Summary:
Marsh reported that its clients filed 105 cyber incidents in the last two weeks of October, which is more than double the 48 incidents recorded in the final two weeks of May, according to data the insurance broker released and Reuters reported on November 17, 2026. Meredith Schnur, who leads the US and Canada cyber practice at Marsh Risk, told Reuters in an interview this week that attackers are using AI enabled and agentic tools to identify vulnerabilities, and she said AI could be attributed to a significant number of the incidents. She said the speed and scale of AI tool adoption, combined with organizations taking longer to contain attacks and respond to incidents, were the main factors driving the recent increase in cyber incident volumes. Schnur said AI is not a peril but an amplification of risk in all areas, and she said the technology lets attackers find and exploit longstanding vulnerabilities such as unpatched software, exposed systems and weak identity controls at a much faster pace. The rise in reported incidents requires businesses and their insurers to contend with attacks that spread faster and reach more targets, because AI tools that are becoming more widely accessible let attackers scale their operations with fewer resources.

GlobalData expects global cyber insurance premiums to rise 6.9% to $16.6 billion in 2026, before growth accelerates to 10% in 2027 to reach $18.3 billion, as businesses respond to rising attack frequency. The Marsh figures compare the final two weeks of October with the final two weeks of May, and the 105 incidents more than double the 48 recorded in the earlier period. The report ties the increase to AI adoption and to slower containment and response times, and it says the wider availability of AI tools is widening the pool of potential targets and putting pressure on businesses. Schnur, the US and Canada cyber practice leader at Marsh Risk, is the person the articles identify as explaining the data, and she attributed a significant share of the incidents to AI in her interview with Reuters this week. She said the signs that attackers are using AI enabled and agentic tools to identify vulnerabilities are happening, and she described AI as an amplification of risk in all areas rather than a peril in itself.

She said the speed and scale of AI tool adoption, together with organizations taking longer to contain attacks and respond to incidents, were the main factors behind the recent increase in cyber incident volumes. The reporting was by Noor Zainab Hussain and Manya Saini in Bengaluru, with editing by Shilpi Majumdar, and the story was published by Reuters and carried by Insurance Journal. The context the articles give is a cyber insurance market that GlobalData expects to grow faster over the next two years as businesses respond to rising attack frequency, with premiums reaching $16.6 billion in 2026 and $18.3 billion in 2027. The articles do not say what Marsh or insurers will change in response to the data, and they do not describe any new policy terms or claims figures beyond the incident counts and the premium forecasts. What happens next, according to the articles, is continued growth in cyber insurance premiums at a faster pace over the next two years, driven by the rising frequency of attacks that the Marsh data shows.

stories.Headline: ROBOTERA deploys humanoid robots across China Post network in Guangdong to tackle labor shortages
stories.Summary:
Beijing Xingdongjiyuan Technology Co., Ltd., known as ROBOTERA, deployed humanoid robots across the China Post Group Guangdong Branch network on November 17, 2026. This initiative represents the most geographically extensive use of embodied intelligence robots within the logistics sector to date. The rollout covers 11 postal hubs located in eight different cities across Guangdong Province. These cities include Guangzhou, Shenzhen, Dongguan, Jiangmen, Shantou, Shanwei, Jieyang, and Heyuan.

The project requires the robots to handle high-volume sorting and cross-regional logistics coordination in a demanding environment. These machines utilize a self-developed five-finger dexterous hand for flexible parcel handling and offer multiple power options for continuous operation. Since a pilot began at the Guangzhou Postal District Center in March 2026, the robots have processed over 1,500 parcels per hour. This technology changes the workforce by allowing humans to move from strenuous frontline tasks to roles in quality control, operations coordination, and robot maintenance.

ROBOTERA and the China Post Group Guangdong Branch are jointly responsible for implementing this large-scale industrial productivity project. The company stated that its AI-native, full-stack technology approach helps translate embodied intelligence into new productivity for the logistics sector. They explained that these robots fill critical capacity gaps caused by persistent labor shortages and high workforce turnover. This support is especially vital during peak shopping seasons when parcel volumes often surge to several times their normal levels.

Guangdong serves as a primary validation site because it is the largest province in China by express parcel volume. The integrated solution has already been adapted for various parcel types and sorting configurations across postal operations in East China. These systems include adaptive speed control and irregular-item rejection to prevent collisions, jams, and missed items. ROBOTERA intends to continue collaborating with industry partners to integrate embodied intelligence into more real-world workflows.

stories.Headline: Family physician Mara Gordon uses an AI scribe on her phone to draft notes but reviews and signs each one
stories.Summary:
Dr. Mara Gordon, a family physician in Camden, N.J., wrote in a piece published November 17, 2026, that a reader asked whether to worry about an artificial intelligence scribe recording private medical conversations. The reader said her doctor had started recording office visits with an AI scribe and that she said yes when asked if she was comfortable. The reader said that in hindsight she felt a little freaked out. Gordon wrote that AI scribes are all the rage in medicine right now. Gordon wrote that doctors use them to take notes everywhere from the gynecologist's office to the emergency room.

Gordon wrote that she first asks the patient if they are comfortable using the service. Gordon wrote that if the patient says yes, she starts recording using an app on her smartphone, usually set down on the desk in the exam room. Gordon wrote that the scribe uses "automatic speech recognition," which records the conversation and automatically distinguishes between the doctor's and patient's voices. Gordon wrote that sometimes, when a family member accompanies the patient, the app needs to distinguish between three or more voices. Gordon wrote that when the visit ends, the recording is transcribed and a large language model geared toward medicine converts the raw transcript into a medical note.

Gordon wrote that the notes follow a standard format specific to the specialty and the type of visit. Gordon wrote that the notes reflect what the patient told the doctor, physical exam findings, and the doctor's medical decision-making. Gordon wrote that she is ultimately responsible for the content of the AI-generated note and always reads them carefully before clicking "sign" and adding them to the medical record. Gordon wrote that most AI scribe software makes doctors sign a user agreement stating doctors are liable for everything they write in the medical record, even if a scribe helps them. Gordon wrote that when the AI-generated notes are factually accurate, she almost always ends up editing them to make her clinical decision-making more clear.

Gordon wrote that she talked to Dr. Eileen Kim, an assistant professor of internal medicine at the University of California San Diego who specializes in clinical informatics. Gordon quoted Kim saying that an overburdened doctor seeing too many patients has an AI tool offered that seems like a great solution but no time to adequately review everything. Gordon quoted Kim saying the note goes into the chart and another AI tool reading the notes propagates errors throughout the chart. Gordon wrote that she comes across erroneous information in the electronic health record all the time and that it is hard to know how much is related to AI and how much to human error. Gordon wrote that many AI scribes can only be used with English-speaking patients, and that health equity advocates fear this means unequal access that could further widen health disparities.

Gordon wrote that she has been an eager adopter in her own primary care practice. Gordon wrote that she uses an app on her phone that records her conversation with a patient and then uses AI to write a preliminary summary for the medical record. Gordon wrote that it saves her time and helps her focus more fully on her patient, so she can make eye contact rather than stare at the computer screen. Gordon wrote that she shares her patients' concerns about privacy and how AI scribes might impact the doctor-patient relationship. Gordon wrote that she worries corporate health systems will pressure doctors to use time saved with an AI scribe to squeeze in even more patients, and that artificial intelligence might one day put her out of a job.

Gordon wrote that there are lots of AI scribes on the market, ranging from products embedded within the electronic medical record to free apps a doctor can download on her phone. Gordon wrote that most scribes use a smartphone's recording capabilities to "listen in" on the conversation, though some use a desktop computer or a separate recording device. Gordon wrote that she uses her personal smartphone, as do many physicians she knows, and that she once got notification pings from her book club's group chat while recording a patient visit, which made her put the phone in "do not disturb" mode. Gordon wrote that conversations are not stored on her device but uploaded directly to a HIPAA-compliant cloud, where the data is transcribed into the AI-generated clinical note, and that most scribe systems then delete the recording and the note after a set period of time. Gordon wrote that HIPAA means the program was designed in accordance with the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, a federal law designed to protect patients' privacy, and that the software company is responsible for safeguarding the data at every step, encrypting it, controlling access, protecting against data breaches, and being liable if data is leaked.

Gordon wrote that she recently saw a patient with metastatic cancer who did not believe he had cancer despite multiple conversations with her, his oncologist, and his surgeon, and that she had even, with his permission, called his spouse. Gordon wrote that the AI scribe did not get this tricky situation right and that the note simply said the patient had been misdiagnosed rather than reflecting the nuances of the conversation. Gordon wrote that she often catches other errors, like mistaking a patient's gender or age, and that the scribes are known for mistaking "I do" statements with "I do not," where the difference between "I do have chest pain" and "I do not have chest pain" can be a matter of life and death. Gordon wrote that most AI scribe companies delete recorded conversations within a set period of time as a security feature, to protect patient privacy and protect doctors from lawsuits, and that there is widespread concern the transcriptions could be used in medical malpractice lawsuits. Gordon wrote that some researchers call the recordings "digital gold" that could assess the quality of AI-generated notes or study physician-patient communication, and that for now recordings of regular appointments, unless a patient is enrolled in a research study, are not used for research.

Gordon wrote that most of her patients readily agree to the AI scribe, but occasionally patients worry the data isn't really secure or could be used to identify them in the future. Gordon wrote that if a patient doesn't want the AI scribe, she just takes notes on the computer while they talk, as she did for years before the scribes became available. Gordon quoted Kim saying AI is "just everywhere" and it would be impossible to separate it, and that software relying on machine learning is used for billing, clinical decision-making, and communication between the doctor's office and patients. Gordon wrote that AI is often used in risk calculators, like tools that estimate a patient's risk of heart disease based on variables like cholesterol levels and blood pressure, and in "early warning" systems that notify clinicians their patients might be vulnerable to high-risk conditions like sepsis based on vital signs and lab values. Gordon quoted Kim saying it is basically impossible for patients to opt out entirely from having AI involved in their medical care "unless you're so healthy that no risk calculators ever come near you."

Gordon wrote that she asked Kim, a primary care doctor like her, whether AI would replace them in the coming years, and whether an AI scribe that could ask the same questions she does could generate a treatment plan as good or better than the one she recommends. Gordon wrote that Kim thought AI might change how patients experience primary care, possibly for the better if AI scribes allow doctors to focus more on their patients and less on the computer. Gordon wrote that the article ends there, leaving Kim's ultimate answer about replacement unstated. Gordon wrote that readers can send health questions to thrive@npr.org. Gordon wrote that she is happy to have robots help with her administrative tasks but still takes pride in being a human doctor with human intelligence.
