stories.Headline: Columbia professor Sandra Matz finds AI assistance reduces the uniqueness of people's choices
stories.Summary:
Professor Sandra Matz of Columbia University ran an experiment with the ice cream store Baskin Robbins, which is famous for its 31 flavors, offering a different one every day for a full month without repetition. When she handed the decision-making power of flavor selection to ChatGPT, the brand with a huge variety of flavors basically only had two choices in the eyes of AI, Walnut Cream and Mint Chocolate Chip. She asked the question repeatedly 100 times, and ChatGPT gave only these two options 96 times. Matz said in her TEDx speech that if this continues for a long time, Baskin Robbins may eventually only have these two flavors left, because if no one chooses the other 29 flavors anymore, merchants would have no reason to keep offering them. Matz believes that AI is inadvertently flattening the diversity of human choices.

Matz and her team analyzed more than 110,000 real social media choices and experimental data from 1,000 American users. They found that whether using a general LLM agent or a personally adjusted version, the uniqueness of the choices people make with AI assistance will decrease significantly. Although the personalized version slightly alleviates the convergence between people, it compresses the breadth of an individual's own choices at a deeper level. When you tell ChatGPT what flavor you like, AI will 100% recommend that explicitly stated favorite, without any deviation. A 2025 study analyzed 2,200 college application essays and found that in terms of collective diversity growth rate, human contributions are more than three times that of GPT.

Matz said that algorithms focus on exploitation, continuously reinforcing options that have already proven to be effective. She said this is beneficial to businesses and sometimes necessary for consumers, because there are far too many choices in modern life. She said that without AI to help filter, we can hardly cope with the complexity of modern life. She said that AI systems, especially recommendation models trained on massive user data, tend to optimize short-term satisfaction by making you click, making you stay, and preventing you from churning. She said that in the face of massive data, what the majority likes is an easily accessible signal.

New York Times reporter Kashmir Hill handed over all the decision-making things for a whole week to AI, including where to eat, what clothes to buy, and what shows to watch. After a week, she felt that she had fallen into a certain basic state, with life becoming predictable and choices impeccable, but there were no more surprises. She began to miss the occasional wrong turn, walking into a restaurant she would never have gone to, and accidentally finding it more delicious than the recommended ones. Italy briefly banned ChatGPT in 2023 due to data privacy issues, and researchers took this opportunity to conduct a natural experiment, analyzing the marketing content of restaurants on social media.

During the ban, the lexical similarity of the content decreased by 15%, the syntactic similarity decreased by 12%, the semantic similarity decreased by 2%, while the user interaction rate rose by about 3.5%. Studies tracking changes in writing complexity of academic papers, news reports and Reddit texts before and after the large-scale popularization of ChatGPT found that the variance decreased by between 21% and 50%. In the field of recommendation system research, this kind of phenomenon is called the rich get richer effect. Guided by algorithms, users may browse a wider range of categories, but their final purchase behavior is more concentrated on popular products, and overall sales diversity decreases instead.

Byung-Chul Han wrote in The Disappearance of the Other that the spread of homogenization is not cancerous, but somnolent, and that it does not encounter resistance from the immune system. Byung-Chul Han described affirmative violence as a kind of harm composed of excessive similarity and excessive smoothness, without heterogeneous friction, no resistance brought by the Other, only continuous consent and appropriateness. The article says that the bias of recommendation systems towards exploitation is a long-standing structural problem, and the emergence of large language models only extends this mechanism from content recommendation to the level of decision-making agents. Some people are actively asking AI to provide unexpected options, asking it to give some options that you are not often asked about but worth trying.

Some people choose to deliberately not use AI in certain decisions, because its suggestions are so good that it has optimized away the possibility of taking a wrong turn. The article says that actively making mistakes has become one of the few ways for humans to defend their aesthetic power in the AI era. The article asks what evidence can be presented to prove that heterogeneity still exists in the human soul. The article says that if we do not want life to become a standard curve in the algorithm's statistical table, this question remains open.

stories.Headline: Secure Code Warrior finds budget AI models can produce safer code than premium versions
stories.Summary:
Secure Code Warrior released findings from its SCW AI Trust Index on November 18, 2026, regarding the security of AI-generated code. The research tested more than 30 AI models from companies including OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Alibaba, and Mistral to evaluate their safety. This study used AI systems to build over 15,000 applications and 41.3 million lines of code across 11 programming languages. The results showed a 15-fold gap between the best and worst performers, with vulnerabilities ranging from 0.24 to 3.66 per 1,000 lines of code.

The findings indicate that curated security rule sets can reduce measured risk by as much as 70 percent. While GPT-6-Astra-High led or tied for first in four frameworks, fifteen different models ranked first in at least one of the 11 frameworks. Budget models sometimes outperformed premium ones, such as GPT 6 Luna which cost USD $0.10 a run and had a risk score of 19.4. In contrast, Claude Opus 5.5 cost USD $8.17 a run and recorded a higher mean risk score of 43.6.

Pieter Danhieux, the Co-Founder and Chief Executive Officer of Secure Code Warrior, stated that assumptions about newer or more expensive models are not always correct. He explained that models do not use secure coding by default, meaning the prompts and rules provided determine the safety of the output. Danhieux emphasized that security leaders need an evidence-based view of inherited risks because model behavior can shift with every new release. He argued that this highlights the critical need for strong governance regarding how AI coding models are utilized.

These results arrive as software teams rely more on large language models for their daily coding work. External survey data suggests that AI will likely account for 65 percent of committed code by 2027. This trend increases the pressure on security teams to understand the specific risks tied to different models and prompting strategies. The company noted that human-only commits typically introduce fewer vulnerabilities, citing Stanford University research that found roughly 0.08 vulnerabilities per 1,000 lines.

stories.Headline: Google adds TPU 8i Max and TPU 8tx to its eighth-generation AI chip line-up
stories.Summary:
Google expanded its eighth-generation Tensor Processing Unit line-up with two new systems, TPU 8i Max and TPU 8tx, bringing its TPU releases this year to four systems, according to an announcement reported on 18 November 2026. TPU 8tx is aimed at secure and confidential inference, while TPU 8i Max is designed for workloads that need large context windows and greater compute density within the same rack footprint. Google said the launch reflects broader demand from customers using AI for model training, inference and autonomous agents. It added that TPUs are now used by nearly 100 customers, including frontier laboratories, trading firms, retailers and universities. TPU 8tx is built on the same silicon as TPU 8t and is paired with fifth-generation AMD EPYC CPU hosts, and Google said it is intended for regulated enterprises and government users that want to run models and agents alongside sensitive data.

According to Google, TPU 8tx protects data and model weights while they are in use through hardware-level confidential computing, and it uses the same Boardfly network introduced for lower-latency reasoning workloads, delivering up to half the latency of TPU 8t with a near-zero performance penalty. TPU 8i Max combines two low-latency TPU 8i chips into a single package, doubling compute, SRAM and high-bandwidth memory bandwidth compared with TPU 8i, according to the company. Google said the design fits twice the silicon into the existing rack footprint, allowing data centres to deploy more compute per square foot and per watt. The launch expands Google's eighth-generation TPU family to four products: TPU 8t for large-scale training, TPU 8i for lower-latency reasoning, TPU 8tx for confidential computing and TPU 8i Max for high-context workloads. Google said this system-level approach allows it to respond more quickly to changing customer requirements than waiting for a full new chip generation, and that rather than redesigning silicon each time, it modifies the surrounding compute, networking, storage and packaging to create more specialised systems.

Google said businesses are asking for accelerators that can reason across AI models' massive context windows as computing moves from human to agent scale, and that some highly regulated customers are asking for specialised encryption capabilities for unique workloads. Alongside the hardware additions, Google outlined software efforts including native PyTorch code and Hugging Face models on TPUs through the open-source TorchTPU project, TPU back ends for open-source inference engines including vLLM and SGLang, and a TPU agent suite in preview. Google said its open-source XLA Serving Engine allows customers to train models in Python and serve them in a C++ runtime across TPUs, GPUs and CPUs, while Agent Compute Engine suspends and resumes idle agent sessions to reduce infrastructure costs. Google said TPU Sync can reduce key-value transfer latency and time to first token by more than 90%, and that GKE dynamic slicing now lets users reconfigure TPU topologies on demand, cutting job start-up times by up to five times and improving fault recovery by up to 4.5 times. Google also said it has been using AI tools from Google DeepMind in its chip design process, including AlphaChip reinforcement learning systems and Gemini-based design tools, which it said have helped cut parts of chip layout work from weeks to hours.

stories.Headline: Google reports attackers use AI agents to automate vulnerability exploitation at machine speed
stories.Summary:
Google Threat Intelligence Group reported on November 17, 2026 that threat actors are using AI-powered agentic workflows to automate vulnerability discovery and exploitation, which accelerates attacks to machine speed and reduces the time defenders have to patch systems. The group observed financially motivated and state-sponsored groups adopting these tools at large scale after earlier experimental use. GTIG highlighted the use of CAIRN, an open-source multi-agent penetration-testing framework, in an attack against the U.S. aerospace sector. Suspected North Korean hackers also used Claude Code to deliver malware, according to the report. Researchers estimate that unsophisticated, fully autonomous attacks requiring little human interaction will emerge within the next three months, while sophisticated fully autonomous agentic attacks are likely within six months.

The FBI warned last week that multiple threat actors have weaponized the ARTEX AI pentesting framework since August, with attacks targeting organizations in financial, government, technology, defense, and healthcare sectors. Google states that attackers systematically abuse open-source pentesting suites including ARTEX, CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI, and HexStrike AI, which facilitate adaptive attacks against internet-exposed endpoints vulnerable to low-complexity flaws that large language models can easily exploit. GTIG's AI Threat Tracker report cites a multi-agent system called exploit_agent that fully automated vulnerability finding and exploitation against French media, entertainment, and education websites. GTIG identified an exposed staging server hosting the framework, which integrates with multiple frontier and local LLMs, analyzes software updates on popular web apps to find flaws, and automatically attempts to exploit them. The deployment of such frameworks dramatically decreases patch time and produces false leads, as seen with PHP2Shell, where hundreds of purported AI-generated proof-of-concept exploits appeared quickly and added a significant burden on defenders who must verify code and develop protections.

Beyond automated attacks, Google also observed UNC6836 using modified Claude Code to deliver the SOMBERMEME backdoor against cryptocurrency firms. AI is also routinely used in influence operations by state-backed groups, commercial vendors, and political networks. LLMjacking has become widespread, with attackers exploiting this new revenue stream at significant cost to affected organizations. The New York Post reported that Russian AI bots pulled off the first fully automated cyber attack and that Google caught them.

stories.Headline: Miro finds AI boosts individual productivity but not team collaboration
stories.Summary:
Miro released research on 17 November 2026 examining how artificial intelligence is affecting productivity and team performance in Australia and New Zealand, and the study found a clear gap between gains in individual productivity and broader organisational results. The survey covered more than 9,500 leaders and workers globally, including 1,031 respondents in Australia and New Zealand. It found that 83 per cent of workers said AI had improved their individual productivity at work, while 72 per cent said it had increased output speed. That uplift was far less clear in other areas, with only 59 per cent of respondents in Australia and New Zealand saying AI had improved output quality.

A majority of respondents said AI had not improved decision-making or collaboration between colleagues and teams, and one in four said it had not improved organisation-wide productivity. Another 23 per cent said AI had not delivered better business outcomes such as revenue growth, cost reduction or operational efficiency. The survey found that 69 per cent of respondents said most AI-assisted work happens in private sessions rather than shared spaces, and half of enterprises reported difficulty with information silos that limit access to shared context across systems. Another 37 per cent of leaders said visibility into how AI is being used was poor or non-existent, while 63 per cent reported compliance and security concerns in the absence of unified governance.

Pete Bradd, Chief Evangelist at Miro, said individuals are getting more capable while the connections that make a team smart are getting thinner, and he pointed to research linking team intelligence to social perceptiveness and equal turn taking more than to the intelligence of individual members. He said the data points to the wrong direction, citing that 44 per cent say AI has made their culture less collaborative and 31 per cent feel disconnected from colleagues because of increased AI use. Dave Ross, Product Evangelist Leader at Miro, said customers report gains in AI-driven productivity at the individual level but many find scaling these gains across the organisation a challenge. He said faster execution is a benefit, but decision-making and decision quality is the real bottleneck, and the research points to a growing need for a place where AI and people can collaborate on critical decisions instead of in fragmented individual single-player tools.

The survey also found that nearly half of respondents said context switching had increased over the past year, while 59 per cent said they faced a higher volume of AI-generated output to review. Just over half, or 53 per cent, said they were seeing more low-quality AI-driven output that requires extra human review and rework, and more than one in 10 said decision-making, creativity, collaboration and work-life balance had worsened because of increased AI use. On workplace culture and role design, 65 per cent of workers worried role boundaries would blur, 49 per cent feared related roles would merge, 48 per cent were concerned about a decline in collaboration culture, and 22 per cent said work felt lonely because of increased AI use. Miro said its survey found that two-thirds of enterprise decision-makers planned to implement what it described as an AI workhub within 12 months, and the wider dataset covered respondents in product development, IT, operations and other functions across North America, Europe and Asia-Pacific.

stories.Headline: NAVER launches AI Tab to turn search answers into purchases and bookings
stories.Summary:
In June 2026, NAVER launched “AI Tab,” a new service that combines generative AI technology with the search assets NAVER has built up over many years. NAVER published the “NAVER AI Tab Service Brief” together with a research team led by Professor Kim Kyung-oe of Yonsei University. The brief is an in-depth look at how AI Tab is being used, based on real service data. AI Tab goes beyond simply providing search results and tailors its answers to each user’s question. It brings together rich information updated in real time across NAVER, from restaurant reservation availability to authentic product reviews.

AI Tab builds its answers from experience-based information accumulated across NAVER Cafe, Blog, and Jisik-iN. It brings together into a single answer the posts that NAVER users used to search for and compare on their own. It also cites its sources, so users can visit the original posts to explore more examples. When generating an answer, AI Tab draws on the NAVER service that best fits the question. If a user asks about a product, it calls on NAVER Shopping; if they ask about a place, it calls on NAVER Map/Place, and reflects those results in its answer.

According to NAVER’s internal survey, more than half of AI Tab users said that seeing an AI answer led them to actually make a purchase, book a reservation, or visit a place. Real service data showed the same trend, with click-through rates for NAVER Shopping and Map/Place within AI Tab each exceeding 40%. Professor Kim Kyung-oe of Yonsei University, who led the research, said he had been using AI Tab even before starting the research and felt that finding information had become much easier. He said AI Tab summarizes the key points first, so he could choose to look only at what he needed. He also said he finds AI Tab especially useful in everyday moments, like looking for places to visit or comparing products.

Kim said the biggest change is that search is becoming more like a conversation, with people asking questions in full sentences and following up based on the answers. He said analysis of AI Tab confirmed this shift, with users in their teens and twenties showing a relatively high share of multi-turn usage, exchanging several questions with the AI. He said users in other age groups showed different behaviors, such as checking the sources of the information AI provided or verifying it through additional searches. He said AI is not simply replacing traditional search but changing the very way users explore and use information. He said users treat AI answers as a starting point to explore and compare further, and then turn that into actual choices and actions.

Kim said AI Tab’s greatest strength is its ability to connect users’ information search to real action. He said people need qualitative information such as other people’s experiences, reviews, and ratings, but also concrete information such as price, location, business hours, and reservation availability. He said NAVER has years of accumulated content on Blog and Cafe, plus a wide range of services such as Shopping, Map, and Reservation. He said AI Tab can provide both the qualitative information users need to make judgments and the concrete information they need to act, and then connect that to actions like purchases and reservations. He said that with typical generative AI services the answer itself is often the final output, and users have to move to another service to buy or book something.

Kim said it will become increasingly difficult for services to stand out simply by providing accurate and useful search results or answers. He said competitiveness in the search market will depend not just on how well a service provides information, but on how effectively it helps users turn that information into real decisions and actions. He said he hopes AI Tab evolves beyond a service that simply answers questions accurately into one that helps users achieve their goals more easily and efficiently. He said it is important to understand users’ context and goals, organize the information they need, and naturally connect it to their actual choices and actions. NAVER said it will continue to develop AI Tab so it can better understand each user’s goals and help them take real action.

Articles.Title: Adding AI to the Search Experience: NAVER AI TAB Service Brief - NAVERCorp.

stories.headline_source: Adding AI to the Search Experience: NAVER AI TAB Service Brief

stories.Headline: Nearly 60% of legal leaders say AI adoption outpaces governance, survey finds
stories.Summary:
A survey published by Diligent Institute and Wilson Sonsini on 16 November 2026 found that nearly 60% of senior legal leaders believe AI adoption is moving faster than governance in their organisations, and it put average board readiness to oversee AI risk at 2.9 out of 5. The Q4 General Counsel Risk Index draws on responses from about 200 General Counsel, Chief Legal Officers and other senior legal executives. It found that 41% of respondents have yet to reach a basic AI governance framework, including 14% with no formal approach and 27% still developing policies and guidelines. About 70% of respondents represented organisations based in North America, while 51% came from private companies and 28% from publicly held companies. Respondents ranked regulatory change as the leading risk facing their organisations, cited by 55%, with AI-related risk at 49% and cyber threats at 47%.

Some 59% of legal leaders said their organisation faced a high level of risk, while workforce, culture and talent issues were cited by 34%, geopolitical conflict by 26% and supply-chain disruption by 24%. Around 67% of respondents said legal reviews vendors and assesses privacy, data, confidentiality and intellectual property issues tied to AI systems, but only 23% said their legal teams regularly brief the board or senior leadership on AI-related risks. The survey also tracked shifts from the previous quarter, with regulatory change rising from 48% to 55%, AI-related risk from 39% to 49% and cyber threats from 39% to 47%, while concern about geopolitical conflict fell from 52% to 26%. Dottie Schindlinger, Executive Director of Diligent Institute, said nearly six in 10 legal leaders report that AI adoption is outpacing governance and that the gap is a risk in itself, because as AI spreads it becomes harder to keep clear visibility into how it is used, what data it touches and who is accountable. She said boards do not need every director to be an AI expert, but they do need enough fluency to challenge assumptions and ensure oversight keeps pace with adoption.

Sachin Kohli, Partner at Wilson Sonsini, said that as risks like AI and cybersecurity evolve at breakneck speed, boards need a clear understanding of their potential legal, regulatory and disclosure implications and of how management is responding. He said legal leaders have a critical role in connecting these risks across the enterprise, working alongside risk, compliance and security to translate complex challenges into actionable insights and give boards visibility to anticipate emerging risks. The research adds to a broader debate over whether companies are putting enough controls around fast-moving AI deployments, and for Australian businesses it comes as regulators including ASIC and APRA continue to press boards for stronger accountability and better visibility over operational risks. The articles do not say what happens next beyond that.

Articles.Title: AI adoption outpaces governance, legal leaders warn - IT Brief Australia

stories.headline_source: AI adoption outpaces governance, legal leaders warn

stories.Headline: BSI survey finds half of business leaders say AI cuts entry-level roles
stories.Summary:
Research commissioned by the British Standards Institution, the UK's national standards body, has found that businesses are increasingly using artificial intelligence to do work traditionally performed by junior employees. Half of the 1,287 business leaders surveyed, 49%, said AI has already reduced entry-level opportunities for starters, and the same proportion expect their organisation to cut entry-level roles because of AI. In a separate finding, 52% of respondents said AI is reducing junior headcount, up from 45% who said the same last year. The report, Human by Design: Thriving in the AI Workforce, was published as the Milburn review into the sharp rise in young people not in education, employment or training was released.

The report notes that 59% of business leaders see AI as crucial to their organisation's growth, but it warns that cutting jobs may build future problems by severing the talent pipeline through which inexperienced workers become experienced ones. It says removing entry-level work may deliver short-term efficiencies, yet organisations will still need employees who have skilled up and progressed internally, and that people develop judgement and expertise by doing the work themselves with the guidance of a human mentor. BSI also finds that people consulting chatbots rather than colleagues endangers the routes by which core expertise and skills develop, and it argues that AI's greatest long-term risk to the workforce may be eroding the career pathways, learning opportunities and sense of purpose through which people develop expertise, confidence and ambition. Rather than handing work to AI, BSI says organisations should assess the value employees bring and redesign jobs so that learning, judgement and progression are preserved.

Kate Field, global head of human and social sustainability at BSI, said the sentiment seems to be to adopt AI or die, but too little thought is being given to the long-term consequences of replacing human talent with AI. She said there are serious questions about what working alongside AI means for people's psychological safety and wellbeing at work, and about the repercussions of decisions that could corrode skills development or reduce opportunities for collaboration and creativity. BSI warns that automation could worsen youth unemployment, saying that while AI is far from the sole cause, there are fears it is poised to exacerbate an already significant challenge with consequences that will reverberate for generations. The standards body says policymakers face pressure to ensure education and training keep pace with a labour market being reshaped by AI, and that if this happens, new workers will be valuable to employers because they will be able to adapt as AI transforms requirements.

Articles.Title: Half of employers say AI is reducing entry-level opportunities - Computing UK

stories.headline_source: Half of employers say AI is reducing entry-level opportunities

stories.Headline: EY survey finds 77% of tax leaders expect AI agent benefits but 71% remain at nascent maturity
stories.Summary:
EY has published its 2026 Tax and Finance Operations Survey, which found that interest in AI agents in tax functions has risen sharply, according to IT Brief Australia. The survey gathered responses from 1,600 Chief Financial Officers and senior finance and tax leaders across 30 jurisdictions and 22 industries. The findings show a gap between expectations for AI and the ability of tax and finance teams to put those plans into practice. While 77% of respondents said they expect AI agents to benefit the tax function, up from 21% a year earlier, 71% said they remain at a completely nascent or exploratory stage of maturity. Data issues emerged as the main obstacle, with 64% of tax and finance leaders identifying insufficient AI-ready data as the biggest barrier to advancing AI initiatives.

Only 16% considered their tax function highly effective at accessing, organising, using and reusing data, and among respondents who said their function is not effective with data, 61% pointed to data silos and 52% cited poor data quality. A further 43% said the inability to execute a sustainable data, AI and technology strategy was the biggest challenge to delivering their function's purpose. The survey also found that 83% said building a workforce in which humans work alongside AI agents is important, while 81% said hiring professionals with AI-related skills is a priority, and 60% ranked strategic thinking and problem-solving among the five most critical skills for future tax professionals. Marna Ricker, Global Vice Chair-Tax at EY, said many organizations have already invested in AI and the challenge is transforming their data, governance and talent capabilities to ensure they get return on their AI investments. She said ambition alone will not be enough as AI becomes embedded in business decision-making, and that tax leaders have an opportunity to use trusted data, knowledge, AI and human judgment to unlock capital.

Stuart Lang, Global Tax and Finance Operate Leader at EY, said the future tax function won't separate compliance from insight, and that every filing and reconciliation generates trusted data and knowledge that can become a source of tax intelligence for the business. He said realizing that potential will require leaders to make deliberate choices about workforce and talent priorities, investing not only in technology but in people skills and culture. Beyond AI adoption, the survey found that 79% of organisations are adapting operations in response to geopolitical developments, and nearly two-thirds, or 64%, are not fully prepared for real-time tax demands as tax administration becomes more digital and immediate. Among respondents already using co-sourcing, 86% said it gave them a greater ability to focus on higher-value activities, 78% reported improved tax risk management, and 77% said it helped them navigate legislative and regulatory change more successfully. With most respondents still in the early stages of AI-agent maturity, the survey points to a market in which ambition is running ahead of execution.

Articles.Title: EY survey finds tax teams keen on AI, but data lags - IT Brief Australia

stories.headline_source: EY survey finds tax teams keen on AI, but data lags

stories.Headline: TCS study finds 84% of executives rank productivity as AI's top benefit but only 10% let agents decide without approval
stories.Summary:
Tata Consultancy Services published a global study on enterprise artificial intelligence adoption, IT Brief Australia reported on 18 November 2026. The study found that 84% of executives cite productivity as AI's top benefit. The research was based on responses from 1,333 senior business and technology leaders across 25 countries. These included 44 respondents in Ireland from 11 industries. The findings point to a gap between the value companies say they get from AI tools and their willingness to let AI systems act independently.

Only 10% of global enterprises said they allow AI agents to execute decisions without human approval across multiple functions or business areas. Nine per cent said they have AI agents that can securely orchestrate workflows across enterprise applications. Security, risk and governance emerged as the main factor shaping deployment decisions worldwide, ahead of cost, speed and ease of deployment. In Ireland, leaders identified cost, speed and ease of deployment as the main driver of AI deployment. Seven per cent of Irish enterprises said they allow AI agents to execute decisions without human approval across multiple functions or business areas, compared with 10% globally.

Amit Kapur, Chief AI and Services Transformation Officer at TCS, said the shift is clearly in AI moving from assisting people to taking more autonomous action with deep access into an enterprise. He said productivity is clearly where enterprises are seeing the greatest value from AI today, with 84% of executives ranking it as the leading source of value from their AI investments. He said 10% have also indicated that they have seen an uplift in revenue. He said concerns around security, governance and resilience seem to be holding organisations back, and rightly so. He said deploying AI responsibly, with the right guardrails and enterprise controls, will be the big focus in the next stage of this journey.

On model independence, 86% of Irish respondents said it was an important factor in AI investment decisions, versus 90% worldwide. Thirty-nine per cent of Irish respondents identified AI sovereignty-related requirements as a high or very high organisational risk, above the global figure of 34%. Across Europe, 43% of respondents described sovereignty-related requirements as a high or very high organisational risk. Although 90% of respondents said model independence matters in investment decisions, only 7% reported having organisation-wide provider-switching continuity plans. Thirty-nine per cent of enterprises said they are still assessing whether AI initiatives generate enough value relative to token and compute costs.

Forty-four per cent of respondents said important business knowledge remains embedded within employees or scattered across fragmented documentation. Globally, 46% of respondents said they had targeted deployment of open-source AI for selected use cases, while in Ireland the figure was lower at 32%. The proportion of leaders who said it is still too early to determine AI's impact on the workforce rose from 4% in 2024 to 19% in 2026. North America showed stronger scores on some enterprise AI foundations, while Europe recorded greater concern about sovereignty. The UK and Ireland stood out on operational resilience, with comparatively stronger levels of AI continuity planning and governance integration.

The survey covered senior leaders from organisations with annual revenues ranging from USD $500 million to more than USD $20 billion, spanning 12 industries. Respondents included C-suite executives, divisional leaders, Senior Vice Presidents and Vice Presidents. On 12 November 2026, the Federal Reserve Board published working paper FEDS 2026-074, titled Artificial Intelligence and the U.S. Economy: Current Evidence. It was authored by Federal Reserve Board economists Nick Carollo, Leland D. Crane, Daniel Garcia Molina and Joseph Nichols. The paper documents that U.S. capital commitments for AI data centers have surged past $1 trillion while aggregate macroeconomic productivity gains and labor market disruptions remain muted.

Articles.Title: TCS study finds AI productivity gains outpace trust - IT Brief Australia
Fed Study: AI Data Centers vs Productivity Gains

stories.Headline: Plaud urges Australian employers to put privacy and consent at the centre of workplace AI use
stories.Summary:
Plaud, an AI device and software company, used comments from Megumi Yoshinaga, its Head of APAC and MEA Growth, to urge Australian employers to make privacy and consent central to workplace AI use as AI assistants become more common in meetings and office work, according to an IT Brief Australia article published on 17 November 2026. Yoshinaga said organisations should focus not only on what AI tools can do but also on what information they capture, where it is stored, who can access it and whether it can be deleted. The comments focus on AI note-taking and transcription tools, whose conversations can include customer details, personal data, intellectual property, commercial discussions and confidential plans, which such tools can reproduce quickly and at scale. A recurring concern is the use of personal AI accounts for work conversations, which Yoshinaga said can leave transcripts and company knowledge spread across personal accounts or cloud folders with uneven access controls.

Plaud argues that workplace AI discussions in Australia are entering a new phase in which trust matters as much as functionality, since early adoption focused on speed and convenience such as generating content, summarising meetings and automating tasks. Yoshinaga said that as different AI tools offer similar outputs, organisations are likely to look beyond product features, so privacy, security and user control will play a larger role in procurement and deployment decisions. On consent, she said employees and meeting participants should not be left guessing whether a conversation is being recorded or transcribed, and that employers should build consent into normal workflows so participants understand what is captured, why, who may access it and what happens afterwards. On ownership, she said organisations should be able to identify where information created by AI assistants resides and who has authority to remove it, arguing that transcripts become company records as soon as they are produced and may carry obligations around access, retention, security and deletion, a problem made more complex because the person who starts a recording is not necessarily the only person whose information is captured.

Yoshinaga said technology providers also have a responsibility to make privacy choices understandable, with settings not hidden behind technical complexity so users can make informed choices without specialist knowledge. Plaud said its approach includes a default policy under which user content is not used to train its own or third-party AI models unless a user has given explicit, informed consent in advance, and that user data is encrypted and stored on regional cloud infrastructure based on the user's location. For employers considering AI note-taking tools, Yoshinaga said they should examine what information is captured, where it is processed and stored, whether it is used to train models, how long it is retained and how much control users or organisations have over deletion, and she pointed to centrally managed workspaces as one way to gain clearer oversight of users, devices, subscriptions and collaboration. She said that when every product can summarise a meeting, a key question is whether you would trust it in the room.

Articles.Title: Plaud urges Australian employers to tighten AI privacy - IT Brief Australia

stories.headline_source: Plaud urges Australian employers to tighten AI privacy

stories.Headline: MathWorks expands TÜV SÜD certification to cover AI tool guidance for functional safety workflows
stories.Summary:
MathWorks has expanded TÜV SÜD certification for MATLAB, Simulink, Stateflow and System Composer to include generic AI tool classification guidance under ISO 26262, the automotive functional safety standard governing electrical and electronic systems in vehicles, according to an announcement reported on 17 November 2026. The certification applies to selected AI-assisted engineering workflows in functional safety applications and covers products included with the company's IEC Certification Kit. It focuses on Model-Based Design workflows that use the Simulink Agentic Toolkit for model development, model review and test-case generation. MathWorks said it is the first tool vendor to provide this type of guidance for selected AI-assisted workflows in functional safety, based on specific use cases evaluated by TÜV SÜD.

The guidance is intended to show how AI-assisted workflows can be introduced into safety-critical development in a controlled, auditable way, with scope covering work on Simulink models, model reviews and the generation of test cases tied to engineering processes. MathWorks said its approach links agentic AI systems directly to Model-Based Design workflows rather than limiting their use to text prompts, and the Simulink Agentic Toolkit lets AI agents interpret model structure, create and modify designs, run simulations, generate tests and connect requirements to models. The toolkit combines Simulink-specific tools with skills developed by the company's engineers and domain specialists for tasks including model development, algorithm specification, plant modelling, testing, validation and requirements generation, while engineers remain responsible for validating outputs produced with AI assistance. The Polyspace Agentic Toolkit extends AI-assisted workflows into software analysis and verification, including code robustness analysis, coding-standard compliance and defect detection, and the underlying framework is built on Model Context Protocol, which supports AI agent platforms including GitHub Copilot, Codex, Gemini CLI and Claude Code.

Michael Carone, Principal Product Marketing Manager for the Simulink Platform at MathWorks, said engineering teams are looking for ways to benefit from agentic AI without sacrificing the rigour that system development demands. He said that by connecting AI agents to Simulink models, simulations and testing workflows, MathWorks is helping engineers apply agentic AI within established engineering processes while preserving the accountability required for complex engineered systems. The move comes as engineering teams assess how AI can be used in sectors where traceability, validation and review are mandatory, and safety-related industries such as automotive typically require documented processes showing how designs were produced, checked and approved. MathWorks, founded in 1984 and headquartered in Natick, Massachusetts, employs more than 6,500 people across 34 offices worldwide.

Articles.Title: MathWorks expands TÜV SÜD certification for AI workflows - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: Abhijit Bhaduri and Karen Blake urge employers to audit AI hiring tools for bias and keep human oversight
stories.Summary:
AI recruitment tools can process applications quickly, but systems trained on historical hiring data may repeat existing biases and reject candidates with unconventional experience, Computing UK reported on 17 November 2026. The article said the increasing use of artificial intelligence in recruitment has made candidates feel their own true voice is unacceptable. It said applications are tweaked to make them more machine-parsable and chatbots are deployed to craft "more professional" CVs. It said the result is that all applications start to look alike, each written in slick, bland corporatese. It said the majority will be rejected automatically, without a human being as much as glancing at them.

The article said employers should combine automation with human intervention, examine rejected applications, track outcomes across demographic groups and scrutinise training data before procuring hiring technology. It said keyword filters may misinterpret career gaps, caring responsibilities and informal business experience. It said employers should audit rejected candidates and measure progression through each recruitment stage. It said IT and HR leaders should examine training data, bias controls and human-oversight provisions before buying recruitment software. It said these steps should be taken at the procurement stage if possible.

Abhijit Bhaduri, a former Microsoft general manager for global learning and development and author of the forthcoming AIdentity, said "It's a very, very poor system." He said automated systems cannot judge what really makes people tick, nor can they predict how they will perform as part of a team. He said "I think it's absolutely stupid to outsource the best part about building a really unique combination of people and to do it through machines. It's a tragedy." He said HR AI systems can be efficient for sorting but can be used the wrong way, optimising what can be measured rather than what makes an individual valuable.

He said organisations need to stop confusing efficiency with effective hiring. Karen Blake, head of the Equality, Diversity, and Inclusion in Science and Health coalition and a member of the Women in Tech Taskforce at the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport, said automated tools have introduced a distance between candidate and hirer. She said many talented people are being screened out, often without feedback and sometimes within hours of applying, while organisations become increasingly indecisive with roles left open for months. She said someone who spent three years caring for a parent with dementia has learned patience and judgement, and someone who helped run the family shop as a teenager probably understands margins and customers better than most graduates. She said biases built unwittingly into automated systems particularly disadvantage returners, women, neurodivergent candidates, older workers and those with unconventional career paths.

She said "These systems process applications in huge numbers, so a single flaw gets repeated thousands of times and ends up deciding who is treated as a candidate at all." The article said the recruitment playing field has never been level, and those who went to the right school or have been coached in professional-sounding corporate language have always had an advantage. It said the mass standardisation of speech patterns by LLMs has created a new norm that "feeds recruitment's oldest habit of hiring the safe bet," Blake asserted. It said the promise that AI will reduce headcount is already threatening the first rung of the career ladder in several professions.

It said Bhaduri believes future jobs will arise at the intersections between existing disciplines, and that hunar, "the irreducible human signature formed by lived experience, judgment, taste, memory, victory, failure, culture, instinct and practice," cannot be replicated by AI. It said Bhaduri suggests choosing three candidates from an automated system but seven from a different system where somebody who doesn't fit the mould can come in. The article said Blake advises focusing on being curious rather than looking impressive, and that your network matters far more than your followers. It said Bhaduri insists developing hunar means avoiding becoming over-reliant on chatbots, starting with the human first.

It said overuse of chatbots risks reducing an individual's distinctiveness towards a common denominator and has a deleterious effect on memory and sense-building. It said Blake states "AI tools are often trained on your past hiring and can only find people who look like your past, and your past is rarely what your future needs." It said recruitment tools are often bought for reasons of speed and cost, but procurers should also scrutinise the training data and measures used to reduce bias. More to follow.

Articles.Title: AI has broken recruitment. Here’s how employers can fix it - Computing UK

stories.headline_source: AI has broken recruitment. Here’s how employers can fix it

stories.Headline: Harvey Nash lets non-IT staff build AI tools under guardrails, CIO Ankur Anand says
stories.Summary:
Harvey Nash has spent several months running an approach it calls Citizen AI, in which employees outside the IT department build their own AI tools, agents and prototypes inside clear guardrails, according to Group CIO Ankur Anand, who described the work in a case study published by Computing UK on 17 November 2026. The company says the method joins a growing group of businesses taking the same route, and it treats the effort as much as a way to build a culture of innovation as a technology programme. Anand said the aim is to put AI into the hands of the people who best understand Harvey Nash's clients, processes and business problems, and to let them experiment within defined limits. The article gives one worked example, in which a content manager built a content agent that lets recruitment consultants find approved posts and assets, personalise them to their role and tone, and publish them to their social channels.

The approach changes how ideas become systems at the firm. Anand said that turning an idea into a technology solution once required specialist skills, funding and space on a development roadmap, and that AI now lowers that barrier so people can test whether an idea solves a real problem before the organisation commits significant resources. The goal is not to create hundreds of unofficial production systems but to support experimentation, after which Technology takes a proven concept and makes it enterprise-ready by addressing architecture, security, data protection, integration, testing, resilience, support and ownership. Harvey Nash uses Microsoft Copilot as its approved general-purpose enterprise AI environment, and its policy requires other AI applications used for company business to be approved by Group Technology, with specific protection for company, client, candidate, supplier and personal information. The company separates general AI use, agent creation and more advanced capabilities so that access reflects what someone is trying to achieve, and it distinguishes simple agents business users can build themselves from complex ones involving integrations that need technology team support.

Anand said guardrails are essential but should not make experimentation so difficult that innovation stops, and he set out expectations around an approved environment, controls on sensitive information and appropriate human judgement. He said the most important capability for an AI citizen is not necessarily coding but understanding a problem well enough to describe it, knowing its context and data, and judging whether the result is useful, and that people still need AI literacy to understand data sensitivity, test outputs and know when human accountability is essential. He said anyone who uses AI owns the work that comes out of it, so a person who sends an AI output in a client proposal, candidate email or board paper is accountable rather than the tool, and he said managers must make clear what data can and cannot go into an AI tool and give people time to learn. Every agent that moves beyond personal use needs a named owner who answers for what it does, what data it touches and whether it still does its job, with owners reviewing access as roles change and switching off agents that are no longer used or safe. Anand also flagged cost as an easily overlooked guardrail, saying agentic AI increasingly has consumption-based economics, so Harvey Nash monitors usage rather than treating AI as unlimited computing.

Anand described IT's role as changing, saying his team does not need to originate every innovation or build every prototype but should create an environment where innovation can emerge safely, identify the proof points that matter and turn the strongest ideas into secure, resilient enterprise capabilities. He said Citizen AI is about dramatically increasing the number of experiments an organisation can run, giving people at the coalface the freedom and guardrails to turn ideas into proven concepts, with Technology stepping in to scale an idea once it shows real value. The article does not say what results Harvey Nash has measured beyond the ability to count posts created through the content agent, which includes a gamification element to encourage usage. It also does not say what happens next beyond the stated plan of moving proven ideas into enterprise-ready systems.

Articles.Title: How Harvey Nash is embracing ‘Citizen AI’ for faster experimentation and adoption - Computing UK

stories.Headline: Genesis AI raises 500m dollars with Nvidia backing to build a general AI brain for robots
stories.Summary:
Genesis AI raised 500 million dollars in a Series A round during November 2026. The physical AI company received backing from Nvidia to build models for various robots. This funding follows a seed round of 105 million dollars from over one year ago. The startup now holds a valuation of 3.5 billion dollars after this latest investment. It represents one of the largest robotics funding rounds in Europe for the current year.

The company operates in France and the United States with support from Bpifrance and Ericsson. Other investors include Khosla Ventures, Neura Robotics, Samsung, and Zoom. The startup aims to create a general AI brain for robots to use. This system will allow robots to learn tasks through observation and a few examples. It seeks to move beyond the current need for specific, hand-coded instructions for every action.

The company is led by founders and executives including Ck ndpiu and q ixcm. They stated that the current approach to robotics is too specific and limited. They believe that AI should allow robots to learn from a few examples. The goal is to create a system that works across many different robot types. This approach aims to make robot training faster and more flexible for users.

The technology affects the robotics industry by reducing the need for manual coding. Other companies like Mosaico raised 7.5 million euros to help manage sensor data. Mosaico was backed by Connect Ventures, OpenOcean, and United Ventures in Italy. This Italian startup helps companies organize the vast data needed to train AI models. They aim to solve the data problem that slows down robotics development.

Genesis AI is part of a broader trend of high venture capital in robotics. Other firms like Bleu Robotics in Paris raised 5 million euros in pre-seed funding. Enact Intelligence also raised a large pre-seed round in Switzerland recently. TSMC is launching a 500 million dollar fund to support future chip titans. This fund targets startups and suppliers to broaden the ecosystem during the AI boom.

Genesis AI will now work to deploy its general AI brain across robots. The company plans to scale its operations in France and the United States. TSMC intends to find the next Nvidia or Broadcom through its new fund. The articles do not state when the general AI brain will be released. They also leave open how Mosaico will scale its data management tools.

Articles.Title: Robotics startup Genesis AI raises $500m backed by Nvidia
Exclusive: Italian robotics startup Mosaico raises €7.5m to tackle AI’s data problem

stories.Headline: Vection wins Italian business award in Melbourne for its Algho sign language AI system
stories.Summary:
Vection Technologies won an Innovation Award at the Italian Business Awards 2026 in Melbourne for its Algho Sign Language system, with UNOX presenting the award at the annual event hosted by the Italian Chamber of Commerce and Industry in Australia for Victoria and Tasmania. The company said the recognition highlights a product designed to let deaf people hold live conversations in sign language with an AI agent, supporting two-way conversations in International and Italian Sign Language. The system reads hand gestures, posture and facial expressions, then responds by signing in real time rather than using pre-recorded video. According to Vection, the sign-recognition tools, generation models and 3D agents used in the system were developed internally and integrated into its broader Algho conversational AI platform. The sign language system is already operating in several Italian transport hubs, including Roma Termini and Milano Centrale railway stations and Cagliari airport.

At Milan Bergamo Airport, Vection said its accessibility system, developed with Sorint.tek, serves as the main self-service terminal for passengers with disabilities, and it also serves wheelchair users and blind passengers. Based on unaudited airport data cited by Vection, 97% of passengers with disabilities can use the system independently, compared with 38% on a standard kiosk. The product was developed with ENS, Italy's national association for deaf people, and the National Research Council of Italy, and Vection also said it is developing real-time human interpreter support as an additional feature. The award comes as the business expands in Australia following its acquisition of Digital Experience Labs, which Vection described as an applied AI, process automation and decisioning services business. Vection said Algho Sign Language is one application of its broader Algho AI platform, which allows organisations to build and deploy AI agents without coding and is used for customer engagement, internal knowledge management, business process automation and decision support.

Earlier this year, Vection announced about AUD $4 million in new Algho AI contracts across 10 industry sectors in Italy, including rail transport, healthcare, water utilities, hospitality and education, and it said those contracts were close to the AUD $4.6 million in AI contracts it secured in the whole first half of FY26. In a separate agreement, the company announced a three-year framework deal with Swiss technology company URBANnext to commercialise Algho across European smart cities, public infrastructure and urban services, including a minimum annual purchase commitment of AUD $2.5 million and a minimum aggregate contract value of AUD $7.5 million over the initial term. Vection linked the latest award to its work on practical uses for AI in public-facing services, and it has positioned Algho as a platform for use across multiple sectors as well as in accessibility settings. Luis Nejo, Chief Executive Officer APAC at Vection Technologies, said the company was proud to receive the recognition from the Italian business community in Australia and that Algho Sign Language shows what inclusive AI can do outside the lab, with deaf passengers in some of Italy's busiest stations and airports now able to ask for help in their own language in real time.

Articles.Title: Vection wins award for sign-language AI in Melbourne - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: Liquid AI releases d1.2 and d1.2-ultra decision models that accept text, images and audio
stories.Summary:
Liquid AI released two new decision models, d1.2 and d1.2-ultra, on November 17, 2026, according to MarkTechPost. A decision model does not write text, because it returns calibrated probabilities over a fixed set of answers instead. The d1.2 family now accepts text, images and audio, and it adds five new answer types. The d1.2-ultra model scores 75 on the Artificial Analysis Decision Index v2.1, which is the top score among decision models on that index.

The models run only on the hosted Liquid API, and no weights are available yet, though Liquid AI says it will open them at some point. Parameter sizes are not disclosed, and the models take up to 65,536 input tokens per question and 128 questions per call. The d1.2 model scores 69 on the same index, and Liquid AI reports a 0.8-point calibration error for d1.2-ultra across 13 benchmarks in its own test. The new answer types cover reading a value, finding every span, locating objects, estimating a number with a range, and picking every option that applies. Audio can be the subject of a question or the question itself, the API takes 16-bit PCM WAV at 10 tokens per second, and both models answer 95% to 97% of questions correctly on held-out ESC-50 and FLEURS recordings.

The index combines six evaluations, with AA-Paperclip carrying 30% of the weight, four others carrying 15% each and When2Call carrying 10%, and its Decision Score penalizes confident wrong answers. On the chart shared by Liquid AI, Drex Max v1.1, SubQ Snap 1.2 and GLiDE v1.2 follow at 73, and d1.2 at 69 is 2 points below the deprecated d1-ultra at 71. Liquid AI argues that no model scores higher than d1.2 for less money, and it says d1.2 is faster and costs less than half as much as d1.2-ultra. The earlier d1, d1.1 and d1-ultra models are now deprecated and do not support audio or the new tasks. The calibration figures come from Liquid AI's own test on held-out splits of public datasets, and no public benchmark exists yet.

Articles.Title: Liquid AI Releases d1.2 and d1.2-ultra: Omnimodal Decision Models That Top the AA Decision Index

stories.Headline: Knightcorp report warns AI and cloud gaps leave insurance cover open to dispute
stories.Summary:
Knightcorp has launched its Forerunner Report - Technology, which examines insurance issues linked to AI, cyber risk, cloud exposure, directors' liability and connected devices, according to an article published by IT Brief Australia on 16 November 2026. The research argues that insurance reviews are struggling to keep pace with how technology businesses now operate, particularly when companies rely on AI tools, cloud infrastructure and third-party software platforms. It presents insurance less as an annual procurement exercise and more as part of broader risk governance for finance leaders, boards and technology teams. One of the report's central findings is that policy wording may not clearly address AI-related claims, and Knightcorp said some professional indemnity and cyber policies are silent on AI, which could leave room for disputes over whether cover applies when businesses build AI into their own products or use AI embedded in third-party platforms. The report says AI exclusions are appearing in some policy wordings, citing Lander & Rogers, which adds pressure on companies to check whether their existing insurance arrangements match their use of the technology.

On cloud cover, Knightcorp said undeclared systems, or systems that do not fit a policy's wording, can become a point of dispute during claims, and it suggests businesses map third-party systems that handle client data and then test how each one is treated in policy applications and wording. The report applies the same logic to connected hardware, saying companies that make or supply smart devices should check whether new mandatory security standards apply to them, including rules banning universal default passwords on in-scope consumer devices manufactured after a specified threshold. It also highlights action by the Australian Securities and Investments Commission over misleading sustainability claims, noting that penalties in greenwashing cases involving Mercer Superannuation and Vanguard Investments fell on the companies involved, and it notes that organisations covered by the Privacy Act that use automated decision-making in certain ways will need to disclose that use in their privacy policies. Trent Brown, Chief Executive Officer of Knightcorp, said the issue for companies is whether insurance arrangements still reflect the pace of change inside technology businesses, and he said the question is no longer simply whether a company is insured but whether its risk and insurance arrangements still reflect the business it has become. Brown said that uncertainty is most likely to surface in policy interpretation and claims handling, particularly once an incident has already occurred.

Justin Geldart, Account Director at Knightcorp, said that where a policy is silent on AI the outcome is uncertain and coverage can be disputed, and he encouraged technology leaders to ask how their cover treats AI they build versus AI they buy because the answer can differ. Jessica Tanner, Technology Account Director at Knightcorp, said claims tend to be tested on what was declared and how the policy defines it, and that for a technology business the practical question is whether the wording and the application reflect the platforms the business actually relies on. The report also refers to a Federal Court development in the Medibank matter, where Deloitte reports prepared after the cyber incident were found not to be protected by legal professional privilege, underlining the importance of how post-incident reviews are commissioned. It includes several tools intended to help organisations assess these questions, including a matrix of exposures, a broker checklist for AI risk, examples of where claims uncertainty can begin, and an 11-question insurance readiness checklist. It also features a client endorsement from Spriggy Co-Founder Alex Badran, who said that before working with Knightcorp it felt like the company was trying to piece together off-the-shelf solutions from different providers and that Knightcorp spent the time to understand its unique needs and built insurance solutions to fit its business.

Articles.Title: Knightcorp warns tech leaders over AI & cloud gaps - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: NVIDIA releases NVKE and NVKR as open-source projects for managed Kubernetes on GPU infrastructure
stories.Summary:
NVIDIA released two open-source projects, the NVIDIA Kubernetes Engine (NVKE) and the NVIDIA Kubernetes Recipes (NVKR), for running managed Kubernetes on GPU infrastructure, and both were recently announced as components of the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform. NVKE serves as the control plane for a managed Kubernetes service, while NVKR builds the OS images, container images and packages that those clusters depend on. Both projects ship under the Apache 2.0 license and are currently in public preview. NVKE is written in Go, uses upstream Kubernetes, kubeadm and Cluster API, and has no runtime dependency on NVKR.

A local evaluation of NVKE needs 6 CPUs, 12 GiB of RAM and 100 GiB of disk with no GPU, while a full footprint calls for 3 CPU servers for the management cluster, 3 CPU servers per workload control plane and a pool of GPU worker nodes. The software runs on your own NVIDIA GPU bare-metal servers provisioned through NVIDIA Infra Controller (NICo), and node images build for both amd64 and arm64. No throughput or provisioning-time benchmarks are published, and the quality signal is certification rather than speed, with conformance testing on Kubernetes 1.36. After install, the NVKE API serves plain HTTP on port 30080 with authentication off, and there is no management-plane upgrade or backup procedure.

NVKR is a build system with declarative Definitions that produces executables, container images, Helm charts and node images, and its Recipes define validated combinations of software versions and GPU generations. Hosted workflows attach signatures, SBOMs and provenance to digest-pinned OCI references, and NVKR can also build artifacts for other Kubernetes management systems. A node must present an attested SPIFFE identity before it gets join credentials, and the README says SPIRE uses TPM for this, while per-cluster etcd encryption is available. An OpenTelemetry-based Helm chart exports logs, metrics and traces over OTLP, and three companion projects plug into workload clusters: AI Cluster Runtime for the GPU runtime, NodeWright for node packages and NVSentinel for break-fix automation.

The repo describes NVKE as a self-hosting factory for Kubernetes clusters rather than a distribution, and it exposes a REST API and controllers on a management cluster. Customers get standard clusters and use kubectl, while the operator manages them through the NVKE API or the nvkectl CLI. Bootstrap begins when nvkectl bootstrap site starts a temporary single-node kind cluster on a bootstrap host, after which NVKE requests 3 servers from NICo, which boots them from the node image before the temporary cluster is deleted. Compared with Gardener from SAP and Kamaji from Clastix, NVKE uses a dedicated control plane per cluster with its own etcd and node pools, and the articles give no further details on what happens next.

Articles.Title: NVIDIA Open-Sources NVKE and NVKR for Managed Kubernetes on GPU Infrastructure

stories.Headline: Pronto Software marks 50 years with accelerated AI investment and security-first ERP roadmap
stories.Summary:
Melbourne-based ERP company Pronto Software is marking 50 years in business, using the anniversary to highlight an accelerated investment in artificial intelligence that it has been developing since 2021, when it began exploring machine learning before speeding up its roadmap after generative and agentic AI emerged. Managing Director and CEO Chad Gates, who has led the company for a decade and joined 21 years ago, said the rapid pace of development has forced software providers to reconsider how they build and deliver products. Pronto has taken what it describes as a deliberate, security-first approach, building its own GPU infrastructure within Pronto Cloud and hosting large language models internally while still allowing connections to external models so it is not dependent on a single provider. The architecture is designed around authentication, permissions and access controls so that AI agents and connected systems cannot access information or perform actions beyond their authorised capabilities. Gates said the company took the position early that it would provide a high-trust model, describing AI as a capability rather than a technology and saying the data is where the value lies rather than the AI itself.

He said customers are primarily concerned with two issues, security and productivity, wanting to know how AI can improve efficiency while worrying about exposing sensitive information or investing in technology that fails to deliver returns. Pronto has operated debt-free since its inception, and Gates said its independent ownership structure and local presence remain competitive advantages against large multinational providers, particularly with owner-operated customers who can speak directly with staff. He said the technology will change dramatically but the truth should never change. Looking ahead, Gates said AI will fundamentally change how employees interact with ERP platforms, potentially reducing the need for traditional interfaces filled with screens, forms and menus as staff increasingly rely on AI assistants and agents to retrieve information, generate reports and interpret business data through conversation.

He suggested future product development could become less reliant on building dedicated screens for every new feature, with AI generating interfaces and reports when users need them. He identified agent-to-agent communication as another significant area of development as businesses deploy larger numbers of autonomous agents, raising questions around coordination, permissions and the management of data and workflows. Quantum-safe encryption is also a priority, with Gates warning that advances in quantum computing combined with increasingly capable AI systems could create considerable security challenges that providers need to prepare for before the technology becomes mainstream. Gates believes the scale and speed of change now underway will exceed anything the business has experienced previously, and he said the challenge will be continuing to innovate while maintaining the security, reliability and customer relationships that have underpinned the company's longevity.

Articles.Title: Pronto Software marks 50-year milestone with AI-focused ERP roadmap - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: Instructure launches Foundry venture and Athena AI study coach for Canvas
stories.Summary:
Instructure has launched Instructure Foundry, a standalone venture focused on AI development for education, and its first project is Project Athena, an AI study coach designed to work with Canvas, according to an announcement reported on 17 November 2026. The venture brings together small teams to develop and refine new products with input from educators and institutions, while Instructure continues developing its existing platforms, including Canvas, Mastery and Parchment. Project Athena is being built to give students study support based on material already in their Canvas courses, using course content, assignments and upcoming assessments to generate personalised quizzes, study guides and coaching prompts. Athena will connect to the learning environment through a read-only link governed by existing student permissions, and Instructure said student conversations with the tool will not be used to train external AI models. In the United States, Hinds Community College is involved in the initiative following an initial pilot, and the project is expected to extend access to its 7,000 students.

The tool is intended to give students extra support outside classroom and tutoring hours, and by drawing on a student's own course context in Canvas it is expected to identify gaps in understanding and adjust prompts as learning progresses. Instructure said the structure is intended to help it move faster on emerging technologies without affecting the stability of products already used by schools, universities and vocational education providers. Shiren Vijiasingam, Chief Product Officer at Instructure, said AI has changed what is possible, with small teams now able to build and test new ideas faster than before, and he said Foundry gives those teams space to iterate on emerging solutions rapidly while core products continue to get sustained investment. He said Project Athena represents what Instructure believes responsible AI in education should look like, grounded in learning science, connected to the learning environment and built to support understanding through skill mastery, and he said it will coach toward mastery rather than answers. Zach Pendleton, Chief Architect at Instructure, said the pace of change has outrun the conventional roadmap, and he said investors have provided incremental funding so the venture does not compete with investment the core products need.

He described Instructure as running two tracks, one that serves and scales what it has built and one that explores what is next. The launch reflects a wider debate in education over how institutions should use AI while protecting student information, maintaining academic integrity and keeping educators central to teaching, and providers in Australia and elsewhere have been weighing whether to adopt new tools within systems they already use or through separate applications. The announcement comes as education providers seek AI tools that can be integrated into existing platforms rather than used as standalone consumer applications, which creates pressure on software companies serving the sector to show both speed of development and controls around privacy, security and educator oversight. Athena is under development and is being created with educators and institutions, and as the first project to emerge from Foundry it will test whether tightly integrated AI study support can gain traction with institutions seeking more direct control over how students use generative AI.

Articles.Title: Instructure launches Foundry & Athena AI study coach - IT Brief Australia
