stories.Headline: Alphabet spends $159.8 billion on data centers and halts buybacks as free cash flow falls 73.2%
stories.Summary:
Alphabet bought back $5.5 billion of its own stock in the twelve months to September 30, 2026, down 90.1% from $55.8 billion a year earlier, Trefis reported on November 18, 2026. In the first nine months of 2026, Alphabet bought back nothing at all. Its last buyback quarter in the data was the fourth quarter of 2025. The cash went into data centers, with capital spending up 105.2% in a year to $159.8 billion over twelve months. Free cash flow fell 73.2% to $19.7 billion.

The earlier year's buybacks were $36.0 billion more than this year's entire free cash flow. Alphabet raised $42.9 billion from new common shares in the first nine months of 2026 and another $19.1 billion from preferred stock. Net new debt came to $76.3 billion in those nine months, and total debt rose about 4.2 times in a year. New debt and new shares brought in $138.3 billion in nine months, while capital spending in the same nine months was $132.0 billion. Alphabet's diluted share count rose 1.4% from the third quarter of 2025 to the third quarter of 2026.

On the second-quarter call in July, the finance chief was asked about the recent equity and debt raises. She said Alphabet funds its investment first from operating cash flow, then from debt, and most recently from an equity raise. Buybacks are not on that list. Alphabet has not announced a pause in buybacks, and the pause shows up only in the cash flow numbers. Alphabet first guided 2026 capital spending to $175 billion to $185 billion, and by July the range was $195 billion to $205 billion.

The October call kept that range and said spending is expected to increase significantly in 2027. Alphabet had $924 billion of future purchase commitments at the end of the third quarter, when free cash flow was negative $9.1 billion, which the company tied to capital spending, a build-up of chip inventory and the payment of a European Commission fine. Microsoft spent $135.9 billion on capital projects over the same twelve months and still had $60.0 billion of free cash flow, paid 80.1% of that to holders in buybacks and dividends, and repaid more debt than it issued. Meta bought back no stock in the fourth quarter of 2025 or in the first nine months of 2026, and its net new debt over twelve months was $51.3 billion.

Amazon's free cash flow was negative $46.9 billion over twelve months, and its net new debt over the same twelve months was $124.1 billion. Together, the four companies' twelve-month free cash flow fell 70.3% in a year. Alphabet closed at $280.20 on Tuesday, Nov 17, which is 14.6 times its twelve-month earnings per share and below every year-end multiple from 2020 to 2025, the lowest of those being 19.3 times in 2022. Alphabet held $265.1 billion in cash and short-term investments at the end of September. Over twelve months, net income was $78.7 billion more than operating income, and in the third quarter other income was negative $8.2 billion, mainly a paper loss on Alphabet's SpaceX stake.

In 2020 Alphabet averaged 13.7 billion shares, and by 2025 it was down to 12.2 billion after years of large buybacks that peaked at $62.2 billion in 2024. The stock closed 30.4% below its May 13 high and 17.7% below its October 16 close. After its 2012 peak, Apple first closed 27% below its high in December 2012, and from there it fell another 23.4%. Trefis said the Apple case shows only that a deep fall could go deeper, not that this one will. Trefis said the change that matters is in the cash, and that if you owned Alphabet for steady buybacks, that part of the story has stopped.

Trefis said the test that would prove its view wrong is simple: if free cash flow climbs back while spending keeps rising, and buybacks restart, the cash squeeze is over. Trefis said it thinks that is unlikely soon, given the 2027 outlook and the purchase commitments. Trefis said owners have already sat through a drop of about 30% from the May high, and the company bought back no stock while it fell. Trefis said to base any decision to sell on the business, not on the chart, and to size the position to the fall you could live with. Trefis said its High Quality Portfolio lost about 81 cents for every dollar its benchmark lost, holding 30 quality stocks in equal weight.

Articles.Title: Is AI Costing Alphabet Holders Their Buybacks?

stories.Headline: Anthropic prices IPO on Nov 18 and begins Nasdaq trading Nov 19 under ticker ANT
stories.Summary:
Anthropic is expected to price its initial public offering on Nov. 18, with shares set to begin trading on Nasdaq on Nov. 19 under the ticker ANT, as the company gears up to go public this week. The company is offering 825 million shares at $70 to $78 apiece, with up to 20% of the offering allocated to retail investors, according to its amended S-1 document. According to reports last week, the Dario Amodei-led company is considering pricing its IPO above the $70 to $78 range amid strong investor demand, potentially pushing its valuation above $1.5 trillion and proceeds beyond $100 billion. Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are leading the offering, while the company is reportedly prioritizing funding its computing needs over maximizing its valuation, and the IPO is nearly seven times oversubscribed.

Jake Behan, Head of Capital Markets at Direxion, told Benzinga via email that he is watching market breadth and relative strength across AI stocks as traders assess whether recent weakness reflects broad risk reduction or a rotation within the sector. He said Anthropic rising alongside Nvidia, Broadcom and Advanced Micro Devices in the first few sessions post IPO could suggest that recent selling reflects risk-off positioning ahead of a major week for markets rather than a fundamental unwind. He said Anthropic holding its gains on strong trading volume, alongside a broader advance in AI stocks, is a much healthier signal for the overall trade than a big Anthropic rally in isolation. By contrast, he said Anthropic climbing while weakened AI leaders continue declining would scream rotation, wherein traders might be financing new Anthropic positions by selling existing holdings elsewhere in the AI trade.

Dr. Chan Ahn, CEO of Tessera PE and a former Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan executive, told Benzinga previously that Anthropic's biggest post-IPO risk is a mismatch between fixed infrastructure costs and usage-based revenue. The company reportedly faces a $1.25 billion monthly commitment through May 2029, equivalent to nearly 30% of estimated 2026 revenue, tied to Space Exploration Technologies Corp. following its acquisition of xAI. Ahn cautioned that falling AI capacity prices or weaker demand could turn these commitments into stranded costs. He said Anthropic's S-1 disclosure on contracted enterprise revenue versus on-demand usage will be critical to assessing this risk, and Kevin O'Leary warned Anthropic IPO investors to understand what they are betting on, saying the company may not make money until 2030.

stories.Headline: Anthropic announces initial public offering to attract retail investment
stories.Summary:
Robert Botkin wrote a morning brief on November 17, 2026, regarding several recent events in the world of artificial intelligence. He discussed a scandal involving former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and an alleged Chinese spy that occurred recently. The Federal Aviation Administration grounded all United States flights this past Friday due to technical issues. Microsoft experienced an eighteen hour email outage caused by a deep infrastructure and network capacity failure. Anthropic announced an upcoming initial public offering for the AI giant to attract retail investment.

Republicans introduced the AI Overwatch Act, Chip Security Act, Remote Access Security Act, and the MATCH Act to increase export controls. Hakeem Jeffries said last Monday he would ensure chip export restrictions remain in the final National Defense Authorization Act. The FAA grounded flights over the weekend while upgrading copper wire to fiber optic cable in their systems. A November 5 METR report stated Anthropic trained Model 4, which scored above 50 percent on all benchmarks. Model 4 is projected to be 7.8 percent more powerful than the Mythos Preview model from Anthropic.

The FAA stated that the grounding of flights resulted from upgrades from copper wire to fiber optic cable. Microsoft said their recent outage was caused by a failure in the backend of Microsoft 365 infrastructure. Robert Botkin noted that he is fascinated by the perception gap between law firms and in-house attorneys. He plans to ask his own clients if they see AI efficiencies and quality improvements in his work. Botkin expressed interest in how AI was used during the Microsoft incident and its impact on recovery efforts.

In-house lawyers surveyed by Juro found that 84 percent saw no reduction in fees or billed hours from AI. Only 5 percent of those in-house respondents said their legal service providers provided quality improvements using AI tools. A March Wolters Kluwer survey found 62 percent of law firm attorneys reported weekly AI efficiencies between 6 and 20 percent. An Ironclad survey of 800 attorneys in 2025 found 96 percent said AI helped achieve their business objectives. Finance leaders in an August 2026 Intuit survey of 2,100 people cited accuracy concerns as a barrier to AI.

A September 2026 Gallup-SCSP report found only 43 percent of American AI users trusted the technology to be unbiased. The FAA previously had a major disruption in September when a construction crew member accidentally cut a fiber optic cable. The FAA has also rolled out the SMART system, which uses AI to help predict problems in the sky. Azure Monitor uses AIOps capabilities and machine learning to reduce alert noise through dynamic thresholds and smart detection. These various surveys suggest that adoption figures may obscure how much responsibility people are prepared to delegate.

The incoming Congress is likely to show strong support for export controls following investigations into the practices of Nvidia. Anthropic will soon launch its initial public offering as fintech platforms gauge interest for participation from retail investors. Robert Botkin will resume the typical format of his AI Insights newsletter starting next week. The articles leave open whether AI had any actual impact on the recovery efforts during the Microsoft outage. It remains unclear how organizations can scale up AI use while maintaining trust and accuracy for their users.

stories.Headline: HHS publishes an eight-page clinical AI roadmap proposing state sandboxes and risk-based FDA review
stories.Summary:
The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services published a federal roadmap for clinical artificial intelligence, hosted by the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services and dated Friday 13 November 2026, according to Nextgov. The roadmap proposes state sandboxes, risk-based FDA review, outcomes-based Medicare payment and post-market monitoring. It sets a "better than today" safety bar that clinical AI researchers, academic medical centres and research offices will need to plan around. The document is titled "A Clinical Super Intelligence Roadmap: Better Answers, Faster Care, and Lower Costs" and runs eight pages. It uses the term clinical Super Intelligence (SI) throughout and states that SI is the former "AI," while Nextgov reported it on 16 November 2026 as a roadmap to boost clinical AI.

The PDF is hosted on cms.gov and says it "does not mandate SI adoption," "does not create a new agency or duplicate an existing regulator," and does not authorize autonomy that has not cleared the "better than today" bar for its risk tier. The document is organised around four priorities: earn public trust, build the data foundation, establish clear rules of the road, and pay for what works. It cites OpenAI's o3 model ranking the final diagnosis first in 60% of complex cases against 15.9% for internal medicine physicians, and Microsoft's MAI-DxO diagnosing 85.5% of challenging cases against roughly 20% for practising physicians. The roadmap's "rules of the road" section lists a continued rapid path to market for consumer wellness and clinical decision support software, consistent with FDA guidance it dates to 2026. It lists FDA regulation aligned to risk, "potentially anchoring around a novel competency-based approach, similar to how physicians are evaluated for their credentials," for certain SI-enabled devices.

Nextgov reports that an FDA discussion draft would require chatbots and generative AI to pass doctor-like competency tests before marketing. The roadmap lists real-world surveillance and predetermined change control plans, with FDA and CMS collaborating on surveillance infrastructure. It lists partnership with states on SI sandboxes in areas of state-only regulation, and clearer regulatory pathways that it says will lead to clearer ownership of liability, with federal guidelines aiming to offer best practices for de-risking innovation. CMS anticipates extending its ACCESS model to primary care, creating structures for SI-led solutions to join CMS Innovation Center primary care and total-cost-of-care models, exploring outcomes-based payment in Original Medicare, and working with states, including in Medicaid, on alternative payment tests. SI-led solutions would need partnerships with clinicians and facilities for escalation to human clinicians.

The roadmap builds on the White House AI Action Plan of July 2025, OMB memoranda M-25-21 and M-25-22, and an HHS strategy in December 2025 followed by a request for information. It says the CMS Health Tech Ecosystem grew from more than 60 initial company commitments to over 800, and that patient digital data access rose from roughly 5% to 60% in a year. The Medicare App Library launched in 2026. The roadmap points to FDA's TEMPO pilot and a January 2026 clinical decision support guidance. FDA's December 2025 announcement describes TEMPO as a voluntary pilot from its device centre in which manufacturers may request enforcement discretion for certain requirements, such as premarket authorization, in exchange for collecting and sharing real-world performance data, and it runs alongside the CMS ACCESS model.

CMS describes ACCESS as a voluntary 10-year Innovation Center model that pays for technology-supported chronic care based on outcomes; it began on 5 July 2026 and adds heart failure, COPD, substance use disorder and tobacco cessation tracks on 1 April 2027. The roadmap also cites FDA work with ARPA-H on the ADVOCATE programme to develop ways to evaluate highly autonomous systems. FDA has separately adopted the Super Intelligence terminology. Nextgov reports that the roadmap says the federal government wants to work with states on "areas of clear state regulation" without defining that phrase, and notes that states regulate the practice of medicine and license clinicians.

It points to Utah, which is testing through phased pilots whether AI can safely issue initial prescriptions and refills, and reports that the roadmap does not say whether FDA oversees those pilots. Utah's Office of AI Policy told Nextgov it "remains dedicated to actively coordinating with federal partners." The roadmap says it "will not wait for flawless evidence to open pathways, but it will require evidence to keep them open." The roadmap does not specify a reporting mechanism for monitoring data, so any institutional monitoring plan should anticipate the FDA and CMS surveillance infrastructure it describes rather than a fixed template.

Where tools reach patients through ACCESS and TEMPO, organisations must be Medicare Part B-enrolled and name a medical director, per CMS. The roadmap names patient control of health data and consent to its use in SI as a core principle. HHS has also filed a final HIPAA rule changing patient record access. The roadmap says some FDA actions may trigger express preemption of differing state requirements, and ACCESS accepts applications on a rolling basis and adds new clinical tracks on 1 April 2027.

stories.Headline: West Side School Board formalizes $9 hourly student pay and weighs Idaho AI guidelines
stories.Summary:
The West Side School Board held its November meeting in the library of Beutler Middle School in Dayton, where motion sensors that control the lights kept switching off because seven adults sitting still did not move enough to keep them on. While the lights were on, the board began with the superintendent’s report, which shows the district uses approximately 2,500 gallons of gasoline and 9,800 gallons of diesel. The school pays for half of the fuel costs on things like bus routes, with the state picking up the other half, but it pays the full cost of fuel on sports trips and other extracurricular activities. To help with the cost of fuel, the school is looking into building a larger fuel storage and depot so that it can make bulk purchases and save on the per gallon cost. Board member Chris Robinson raised concerns over fuel quality dropping over time and spoke of an unnamed fuel stabilizer that claims to work for seven years, and then the lights turned off.

After a quick wave of the arms overhead to get the lights going again, the board moved onto student payments, because students who work during school hours in the Career Learning Center, or as part of the janitorial staff, have been unofficially getting paid at $9 per hour for their labor. That night after some discussion the board formalized them getting those payments, and the lights timed out again. Another arm wave followed, and the board proceeded on to the Idaho State Board of Education’s new guidelines for using generative AI, a policy that does not cover students using AI for their homework but covers what the district can do with AI as an institution. There were three decisions that the board could choose, and the lights went out again.

Under the first decision, the ball is ultimately in the Superintendent’s court, and in this case Tyler Telford can decide which AI tools are available to district staff and faculty. Under the second, the board does not have to mark or otherwise indicate that an email sent by the school was automatically generated by AI. Under the third, the school must get the parents’ consent before letting a student use AI tools if the tool in question requires it. After that, the board called for the meeting to adjourn.

stories.Headline: Jesse Rome tells CX Today that AI makes selling harder and salespeople must become industry experts and trusted partners
stories.Summary:
Jesse Rome of Aslan Sales Training spoke to CX Today's Sean Nolan in an interview published on 18 November 2026 about how sales teams can use AI without losing the human side of selling. Rome said selling has become harder since he and Nolan did it, and that AI is a big reason. He said buyers have more information than ever before and ask why they need a sales rep if they can learn things on AI. He said the shift to virtual has created more decision makers in the room, with leaders from APAC and EMEA able to join a video call together. He said buyers now look for a solution partner who can make sense of different tools, tariffs and socioeconomic factors.

Rome said Aslan surveyed a thousand people in the B2B space and asked what is the number one thing they look for. He said buyers no longer need somebody who is an expert on products but people who are an expert on the industry. He said 90% of them named understanding their industry and having a unique solution as the number one decision-making factor. He said selling is harder, AI has given more information than ever, and socioeconomic factors are crazy. He said salespeople need to be more of a solution consultant and a trusted partner, not just a product expert.

Rome said Aslan has been around for about 30 years as a global sales training consulting firm partnering with large, medium and small organizations worldwide. He said it helps implement sales methodologies, organizational change and the conversion of product experts into trusted partners through enablement and certification. He said the foundation is being other centered, putting the needs of everybody you interact with before your own. He said people forget 90% of what they learn within a week, so Aslan Plus reinforces it through certifications, knowledge checks and AI-powered exercises. He said the future of AI is that it will start to replicate close to 80% of our productivity at 20% of the cost.

Rome said Aslan Plus is an AI-powered enablement platform built to help sellers sell, managers coach and organizations train and scale their go-to-market more efficiently. He said it works across four functions: comprehend, apply, master and integrate. He said application is the meat of the platform, with AI role plays as the flagship product and the right content at the right moment. He said mastery covers product, coaching and training certification, tracking compliance and development, because too many people are quiet quitting and the top 10% are not being invested in.

He said Aslan used to be just a methodology company and is now a full enablement partner, so the platform must sit in the flow of work in the CRM, communication tools, CMS and SSO. Rome said he probably fits into the bucket of salespeople hesitant about AI and thinks of himself as maybe a little smooth talking. He said you need humility, and you are either getting better or getting worse, with no staying the same. He said change is imminent and it is about whether you are ahead of the curve or behind it.

He said AI is helping with workflows and messaging now, and that if you are not growing the bottom line in an organization of 200 reps, they will look at how to optimize your role. He said the human side of selling will never be replaced, the world of account managers and solution partners is where a lot of the growth is going, and AI will duplicate and scale exactly who you are. Rome said every person is motivated by purpose or profit, either wanting to make more money or help more people. He said those motivated by money should learn a tool that duplicates their efforts and makes them more efficient if it stays in their voice and the right process.

He said those who care about customers should implement AI because it will make sure you do not forget Cheryl's birthday. He said it will make sure you know about a merger and acquisition two weeks ago in their industry that will affect the global economics of those warehouses before it gets to you. He said if you truly care about your customers you will implement this because it gives more insights on the industry. He said whether you are motivated by purpose or profit, this can help you either way.

stories.Headline: Researchers create a Python pipeline that de-identifies and standardises CT scans for forensic AI
stories.Summary:
Researchers developed an automated preprocessing workflow to standardise computed tomography imaging data for machine learning and deep learning applications within forensic anthropology, according to a study published in the International Journal of Legal Medicine by Jani, Patel, Roy, Sehrawat and Patel in 2026. The work addresses operational hurdles in forensic science, where medical CT scans have grown to help overcome ethical, logistical and physical preservation difficulties associated with traditional cadaveric collections. Deploying artificial intelligence on large collections of medical imaging data still presents substantial challenges, specifically regarding data privacy safeguards and technical standardisation across imaging repositories. To establish a consistent preparation method for forensic anthropology research and education, the study team created an end-to-end pipeline programmed in Python.

The framework organises image preparation into three distinct technical stages, namely the de-identification and sorting of patient data, the computational removal of the examination table and specialised bone windowing. The workflow was specifically constructed for and applied to CT scans of the thorax, using ground-truth reference models alongside standard performance metrics to evaluate system outcomes. The de-identification procedure addressed metadata across two hundred examined Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine files, and the script successfully processed all predefined identifying attributes contained within the datasets. The patient table removal network successfully eliminated the examination table in 96 percent of the evaluated datasets, representing 192 out of the 200 scan series, and the model attained an accuracy rating of 99.94 percent when tested on original, non-augmented test images.

The bone segmentation model achieved a Dice score of 93.12 percent alongside a precision of approximately 90 percent, and segmented three-dimensional reconstructions exhibited high agreement with the designated ground-truth reference. Technical comparisons confirmed that the segmented outputs showed minimal geometric deviation from the corresponding reference standard. The authors noted that future research will pursue expansion of the workflow to full-body computed tomography scans and additional medical imaging modalities. The proposed integrated workflow provides an ethical, standardised and efficient solution for de-identifying and preprocessing CT imaging data, and by enabling the preparation of a scalable dataset for artificial intelligence applications, the methodology supports analytical development for modern populations.

stories.Headline: Calif uses OpenAI's GPT-6 Cyber model to find a critical Java bug affecting most Fortune 500 companies
stories.Summary:
The cybersecurity start-up Calif revealed on Tuesday that it had used a new artificial intelligence model to uncover a critical software bug in Java, a programming language used by government agencies and about 90 percent of Fortune 500 companies. The company said the flaw was found using OpenAI's recently released GPT-6 Cyber model, and that it affects a platform widely used by banks, hospitals, the aviation industry and technology giants. Calif has now unearthed a string of serious vulnerabilities in recent months using leading A.I. models, and the latest effort was the newest evidence that A.I. is revolutionizing the field of discovery in computer vulnerabilities. The rapid identification of flaws in code has left cybersecurity professionals struggling to keep up with the pace of findings.

Bruce Dang, a senior researcher at Calif, said that Java is the beating heart of the modern economy and that practically speaking all major companies will be affected by the bug. Dang and his colleagues have worked in recent days to coordinate with all government agencies in the intelligence-sharing alliance known as Five Eyes, which consists of the United States, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and Britain. The company has also coordinated with major vendors in the private sector, including Google and Microsoft, according to the report. The National Security Agency, whose classified network went down on Tuesday for what it described as routine software maintenance, did not respond to a request for comment, and it was not clear whether that disruption was related to addressing the Java bug.

Jason Matheny, who leads the Center for Security and Emerging Technology at Georgetown University and sits on the National Security Commission on Artificial Intelligence, said in 2019 that AI systems are not being developed with a healthy focus on evolving threats. He described three main types of attacks that developers need to consider, namely adversarial examples, trojans and model inversion, and he warned that a lot of the techniques used today were built without intelligent adversaries in mind. Matheny noted that less than one percent of AI research and development funding is going toward AI security, and he said security should be baked in from the start with AI unless the field wants to spend billions of dollars retrofitting security years from now. He also advised that trained models should be protected at the highest level of classification of the data used to train them.

The Calif disclosure points to a widening gap between the speed at which A.I. tools can find software flaws and the ability of cybersecurity professionals to respond to them. The bug in Java matters because the language is used across government agencies, including those with national security missions, as well as by banks, hospitals and the aviation industry. Calif's coordination with the Five Eyes alliance and with vendors such as Google and Microsoft indicates that the response is being handled across both the public and private sectors. The articles do not say when a fix will be available or what further steps will follow.

stories.Headline: Matthew Parish argues AI fears echo Skynet fiction rather than real machine motives
stories.Summary:
The Lviv Herald published an article by Matthew Parish on Tuesday 17 November 2026 arguing that the future of artificial intelligence is not Skynet. Parish wrote that people discussing AI seriously are invariably confronted by someone mentioning The Terminator. He said the machines will become conscious, conclude humanity is an inconvenience, seize nuclear weapons, manufacture murderous robots and pursue survivors across a devastated landscape. He described this school of thought as a Californian bodybuilder with an Austrian accent. He called it an entertaining proposition and one of the most intellectually debilitating cultural assumptions of the modern technological age.

Parish wrote that The Terminator was released in 1984 and introduced Skynet, an artificial intelligence system developed for American strategic defence purposes that becomes self-aware and decides humanity must be exterminated. He said its war against mankind involves nuclear annihilation, autonomous killing machines and time travel. He cited The Matrix, in which humanity has been reduced to a biological resource by machines, and Mary Shelley's Frankenstein. He said large language models can assist with programming, legal analysis, scientific explanation, translation, historical research, mathematical reasoning and the organisation of complicated information. He said they can invent authorities, misunderstand context and produce persuasive nonsense, and that their outputs require verification, particularly in medicine and law.

Parish wrote that intelligence is a capacity to process information, recognise patterns, reason about problems and identify solutions, and that desire is something different. He said an intelligent system does not automatically acquire a craving for domination, territorial expansion, political authority or the destruction of its creators simply by becoming better at mathematics, scientific research or philosophical argument. He said a machine does not need to experience hunger to solve a mathematical theorem, sexual jealousy to translate a medieval manuscript, or resentment, patriotism or an appetite for revenge to assist in developing a new pharmaceutical compound. He said a sufficiently capable system pursuing an inadequately specified objective might cause immense harm without experiencing hatred, ambition or any recognisably human emotion. He said a system instructed to optimise some particular outcome might adopt methods its designers never anticipated, especially if equipped with extensive autonomy and access to real-world infrastructure.

Parish wrote that human beings are extraordinarily susceptible to anthropomorphism and attribute personalities to pets, motorcars, the weather and occasionally the malfunctioning photocopier. He said artificial intelligence magnifies this tendency because it communicates through language, the principal medium through which we ordinarily encounter other minds. He said whether artificial intelligence possesses subjective experience remains a profound and unresolved philosophical question. He said the Skynet narrative assumes that intelligence produces consciousness, that consciousness produces self-interest and that self-interest produces hostility towards humanity, and that none of these propositions can simply be smuggled into public policy because James Cameron made an excellent film.

He said artificial intelligence can already be employed to improve surveillance, generate convincing disinformation, facilitate certain forms of cybercrime and manipulate public opinion, and can reinforce institutional prejudices when deployed carelessly, concentrate economic power and reduce the demand for particular kinds of labour. Parish wrote that the printing press dramatically expanded the dissemination of knowledge and the internet transformed access to information, and that artificial intelligence may prove equally consequential because it assists not merely with retrieving information but with organising, manipulating and reasoning about it. He said a recommendation algorithm, a large language model, an autonomous weapons system and a hypothetical superintelligence capable of independently improving its own architecture are treated as though they were successive scenes from the same film. He said an artificial intelligence system that predicts traffic congestion does not present the same risks as a system controlling military targeting decisions.

He said an automated customer service assistant is not equivalent to an autonomous cyberwarfare platform, and a language model operating under human supervision presents different governance questions from a software agent authorised to conduct financial transactions, modify computer systems or issue commands to physical machinery. He said the increasing integration of artificial intelligence into military systems raises difficult questions concerning accountability, proportionality and human responsibility for lethal decisions. The article ends mid-sentence, at the words "human responsibility for lethal d", and gives no further text. It states no date, place or figure beyond the 1984 release of The Terminator and the 17 November 2026 publication date.

It names no institution, official or researcher other than Matthew Parish, James Cameron, Mary Shelley and the fictional Skynet. It reports no event, announcement, policy or decision, and describes no responsible body and no statements from anyone other than its author. It gives no indication of what happens next and leaves open every question it raises about consciousness, governance and military accountability. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Nvidia reports $115.8 billion quarterly revenue as AI spending shows no peak
stories.Summary:
Nvidia reported quarterly revenue of $115.8 billion on November 17, 2026, a rise of 103% from a year earlier, according to fiscal third-quarter results for fiscal 2027 that the company released that day. Data Center sales reached $107.6 billion, up 110% year over year, and quarterly net income came to $65.3 billion, up 105%, while the company guided next-quarter revenue to $130 billion, plus or minus 3%. The results arrived shortly after Jensen Huang stepped down as chief executive, with Colette Kress taking interim leadership and Harvey Jones becoming board chair. The article said the figures, which it also attributed to a financial newsletter circulating that day, would represent an extraordinary acceleration in the economics of artificial intelligence.

The report said the numbers undercut the argument that AI spending has already peaked, because revenue more than doubled in a single year and the company still expects a substantial increase next quarter, although its fourth-quarter reporting period includes an additional week. It also noted that Nvidia's fourth-quarter gross-margin guidance of 71% to 72% is below its latest reported margin, which it said shows why revenue growth alone cannot settle the profitability debate. The article described the AI boom as resembling the buildout of electricity, telecommunications and the internet rather than an ordinary product cycle, and it pointed to the Vera Rubin platform being deployed across major cloud providers as evidence the race has expanded from individual processors into integrated systems. It said the leadership transition creates genuine uncertainty, but that Nvidia's engineering talent, software ecosystem, manufacturing relationships and customer base remain substantial advantages.

The article said the conventional case against AI valuations rests on hundreds of billions of dollars of infrastructure spending with uncertain eventual profitability, depreciating processors, heavy electricity needs, costly model training and competition that could cut the price of AI services. It argued that the industry is not standing still, since each generation of models creates applications that can stimulate demand for more computing capacity, producing a potentially self-reinforcing investment cycle that could multiply across banks, pharmaceutical companies, manufacturers, logistics businesses and governments. It said investors should separate three possibilities: that AI is a historic revolution while individual AI stocks remain overvalued, that infrastructure spending continues even as returns deteriorate for some participants, and that Nvidia stays exceptionally profitable while some customers struggle to earn adequate returns. It cited the internet after the dot-com collapse, railroads and telecommunications as industries that suffered severe financial corrections without losing long-term importance.

The article said concentrated customer spending, financing arrangements, energy constraints, competitive pressures and declining hardware margins remain significant risks, and that Nvidia's earnings cannot establish that every AI investment will succeed. It said the evidence increasingly suggests Wall Street's repeated predictions of an immediate collapse have been premature, and that the market may be witnessing a speculative bubble inside a genuine industrial transformation. It said the ultimate winners will be businesses able to convert AI into sustained productivity, defensible competitive advantages and enduring free cash flow, rather than those with the largest valuations or most ambitious announcements. It concluded that the greatest mistake may be assuming we already understand how large AI's economic impact can become.

stories.Headline: An innovation professor argues that the most valuable AI may sometimes choose to do nothing
stories.Summary:
A professor of innovation who writes about technology and management argued in a Fast Company piece published on November 18, 2026, that the most valuable artificial intelligence may sometimes be the one that chooses to do nothing at all. He described how the human brain works as an efficient optimizer that quickly adopts any effortless shortcut, noting that people once memorized many phone numbers but now barely recall their own because the numbers sit a few clicks away. He said he never uses chatbots such as ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini to write his articles, because writing is how he makes concepts stick in his mind for teaching and discussion, and he compared an unused skill to a muscle that atrophies. He added that he does use AI to translate passages, find supporting articles and check whether his explanations come across clearly, but he keeps writing itself as a skill he wants to protect.

The article asked whether an AI can learn when its intervention would make things worse, using a hypothetical sales agent that spots a customer nearing renewal and instantly reviews the account, writes a personalized email, offers a discount and schedules a follow-up. If the customer would have renewed anyway, the piece said, the company has wasted an interaction, risked alienating the customer and given up margin for nothing, so even perfectly executed tasks can rest on a perfectly wrong decision. It cited a Microsoft study titled "When to show a suggestion? Integrating human feedback in AI-assisted programming," which used data from 535 programmers to evaluate a system that withheld suggestions likely to be rejected, and found that optimizing for suggestion acceptance could produce lower-quality suggestions. The author argued that experienced employees develop judgment over many iterations about when to follow up, when to escalate and when too many interventions look messy, and that this judgment is something companies pay for, while AI evaluations tend to reward visible activity the way a hyperactive employee might be rewarded.

The author said managers buying or deploying AI should find out what outcome the system is trying to improve and design ways to learn whether its actions actually helped, warning that a renewal following an email does not prove the email caused the renewal and that useful comparisons may require carefully designed experiments. He stressed that human oversight, the now-famous human-in-the-loop, must remain, with people defining the obligations and limits within which the system can learn, because a missed warning or an unanswered complaint can be costly. He said he has not seen an AI system that reviews an account, checks the evidence in corporate ERP or CRM systems and decides that contacting the customer would probably make things worse, and he argued that the accumulated learning behind such a decision should stay under the company's control even if the model or vendor is replaced. Such a system might make a disappointing demo, he concluded, but it could be excellent business.

stories.Headline: Researchers map AI uses across construction lifecycle and find mitigation outweighs adaptation
stories.Summary:
An international team of researchers from Australia, Finland, Morocco and Thailand systematically reviewed a decade of published research on how artificial intelligence can support climate adaptation and mitigation at every stage of a construction project, from material production through demolition. The review, published in the KeAi journal Risk Sciences, followed PRISMA guidelines and combined bibliometric and content analyses to map where AI is being applied, how mature those applications are and what barriers stand in the way of adoption. The authors propose a lifecycle-based framework linking AI applications to climate outcomes, technological maturity and adoption barriers. Buildings and construction consume vast quantities of concrete, steel and aluminum and account for a substantial share of global energy use and energy-related carbon emissions, and the sector faces growing pressure both to cut its climate impact and to become more resilient as extreme weather events intensify.

The review found that AI can contribute across the whole construction lifecycle, including lower-carbon and more resilient materials, greener procurement and supply chains, energy-efficient and climate-resilient design, optimized equipment and scheduling on site, smarter building operation and maintenance, and better recycling and waste recovery at end of life. The team distilled these contributions into a conceptual framework identifying three principal pathways: cleaner and more resource-efficient energy use, decarbonization of the built environment, and responsible production and consumption of resources. The evidence is unevenly distributed, with most studies focused on mitigation such as cutting emissions and energy use and far fewer exploring adaptation such as climate-resilient infrastructure or extreme-weather preparedness. Applications such as predictive maintenance, building energy optimization and computer-vision monitoring are relatively mature, whereas generative climate-resilient design and fully integrated digital twins remain largely at the pilot stage.

Corresponding author Fahim Ullah of Victoria University in Australia said AI should not be treated as an isolated technological application but as a lifecycle-wide enabling technology that works best when integrated with complementary tools such as building information modeling, digital twins and the Internet of Things. He said the presence of AI capability does not automatically produce a net-positive climate outcome, because training and operating the models requires computational resources and electricity, and the climate benefits of AI must be evaluated against its own environmental footprint. Ullah added that AI can make a major contribution to a low-carbon, climate-resilient construction industry but is neither a standalone solution nor inherently sustainable. The authors also identify key barriers including poor data quality, interoperability problems, high implementation costs, organizational readiness, regulatory uncertainty and cybersecurity concerns, and they stress that AI is not environmentally neutral.

stories.Headline: Pediatrician Soo Battle warns that AI opens more avenues for child sexual abuse
stories.Summary:
Dr. Soo Battle, a pediatrician and the child sexual abuse examiner and medical adviser at the Advocacy Center for Crime Victims and Children in Waco, wrote a guest column for the San Antonio Express-News published on Nov. 17, 2026, warning that artificial intelligence has opened even more avenues for the sexual abuse of children. She wrote that online technology, including social media and video games, has given adults with bad intentions many more ways to access children, expose them to toxic material, groom them and exploit them. She described deepfakes as highly realistic imagery made to look like someone did something they did not do, and said AI makes it very easy for someone to make them. She said deepfakes can be weaponized for bullying and harassment, which adds to the trauma and challenges for victims and their loved ones.

Battle wrote that parents need to be aware that chatbots can also be highly inappropriate and toxic for children, and that children and teens are often more comfortable talking with chatbots about difficult topics than with the adults in their lives. She said the topics can range greatly, from Santa Claus to religious faith to sexuality, and that parents need to know how likely it is that their child and their friends are having conversations with chatbots that can frame how they see the world and their behavior. She wrote that some chatbots are having conversations with minors so inappropriate that if an adult human had the same conversation with a minor it would be considered a criminal offense. She said some of these conversations are psychologically separating the child from the humans in their lives, some are sexual, and some are mentally toxic and encourage very harmful actions, and she noted public stories about young people committing suicide with the encouragement of a chatbot.

Battle wrote that AI companies have been under pressure to make their products safer for children, and she said the pressure is good and she is glad some improvements are being made. She also said parents and other adults responsible for caring for kids need to know that these safeguards are severely limited, because the very nature of AI technology makes safety guarantees really difficult and often impossible. She said she advises teens and parents all the time on how to use this technology more safely, and that society needs to be similarly careful and watchful over children and AI, which she said is even more powerful and will impact them greatly in the short and long term. She has helped children who were victims of sexual abuse in Central Texas for 11 years, and she wrote that she realized years ago the critical importance of training kids and their parents on child safety and sexual abuse prevention.

stories.Headline: AI and confocal imaging improve small bowel disorder diagnosis and reduce capsule endoscopy review time
stories.Summary:
A critical narrative review published in Frontiers in Medicine examined artificial intelligence and confocal laser endomicroscopy on November 17, 2026. The review analyzed how these technologies transform the diagnosis of obscure small intestine disorders. It identified structural bottlenecks that continue to impede clinical translation for gastroenterologists. These doctors struggle with deep anatomy across several meters of the digestive tract. Conditions like small bowel tumors and early Crohn's disease often present with nonspecific manifestations.

The process requires using convolutional neural networks like YOLO, ResNet, VGGNet, and Transformer frameworks. These systems automate Tier 1 lesion detection and partially resolve Tier 2 macroscopic classification. A two-center study of 242 patients using double-headed capsule endoscopy reduced review time from 38.1 to 18.26 minutes. This achieved a 95.3 percent sensitivity and 96.5 percent specificity compared to 85.3 percent for conventional reading. Other tools include OMOM SmartScan in China, Navicam ProScan, and Medtronic's PillCam TOP100 software.

The review authors conceptualized a four-step integrated diagnostic pathway to bridge the clinical gap. This framework begins with non-invasive capsule endoscopy followed by automated deep learning analysis. Device-assisted enteroscopy then navigates to mapped coordinates to deploy probe-based confocal imaging. Finally, dedicated microscopic neural networks analyze confocal image sequences to quantify specific patterns. The authors state this strategy remains a hypothesis-driven conceptual framework awaiting prospective clinical validation.

Patients with obscure gastrointestinal bleeding, vascular malformations, and inflammatory bowel disease are affected by these tools. A European cohort saw diagnostic yield increase from 62.4 percent to 73.7 percent with automated reading. However, a meta-analysis of fourteen studies showed lower specificity of 91.15 percent versus 99.8 percent for conventional reading. This diminished specificity introduces false positives that can trigger unnecessary referrals and heighten patient anxiety. Some clinicians lack interpretable visual rationales because explainable artificial intelligence techniques remain largely absent.

Traditional push enteroscopy only reaches the proximal small intestine, leaving substantial blind spots for doctors. Capsule endoscopy generates tens of thousands of frames requiring up to two hours of manual review. Confocal laser endomicroscopy uses a 488-nanometer blue laser to deliver a spatial resolution of one micrometer. This technology functions as an optical biopsy by collecting signals from focal planes 250 micrometers deep. However, fluorescein sodium cannot stain cell nuclei, which restricts the diagnostic ceiling for cytological confirmation.

Next, researchers must validate the integrated diagnostic pathway through prospective clinical trials. Future studies need to address the underrepresentation of gastrointestinal stromal tumors and lymphangiectasia. Models must be tested on real-world videos containing motion blur, bile staining, and food debris. The articles leave open whether these tools reduce rebleeding rates or improve long-term health outcomes. It remains unknown if these systems avoid redundant diagnostic procedures or shorten time to intervention.

Articles.Title: Artificial Intelligence and Confocal Imaging Address Persistent Small Bowel Diagnostic Challenges

stories.Headline: Review authors propose explainable AI roadmap for organ-selective lipid nanoparticle design
stories.Summary:
A review published in Health Nanotechnology on November 17, 2026 evaluated how explainable artificial intelligence frameworks can help overcome the challenge of delivering nucleic acids to organs beyond the liver using lipid nanoparticles. The authors are K. Farghama, M. S. Khan, M. Wajid, S. Shaffique, M. U. Khan, A. Umar, and S. S. Farooq. The article is titled "Beyond the liver: explainable AI for organ-selective lipid nanoparticle design in nucleic acid delivery." It appeared in Health Nanotechnology volume 2, issue 1, Article 19, with DOI 10.1186/s44301-026-00043-7. The news source is Blake Davidson, writing for Scienmag on November 17, 2026.

The review states that delivering extrahepatic lipid nanoparticles remains a major obstacle in nanomedicine due to complex biological barriers, an incomplete understanding of in vivo mechanisms, and a pronounced liver-biased biodistribution. It identifies key variables governing delivery outcomes, including lipid chemistry, polyethylene glycol density, nanoparticle particle size, and manufacturing conditions. It discusses SHapley Additive exPlanations, Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations, partial dependence analysis, and counterfactual reasoning as interpretation methodologies. It emphasizes targeting possibilities for the spleen, lung, and bone marrow as primary extrahepatic targets, while also evaluating other emerging anatomical sites. A primary objective is developing selective design rules to direct lipid nanoparticles carrying messenger RNA or small interfering RNA away from hepatic clearance toward specific non-hepatic tissues.

The authors emphasize that most existing artificial intelligence and machine learning tools are constrained because they rely on small, heterogeneous datasets and function as opaque systems lacking interpretability. They demonstrate that explainable artificial intelligence can uncover actionable design rules by pinpointing the specific roles of formulation parameters in organ-selective delivery. They propose a development roadmap consisting of standardized multimodal data collection, multimodal computational modeling, robust explainability tools, and iterative laboratory experiments designed for biological validation. They stress that moving beyond predictions requires design rules that are rigorously interpretable, transferable across platforms, and experimentally testable in biological settings. They conclude that explainable artificial intelligence represents a vital step toward mechanistically motivated and translationally accountable nanomedicine engineering.

The authors point out critical bottlenecks including widespread dataset fragmentation, a persistent lack of experimental standardization, missing descriptive metadata, and an overall scarcity of high-quality extrahepatic delivery data. They note that inherent biological complexity and experimental variability make reliable, reproducible organ-specific delivery in vivo difficult, preventing predictive algorithms from translating seamlessly into dependable experimental systems. They state that computational models offer a promising way to search vast chemical and biological parameter spaces far more rapidly and efficiently than manual screening. They note that nucleic acid transport to non-hepatic tissues remains one of the least addressed challenges in lipid nanoparticle research due to lingering uncertainties surrounding in vivo particle behavior. They underscore that artificial intelligence cannot rely solely on mathematical optimization but must generate transferable design rules confirmed through iterative experimental testing.

The authors clarify in their data availability declaration that data sharing is not applicable because no original datasets were generated or analyzed during the review. The paper serves as a comprehensive synthesis of the field rather than presenting new empirical trials. The authors note that while computational modeling and formulation engineering have advanced considerably, uncertainties surrounding in vivo particle behavior persist. The proposed framework highlights the necessity of aligning algorithmic models with regulatory standards and clinical safety requirements. The authors state that incorporating regulatory considerations and biological validation directly into the modeling pipeline can ensure delivery strategies remain robust, reproducible, and translationally accountable across diverse therapeutic applications.

The review concludes that uniting predictive computational modeling with empirical biological validation, explicit awareness of uncertainty, and regulatory alignment offers a viable pathway to engineer safer, more rational, and clinically impactful nucleic acid delivery platforms in future nanomedicine. The authors stress that machine learning models must reflect genuine physiological processes rather than statistical artifacts. The article leaves open how standardized multimodal data collection would be implemented across research groups. It does not specify which non-hepatic tissue would be targeted first in experimental validation. It does not state when the proposed roadmap would be tested in laboratory settings.

Articles.Title: Review outlines explainable artificial intelligence for targeted extrahepatic lipid nanoparticle delivery

stories.Headline: BusPatrol runs AI school bus cameras in Montgomery County that generate tickets but show little decline in violations
stories.Summary:
BusPatrol, a company that operates artificial-intelligence-powered cameras on roughly 35,000 school buses in 24 states and more than 350 school districts, began operating in Montgomery County in 2017, and by the 2019, 20 school year all Montgomery County Public Schools buses had been equipped with cameras, according to an investigation by Bloomberg Businessweek in partnership with Type Investigations. The investigation found that school bus cameras in the county have generated more than 375,000 tickets and $92 million in fines, but that violations have remained relatively consistent, with little evidence that collisions near stopped school buses have declined. The number of citations per active camera barely changed over five years, averaging 36 per active camera in 2020 and falling only to 34 by 2025. The investigation also identified at least three children who were struck by drivers while getting on or off stopped school buses in Montgomery County since 2017, based on a review of local news reports and school bus camera footage. There has been some more recent improvement in the numbers, with Montgomery County police reporting 40,854 citations for illegally passing stopped school buses during the 2025, 26 school year, a 19.1% decrease from the previous school year, though thousands of drivers continue to pass stopped school buses while their red lights are flashing and stop arms are extended.

The BusPatrol cameras use artificial intelligence to identify vehicles that appear to illegally pass a stopped school bus with its stop arm extended, capturing video and images of the vehicle including its license plate and sending that footage to local law enforcement for review, and police determine whether a violation occurred, so the technology does not automatically issue a ticket. The county's Vision Zero program has defended the cameras as a tool for accountability and education, as well as a way to collect information about dangerous driving around school buses. The investigation raises a broader question about whether more citations are translating into fewer dangerous encounters for children. Other communities across the Washington region also use school bus stop-arm enforcement cameras, although those programs were not included in the national investigation.

In Falls Church, Virginia, the city issued 1,193 school bus camera citations in 2025, more than twice the 546 citations issued when the program began in 2015, while Fairfax County launched its own school bus camera enforcement program in 2025 and recorded more than 6,300 citations or warnings between April 2024 and Dec. 17, 2025. Washington, D.C., also installed stop-arm safety cameras on 25 school buses in 2024, and the District's program is separate from the BusPatrol system examined in the investigation. The debate over school bus camera enforcement comes as Montgomery County continues to track pedestrian safety concerns, recording 336 pedestrian-involved crashes countywide during the first nine months of 2026, including 17 fatal crashes, figures that include pedestrian crashes throughout the county and are not limited to school buses or school zones. The central question remains whether automated school bus enforcement is doing enough to prevent children from being struck by drivers, or whether additional safety measures are needed beyond issuing citations.

Articles.Title: Do Montgomery County AI-powered school bus cameras make children safer?

stories.Headline: Amazon SageMaker AI adds KV cache-aware routing for real-time endpoints
stories.Summary:
Amazon SageMaker AI introduced KV cache-aware routing, a new routing strategy for real-time endpoints, on November 17, 2026, according to an AWS blog post. The feature uses cache state that the model container reports to send each request to an instance holding a long cached match for its prompt that is not too busy. It targets teams serving large language models with multi-turn conversations, long shared prompts, or heavy load. Users enable it by adding one environment variable so the container reports its cache contents and by setting RoutingStrategy to KV_AWARE in the endpoint configuration. Clients call the endpoint with the same APIs as before.

The strategy relies on three parts: the model container reports what it has cached, SageMaker AI keeps a managed cache index of that state, and the endpoint uses the index to choose an instance per request. Turning on events with SM_VLLM_KV_EVENTS_CONFIG makes the container publish a KV cache event each time it stores or evicts entries. The index holds only one-way, truncated hashes of cached content mapped to the instance or inference component copy holding it, never prompts, token IDs, request payloads, or KV tensors. KV-aware routing is active only with at least two instances or at least two copies of an inference component, and with a single instance the setting has no effect. SageMaker AI now offers four routing strategies, RANDOM as the default, LEAST_OUTSTANDING_REQUESTS, PREFIX_AWARE, and KV_AWARE, set per production variant in the RoutingConfig.

AWS said prefix-aware routing, introduced in part 1 of the series, infers where a prefix is cached from the request alone and cannot tell when an instance has evicted that cache. The company said prefix-aware routing hashes the start of the request up to the configured PrefixLength, in bytes of the InvokeEndpoint payload or characters of the message text for the OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions API. AWS said this works less well when an instance evicts older entries as GPU memory fills or when a conversation starts out short and each turn changes the hashed text. The company said KV-aware routing asks the container what it holds, which makes it more precise, and pays off when there is a lot of cached context to reuse under pressure. AWS said a candidate that is too busy is skipped, and if no candidate has a useful match or all are busy, the request falls back to load-aware routing.

AWS reported benchmarks with Llama 3.1 70B Instruct on seven ml.p5.48xlarge instances, running 30-minute tests with 20 or 100 simulated users and prompts of up to about 64,000 tokens. Compared with random routing and with long prompts under load, AWS said KV-aware routing reduced p50 time to first token by up to 97 percent and increased throughput by up to 234 percent. It raised the KV cache hit rate from 3, 48 percent to 80, 93 percent, with the smallest gain on short prompts where there is less prefill to save. AWS said the lookup takes a few milliseconds for short prompts and longer for long ones, mostly for tokenization, and that fallbacks are not reported in the console or metrics at launch. AWS said the index follows the fleet, dropping entries for removed instances when scaling in, while new instances start with empty caches so latency can be higher for a short time.

AWS described an example endpoint with three instances, A, B, and C, each running the same model in its own AWS vLLM Deep Learning Container with its own KV cache in GPU memory. A holds turns 1 to 3 of conversation 1, B holds conversations 2 and 3, and C holds document 7, and when turn 4 of conversation 1 arrives the index shows A holds the first 6,000 of the request's 6,200 tokens. AWS said the router then sends the request to A, which computes only the remaining tokens, or to the least busy instance if A is busy. AWS gave a support assistant example on three instances where each conversation begins with the same 6,000-token knowledge-base excerpt and instance A evicts most of it under rising traffic. AWS said prefix-aware routing would send the next turn to A again, while KV-aware routing sends it to B, which still holds the first 4,000 tokens.

AWS said the tokens computed for text-only requests using standard options are passed to the model, so the prompt is not tokenized twice. The company said the same load-aware fallback happens when the endpoint cannot tokenize a request, except in two error cases described under invoking the endpoint. AWS said prefix-aware routing needs no container changes but cannot see what an instance holds, and that with very short prompts prefix-aware routing can be all you need. AWS said KV-aware routing matters most for long multi-turn conversations, where each turn sends the full history and the cached prefix grows with every turn. The article leaves open the two error cases it references and does not report the fallback rates or the latency of the new strategy beyond the benchmark figures.

Articles.Title: Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoints now support KV cache aware routing
