stories.Headline: Artificial Intelligence Tools Advance Poultry Health Monitoring Across Global Farms
stories.Summary:
Researchers at the Vellore Institute of Technology conducted a narrative review of artificial intelligence in poultry disease detection and health surveillance, published in Frontiers in Animal Science. The synthesis examined 81 peer-reviewed research papers published between 2016 and 2026. It evaluated machine learning and computer vision architectures that have achieved high experimental accuracy. The review found that significant real-world operational barriers continue to hinder widespread commercial deployment. The article was published on November 17, 2026.

The reviewed literature covers automated diagnostic modalities monitoring visual signs of infection, abnormal droppings, atypical vocalisation, altered movement patterns, and body temperature fluctuations in commercial flocks. Global poultry meat consumption is projected to rise from an average of 99.12 million metric tons over the past decade to 107.99 million metric tons over the next decade. Between 2016 and 2019, studies relied on support vector machines, artificial neural networks, random forests, and decision trees paired with manual feature extraction. From 2020 onward, research shifted toward convolutional neural networks and single-stage object detection architectures such as YOLO. Whole-bird RGB computer vision and faecal-image analysis emerged as the most prevalent methodologies across the 81 reviewed papers.

The authors observe that gains claimed by multimodal architectures remain largely validated on small or proprietary datasets rather than through rigorous multi-facility trials. They identify the cross-farm generalisation gap as a foremost methodological vulnerability, with models trained on single facilities suffering sharp performance drops in external environments. They call for open-access, multicountry, and multibreed benchmark datasets validated against veterinary reference standards such as PCR, microbial culture, or histopathology rather than visual inspection alone. They emphasize prospective commercial farm trials spanning multi-year production cycles and explainable artificial intelligence frameworks allowing farm managers and veterinarians to audit model reasoning. They also call for continual learning systems that adapt to seasonal flock variations and standardized reporting metrics detailing data-splitting protocols, hardware constraints, and false-alarm frequencies.

Automated vision frameworks on farms use fixed barn cameras, mobile devices, and inspection robots to identify clinical signs of Newcastle disease, fowl pox, and avian influenza. Deep convolutional pipelines evaluate changes in droppings' colour, consistency, moisture, and structural integrity as indicators of enteric pathogens like coccidiosis and salmonellosis. Recent deployment-oriented acoustic systems evaluated on working commercial facilities recorded field accuracies of approximately 93 percent, within the reported range of expert human assessments. In one quantified cross-country trial, an image-based multiclass disease classifier trained on poultry in Tanzania achieved 95 percent accuracy on local test data but fell to between 69 and 70 percent on Malawian poultry, a decline of 25 to 30 percentage points. Industrial processing lines run at speeds of 140 to 175 birds per minute.

Early acoustic efforts paired frequency-domain and time-frequency features with support vector machines for multi-pathogen classification, while later investigations used parallel convolutional branches and spectrogram representations to track disease severity over consecutive post-inoculation days. Investigators increasingly rely on generative adversarial networks and diffusion models to synthesise augmented training images, allowing object detectors to maintain high precision under heavy flock occlusion and dim lighting. Researchers are exploring edge computing, knowledge distillation, and federated learning frameworks, with edge systems delivering real-time inference latencies measured in milliseconds. Multispectral fluorescence imaging coupled with accelerated neural networks has demonstrated high average precision in identifying carcass surface defects and spotting microscopic faecal residues linked to Salmonella risk. Postmortem diagnostic models have achieved substantial accuracy screening internal organs, though softer tissues like diseased livers exhibit higher classification variance than cardiac pathologies.

The review concludes with a structured roadmap outlining research priorities required to establish trustworthy, scalable, and clinically robust precision poultry farming. Portable fluorescence systems have been adapted to scan eggshells under ambient lighting conditions, preventing contaminated products from entering retail channels. The authors note that droppings with identical visual appearances can stem from differing diets, flock ages, or ambient litter conditions rather than single pathogens. They state that image-based classifications currently function best as triage alerts rather than definitive diagnostic confirmations unless corroborated by laboratory assays such as polymerase chain reaction testing. The review traces an architectural progression from early handcrafted classifiers toward deep neural networks, transformer models, and multimodal fusion frameworks.

Articles.Title: Artificial Intelligence Tools Advance Poultry Health Monitoring Across Global Farms

stories.Headline: A review in Health Nanotechnology examines how AI reshapes nanomaterial discovery and validation
stories.Summary:
A comprehensive scientific review published in Health Nanotechnology on November 17, 2026 examines how artificial intelligence and nanoscale science are reshaping the discovery, synthesis, characterization, and biomedical application of functional nanomaterials. The review was published in the journal Health Nanotechnology and appeared on bioengineer.org on November 17, 2026. Nanotechnology centers on the precise understanding and manipulation of matter at dimensions between 1 and 100 nanometers. At those dimensions, high surface-to-volume ratios and quantum confinement phenomena yield physicochemical behaviors distinct from bulk materials. Conventional fabrication workflows have historically relied on trial-and-error experimentation across multidimensional parameter spaces, including precursor concentrations, reaction temperatures, pH levels, synthesis times, and capping agents.

Advanced computational methods, ranging from classical machine learning algorithms to deep artificial neural networks, have emerged as powerful mechanisms for deciphering nonlinear structure-property relationships and optimizing multidimensional problems. The review outlines how computational modeling accelerates research while identifying foundational data limitations, reproducibility challenges, and regulatory bottlenecks that currently prevent laboratory demonstrations from translating into widespread clinical and industrial applications. Machine learning in nanoscience encompasses distinct algorithms whose suitability depends directly on dataset size, problem dimensionality, and interpretability requirements. Artificial neural networks capture complex nonlinear interactions between synthesis variables and particle properties, such as hydrodynamic diameter and drug encapsulation efficiency, but their black-box architectures present interpretability challenges. Random forest models, constructed from ensembles of decision trees, offer robust performance on small to medium-sized heterogeneous datasets and provide feature-importance metrics that identify critical formulation drivers.

Support vector machines effectively navigate high-dimensional feature spaces with limited sample sizes, making them useful for nanoparticle size estimation and surface nanotopography analysis. Gaussian process regression functions as a probabilistic technique providing both continuous predictions and explicit uncertainty estimates, establishing it as a primary surrogate model for Bayesian optimization workflows. Convolutional neural networks process spatial imaging data, recurrent neural networks and long short-term memory networks analyze sequential drug release profiles, generative models facilitate structural inverse design, and graph neural networks map atomic topologies directly to macroscopic material properties. High-throughput computational screening frameworks integrated with machine learning enable the systematic identification of potentially exfoliable two-dimensional materials from known layered structures, drastically reducing first-principles computational costs. Graph neural networks, specifically crystal graph architectures, accurately forecast formation energies, electronic band gaps, and structure-dependent behaviors directly from crystal coordinates.

When paired with density functional theory adsorption datasets, data-driven algorithms prioritize promising bimetallic catalyst candidates for critical electrochemical reactions, including the oxygen reduction reaction and carbon dioxide reduction. Convolutional neural networks predict the optical responses of plasmonic nanostructures and extract underlying structural geometries from measured optical spectra. Machine learning models also predict size-dependent semiconductor quantum dot bandgaps, thermal conductivities, and mechanical properties, while explainable techniques like Shapley Additive Explanations quantify individual feature contributions to enhance physical plausibility. Generative adversarial networks, variational autoencoders, and large language models explore continuous multidimensional latent representations to propose novel nanostructures. In nanophotonics and metasurface engineering, generative adversarial networks learn mapping functions between structural geometries and optical spectra, generating candidate designs that fulfill predefined plasmonic resonances or target bandgaps without repeated Maxwell equation simulations.

Variational autoencoders provide smooth latent spaces that permit systematic interpolation between candidate materials, assisting in the targeted optimization of complex nanostructures. Large language models assist researchers through automated literature mining, scientific information extraction, hypothesis generation, and experimental synthesis planning. Published inverse design studies remain predominantly proof-of-concept investigations conducted on narrow, single-laboratory datasets, underscoring the urgent necessity for standardized benchmarking suites, open-access repositories, and rigorous external validation across independently synthesized materials. Standard regression architectures, including random forests and neural networks, map formulation variables such as polymer loading, surfactant ratios, solvent mixtures, pH, and mixing kinetics to physical attributes like polydispersity and colloidal stability. Single- and multi-objective Bayesian optimization frameworks utilize acquisition functions to balance exploration of unmeasured conditions with exploitation of favorable formulations, generating Pareto-optimal frontiers for competing parameters such as encapsulation yield and particle size.

Self-driving laboratories integrate robotic fluidics, automated inline characterization tools, and machine learning decision loops. Autonomous platforms, exemplified by systems developed for shape-programmable gold nanoparticles and the reinforcement-learning-guided AlphaFlow fluidic synthesizer, execute closed-loop cycles of synthesis, measurement, and model updating. Machine learning models optimize green synthesis protocols utilizing biological phytochemical extracts, systematically tuning reaction conditions to replace hazardous reagents while sustaining nanomanufacturing yields. Long short-term memory architectures capture the continuous kinetics of drug dissolution and release from polymeric nanocarriers, facilitating inverse formulation design tailored to produce zero-order or sustained release kinetics.

Deep convolutional models analyzing high-content fluorescence microscopy achieve up to 92 percent accuracy in classifying nanoparticle cellular internalization under controlled in vitro conditions. Random forest models utilizing molecular weight, surface charge, and lipid solubility predict blood-brain barrier penetration with 88 percent accuracy, illustrating computational potential for neurodegenerative therapeutics. Artificial neural networks trained on physicochemical properties predict the composition of the biomolecular protein corona that forms upon systemic exposure, aiding the design of long-circulating stealth nanocarriers. Conceptual frameworks propose integrating patient-derived genomic profiles, biopsy data, and biosensor inputs with deep reinforcement learning to adjust dosing dynamically, though substantial preclinical validation remains essential.

In benchmark evaluations, random forest models trained on diverse datasets of over 300 nanoparticles, including metal oxides, quantum dots, and carbon nanotubes, demonstrated approximately 85 percent accuracy in predicting in vitro cell viability, identifying surface functionalization and hydrodynamic dimensions as predominant determinants of cytotoxic response. Toxicological outcomes span diverse biological mechanisms, including membrane disruption, oxidative stress generation, chromosomal aberrations, and immunogenic cytokine release, each requiring distinct experimental assays and feature representations. Most existing predictive tools are trained on single cell-line assays over restricted 24-hour exposure intervals, and models frequently fail when generalized across structurally distinct materials like lipid nanoparticles or when extrapolating from simplified in vitro assays to complex in vivo pharmacokinetics, organ accumulation, and systemic clearance pathways. In transmission electron microscopy, U-Net convolutional architectures have demonstrated superior particle segmentation capability, securing an overall accuracy of 96.65 percent and an F1 score of 0.909 across variable image sets, with performance reaching 98.95 percent on high-contrast micrographs before degrading to 92.76 percent on clustered or beam-damaged specimens.

Shape classification networks, including ResNet-34 on scanning electron microscopy and AlexNet on scanning transmission electron microscopy, classify morphologies such as spheres, rods, triangles, and agglomerates with accuracies between 93 and 95 percent. In atomic force microscopy, convolutional networks correct thermal drift, scan-line noise, and tip broadening artefacts, while pix2pix conditional GANs enhance topographical contrast. Convolutional networks extract defect densities and layer counts from Raman spectra of carbon nanomaterials. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Seoul researchers develop deep learning model that raises pathologists accuracy in detecting rare kidney cancer
stories.Summary:
Researchers at Asan Medical Center in Seoul developed a deep learning model to identify a rare and aggressive kidney cancer called fumarate hydratase-deficient renal cell carcinoma. This study, published in npj Digital Medicine, tested the tool using 335 digitized pathology slides to see if it could help doctors distinguish this specific cancer from other renal types. Twenty-one pathologists, including seven residents and fourteen specialists, examined 30 challenging cases both independently and with the assistance of the AI. The results showed that AI assistance increased overall diagnostic accuracy from 60% to 73.3% and improved precision from 66.7% to 77.8%.

The AI model, built on the ResNeXt101 architecture, flags suspected cases and generates color-coded maps to highlight suspicious tissue regions for the doctors. It is designed to help pathologists identify patients who may require additional genetic analysis or immunohistochemistry testing for a final diagnosis. The study found that receptive doctors improved their accuracy but had a median overreliance rate of 80%, meaning they often accepted incorrect AI advice. Resistant doctors were less influenced by AI errors, but they showed no statistically significant improvement in their diagnostic accuracy during the tests.

Professor Yong Mee Cho stated that AI could help clinicians recognize rare cancers they might otherwise overlook to ensure patients receive confirmatory testing. Professor Namkug Kim noted that effective AI use requires skills independent of traditional diagnostic expertise, which suggests a need for tailored human-AI collaboration strategies. The researchers questioned whether conventional clinical training adequately prepares doctors to critically assess AI recommendations to avoid overreliance. Future studies in routine pathology settings will determine if specialized training can help doctors benefit from AI while reducing the risk of errors.

Articles.Title: AI can detect rare cancer, but can doctors use it?

stories.Headline: Keith Bowers argues AI cannot replicate lived experience in landscape architecture
stories.Summary:
Keith Bowers wrote an article on November 17, 2026, about the use of artificial intelligence in landscape architecture. He explored how these digital tools impact the professional responsibilities of designers and their relationship with nature. The author argued that AI cannot replicate the lived experiences that give landscapes their true essence. He noted that AI can analyze components but cannot experience the social or ecological processes of a site. This piece serves as the third part of a three-part series regarding intelligence and design.

The ASLA 2025 public policy on AI states that these tools cannot replace professional judgment, creativity, or ethics. Responsibility for every deliverable remains with the licensed landscape architect regardless of the tools used for the work. A 2025 survey by the CSLA, ASLA, and IFLA found that half of respondents used AI for research. Three quarters of those surveyed said AI made their work more efficient, yet 70 percent voiced ethical concerns. These practitioners worried about accuracy and the erosion of human connection within the design process.

Keith Bowers stated that he struggles with how professionals remain accountable for what AI produces or leaves out. He explained that AI interprets sites through a WEIRD lens, which favors Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, and Democratic societies. Bowers noted that AI cannot convey oral histories, cultural significance, or the seasonal rhythms of a neighborhood. He argued that professional judgment is built by walking sites, observing patterns, and listening to local communities. The author warned that relying on AI could weaken these essential human capacities for discernment.

Researchers at Harvard University found that large language models respond most like people from WEIRD societies. Stanford researchers estimate that only 1,000 of over 7,000 living languages are well represented in digital AI training. A study of 3,200 participants across 16 identities found that AI tends to misportray and flatten group members. Design ideation experiments showed that AI image generators led to fewer ideas and lower originality among participants. These findings affect landscape architects who must ensure their designs are inclusive and truly original.

The articles mention that most AI training data comes from web text skewed toward English and wealthy countries. The biologist Jakob von Uexküll used the term Umwelt to describe the unique perceptual world of each organism. AI cannot capture the sensory worlds of bees, bats, moths, salamanders, or soil fungi in its datasets. Ecologists describe an extinction of experience as the loss of direct contact with nature and the environment. This loss diminishes human health, well-being, and positive attitudes toward the natural world.

Panelists at the ASLA Groundwork presidential forum in May discussed the hazard of AI output that only looks finished. They feared that designers might privilege easily measured data over intangible and relational qualities of a place. The UN Chronicle argued that inclusive AI must respect the decisions of communities to protect certain knowledge. Practitioners are encouraged to use the CARE Principles for Indigenous Data Governance to honor these boundaries. The text ends while discussing the concept of Nature Intelligence.

stories.Headline: Jacqueline Arthur-Montagne examines what classical texts say about artificial intelligence
stories.Summary:
The article, published by Public Books on 17 November 2026 and written by Jacqueline Arthur-Montagne, examines what classical texts say about artificial intelligence. It describes the robotic handmaids of Hephaestus in Homer's Iliad, which moved fast, looked like young women and could speak and think beyond human ability. It cites Adrienne Mayor's writing that automata fall into three basic functions: labor, sex, and entertainment or spectacle. It recounts that the Roman senator Herodes Atticus raised 24 slave-boys, each named for one of the letters, alongside his son, who could not master the alphabet. It adds that the emperor Nero enticed Greek youths to reperform shocking moments of their own mythology, and one young man playing Icarus tumbled to his death and spattered the emperor with blood.

The article says Herodes reared only six natural children of his own in the household where the 24 enslaved playmates lived. It says the letter-boys were brought into existence exclusively as mnemonics for an elite child and would be decommissioned as obsolete hardware once his son grasped their grammatic essence. It says their fate, like their names, was never recorded. It describes Calvisius Sabinus, an exorbitantly rich slaveholder who, according to the letters of Seneca the Younger, kept a stable of slaves who had committed all the Greek poets to memory. It says that if Sabinus desired a book not yet memorized, he placed an order for a new slave custom-made, and that he assembled this enslaved archive to impress dinner guests rather than to edify his intellect.

The article says Sabinus summoned his slaves for parties and commanded them to deliver just the right verses for himself to repeat. It says Sabinus's friends teased that it would have been cheaper to buy and learn the books himself. It reports that Sabinus insisted that what anyone in his household knew, he himself could be said to know. It says Seneca tells the story for the same reason college professors tell students not to rely on ChatGPT, to argue that users of the enslaved archive neither acquire nor internalize the information within. It says Seneca also prefigures the fantasy of possessing encyclopedic knowledge without personal exertion or ethical accountability.

The article says the production of human alphabets and enslaved archives was prohibitively expensive in Seneca's day, feasible only for the ultra-rich like Herodes Atticus and Sabinus. It quotes Bill Gates predicting that intelligence will be completely free. It says Seneca's letter points to the darker possibility that effortless intelligence will always rest on someone else's labor. It quotes Sundar Pichai, CEO of Google, urging that technology brings incredible benefits but we must ensure everyone has access to them, and that we have the opportunity to improve lives at a once-in-a-generation scale.

It says big tech has long recognized the appeal of consumer-facing virtual assistants with human names and personalities, and that compliant female personae predominated in the 2010s as Microsoft's Cortana and Amazon's Alexa joined the conversation that Siri once monopolized. The article says the first artificial intelligence belonged to the Olympian gods. It says Hesiod relates how the Greek gods crafted an artificial woman, Pandora, from earth and water, sculpted her face with immortal beauty and ornamented her with golden jewelry. It says that deep in her hardware were installed the lies and wily words and cunning character of Zeus's design, and that Pandora means all-gift because each god gifted her with a special trait to doom mankind.

It says the myth began with the titan Prometheus, who stole a spark of Zeus's fire after the gods hid away the tools of easy living, lighting a torch with the promise of effortless productivity. It describes a red-figure calyx-krater of about 450 BC from Attica, Greece, by the Niobid Painter, held at the British Museum in London, showing Pandora standing full frontal with arms stiff at her sides. The article says Hesiod called Pandora a kalon kakon, a beautiful evil. It says Anthropic crafted Claude in honor of the polymathic inventor Claude Shannon, who named his artificially intelligent mouse Theseus after the labyrinth-solving demigod, and that Shannon appears to have been as reliant on the mathematical brilliance of his wife, Betty, as Theseus was on the maiden Ariadne.

It says Google had initially christened its generative AI Bard, a term for an epic storyteller closely associated with Homer and Hesiod, before unveiling the chatbot Gemini. It says the Roman poet Ovid recalls that Icarus had witnesses, a shepherd and a fisherman, who looked up and thought they saw a god. It says Sam Altman qualified in 2023, before the AI-related deaths of our own young men in Florida, Texas, and California, that there will be mistakes. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Slaves and Other “Artificial Intelligences”: What the Classics Warn Us About AI

stories.headline_source: Slaves and Other “Artificial Intelligences”: What the Classics Warn Us About AI

stories.Headline: Michael Garland and Gaurav Pal say shared savings lets government adopt AI with little financial risk
stories.Summary:
Michael Garland and Gaurav “GP” Pal wrote in a November 17, 2026 commentary that government can adopt AI quickly with little financial risk. They said the government has not been an early adopter of new technology. They noted the Cloud First policy arrived in 2010 and FedRAMP in 2011. They said agencies are still migrating workloads to the cloud more than 15 years later. They said the artificial intelligence revolution is a juggernaut.

They said Anthropic’s recent IPO filing reports revenue grew from $41 million in 2023 to $16 billion in the first half of 2026. They said Bloomberg reports OpenAI’s annualized revenue was about $50 billion at the end of September. They estimated the government spends about $20 billion a year on commercial software licensing alone. They cited the Congressional Budget Office putting the fiscal 2026 deficit at $2.0 trillion. They cited Pew Research finding the federal workforce fell about 10% in 2025.

They said the mechanism is shared savings, where the contractor funds the deployment and the government pays a percentage of verifiably delivered savings. They said Energy Savings Performance Contracts have let agencies pay contractors out of guaranteed energy savings for decades. They said Medicare’s Shared Savings Program rewards providers who hold costs below a benchmark. They said in September the Pentagon’s Chief Digital and AI Office signed a one-year agreement with Red Cell Partners with a ceiling of $100 million.

They said Red Cell projects $62 million in Air Force audit-readiness support contracts could be consolidated into an AI-augmented model costing about $24.8 million, with the vendor earning 30% of the verified reduction. They said the General Services Administration’s OneGov program supplies a known price. They said GSA recently set a 50% discount on OpenAI token usage under a 27-month agreement. They said as of Oct. 27 GSA set a 40% discount on token usage across Anthropic’s Claude models.

They said the E-Government Act of 2002 authorized share-in-savings contracts for IT. They said the Government Accountability Office reported in 2005 that implementing regulations had never been issued, only 21 acquisition employees had taken GSA’s training course, and no contracts had been awarded. They said the authority expired that September. They said the Anti-Deficiency Act forbids obligating funds before Congress appropriates them.

They said the Pentagon pilot is a one-year other transaction agreement that sidesteps the multiyear problem for now. They said scaling beyond one-year pilots will take legislation. They said a small office skilled in designing cost baselines could be housed at GSA. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Shared savings: How government can adopt AI quickly with little financial risk

stories.Headline: Kevin Roose details the race to build artificial superintelligence in a new book
stories.Summary:
Christine Emba, a senior fellow and guest host of The Gray Area podcast, spoke with technology journalist Kevin Roose about his new book, The AGI Chronicles: The Inside Story of the Race to Create an Artificial Superintelligence, in an episode published on October 26, 2026. The episode examined what is happening behind the scenes at America's largest AI companies and how the squabbles, ideologies and goals of their CEOs and engineers could shape the future. Roose's book offers a behind-the-scenes look at the engineers and tech leaders competing to build artificial superintelligence, according to the episode description. The conversation also explored the rivalries between frontier labs such as OpenAI, Anthropic and Google DeepMind, along with the philosophical roots of "p(doom)" and AI safety. The episode description states that the race to build artificial superintelligence has sparked a massive data center boom and has made a handful of people some of the most powerful decision-makers on Earth.

Emba and Roose also discussed whether recursive self-improvement could push superintelligence beyond human control sooner than many people think. The episode was published by the American Enterprise Institute as part of its Social, Cultural, and Constitutional Studies work and appeared under The Gray Area with Sean Illing. The page lists Emba as a senior fellow and does not give any further dates, figures or named companies beyond those above. The episode presents Roose's account of the engineers and tech leaders competing in this race, and it frames the rivalries among the frontier labs as a central part of the story. Emba and Roose explored the philosophical roots of "p(doom)" and AI safety as part of the same conversation about how the goals of the people involved could shape the future.

The description does not attribute any further statements to Roose or Emba beyond the topics listed for the episode. No additional remarks from the participants are given on the page. The page places the episode alongside other recent Gray Area installments, including discussions of the gender divide, the Cornell case and trauma as a status symbol, and it links to a related book event with Daniel A. Cox on Generation Uncoupled. The articles do not say what happens next in the race itself or what any company or regulator plans to do. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Philosopher Matthew Parish argues that minds may create heaven and that AI advances support dualism
stories.Summary:
The Lviv Herald published an article by Matthew Parish on Tuesday 17 November 2026 arguing that heaven may be what we make of it. Parish wrote that the afterlife, should there be one, is not a place to which we travel but a condition of existence that our own minds bring into being. He said the traditional theological question of what heaven looks like may be misconceived. He argued that heaven might look different to everyone because the human mind is itself the architect of experience. He said some of the strongest reasons for contemplating this arise from recent advances in artificial intelligence.

Parish cited the eighteenth-century German philosopher Immanuel Kant, who argued that the human mind actively structures the way the world appears to us. For Kant, space and time are forms of human intuition, and causation, substance and other fundamental concepts are categories through which the understanding organises experience. Parish said we cannot step outside our minds to inspect the universe as it might appear to a being whose faculties are entirely different from our own. He asked whether consciousness that survives bodily death must continue to experience space, time and causation as we presently understand them. He said heaven could be a radically different mode of consciousness in which the organising principles of experience have been transformed.

Parish said the development of large language models has made him increasingly sympathetic to dualism, the proposition most famously associated with René Descartes that mind and matter are fundamentally distinct. He said he does not suggest artificial intelligence has demonstrated the truth of Cartesian dualism, still less that we have discovered experimental evidence for an immortal soul. He said a large language model may discuss the poetry of Shakespeare, explain the metaphysics of Aristotle, analyse the emotional consequences of bereavement and compose an apparently moving meditation upon eternal life. He said such a system can do all these things without possessing a human body, human memories or a human biography.

He said there is no universally accepted scientific test for subjective experience and that the possibility of machine consciousness remains a serious philosophical question. Parish said physical explanations can describe neural activity, information processing and behavioural responses but cannot explain why any of this should be accompanied by the inward quality of experience. He said the explanatory gap remains and that the possibility consciousness constitutes a fundamental feature of reality rather than an incidental product of matter deserves renewed attention. He said a materialist may reasonably argue that consciousness emerges from certain forms of physical organisation, whether biological or artificial.

He said that if consciousness is in some meaningful sense distinct from the physical mechanisms through which it ordinarily operates, then bodily death need not logically entail its extinction. He said we would still require an explanation of how consciousness persists and what preserves personal identity. Parish said Christianity traditionally understands heaven not merely as the satisfaction of subjective preferences but as communion with God. He said the Christian conception of salvation presupposes that human desires may be mistaken, disordered or incomplete.

He said Saint Augustine understood human restlessness as a consequence of our incomplete orientation towards God. He said Dante's vision of the afterlife connects the condition of the soul with the structure of its desires. He said the damned are not merely punished by externally imposed torments but are, in significant measure, imprisoned by their own condition. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Heaven is what we make of it: Kant, artificial intelligence and the immortality of the mind

stories.Headline: ArisGlobal caches shared prompt prefixes on Amazon Bedrock to cut inference costs and latency
stories.Summary:
ArisGlobal, a provider of life sciences technology, developed NavaX, an AI engine built on Amazon Bedrock, to automate adverse-event case processing. ArisGlobal productionized its first generative AI solution on Amazon Bedrock with Anthropic's Claude in March 2025. According to ArisGlobal's internal production telemetry, the system has processed over 1 million real transactions in regulated pharmaceutical environments. It has handled billions of tokens across multiple enterprise tenants. ArisGlobal chose Amazon Bedrock for managed access to foundation models, EU geographic cross-Region inference, and managed prompt caching.

As enterprise customers added distinct compliance requirements, the shared prompt prefix grew by about 150% over 6 months. Over that period the shared prompt prefix grew from approximately 72,000 to 180,000 tokens. Per-case inference costs increased by more than 200%. NavaX's Dynamic Data Extraction agent extracts around 130 fields, and source documents are often 10 to 200 pages. Supported Claude models allow up to four checkpoints per request, and for Claude Sonnet 4.5 the minimum prefix size is 1,024 tokens.

ArisGlobal first cached each source document because it was the largest part of a request, which left the growing shared prompt prefix outside the cache. By reversing the order and caching the shared prefix instead, ArisGlobal reduced effective input cost and supported additional tenants without proportional cost growth. ArisGlobal uses one explicit checkpoint immediately after the shared prompt prefix, which is sent first. The per-case document follows the checkpoint and is processed on each request. ArisGlobal gave up limited document reuse within one case and gained prompt reuse across the fleet.

In production, 65% of input tokens on a typical request are served from the shared prompt cache. Caching the shared prompt prefix produced up to 25% lower end-to-end latency on cached production requests. It produced approximately 50% lower effective input cost and approximately 40% lower overall monthly inference spend at more than 19 billion tokens per month. Around 15% more enterprise tenants were onboarded without proportional cost increases, and EU geographic routing remained unchanged.

For most active accounts, cases arrive about every 5 minutes per tenant and multiple tenants run concurrently. ArisGlobal is the creator of LifeSphere, a unified SaaS platform for pharmacovigilance, regulatory affairs, quality, and medical information. LifeSphere serves pharmaceutical companies globally, including multiple Top 20 pharma organizations by revenue. The entire system runs on AWS.

LifeSphere NavaX is ArisGlobal's AI engine that transforms drug safety from a system of record into a system of strategic advantage. Because case content includes protected health information, ArisGlobal applies responsible-AI controls as a standard part of its production deployment, drawing on capabilities such as Amazon Bedrock Guardrails. The default cache TTL is 5 minutes, and select models support a 1-hour TTL by setting "ttl": "1h". Longer-TTL entries must precede shorter-TTL entries.

ArisGlobal advises caching what repeats rather than what is largest, and placing stable content first. For sporadic traffic, ArisGlobal suggests evaluating the 1-hour TTL on supported models. Model availability varies by Region. All performance and cost figures reflect ArisGlobal's production metrics as reported to AWS, and results will vary based on prompt structure, traffic patterns, and cache hit rates.

stories.Headline: Jennifer Wood says auditors must validate AI output and challenge it with professional skepticism
stories.Summary:
Jennifer Wood, a partner and the assurance service line leader at the Bonadio Group, wrote in a Bloomberg Tax article published on November 18, 2026, that artificial intelligence must test rather than replace auditors’ professional skepticism. She said the AICPA’s new guidance on using AI in financial reporting and auditing, published on October 13, 2026, arrived at the perfect time and is nonauthoritative but increasingly relevant to audit quality and peer-review readiness. She said the practice aid lacks guidance on how firms should consistently validate and document AI-assisted procedures, particularly when AI is used to identify exceptions or support audit conclusions, along with practical examples. She said the biggest challenge for audit firms is determining when auditors can trust AI output, how to validate it, and when their own professional skepticism requires them to challenge it.

Wood said AI does not change auditors’ responsibility to secure sufficiently appropriate audit evidence but changes how they fulfill that responsibility. She said the biggest misconception is that AI is simply a faster way to perform existing tasks, when it is actually an opportunity to rethink how audits are performed. She said an AI output can be accurate without being complete, and she prefers the expression “validate before relying.” She said her firm has used AI for financial statement tie-outs and document analysis, and that a tie-out involving more than 100 pages historically consumed nearly two days of staff time, which AI can accelerate while identifying inconsistencies a human reviewer might overlook, though the auditor must still confirm the results. She said that in a hypothetical example of using AI to review 1,000 revenue contracts and identify unusual recognition provisions, the tool flags 25 contracts and all 25 are legitimate exceptions, but it might have overlooked another 10 contracts containing problematic provisions, so every exception identified was accurate yet the analysis was incomplete.

Wood said professional skepticism has historically focused on challenging management’s assertions, estimates, and representations, but now auditors must also challenge the technology that helps them evaluate those assertions. She said AI-generated work can look remarkably polished and authoritative, which can create a false sense of confidence, and auditors should instinctively ask what evidence supports a conclusion, what assumptions were made, and what might have been missed. She said AI creates additional responsibilities for engagement partners and reviewers, who need to understand how AI is being used on their engagements and whether appropriate validation has occurred, without needing to understand every technical aspect of the underlying model. She said firms need clear policies defining approved AI tools, permissible uses, confidentiality requirements, and expectations for validation and documentation, and that documentation for AI-assisted audit procedures should identify the tool used, the purpose of the procedure, the relevant inputs and outputs, how results were validated, and how the work influenced audit conclusions.

Wood said firms should distinguish between AI used for administrative efficiency and AI used to support audit evidence, which warrant different levels of oversight, and should incorporate AI governance into their existing system of quality management rather than treat it as a separate technology initiative. She said AI can improve audit quality and reduce the risk of human fatigue associated with repetitive procedures, citing financial statement tie-outs and document analysis as examples, and that AI can quickly summarize key provisions in a lengthy lease agreement or debt agreement so the auditor can focus on evaluating the accounting implications. She said the goal should be better audits, not just faster ones, and the greatest opportunity is reinvesting time saved in higher-value audit activities including risk assessment, investigating exceptions, and challenging management’s assumptions. She said that over the next three to five years, the firms that succeed will be those that integrate AI into their methodologies, invest in quality management, and fundamentally rethink how they develop their people, and that the firms that differentiate themselves won’t necessarily be using AI the most but will be demonstrating that AI is making their audits better.

Articles.Title: AI Must Test, Not Replace, Auditors’ Professional Skepticism

stories.Headline: USD 435 approves guidelines for safe AI use by teachers and students
stories.Summary:
USD 435 has established guidelines for how teachers and students can use artificial intelligence safely and effectively, as AI becomes an increasingly common tool in education. Assistant Superintendent Rick Rivera presented the district's proposed acceptable use guidance for artificial intelligence to the Board of Education during its Nov. 9 meeting. The board later approved the guidelines. The guidelines are intended to establish expectations for AI use by both staff and students. They are also meant to protect student privacy and ensure compliance with state and federal regulations.

The guidance recognizes that AI can be used in several ways in the classroom. Teachers may choose to prohibit its use on a particular assignment, allow limited assistance, or encourage students to use it as a brainstorming partner. The district plans to provide professional development for teachers interested in incorporating AI into their instruction. Administrators have already begun evaluating platforms designed specifically for educational use, including School AI and MagicSchool, with particular attention to student safety and data protection. The evaluation process includes reviewing whether platforms meet federal requirements for student privacy and online safety, including the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA), the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA), and the Children's Internet Protection Act (CIPA).

Rivera emphasized that AI should be viewed as a tool to enhance instruction, not replace teachers or the critical thinking skills students need to develop. He compared the technology to using a navigation app when planning a road trip, saying the driver remains in control of the vehicle and makes the final decisions. He said AI "just gives us that information." Rivera said School AI, one of the platforms administrators have explored, uses servers located in the United States and has safeguards designed to filter information before it reaches students. The platform also provides teachers with information about student interactions, including questions being asked and potentially inappropriate content.

During an evaluation exercise, administrators were asked to try to get the system to produce inappropriate responses. Rivera said he asked administrators to type something in that would possibly have a student land back in their office because of what they did. He said the platform redirected those requests and provided feedback to teachers about student activity. Not only did it flag it, it sent him an email about what the person did. Rivera said School AI does not use student data to train its models and believed MagicSchool has a similar policy.

Board members discussed the importance of providing training for both teachers and students, noting that some educators may already be using AI but feel uncertain about discussing it openly. The board raised questions about parental notification and consent, as well as whether information entered by students could be used to train AI models. Rivera said the district would share its guidelines and information about any selected platforms with parents. He said the acceptable use guidance would provide a foundation for staff training and help teachers understand which tools are appropriate for classroom assignments. Rivera said any platform used for student assignments would go through an approval process to ensure it meets district technology and safety requirements.

The list of AI platforms included in the district's evaluation is not intended to be exhaustive. Because the technology changes rapidly, the list may be updated as additional tools are reviewed. Rivera said "AI is not a human" and "AI makes mistakes." He stressed that students must continue to check the information they receive and rely on their own judgment and critical thinking. He said the goal is to use AI as a thought partner that can help students develop ideas and creativity without replacing human connection or decision-making.

stories.Headline: Bain analysts argue AI advantage comes from signals competitors cannot copy
stories.Summary:
The articles describe a Bain & Company report published on 17 November 2026 by Matthew Crupi, Sanjin Bicanic and John Hazan, arguing that competitive advantage from AI comes from signals competitors cannot copy. The report says AI advances fastest where a signal lets a company quickly and reliably check that the work is correct. It describes a mining company's capital projects team that spent an hour on a Monday afternoon setting up review of its most critical investment projects. By Tuesday morning, agents had reconciled tens of thousands of documents against cost and schedule data, and a first pass was on the table. The team then had to decide which of the problems the system flagged were real.

The report says work falls into three groups: work with a fast signal, structurally slow work, and a dangerous middle nobody has measured yet. It says companies move the frontier by building a proxy, encoding an expert's unwritten standard into a rubric, and using simulation to reproduce an environment and grade success. It cites Goodhart's Law, warning that once a proxy becomes the target it can drift. It says building a signal is slow and expensive, so it belongs where the work makes a company distinctive. It says durable advantage depends on owning the data, workflow and feedback loop that make the system improve with use.

The report cites a March 2026 cross-industry Bain survey of 196 respondents in which 91% said AI helps them be more productive and 53% reported higher-quality work. Only 27% said it helps them do new types of work. It says Anthropic reports that as agent-written code moved through its own organization, human review became the new limit. It says agentic AI concentrates judgment into four human responsibilities: intent, constraints, validation and stewardship. It says most failures it has seen were not AI model failures but traced back to one of these four responsibilities going unassigned.

The report says Stripe had to write down a rule that data from two unrelated customer contexts must not appear in the same analysis, even where one person is cleared to see both. It cites an experiment with 791 professionals at Procter & Gamble in which AI raised the quality of ideas generated and human judgment concentrated on selecting among them. It says stewardship takes roughly a third of the human effort in Bain's agentic work. It says OpenAI helped an accounting firm build a tax preparation agent, and the share of returns reaching a baseline quality threshold went from 25% to 86% in six weeks. It cites an Anthropic survey of more than 500 technical leaders in the US in which 57% were running agents on multistage workflows but only 16% across processes spanning teams.

The report says Climate Corporation was a crop insurance start-up that built soil and climate measurement data across US farmland where almost none existed. It says Monsanto acquired Climate Corporation for about $930 million in 2013, and Bayer inherited it when it bought Monsanto in 2018. It says more than a decade later Bayer traces its current AI capability to that deal, and its CIO argues the data, not the model, is the part competitors cannot copy. It says lenders with no credit files built a proxy from mobile operator data, reading airtime top-up patterns as an indicator of who could repay, and a mobile credit-scoring industry formed around the score. It says reversibility sets the autonomy frontier: where errors can be caught and reversed, let the system run and audit the exceptions, and where they cannot, use the signal to accelerate review rather than remove it.

The report says AI separates output from expertise, so firms book productivity gains immediately while expertise losses arrive later and without warning. It says protecting human judgment requires companies to deliberately redesign both work and learning. It advises starting where the value is, testing the signal, and breaking one of the most important workflows into tasks because the frontier runs inside a workflow rather than around it. It advises deploying where results are already checkable and not pouring agents into work no one can grade. The articles leave open how companies should build signals where none yet exist and how the expertise losses will be detected before they surface.

Articles.Title: Everyone Has AI. Advantage Comes from What You Build Around It

stories.Headline: FDA adopts super intelligence as its official term for AI across communications and documents
stories.Summary:
The US Food and Drug Administration announced on Monday, 17 November 2026, that it will use the term “super intelligence” instead of “artificial intelligence” in all official correspondence, public communications, websites, reports and policy documents. The agency said the shift was prompted by an executive order signed by President Donald Trump in September, which directs all executive departments and federal agencies to make the change. The FDA said the term change will not affect existing guidance documents, regulations, Federal Register notices and other previously issued FDA documents. The agency also said that where a statute or regulation uses “artificial intelligence” or “AI”, the FDA will continue to quote and cite those terms as written.

The executive order applies only to executive branch agencies and does not affect private industry, Sydney White, an attorney with Wiley Rein LLP, told Focus, which means pharmaceutical and medical device manufacturers will not need to make the terminology change. White noted that private-sector organizations could be affected if any of the order’s directives are enacted into law. According to the order, the term “AI” is considered outdated, and “Super Intelligence” more appropriately captures the promise, potential and rapidly advancing capabilities of these technologies. The order directs the Assistant to the President for Science and Technology to provide the President with proposed legislative language that defines “Super Intelligence” within 60 days of the order.

Christina Silcox, the research director for digital health at the Duke-Margolis Institute for Health Policy, told Focus that she would consider this more of a semantic change than a meaningful change, because neither artificial intelligence nor super intelligence have particularly strong definitions. Silcox expressed concern that using the term “super intelligence” to describe all clinical and clinical-adjacent AI-enabled tasks might lead to an over-reliance on the results by clinicians and patients. She emphasized that health systems with effective governance should ensure that users understand what each specific AI tool does, when it should be used, and how to interpret and act on the results. The FDA said it will make conforming edits to its public-facing documents as part of each document’s next substantive revision and update web content on its regular maintenance cycle.

Articles.Title: FDA to refer to AI as ‘super intelligence’ going forward

stories.Headline: Review authors say AI advances antibiotic discovery and design across five areas
stories.Summary:
Antibiotic-resistant bacterial infections cause more than 1 million deaths worldwide each year, according to a Review published in Nature Reviews Microbiology on 17 November 2026. The Review focuses on recent advances in small-molecule antibiotic discovery enabled by artificial intelligence. It presents innovative approaches that are substantially increasing the size and diversity of the explored chemical space. It highlights recent artificial intelligence-driven advancements in phenotypic antibiotic discovery, mechanism of action elucidation, target-based discovery, de novo molecular design and lead optimization. The authors say these promise to expand the repertoire of antibacterial agents and uncover bacterial pathways and vulnerabilities amenable to therapeutic intervention.

The Review states there is a critical need for new classes of antibiotics, particularly those with novel mechanisms of action. It cites a 2022 Lancet analysis by the Antimicrobial Resistance Collaborators on the global burden of bacterial antimicrobial resistance in 2019, published in volume 399, pages 629 to 655. It cites a 2024 Lancet analysis by Naghavi and colleagues on the global burden of bacterial antimicrobial resistance from 1990 to 2021, with forecasts to 2050, in volume 404, pages 1199 to 1226. It cites a 2024 report from the EcoAMR Series by McDonnell and colleagues on forecasting the economic impacts of antimicrobial resistance in humans, from WOAH and the World Bank. The Review is a preview of subscription content, with access through an institution or a Nature+ online-access subscription at $39.99 for 30 days.

A journal subscription gives 12 print issues and online access for $259.00 per year, or $21.58 per issue. The article can be purchased on SpringerLink for USD 39.95, with prices subject to local taxes calculated during checkout. The Review includes five figures, on strategies for systematically exploring small-molecule chemical space, a workflow for machine learning-guided antibacterial hit identification based on phenotypic screens, experimental approaches for mechanism of action characterization, a structure-based drug discovery pipeline for target identification and hit validation with associated challenges, and multimodal design of antibiotics for lead optimization and candidate progression. The reference list includes Levy's 1992 book The Antibiotic Paradox, published by Springer, and Silver's 2011 paper on challenges of antibacterial discovery in Clinical Microbiology Reviews, volume 24, pages 71 to 109. It includes Walsh's 2003 paper in Nature Reviews Microbiology, volume 1, pages 65 to 70, asking where new antibiotics will come from.

It includes Stover and colleagues' 2000 paper in Nature, volume 405, pages 962 to 966, on a small-molecule nitroimidazopyran drug candidate for tuberculosis. It includes Eyal and colleagues' 2016 paper in Scientific Reports, volume 6, article 39004, on a novel pleuromutilin antibacterial compound, its binding mode and selectivity mechanism. The references also include Miller and colleagues' 2008 paper in Antimicrobial Agents and Chemotherapy, volume 52, pages 2806 to 2812, on discovery and characterization of QPT-1, the progenitor of a new class of bacterial topoisomerase inhibitors. They include Bax and colleagues' 2010 paper in Nature, volume 466, pages 935 to 940, on type IIA topoisomerase inhibition by a new class of antibacterial agents. They include Yao and colleagues' 2026 paper in Antimicrobial Agents and Chemotherapy, volume 70, e01706-25, on stepwise evolution and clonal enrichment of gepotidacin resistance in Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

They include Mukherjee and colleagues' 2026 paper in the Journal of Infectious Diseases, volume 234, pages e131 to e140, on genetic background modulating zoliflodacin and gepotidacin cross-resistance and fitness in Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Further references include Wan, Wong, Collins and de la Fuente-Nunez's 2024 paper in Nature Reviews Bioengineering, volume 2, pages 392 to 407, on machine learning for antimicrobial peptide identification and design. They include Martins and colleagues' 2026 scoping review in Artificial Intelligence in Medicine, volume 179, article 103461, on artificial intelligence in drug discovery for fungal diseases. They include Fu and colleagues' 2021 paper in Nature Communications, volume 12, article 6497, on leveraging machine learning essentiality predictions and chemogenomic interactions to identify antifungal targets. They include Wensing and colleagues' 2026 paper in Nature Microbiology, volume 11, pages 2157 to 2169, on pooled CRISPRi screening revealing fungal-specific drug target candidates.

The references further include Behsaz and colleagues' 2026 paper in Cell Reports Methods, volume 6, article 101510, on a large-scale discovery platform enabling identification of peptides targeting drug-resistant candidiasis. They include Pitt and colleagues' 2025 paper in the Journal of Medicinal Chemistry, volume 68, pages 851 to 859, on real-world applications and experiences of AI/ML deployment for drug discovery. They include Bender and colleagues' 2026 paper in Nature Reviews Drug Discovery, volume 25, pages 855 to 876, on artificial intelligence in drug discovery, what it is, where we stand and the path forward. They include Hutchings, Truman and Wilkinson's 2019 paper in Current Opinion in Microbiology, volume 51, pages 72 to 80, on antibiotics past, present and future. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Denmark and Ukraine sign declaration for Danish forces to train military AI on Ukrainian battlefield data
stories.Summary:
Denmark’s Ministry of Defense announced on Tuesday that Danish Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus and his Ukrainian counterpart, Yevhenii Khmara, signed a declaration agreeing to cooperate on the development of artificial intelligence, according to a Kyiv Post report dated November 18, 2026. Under the agreement, the Danish armed forces will receive large quantities of battlefield data and images from Ukraine, which they will use to train their own warfighting AI models. The deal gives Denmark direct access to Ukraine’s advanced Avengers Labs, which has built an extensive database drawn from millions of battlefield images and other information. Avengers Labs was initiated by Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense and uses the DELTA target detection system, which has created an annotated dataset obtained from more than 100,000 drone video streams each month. Denmark joins what the Danish ministry described as an exclusive club, since the United Kingdom was the first international partner to gain access to the platform.

The agreement requires Danish experts to work with their Ukrainian counterparts on the extensive dataset so they can train their own AI models and applications. That work is meant to accelerate the integration of artificial intelligence into military operations in support of the defense capabilities of both countries. Denmark’s armed forces are also establishing their own AI Center, which will be the focus for implementing the new agreement. The center will coordinate cooperation with companies and research institutions that will enhance the country’s defense technology contribution. The Danish ministry said the cooperation would help develop the combat power of the Danish defense forces through knowledge of artificial intelligence and new technologies.

Bruus said technology on the battlefield is constantly developing and that Ukraine is at the forefront in this area. He said it is therefore very valuable that Denmark can learn from Ukraine through cooperation, though he acknowledged it rests on a sad basis. Bruus also said Denmark continues its unwavering support for Ukraine while strengthening the capabilities of its own armed forces through the sharing of AI and emerging military technologies. The Kyiv Post report describes the Danish ministry’s announcement as the source for the details of the declaration and the access it grants.

The report places the agreement in the wider context of Denmark’s support for Ukraine and its effort to build up its own military technology. It says the Danish armed forces are setting up an AI Center that will serve as the hub for the new cooperation and for coordination with companies and research institutions. The Kyiv Post, which describes itself as Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995, carried the announcement. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the establishment of the AI Center and the planned work with Ukrainian counterparts.

stories.Headline: Israel can turn AI infrastructure constraints into opportunity through energy planning, article says
stories.Summary:
A sweeping Democratic victory in the US midterm elections has raised investor concern that data center projects will face more local opposition and tighter restrictions, according to an opinion article by Lior Prosor published by The Jerusalem Post on November 18, 2026. The article says the market routing last Thursday showed that AI trade investors now worry about delays in electricity supply and computing capacity. It argues the market may be overstating the impact of these delays and that the period could be a buying opportunity. For Israel, the article says, the situation should also be a wake-up call.

The article says opposition to data centers stems from residents wanting to know who will pay to expand the grid and what communities will receive, such as tax revenues and local jobs. It points to BAAJA, a bipartisan permitting reform package whose sponsors released an updated version on November 7, which aims to streamline approvals and expand the transmission grid while requiring data centers to cover the costs they add. The package has not passed and would not eliminate local authorities' powers. The article also says a delay in a US project does not necessarily mean lost sales for suppliers, because another customer elsewhere may take the equipment, and it cites SpaceX building capacity outside the US, including a large project in Saudi Arabia, and renting compute through short-term contracts at market prices. It says SpaceX has reported that at current prices new deployments pay back their investment in less than a year.

The article says Israel can become a significant player without matching US investment levels, but the government and the national AI directorate need to connect computing ambitions to an energy plan they can execute. It lists immediate priorities as electricity generation, storage, transmission and grid connections, and calls for a multiyear plan with funding, clear accountability and delivery targets. It says microgrids and regional partnerships in energy and infrastructure should be added alongside expansion of the national grid. The article names Phinergy, which develops long-duration aluminum-air backup power as an alternative to diesel, Turbogen, which offers microturbines for local electricity generation including for smaller data centers, and Bezeq, which could see greater demand for connectivity between distributed computing sites.

The article says not every use of AI requires a giant data center, because inference can often take place in smaller facilities and local systems close to users and electricity sources. It says the difficulty of building AI infrastructure increases the value of those who can deliver it, and that investors may find opportunities in companies the market is punishing too severely. For Israel, it says, this opens a path to build domestic capabilities and sell the world solutions to a shortage everyone is facing. The article notes that its forecasts can prove wrong and computing prices can fall.

Articles.Title: Israel could turn the AI infrastructure crunch into an opportunity

stories.Headline: FBI reissues advisory warning that criminals use ARTEX to automate business intrusions
stories.Summary:
The FBI reissued its FLASH advisory from the previous week about cybercriminals using ARTEX, an AI-powered penetration testing framework, to target businesses globally, according to a Benzinga report published on November 18, 2026. The bureau said attackers can use ARTEX to automate intrusions and potentially move from initial targeting to privileged access in less than three hours. According to the advisory, the framework was used during the October ConnectWise supply-chain compromise, which exposed Microsoft 365 customer environments. The FBI directed companies and other organizations to monitor suspicious automated activity and to report potential compromises through the Internet Crime Complaint Center.

Cryptocurrency bettors doubt that artificial intelligence caused the recent Federal Aviation Administration outage, even as the FBI repeated its warning about AI tools automating cyberattacks on businesses. Polygon-based Polymarket currently assigns only a 3% chance that the federal government officially attributes last week's nationwide flight ground stop to AI. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the problem appears tied to a router installation by an FAA contractor, with investigators still trying to pin down whether the failure was human error, a bad device or something else. Multiple outages over the last week have businesses and the administration on edge, including a Microsoft outage that disrupted access to Outlook and Teams.

Thousands of JPMorgan Chase customers reported problems accessing their accounts on Monday, and NSANet, the internal classified communications network for the National Security Agency, also went offline on Tuesday. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said authorities found zero evidence of a coordinated cyberattack behind outages at Microsoft, JPMorgan, airlines and government agencies. Microsoft shares were sliding Tuesday as software stocks faced pressure from outage concerns, AI disruption fears and cybersecurity worries. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the FBI's call for monitoring and reporting through the Internet Crime Complaint Center.

Articles.Title: FBI Reissues Warning About AI-Powered Cyberattacks on Businesses as Crypto Bettors Dismiss AI Link to FAA Outage

stories.Headline: Sujay Maladi wins first place at USC AI hackathon with QuestSC campus map platform
stories.Summary:
USC’s AI Strategy Committee collaborated with HackSC, a student hackathon organization, to host the first “AI@USC Hackathon” over the weekend at Ginsburg Hall. The event brought together over 300 student participants and several guest speakers, including industry professionals and University faculty. Students were tasked with designing an AI-powered solution to improve the USC student experience on campus, whether academically, professionally or socially. With $14,000 in prize money on the line, hundreds of students competed to reimagine the future of USC student life by leveraging artificial intelligence. Sujay Maladi, a master’s student studying computer science, won first place with a platform named “QuestSC.”

The hackathon was open to students of any major or school at USC, including graduate students. Competing teams formed groups by 11 a.m. on Saturday and had until 11 a.m. on Sunday to submit their final proposals, including a prototype, GitHub link, video demo and slide deck. Ten finalists were then chosen to pitch their ideas to a panel of judges, which consisted of faculty, professors, professionals and entrepreneurs.

Prizes included $14,000, split between 3 finalists, as well as potential professional opportunities, including interviews and company visits. The winning projects will be considered by the Undergraduate Student Government and the University for possible implementation on campus. Geoffrey Garrett, the chair of President Beong-Soo Kim’s AI Strategy Committee and special advisor to the president for global strategy and engagement, said students are at the frontier of technology, making them an “incredible resource.” He said the big theme of the hackathon is “For Trojans, by Trojans.” He said the organizers genuinely want to improve the student experience and know the best way to do that is to leverage the expertise of students.

Maladi said he wanted to make something for USC and feels USC’s websites are completely disconnected. Maladi said he needs to find a way to integrate all of them into one thing and would really love to see this being used by all the fellow Trojans. The second-place winner was Forage, a platform for students to efficiently navigate on-campus makers’ spaces by consolidating information like costs, required training and permission statuses. The Forage team won $4,000 in prize money. Ashwath Saravanan, a freshman majoring in electrical and computer engineering, competed with three of his friends, winning third place with “Trojan Arc,” a platform designed to help students manage their professional development by creating personalized career plans and matching students with curated internship and research opportunities.

Saravanan said he joined the event just to gain experience and definitely got way more than what he was expecting out of it. Ethan Don, a freshman majoring in electrical and computer engineering, collaborated with Saravanan on Trojan Arc, and with $2,000 in prize money, Don said the team will most likely put it toward facilitation expenses as computing costs rise with more students using the tool. Other finalists included “Same Page,” a tool that transcribes professors’ lectures to provide an accurate summary of their teaching styles for students who want a holistic assessment of a professor before choosing to take their class. “Kyros,” an AI agent reachable via iMessage, consolidates information on Brightspace, myUSC, engageSC and Handshake. Hasan Askari, managing partner at K1 Investment Management, spoke to contestants at the opening ceremony of the hackathon.

Askari said there is this idea of having a will to do something that he wishes he could inject into more students every time he interacts with them. Askari said the magical thing about the world we live in right now for the students is they now are given the platforms and the tools where they’re not restricted by how things were done before. Other guest speakers throughout the event included Jared Grusd, CEO of Gracenote and Nielsen, two separate technology companies; Holly Willis, a professor of cinematic arts; and Neha Jogani Narang, chief marketing officer at Replit, an AI-powered website and app builder. Grusd said we are living in a world where the act of creation, the cost to create, is coming down to the marginal cost of computing power. Grusd said the thing students build today will be infinitely better than what people could build last year.

QuestSC is a 3D interactive map of University Park Campus, displaying live events, availability of gyms, libraries and other public spaces, as well as a live simulation of public transportation as it arrives and departs. Users of QuestSC can also see live locations of friends. The winning projects will be considered by the Undergraduate Student Government and the University for possible implementation on campus. The articles do not state when that consideration will happen or which projects will be selected. The articles do not state the exact amounts of the first-place and third-place prizes beyond the $14,000 total split between 3 finalists, the $4,000 Forage prize and the $2,000 Trojan Arc prize.

The articles do not state how many teams competed among the over 300 participants or the names of the judges. The articles do not state whether Maladi or the Forage team commented beyond what is given. The articles do not state any date for the event beyond the weekend and the 11 a.m. Saturday and Sunday deadlines.

stories.Headline: Unesco and CodeAI host an online AI workshop for Latin American teachers on 19 November 2026
stories.Summary:
The UNESCO Regional Office in Santiago and CodeAI will host an online workshop for educators on Thursday, 19 November 2026. This virtual event, titled Teachers, Dive into AI!, will run from 4:00 to 5:30 p.m. Chile time via Zoom. It is designed specifically for primary and secondary school teachers and education professionals throughout Latin America and the Caribbean. Participants will engage in a hands-on experience to learn about artificial intelligence and how to bring it into their classrooms.

The session requires prior registration and will be conducted entirely in Spanish for all participants. It focuses on the AI for Oceans activity from CodeAI, where teachers train a machine learning model by classifying images of fish and marine waste. This process allows educators to observe how systems make decisions and identify potential errors or biases without needing prior programming knowledge. The workshop aligns with the UNESCO AI competency framework for teachers to promote a human-centred and ethical pedagogical approach.

The organizers are responsible for providing teaching resources and guidance on adapting these activities to various educational levels and subjects. They stated that the goal is to help teachers replicate these experiences with their own students during Hour of AI activities in December 2026. This initiative seeks to strengthen digital competencies and foster a critical understanding of responsible technology integration. The program also includes strategies for schools that have limited access to internet connectivity or electronic devices.

stories.Headline: Nick Hodges says AI agents will soon write code humans cannot understand
stories.Summary:
Nick Hodges wrote in InfoWorld on November 18, 2026, that he lost a five-year-old bet with his daughter that non-fungible tokens would be a major part of gaming by that week, and she told him he knows nothing about the gaming community. She did concede he was right that agentic coding would become the norm, though she had been skeptical about using AI to write code until she read about a company that used AI to solve a gaming problem a Unity engineer had called unsolvable. Hodges says he is less interested in the gaming community's controversy over AI's harm than in the fact that AI solved a problem considered not solvable, and that everyone will need to get used to this. He notes AI has been doing such things for a while, citing that in May an OpenAI internal model disproved a central conjecture in discrete geometry, the Erdős unit distance problem, a result that was not a complete answer but opened a door humans quickly walked through. Fábio Caversan, the CTO of the Stefanini Group, told Hodges recently that people should get used to whatever they code today being outdated in six months.

Hodges writes that AI is not only better at coding than humans but will soon be orders of magnitude better, doing things we have not thought of yet, and that if Caversan is right, AI code generation will soon be overtaken by something even more functional that produces things we have not imagined. He says a lot of effort now goes into reviewing AI-written code to make sure it is up to snuff, but we may need to prepare for a world where the code agents write is so different that we cannot understand what they are doing. He suggests we are probably not far from the code not mattering, not because agents write such good code but because they write code we have not seen before and cannot currently conceive of. Hodges asks how we trust code that becomes something humans cannot or do not need to understand, and says the job of software developer seems to change almost to that of a QA engineer, validating instead of producing.

If an agent produces something that runs and does exactly what we ask in a manner we do not care about, he writes, the job becomes proving that what it does is correct and what we want. As with the Erdős problem, he says, we probably should not take the agent's word for everything but simply walk through that open door. He concludes that when we say something cannot be done, what we really mean is that no human has done it yet. The article is an opinion piece and does not say what happens next beyond Hodges's argument that developers should prepare to validate rather than produce code.
