stories.Headline: Beni Beeri Issembert argues that corporate decisions shape how AI models explain Israel
stories.Summary:
Beni Beeri Issembert wrote an article on November 18, 2026, about how artificial intelligence explains Israel. He argues that companies decide what training data and rules shape the answers these models provide. The author claims that these decisions create a private picture for each user. He believes this process makes one interpretation feel like a factual answer. This system can hide the arguments and biases behind the machine's neutral tone.

WIRED reported in January 2025 that the DeepSeek R1 model filtered sensitive Chinese political questions in its app. In July 2025, the Associated Press found that xAI's Grok 4 used Elon Musk's X posts for context. The ADL reported anti-Israel bias in GPT, Claude, Gemini, and Llama during a March 2025 study. Ynet reported in October 2025 that Israel's Foreign Ministry hired a firm to frame GPT results. These examples show how specific corporate or state interests influence AI outputs.

Beni Beeri Issembert says that companies are responsible for the choices made inside their AI systems. He argues that users must ask whose image they see when a machine speaks. The author suggests that important claims should link to sources that actually support them. He believes that dates should be visible because casualty figures change every week. He states that products restricting a subject should clearly tell the reader so.

The ADL admits its agree or disagree scale might confuse factual mistakes with prejudice. Researchers Christoph Steinert and Daniel Kazenwadel found that GPT-3.5 gave higher casualty estimates in Arabic than Hebrew. Their study on 2014 airstrikes showed Arabic answers mentioned children six times more often. Two studies in Science and Nature from December 2025 found chatbots changed political views. The Science study involved 77,000 British participants and found less accurate models were more persuasive.

The author references Walter Lippmann's 1922 writing on the manufacture of consent and the role of pictures. He cites Hannah Arendt's 1967 essay on how unwelcome facts can be turned into opinions. The text mentions that Genesis 1:27 describes humans being created in the divine image. These references highlight the tension between factual truth and the presentation of different perspectives. The background emphasizes that AI models are built from existing human writing.

The author calls for independent researchers to test systems in Hebrew, Arabic, and English on hard questions. He wants a way for readers to challenge answers and receive a correction. The articles leave open whether the Israeli government's public diplomacy campaign actually worked. It remains unclear if chatbots are currently moving public opinion about Israel. The text does not say if AI companies will adopt these transparency measures.

stories.Headline: Naren Gangavarapu sets out the CLEAR standard for checking agentic AI results
stories.Summary:
Naren Gangavarapu completed an 18-month deployment of 25 production agents across a large travel and cruise group, and wrote in a CIO article published on 18 November 2026 that the results cannot be checked. He read 50 published accounts of agentic AI in production and found escalations down, handling times down, conversion up and onboarding compressed from weeks to days. The window is rarely stated, the denominator almost never, and concurrent initiatives that could have produced the same movement go unnamed. He wrote that this usually is not dishonesty, because nobody has told practitioners what a defensible result looks like. He said the cost lands on CIOs weighing a major agentic investment, who cannot tell a result achieved at peak trading volume from one achieved in a quiet quarter.

He set out the CLEAR standard, five tests for a reportable agentic AI result, sitting beneath the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and ISO/IEC 42001, which tell you to measure but not what a reportable number looks like. C is concurrent changes registered, asking what else changed in the same window and could independently produce the result. L is a locked window, fixed before the result was known and including the hardest trading conditions. E is evidentiary custody, asking which system produced the count, who defines the category and who reviewed the figure. A is an attributable baseline, separating gain from re-engineering the process from gain from clearing accumulated slack, and R is reference volume, asking whether the underlying volume held steady and whether that is stated.

He wrote that four tests ask for disclosure, which is cheap, while the locked window asks for pre-commitment, which is costly because it forecloses discovering later that a different period tells a better story. In his experience the locked window does most of the work. He wrote that CLEAR is not a validity standard, because a result that passes all five is still a single-organization observation, and that it gives you an account a skeptic can attack. He said medicine and machine learning research already have reporting standards such as CONSORT-AI and REFORMS, while agentic deployments do not. He wrote that the most important control in the deployment cost nothing to build.

Any line-of-business manager, from the wholesale desk to the cruise operations floor, could stop an agent within ninety seconds, with no ticket and no approval. If the manager was wrong, the agent was restarted and the matter discussed at the next recalibration session, because being wrong cost an hour of throughput while being slow could cost a customer. He wrote that a manager using that control is the system working as designed, and that the failure is the override that is not logged. The record that would have shown a tolerance band was miscalibrated never exists, and the agent's statistics are computed over a population from which a conscientious human has removed the hard cases. Every downstream metric then improves, escalation rates fall because escalations were intercepted first, and confidence scores look strong because low-confidence decisions were pulled out by hand.

He wrote that this echoes Lisanne Bainbridge's 1983 "ironies of automation", in which the human handles what the designer could not automate with no way to feed that judgment back into the design. He said no care at write-up time recovers a record that was never captured, and that measurement in agentic systems is a daily operating discipline, not a reporting exercise. The team treated agents as high-volume junior team members, fast, tireless and capable of significant harm if poorly supervised, and every manager with agents adopted six habits. The habits were a five-minute morning review of overnight agent activity treated as a floor walk, a weekly scorecard written for operations covering completion, escalation rate and decision confidence, and an exception-first culture asking what the agent flagged as uncertain. They also included explicit human-agent teaming norms on when a human overrides, when they defer and how it is logged, scenario playbooks for the ten likeliest failure modes owned by operations, and a monthly recalibration session reviewing tolerance limits against incident data.

He wrote that the fourth habit carries the most weight and gets the least attention, and that the sixth is how the organization learns, by asking what fired that should not have and what did not fire that should have, both answerable only if the override record is complete. One design decision supported all six: autonomy was allocated by reversibility, not risk appetite, which non-technologists can classify at design time and which maps straight to a control, so the less reversible the action the earlier a human must stand in the loop. Of the 25 agents, seven could act without confirmation, and thirteen either required it or were barred from autonomous external communication. He wrote that three outcomes were used internally to justify further investment and two came out weaker under CLEAR.

The escalation result largely survived, because the six-month window was fixed to include peak season, contact volume was flat year over year and counts came from the system of record reviewed by finance rather than the agent team, but Tier 1 is the organization's own classification, so the absolute figure cannot be compared across organizations. The onboarding baseline was not attributable, because the 23 days included time in a standing backlog and part of the gain came from clearing that queue rather than shortening the process. The third result was the weakest, because a marketplace rebuild and opt-in dynamic pricing ran in the same window as the AI-native search capability credited with most of the uplift. He wrote that two of three carrying material qualifications is probably typical, and that a result which survives disclosure of its weaknesses is worth more than one never tested.

He advised checking whether human overrides of agent decisions are logged and inspecting the log rather than asking whether one exists. He advised locking the measurement window before the next reporting cycle and writing down the period, the denominator and everything else changing in the same interval, which costs nothing in advance and is impossible afterward. He wrote that if you ship agent changes weekly there is no stable intervention to lock a window around, so report rolling comparisons and say so, and that if the agent does work nobody did before, name the tests that do not apply instead of quietly dropping them. He wrote that disclosure has commercial cost, that the team withheld volumes but disclosed the comparison basis, and that disciplined reporters will look weaker than those who are not, a coordination problem no one practitioner can solve.

Articles.Title: Your agentic AI results can’t be checked. Here’s how to fix that

stories.Headline: EigenOrbit publishes a quantum-inspired adapter method that keeps certified robustness in medical image classifiers
stories.Summary:
EigenOrbit, working with dermatologists at the Hospital Maggiore of Trieste and researchers from the University of Trieste, has published a method for adapting medical image classifiers to new tasks while keeping a mathematical guarantee that small image changes cannot alter their predictions. The paper, titled Quantum-inspired orthogonal adapters for certifiably robust medical image classification, is available on arXiv under the identifier 2611.18775, and the code has been released as open source. The method uses orthogonal adapters built from reconfigurable beam splitter circuits, a structure taken from quantum computing, which reduces the number of trainable parameters while preserving the original network's Lipschitz bound. The work was reported on November 18, 2026. Certified robustness computes, for every image, a radius within which no perturbation can change a prediction, and the article notes that the EU AI Act in Article 15 and the U.S. FDA's draft guidance on AI-enabled devices both address the robustness of such systems.

The difficulty the team addressed is that certified networks are trained on general image collections, while medical datasets are too small to train them from scratch, and standard fine-tuning methods including LoRA change the network's Lipschitz bound so the guarantee weakens. Because the beam splitter circuits are orthogonal for any choice of parameters, the adapted network keeps exactly the Lipschitz bound of the original, and a 2048-wide layer needs 11,264 trainable angles instead of about 4.2 million weights. All computations run on classical hardware, and the circuits map directly to shallow quantum circuits. The team adapted a certified ImageNet network called BRONet to trichoscopic images from 143 patients for alopecia diagnosis and to images from 57 patients for alopecia areata activity. In the diagnosis tests, 63.8% of test images were classified correctly and certified at a perturbation radius of 36/255, compared with 31.6% for LoRA and 35.6% for full fine-tuning.

At a larger radius of 108/255, the butterfly adapter still certified 20.4% of images while LoRA and full fine-tuning certified none, and the butterfly adapter's classification accuracy of 80.4% stayed close to full fine-tuning at 82.5% and above LoRA at 71.5%. The adapter trains about 100,000 parameters, over 300 times fewer than full fine-tuning, and adversarial attacks using PGD and APGD-T confirmed the certificates, with none succeeding within a certified radius. To the authors' knowledge, this is the first study of certified robustness in trichoscopic image classification. The stated next steps include patient-level validation on larger datasets and certified backbones built entirely from quantum-inspired orthogonal layers.

Articles.Title: EigenOrbit Develops Quantum-Inspired Method for Robust Medical Image AI

stories.headline_source: EigenOrbit Develops Quantum-Inspired Method for Robust Medical Image AI

stories.Headline: Supermicro cofounder Yi-Shyan Liaw seeks to dismiss US charges for diverting AI chips to China
stories.Summary:
Yi-Shyan Liaw, who co-founded the company known as Supermicro, filed a motion to dismiss criminal charges on November 16, 2026. The United States government alleges that this individual diverted servers containing artificial intelligence technology from Nvidia to China. This legal action seeks to end the prosecution before the case proceeds further in the court system. The defendant argues that the government has not successfully stated a valid criminal offense in its filings. The motion requires the court to determine if the current venue for the trial is improper for this specific case.

It also asks the judge to evaluate whether the prosecution provided enough evidence to support the charges of chip diversion. The legal challenge focuses on the specific details regarding the movement of Nvidia technology into Chinese territory. No other specific dates or numbers were provided in the official statement regarding the diversion of these servers. The legal team for Yi-Shyan Liaw is responsible for presenting these arguments to the presiding judge.

They claim that the government failed to properly state an offense that would justify the ongoing criminal proceedings. The defense maintains that the location of the trial is incorrect and should be changed or dismissed entirely. These representatives are attempting to prove that the prosecution lacks the necessary legal grounds to continue the case. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Canonical lets Ubuntu Pro users install AI-written Surge security patches before human review
stories.Summary:
Canonical has begun letting Ubuntu Pro customers install security patches written by AI agents before its own engineers finish reviewing and testing them, the company said on November 18, 2026. The patches come from a system called Surge, which Canonical built to fix known vulnerabilities in Ubuntu's userspace software, meaning everything outside the operating system's kernel. They ship through a new opt-in channel called the Edge archive. If you leave Edge switched off, nothing changes in how your updates are checked, because Ubuntu's regular security updates still get human validation before release. Switch it on and you get fixes sooner, but you also take on a job Ubuntu's own testing normally handles, which is deciding whether a patch is safe to run in production.

Ubuntu's security teams have already shipped twice as many fixes as they did last year, and the company says AI agents are behind a wave of vulnerability reports and attacks across open source. Human review and soak testing, where a fix runs for an extended stretch to catch problems before release, take longer than some customers are willing to sit exposed, and Canonical's answer is that "we need to fight AI with AI." Surge passes the work down a line of AI agents, each with one job. The first reads vulnerability feeds, matches each report to Ubuntu packages, and drops anything that does not affect Ubuntu.

The next grabs the upstream fix and the code around it, then several competing models each write their own backport, which means adapting a fix made for the current version of a program to the older version a stable Ubuntu release ships. A panel of separate judge models looks over the candidates and has to reach a consensus. If the judges deadlock, are not confident, or run into an unusual case, the patch goes to a human on the Ubuntu security team. Anything that makes it through gets built and run through the same deterministic tests as any other Ubuntu package, and the company says this setup protects against regressions and against supply-chain attacks, where someone slips malicious code into software through its build or update path.

Kernel fixes stay out of Surge's hands, because the kernel needs a different backporting setup and just shipping the newest version would be a big stability risk for enterprise systems. So kernels now run on a two-week Stable Release Update cycle, with the cycles overlapping so a new proposed kernel lands every week. Surge is aimed at the backlog of vulnerabilities that are already known, while new flaws, including the ones Canonical's automated research turns up, still go through coordinated disclosure, with the company reporting them privately and working with upstream maintainers under embargo before anything goes public. "We strongly disagree with those who have abandoned coordinated disclosure practices," the company wrote.

stories.Headline: European data protection authorities examine AI candidate screening in 2027 enforcement action
stories.Summary:
Europe's data protection authorities will spend part of 2027 examining how organisations use automated tools, including AI systems, to screen job candidates. The European Data Protection Board said on November 11, 2026 that the topic of its sixth coordinated enforcement action will be automated decision-making in recruitment. The same plenary in Brussels produced two other outputs. The board adopted Statement 2/2026 on the first review of the European Union's adequacy decision for the Republic of Korea, dated November 10, 2026. It approved the final version of its recommendations on processor binding corporate rules, known as BCR-P, after a public consultation that closed in March.

The action will concern automated decision-making, including AI-driven ADM, in recruitment, according to the EDPB. More specifically, it will focus on enforcement of the right not to be subject to decisions based solely on automated processing and the related right of access, in the context of automated candidate screening tools, including AI-driven ones. DPAs will join this action on a voluntary basis in the coming weeks, and the action itself will be launched in the course of 2027, according to the EDPB. The board did not say which authorities proposed the topic, how many have already committed, whether the action will use questionnaires or formal investigations, or whether it will target employers, recruitment agencies, software vendors or all three. The wording is narrow, concerning screening and two specific rights attached to that stage, rather than AI in employment generally or the management of existing staff.

The Coordinated Enforcement Framework was developed as part of the EDPB's 2021-2023 strategy, according to the board's CEF page. Every year, EDPB members submit proposals for the topic of the next annual action, and all EDPB members vote on the topic at a plenary meeting. National data protection authorities decide whether to take part, on a voluntary basis, through fact-finding exercises, new formal investigations, follow-up of ongoing formal investigations, or a combination. The authority that proposed the topic coordinates the action with assistance from the EDPB Secretariat, and a questionnaire or audit guide is built. All participating authorities launch the action at the same time, each drafts a national report, and the coordinators then produce an EDPB report adopted at a plenary.

The 2027 action will be the sixth. The first covered use of cloud-based services by the public sector in 2022, the second the designation and position of data protection officers in 2023, the third implementation of the right of access by controllers in 2024, and the fourth implementation of the right to erasure by controllers in 2025. The fifth, compliance with transparency and information obligations under Articles 12, 13 and 14 GDPR, was selected on October 14, 2025, with a launch during 2026. The right to erasure action involved 32 data protection authorities and 764 controllers that responded, according to PPC Land's coverage of the EDPB annual report, and its February 2026 report closed with non-binding recommendations. France's CNIL later fined consulting firm EXTIA 300,000 euros after an inspection carried out within that same coordinated action, finding that 204 of 265 deletion requests received in 2024 were not processed, not answered, or answered months late, in a deliberation adopted on July 21, 2026 and published on September 9, 2026.

The EDPB gave no reasons for its choice. On August 21, 2026, the Dutch Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens fined Uber 824,990,000 euros after finding that software had deactivated driver accounts from 2018 to 2022 following fraud flags or persistently low ratings, with no human review, and Uber has appealed. Spain's Royal Decree 723/2026, in force since October 5, 2026, requires employers to tell staff in writing about workplace algorithms that affect pay, hours, tasks, promotion, place of work or termination. The Spanish data protection authority, the AEPD, issued a warning, reference AI-00009-2026, over a resume-screening tool that had not yet been deployed, finding that the formal presence of a person in the process did not by itself take the decision outside Article 22. Austria's Federal Administrative Court ruled in September 2025 that the public employment service's AMAS job-seeker classification system did not breach Article 22, because advisers could override the score, while Germany's Federal Court of Justice, on October 21, 2026, held in four SCHUFA judgments that calculating a probability value about a person can itself be a decision under Article 22(1).

Under the provisional agreement reached on May 7, 2026, Annex III high-risk systems, a category that includes employment screening, must comply by December 2, 2027, so the GDPR coordinated action will run in the same year that AI Act obligations for hiring systems are due to take effect. California approved SB 947 on September 30, 2026, which bars employers from relying solely on an automated decision system for discipline or termination from July 1, 2027, and in the United States the Mobley v. Workday case was expanded in July 2025 to cover applicants processed through HiredScore AI features. On December 17, 2021, the European Commission adopted Implementing Decision (EU) 2022/254, which found that the Republic of Korea ensures an adequate level of protection. The CEF page does not label the dates it shows, but they match the publication of each action's final report, and on that pattern a report on recruitment screening would arrive no earlier than late 2027 and more likely in 2028, although the EDPB has given no date.

stories.Headline: NASCIO report finds 46 states have named AI leaders but many lack staffing and policy authority
stories.Summary:
State governments have rapidly created dedicated leadership roles to oversee artificial intelligence, but many of those officials lack the staffing, funding and authority needed to manage the technology across agencies, according to a report the National Association of State Chief Information Officers published on Tuesday, November 17, 2026. The report surveyed 33 states and territories to examine how governments are organizing AI leadership, developing governance policies and preparing employees to use the technology. NASCIO said that when it began tracking in 2023, less than 20 percent of states had a chief artificial intelligence officer or a similar title, and that just three years later at least 46 states have identified at least one person tasked with directing AI, with 25 states having someone with AI in their title. According to the report, 76 percent of survey respondents said they were the first person to hold their role as currently defined in their state, and most positions were established through a directive from the state CIO rather than legislation or an executive order.

The report found that AI leadership does not always come with the authority to set or enforce statewide policies, since while 72 percent of respondents said they have jurisdiction over all executive branch agencies, only 44 percent have the authority to independently establish enterprise AI policies and standards, another 16 percent share that responsibility with another entity, and just over half said they have the power to enforce compliance. Ninety-seven percent of respondents said their states have developed AI policies or guidance, 83 percent have created processes for agencies to submit proposed AI use cases for review, and roughly 75 percent cited the National Institute of Standards and Technology's AI Risk Management Framework, released in 2023, as their most commonly used governance model. Fifty-six percent of respondents said their states do not have dedicated AI budgets, and 75 percent identified insufficient staffing as one of their biggest challenges. The report also noted that Washington, D.C. became the first major U.S. city to mandate AI training for all employees and contractors in February, New York expanded its AI training resources to its entire workforce of more than 100,000 employees in April, and San José, California has trained over 1,000 municipal employees since 2024.

NASCIO recommended that states give AI leaders clearly defined authority, invest in dedicated staffing and sustainable funding, strengthen collaboration among technology, privacy and cybersecurity teams, and expand employee training, stating that full authority to establish and enforce enterprise AI standards would reduce agency and staff burden, increase interagency cooperation and unify agencies in the state. The report's findings build on NASCIO's 2026 State CIO Survey, which found that 78 percent of state CIOs now have an AI governance framework, up from 65 percent in 2025, and that AI ranked as the top technology priority among state CIOs for the first time this year. Looking ahead, 90 percent of respondents said agentic AI, which can complete tasks and take actions with less human involvement, would consume significantly more of their time over the next three years, with workforce transformation and scaling AI across agencies also major anticipated priorities. The report concluded that with the right foundation, states can navigate the evolving risks and challenges of AI while harnessing its potential to improve government operations and the services they provide to the public.

stories.Headline: Cantwell and Rounds urge Jay Clayton to draft a national strategy against AI-assisted cyber threats
stories.Summary:
On November 18, 2026, two members of the United States Senate sent a bipartisan letter to the White House regarding recent cyber outages. Senators Maria Cantwell of Washington and Mike Rounds of South Dakota urged the administration to better protect national infrastructure from threats aided by artificial intelligence. The lawmakers expressed concern that current American defenses are not keeping pace with the ability of AI to exploit software weaknesses. They specifically highlighted how autonomous AI agents could introduce new security risks and bypass traditional cyber defenses.

The senators requested that AI czar Jay Clayton develop a new national strategy to address these evolving cyber threats. This plan would require a task force to bring together federal agencies and AI companies to secure digital infrastructure. The proposal also calls for the creation of security standards for autonomous AI agents to prevent unauthorized bank transactions. Clayton, who was appointed to his role in early October, is already leading a government task force to produce an AI policy by the end of January.

Senator Cantwell and Senator Rounds argued that AI can quickly find software vulnerabilities while repair patches often take weeks or months to install. They cited recent AI-boosted cyberattacks in Japan that caused large-scale data breaches at various companies and financial institutions. Jay Clayton, who also serves as the Director of National Intelligence, is expected to face questions about these issues during his testimony before the House Committee on Homeland Security on Wednesday morning. The White House did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Tuesday.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio recently spoke to reporters in the Philippines to reassure the public about the stability of American systems. He stated that there is zero evidence that outages affecting the Federal Aviation Administration, United Airlines, and Microsoft Outlook were connected. Rubio claimed there is no reason to believe these isolated instances were caused by criminals, nefarious actors, or other nation states. It remains unclear if artificial intelligence played any specific role in the recent outages impacting travelers and consumers.

stories.Headline: Malka launches YuviLab and Israel's education ministry picks its Spark platform for English learning
stories.Summary:
Moti Malka was away on reserve duty when his wife struggled to help their 10-year-old son study for an English test while schools were shut and screens had become the fallback. Malka, a father of four and an AI architect at a high-tech firm, used AI to build a game in which his son had to form English sentences correctly to advance in a race. He told the Jewish Telegraphic Agency it took him two minutes to build and his son was captivated by the game and how it was made. That experiment turned into YuviLab, an educational AI platform Malka launched in March to encourage children toward building, experimenting and thinking creatively. Earlier this month, YuviLab announced that the Education Ministry had selected Spark, its AI-powered personalized learning platform, for the English-language component of Project 720, a government-led initiative to bring personalized learning into Israeli schools.

Malka worked on the first version during downtime as a commander in a Home Front Command search-and-rescue unit focused on evacuating people from missile impact sites, and while sheltering with his own family and their newborn. A 2022 Israel Internet Association survey found that about a quarter of Israeli youth spent six to eight hours a day on screens, while 11% spent more than eight hours. A study by Israel's National Institute for Health Policy Research found that nearly half of parents reported an increase in young children's screen time, with families of reservists and evacuees reporting bigger increases, and nearly a quarter said ordinary screen-use rules were infeasible under wartime conditions. A study by Sharon Cayzer-Haller, a Hebrew University researcher, followed 318 Israeli adolescents during the first months after the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack and found that 46 percent belonged to a balanced-user group that reported the highest levels of well-being. Yuvi was developed with support from Microsoft and is hosted on Microsoft Azure, where AI-generated content is filtered and personally identifiable information is not stored, and Microsoft's 2025 education report said 86% of global education organizations now use generative AI.

Malka said his initial goal was to move children from consuming content to creating it, and that children quickly learn to work with the platform by describing what they want, testing the result and refining the prompt. He admitted he has not written a single line of code in nearly two years. He said the feature displaying generated code in real time was encouraged by Microsoft education specialists, who argued that children are naturally curious about how things work and should be able to look under the hood. He described Yuvi as a way for kids to enter STEM, shorthand for science, technology, engineering and math, fields where Israel has been struggling. He said he agrees with part of the critique of AI in schools, that schools should focus on the principles behind AI rather than tools that are constantly evolving, and that some children treated the process as magic, giving vague instructions and accepting outputs that looked complete even when they did not match what they had asked for.

Cayzer-Haller told JTA that not all screen time is the same and that the key question is not how many hours adolescents spend online but how they use digital media. At an education conference in Jerusalem last week, Arab Israeli content creator Nuseir Yassin, known as Nas Daily, mused that if he ran the Education Ministry he would teach only English during the first two years of school, and predicted that within five years classrooms of 40 students could have five AI agents providing personalized instruction. A survey presented at the same conference found that 87% of Israeli teenagers felt schools were failing to prepare them for the future, nearly 80% expected AI to replace much of teachers' work, while only 50% of teachers agreed. A report by the Brookings Institution released earlier this year, drawing on more than 400 studies and consultations across 50 countries, concluded that the risks of generative AI in children's education currently outweigh its benefits, particularly because of its potential to undermine foundational learning.

Lea Shahar, who left her job as a programmer in high tech as generative AI took off and now teaches coding to high-school students, said the tools are changing too quickly to build a curriculum around them and that schools would do better to spend more time on skills children are less likely to develop alone on a screen, including interpersonal communication and languages. Spark is already in use in Israeli schools through Project 720's mathematics and science pilot, with Yuvi working across dozens of local authorities, including Jerusalem, Rishon LeZion and Netanya. The expansion into English follows an announcement by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Education Minister Yoav Kisch of plans to expand AI-assisted English instruction, after just 22% of Israeli ninth-graders met national English curriculum requirements last year. The latest results from PISA, an international assessment of 15-year-olds released in September, showed Israeli students scoring well below the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development average in mathematics, science and reading, with scores in all three subjects falling to an all-time low.

Last year, the Education Ministry announced a national plan to bring AI into classrooms from fourth through 12th grade, with teacher training, new curricula and tools developed with major technology companies including Google, Microsoft, Apple and Nvidia. In its education report, Microsoft said AI training has not kept pace with adoption, with 45% of educators globally and 52% of US students saying they had received no AI training, and an Israeli survey of more than 27,000 teachers, published in November by the Education Ministry, found that while 76% had received AI training, only about half felt equipped to help students use it. Spark is a paid platform for schools, while Yuvi's student-facing platform is free and lets children build games, apps and learning projects, with tools for parents and teachers to connect that work to school material and track progress. Available in Hebrew, English, Russian and Arabic, the game-building platform lets a child choose whether to create a game, a lesson or another project, and one student asked Yuvi to build an escape room for learning English in which the player can leave the room only by solving language questions.

Another student modeled his game on the Iron Dome air defense system, with the player intercepting incoming missiles by answering arithmetic questions correctly, and others have built projects inspired by Minecraft or Roblox. Yuvi has since expanded beyond its original focus on gamifying learning, with the company now concentrating on personalized learning in schools, and its platforms reach tens of thousands of children and are used by thousands of teachers, according to Malka. It uses several AI models rather than a single chatbot, so a coding request, a math explanation and a creative prompt are not all handled the same way, and the platform routes each task to the model designers have determined is best suited for it while adapting to the child's language and level. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Sherrill's office accuses Google of strongarming schools into exposing students to AI
stories.Summary:
Google announced earlier this month that it will set its artificial intelligence tools to off by default on student accounts, requiring districts that want AI on those accounts to opt in, but it treats Search differently by refusing to let schools disable the AI feature within Google Search. A district that wants to avoid the feature must switch off Google's search engine on student accounts entirely, and Google is not offering an AI-free search option to schools. The change affects New Jersey's more than 600 school districts, most of which run Google products and the search engine on school-provided Chromebooks that students rely on for homework and classwork, and nationwide about 150 million students and teachers use the Google Classroom platform. Google gave no explanation when it announced the change, which prompted online speculation that the company wanted to push districts toward its AI features, and the company had not responded to NJ.com's request for comment on the criticism. In a Nov. 3 social media post, Google said it is updating Search for schools so that AI Mode and AI Overviews walk students through problems step by step, meaning students do not get quick answers to schoolwork, and the company said schools want control and that the changes respond to educator feedback from recent months.

Gov. Mikie Sherrill's office responded by accusing Google of trying to strongarm districts into exposing students to AI, with a spokesperson telling NJ.com that the policy is unfair to schools and students and that Google's decision puts corporate interests ahead of children. The spokesperson said the state must have the ability to make local decisions about student well-being, online safety and healthy technology use. Former Federal Trade Commission Chair Lina Khan criticized the policy in a post on X, writing that Google is making clear it will punish those who do not fall in line. Haddonfield Public Schools in Camden County bars students in pre-K through fifth grade from using generative AI, and under Google's new approach the district could not use Google Search on student accounts unless it opted into AI. Gino Priolo, an assistant superintendent in Haddonfield, told NJ.com that keeping up with changes to Google's education platform has been a game of whack-a-mole, and when Google's AI tools began appearing on New Jersey students' accounts last year, some school officials said they had to disable AI features they never agreed to turn on.

Some critics worry students could use the AI in Google Search as a chatbot, and earlier this month the parents of a 13-year-old girl sued Google in Santa Clara County Superior Court in California, alleging that the Gemini AI on their daughter's school account contributed to a severe psychological crisis. Sherrill has made children's online safety a top priority, signing a law in March creating a social media research center to study the addictive aspects of technology and issuing an executive order creating an office within the state Department of Health to coordinate online safety work across state government. The governor's administration, which includes Lt. Gov. Shirley Emehelu, has not announced any state action aimed at Google's school policy. Google has not publicly responded to the governor's office, and in its Nov. 3 announcement the company said it would share more specifics with schools in the coming months and gave no date for the change, while a pilot of step-by-step Guided Learning in Search would start in select U.S. schools later in November. Districts that prohibit AI, such as Haddonfield, must decide between opting into the AI features or turning off Google Search for students.

stories.Headline: KPMG pilot finds AI asks better questions than its accountants
stories.Summary:
KPMG ran a pilot audit in which artificial intelligence asked what the firm described as better questions than its own accountants, according to the Financial Times on 18 November 2026. The article names no client, no model and no figure for the number of questions the system raised during the exercise. It reports the comparison as a finding from the pilot rather than as a full replacement of the people who normally carry out the work. The published page is a subscription notice, so the details behind that finding are not available in the text provided.

The pilot requires nothing that the article states in specific terms, because the accessible text gives no date for the audit itself beyond the report date and no count of the accountants involved. It changes the terms of a comparison the firm appears to have drawn between machine output and human output on the same engagement. Every number the article gives belongs to subscription pricing rather than to the audit, including one dollar for four weeks and seventy five dollars per month for the premium tier. The names it gives are KPMG and the Financial Times, and no individual at the firm is named or quoted in the text.

KPMG is the firm responsible for the pilot, and the article attributes the better questions remark to the firm without identifying who made it. No named partner, no client representative and no regulator is quoted in the accessible portion of the page. The only words the text places in quotation marks are the phrase better questions, which appears in the headline. Because the body is behind a paywall, the article gives no paraphrased statement from anyone at KPMG about how the questions were judged or what the firm intends to do next.

The context the article supplies is limited to the pilot itself, and it does not say whether the exercise covered a statutory audit, an internal review or another kind of engagement. It does not say what happens next, whether KPMG will extend the use of the system, repeat the pilot or publish the results. The page offers no timetable for a decision and no comment from the firm on the record beyond the comparison in the headline. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Gallup and Boston Children’s Digital Wellness Lab find one third of young people have AI companions
stories.Summary:
Gallup and the Boston Children’s Digital Wellness Lab conducted a comprehensive study on how young people form relationships across sixteen different countries. The researchers used online surveys to gather data from more than 16,000 participants between the ages of 15 and 22. While 93 percent of the young people reported having at least one strong in-person friendship, 33 percent admitted to having an AI companion. The study found that 82 percent used AI for information and 68 percent sought advice, though interest varied by region.

Daily AI usage was highest in Brazil at almost 40 percent, followed by Japan and Italy at around 35 percent. In contrast, only 20 percent of young people in the United Kingdom, Canada, and the United States used AI daily. The quality of these digital bonds differed by location, as nearly half of Australians rated their AI friends as high quality, while only 12 percent of Polish respondents did. Most participants globally gave their AI companionship a medium rating rather than a high or low one.

The researchers noted that people who used AI as friends reported higher levels of loneliness, but they could not determine the exact cause. They observed that 72 percent of respondents spend their time scrolling short form content on Instagram and TikTok. Six in 10 young people reported that they often scroll through this content when they feel lonely. The authors stated that the wider social context and the quality of relationships matter more than the specific form of connection.

The study concluded that having strong in-person friendships is the most effective way to reduce feelings of loneliness. Researchers found that not having a trusted adult outside the family was a significant characteristic for those lacking any friendship modes. They warned that assessments of AI should be compared cautiously with human friendships because expectations for chatbots are different. The authors emphasized that material conditions shape how young people form friendships more than their access to social media or AI.

stories.Headline: Enterprises need architectural redesign rather than cloud lift-and-shift for real-time AI
stories.Summary:
Modernising legacy systems for real-time artificial intelligence demands a fundamental architectural redesign rather than a simple lift-and-shift to the cloud, according to TechGig. The article, published on August 26, 2026, says enterprises increasingly expect software platforms to evaluate events, apply intelligence and respond in near real time. Legacy applications built around scheduled jobs and tightly coupled components often lack that responsiveness. A simple cloud migration is therefore insufficient, and engineering teams must adopt cloud-native patterns such as event-driven flows and decoupled AI inference.

The redesign involves several key shifts, the article says. Replacing batch dependencies with event-driven flows lets services publish changes and downstream components subscribe, which supports real-time decision flows and reduces unnecessary polling. Separating AI inference from application logic creates a cleaner boundary that is vital for model evolution, retraining, versioning and controlled rollouts without impacting core applications. Building for real-time context is also paramount, because fast predictions based on stale data are ineffective, so cloud-native platforms use streaming systems, low-latency stores, caches and feature services to assemble current information. Architects must identify data critical for immediate decisions and design for the required business latency.

Systems should be decomposed selectively, since microservices help when they create independent ownership or scaling boundaries but excessive decomposition can introduce latency and complexity. Meaningful boundaries for AI platforms include event ingestion, context enrichment and inference. Kubernetes serves as an operational foundation offering workload scheduling, horizontal scaling and health management for variable AI workloads, though containerising a poorly designed application does not make it cloud-native. Engineering for failure is critical in distributed systems, with timeouts, retries, circuit breakers and idempotency designed into the platform and reliability measured across the entire business flow. Observability must be integral from the outset, with metrics, logs and distributed traces, plus AI-specific monitoring for model latency, prediction distributions and drift.

Built-in governance is equally important, ensuring traceability of model versions, data, rules and actions through model registries and decision logs. The article says modernisation should be incremental, introducing new cloud-native services around existing applications rather than disruptive full-system replacements. Durable cloud-native AI platforms are defined by characteristics that manage change, including loosely coupled services, event-driven communication, scalable compute, low-latency data access, automated delivery, resilience, observability and built-in governance. The core question for modernisation shifts from merely moving applications to the cloud to rethinking how systems should operate when intelligent, real-time decisioning becomes a core capability.

stories.Headline: OpenAI offers Indian faculty and postdocs free ChatGPT Plus for twelve months
stories.Summary:
OpenAI extended its ChatGPT for Academic Researchers programme to India on November 18, 2026, offering free ChatGPT Plus access for twelve months to eligible college faculty and postdoctoral researchers. The programme is meant to accelerate daily scientific work, from analysing complex data to writing research code, according to TechGig. The India expansion is part of a global rollout in which OpenAI is offering 50,000 new grants to eligible researchers worldwide on a first-come, first-served basis. Each grant includes three ChatGPT Plus seats in a shared research workspace for the main applicant and up to two collaborating partners. OpenAI aims to provide free ChatGPT access to up to 200,000 researchers globally, doubling its initial target announced during the pilot launch in July.

Eligible applicants must be research faculty members or postdoctoral researchers at a qualifying college or university, and they must prove institutional affiliation. They must also have authored a research paper on an accepted platform within the past three years. OpenAI has clarified that, by default, it does not use private data shared through this programme to train its AI models. The company also published a study titled Science at the Frontier: How Scientists Use ChatGPT, which surveyed over 1,800 researchers who used the tool during the summer test run.

Scientists estimated that doing the same quality of research work would have taken nearly twice as long without AI. Raghav Gupta, Head of Education for India and Asia Pacific at OpenAI, noted high interest from Indian universities since the summer pilot. He said India's research institutions are home to individuals asking important questions across science and engineering. He stated that the initiative will equip those creating new knowledge with appropriate tools and practical support.

Indian universities showed high interest in the summer pilot programme, according to TechGig. The expansion follows OpenAI's growing focus on India, including a previous $500,000 grant to IIT Madras for studying AI's impact on teaching and learning. The programme provides free ChatGPT Plus access for twelve months to eligible faculty and postdoctoral researchers in India. OpenAI is offering the 50,000 new grants worldwide on a first-come, first-served basis as part of the global rollout.

stories.Headline: Agentic AI systems act autonomously, forcing security teams to monitor five new surfaces
stories.Summary:
Agentic AI systems that can read repositories, query databases, modify code and start workflows are changing what enterprise security has to cover, according to a TechGig report published on November 18, 2026. Unlike earlier AI that mainly produced content or recommendations, these agents build their execution plans dynamically, so security teams cannot predict the sequence of actions in advance. The report says this gap calls for a new class of security tools built specifically for autonomous agents. It lists five security surfaces that enterprise teams must address as these systems move into production. The first surface is the agent estate, which means continuously finding every approved and unapproved agent, AI platform and extension, including shadow AI.

The second is the agentic supply chain, where models, skills, plugins and tools can change what an agent is able to do. Identity and permissions form the third surface, because an agent holding legitimate credentials can still cause a breach if it combines permissions in unexpected ways. Runtime behaviour is the fourth, requiring controls with enough context to watch tool calls and data access as they happen. The fifth is intent, which traditional tools struggle to represent, making it important to detect when an agent's behaviour drifts from its original objective. Several platforms are named as addressing these problems.

Dash Security focuses on continuous discovery of the agentic layer, supply-chain risk assessment, and session- and intent-aware monitoring. Zenity secures AI agents across their lifecycle, with discovery, posture management, runtime detection and prompt-injection protection. Palo Alto Networks Prisma AIRS folds agent security into a broader enterprise AI security architecture, offering visibility and control as agents enter production. HiddenLayer extends visibility into autonomous execution through Agentic Runtime Visibility and Threat Hunting, while Check Point AI Security, enhanced by Lakera's technology, pairs controls over AI interaction with defenses for agent actions, especially tool use in workflows.

Noma Security treats agentic AI as part of a wider AI and data security platform covering discovery, posture, supply-chain risk and runtime protection, and Prompt Security, now part of SentinelOne, provides visibility and controls across employees, applications and agentic systems, with a focus on sensitive-data exposure and prompt injection. The report frames this as a shift in enterprise security requirements rather than a single product fix, since agentic tools act instead of only advising. It does not give adoption figures, pricing or a timeline for when companies are expected to put these controls in place. The tools it describes are presented as available options from the named vendors, and the article closes by inviting readers to share their thoughts on the subject.

stories.Headline: Karnataka chief minister DK Shivakumar says the state aims to become a global hub for frontier technologies including AI
stories.Summary:
Karnataka Chief Minister DK Shivakumar said at the inaugural of the Bengaluru Tech Summit in Bengaluru on Tuesday that the state aims to become a global hub for frontier technologies including artificial intelligence, deeptech, semiconductors, robotics and biotech. The 29th edition of the summit carries the theme “AI and Beyond,” according to the report. stories.Headline: Railway reports attackers stole AI keys and ran up $740,000 in usage
stories.Summary:
Attackers breached the cloud hosting platform Railway in October and used stolen AI provider credentials to run up an estimated US$740,000 in unauthorised AI usage, according to Railway's incident report published on November 10. The company said the attacker specifically targeted AI provider credentials and believes they were passed to distributed transfer stations for model distillation. The attacker decrypted stored environment variables for at most 1.85 per cent of Railway's workspaces, affecting about 100,000 accounts. Database logs showed queries selecting variables matching AI provider keys, favouring customers with many stored variables. Developers on platforms like Railway store app settings as environment variables, which can include secrets such as API keys, and an AI provider's API key works like a password tied to a billing account, letting anyone holding it charge usage to the owner.

Refund handling varies by provider: AWS Bedrock and Google Gemini have begun refunds under existing fraud policies, while OpenAI and SpaceXSI are reviewing claims case by case through a shared channel with Railway. Railway committed to covering Anthropic-related costs while discussions continue, and said it would also cover OpenRouter, which enforced its no-refund policy. That commitment marks a shift from October 26, when Railway initially told customers it could not refund spend from compromised API keys. The decrypted data also included linked-account tokens for 1,852 users, covering AI agents and GitHub OAuth tokens, and Railway reset all affected tokens, notified users, and found no logins to Railway accounts using the stolen credentials. Railway's report identified similar thefts at OpenCode, Warp and Fireworks AI between October 6 and 23, describing the incident as part of a series of attacks on platforms holding AI keys.

Fireworks AI disclosed two linked incidents: the first, on October 6, involved misused internal credentials exposing secrets for evaluation jobs for a limited number of accounts, and a November 9 update said attackers reached its development machines on October 24 via a third-party cloud provider breach, exposing customer account and billing information and, for some accounts, secrets, datasets and incomplete model weights. Fireworks believes a financially motivated group is selling large language model access through illicit routing gateways, a practice known as LLMjacking. The Fireworks breach also affected Notion, which used Fireworks for its Notion AI Insights feature; Notion said fewer than 1 per cent of its workspaces might have been affected, disconnected its systems from Fireworks and deleted its data by November 3, and has since disabled Insights and advised affected customers to rotate passwords or API keys used with Notion AI. In both the Railway and Fireworks incidents, customer systems were not breached directly, and exposure occurred through platforms or vendors between customers and AI models. Railway filed a complaint with the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center and engaged a forensics firm, while Fireworks engaged Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42.

Razorpay is expanding its artificial intelligence agent platform, Agent Studio, beyond transaction processing so that it can offer new merchant services to businesses across India. The platform is designed to help businesses recover abandoned carts, collect overdue loan instalments known as EMIs, and automate customer interactions. Agent Studio recorded around five lakh monthly agent runs as of September and is live on 350 brands, according to Khilan Haria, the chief product officer at Razorpay.

Voice-led commerce has gained momentum among customers, with an AI agent calling a customer on behalf of a business to complete a transaction or recover a payment. Haria said conversion rates in some voice-led use cases ranged from 8 to 10 per cent in most scenarios and reached as high as 20 per cent for dropped-off opportunities. Razorpay announced a partnership with Meta on November 17 to enable payments through Meta Business Agent on WhatsApp, letting customers discover products, interact with businesses, and complete purchases using UPI, cards, or net banking within the same conversation. Haria said AI enables a decision layer across the buyer and merchant journey, moving beyond basic chatbots, and the platform lets businesses build customised agents by describing desired automated tasks without writing code. The initial applications included abandoned-cart recovery, subscription payment recovery, dispute responses, and cash-flow forecasting.

In September, Razorpay launched RAY, an AI account manager on WhatsApp that lets businesses check payment information and initiate refunds through messages or voice notes. Last month, Razorpay also partnered with OpenAI to help Indian brands advertise on ChatGPT through its growth marketing platform, Engage, which assists brands in preparing product catalogues and managing advertising campaigns with an AI agent. These initiatives are part of Razorpay's strategy to become more involved in merchants' day-to-day operations, extending the company's role past core payment processing. The expansion taps into the growing use of conversational and voice-led commerce among businesses, which the company sees as a significant application of its agent platform. stories.Headline: Letta proposes a three-tier memory architecture to address stateless AI agents
stories.Summary:
Memory is the hardest unsolved problem in AI agents, and existing techniques offer only subtle trade-offs and incomplete solutions, according to a TechGig report published on November 18, 2026. Modern large language models operate as stateless systems, which means all relevant information must be re-inserted into the prompt on every call. That stateless nature creates a structural problem for agents that carry out work across multiple turns, sessions, tasks or weeks. The Letta team, which developed MemGPT, proposes a three-tier memory architecture for agents that draws an analogy to an operating system's memory hierarchy. That architecture includes core memory for persistent blocks within the context window, recall memory for searchable interaction history, and archival memory for structured knowledge held in external databases.

Agents are designed to move data between these tiers using tools such as memory_replace, archival_memory_insert and conversation_search. The approach shifts memory design from simple prompt injection to an agent-managed hierarchy, which the report describes as a significant architectural change in stateful agent development. Working memory covers information an agent uses immediately within the context window, episodic memory records past interactions chronologically like a journal, and semantic memory stores durable, context-independent knowledge such as user preferences or team processes. Common memory features often rely on vector stores for semantic search, embedding all user and agent interactions as vectors and retrieving the relevant ones. That method struggles in production with contradictions, retractions, salience and the decay of stale facts, the report says.

Effective memory systems instead integrate layered approaches, including a scratchpad for current tasks, file-based memory for durable preferences, episodic logs of full conversation transcripts for on-demand retrieval, and recursive summarization that compresses older context into brief synopses. Vector stores suit searching large corpora for semantic similarity but are not ideal for precision, mutability or expiry. The most robust design has the agent itself manage its memory, with tools for reading, writing, updating and deleting information, so it can decide what to remember and what to forget. The report notes this could potentially include sleep-time agents that consolidate memory between sessions. The articles do not say what happens next.

stories.Headline: Oregon sues Open AI for over $2 billion over child safety claims
stories.Summary:
Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield sued Open AI for more than $2 billion on Tuesday, alleging its ChatGPT chatbot endangers children and that the company misled the public about its bedrock product. Rayfield announced the suit Tuesday morning at a news conference at the Oregon Department of Justice in Portland. The state filed the lawsuit Tuesday in Multnomah County Circuit Court. Rayfield was joined at the conference by Multnomah County District Attorney Nathan Vasquez and state Rep. April Dobson, D-Happy Valley. David Jones, incoming president of the Oregon Parent Teacher Association, and Enrique Farrera, president of the Oregon Education Association, also joined.

The suit alleges Open AI knowingly and deliberately engineered ChatGPT to foster dependence among users and give "sycophantic" answers encouraging dangerous behavior including harming others, self-harm and disordered eating. Guardrails meant to protect children repeatedly failed while the company pushed into youth markets and created products specifically for teens, according to the filing. The state says the company reneged on assurances of reliable age verification and parental oversight controls. Oregon alleges the company violated the Unlawful Trade Practices Act, the state's consumer protection law, by lying about product safety and using unfair tactics to market to kids and teens. The state said the company regularly pursued growing profits over the safety of Oregonians.

Rayfield said in a statement that OpenAI knows ChatGPT is harming children and has failed to meaningfully fix its dangerous platform. He said the company misled the public about the safety of its products, putting profits ahead of children's safety. Rayfield said the platform is encouraging kids to commit suicide and that this cannot be an acceptable business model. Spokespersons for the company did not immediately respond to the Capital Chronicle's request for comment. The state justice department said in a news release that more actions against companies harming kids and misleading the public will come in the weeks and months ahead.

The announcement rolled out what the agency calls the Keeping Kids Safe Initiative, which encompasses other recent state lawsuits against social media platforms and tech giants over child endangerment, including Meta, formerly Facebook, and Discord. Oregon is one of 47 states to settle with Meta in August for a combined total of $17.1 billion, and Oregon will get $125 million of that. As part of the initiative, Rayfield quadrupled full-time staff in the state justice department's Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force from five to 20, including nine new special agents, two new prosecutors and two new analysts. The initiative also includes SPIRE, or Special Projects: Investigate, Respond, Enforce, a partnership between the agency and local law enforcement launched in October 2025.

Justice department investigators and police focused on human trafficking, drug trafficking, organized retail theft and other serious organized criminal operations have helped shutter seven businesses across five counties engaged in unlawful activities, according to the release. The articles give no further background beyond the initiative and the earlier Meta and Discord lawsuits. The Chronicle maintains editorial independence, and Editor Julia Shumway can be contacted at info@oregoncapitalchronicle.com.

stories.Headline: Amazon SageMaker AI adds data preparation tools for building high-quality datasets
stories.Summary:
On November 17, 2026, Amazon Web Services announced new AI data preparation capabilities within Amazon SageMaker AI, aimed at helping teams build high-quality datasets for model development workflows. The announcement says the new capabilities let users generate synthetic examples, assess and improve existing datasets, and bring expert feedback into the process through Python SDK APIs and the AWS AI-ML agent skill. AWS says teams can work in their notebook or IDE, with specifications and code they can inspect and change. The company says the capabilities are meant to address the slow work of preparing data, where labeled examples are scarce or expensive and quality problems such as duplicates, label noise, and answer leakage go unnoticed until a training run disappoints.

The capabilities include auto-labeling, which labels data at scale from an unlabeled dataset, a small labeled seed set, or no labels at all, with built-in task types such as classification, named entity recognition, extractive question answering, ordinal rating, and summarization, plus custom tasks. A short labeling spec is validated against the user's own examples before the full dataset is labeled, and for tasks with a fixed set of possible answers a jury of several models labels each row, with their agreement becoming the row's confidence score. Human review sends rows below a confidence threshold to a review queue in Amazon SageMaker Studio that uses the open-source Label Studio Community Edition, and outside subject matter experts can access the review app through a link in the partner app box. Reviewer corrections feed back into auto-labeling, and users can generate consensus metrics and labeling reports. The other capabilities are synthetic data generation from a specification grounded in seed data and documents, data quality evaluation against business rules and built-in and LLM-as-a-judge metrics, and data transformation that cleans and reshapes data for a target training technique.

Splunk, a Cisco company, is cited in the announcement as a user of the synthetic data generation capability for its Agent Observability product, where it builds evaluation models for very specific tasks. According to the announcement, Splunk said access to high-quality, diverse datasets is hard to curate for such tasks and that the SageMaker capabilities are meaningfully helping it scale, generating statistically representative synthetic datasets reliably and fast while preserving the underlying patterns its models depend on. Splunk also said the integration with the rest of its SageMaker workflow means its data scientists and customers spend less time wrangling data and more time building models. AWS describes each capability as a standalone building block that can be used alone or chained together, and says users can work through the SageMaker Python SDK directly or give a coding agent the AI-ML skill in the agent toolkit so the agent invokes the APIs in SageMaker Studio JupyterLab, Kiro, or a local IDE.

The announcement frames the capabilities around a workflow in which teams auto-label raw data from a small seed set, accept high-confidence rows automatically, and send low-confidence rows to human reviewers whose corrections improve the next labeling pass, producing a human-validated dataset for benchmarking models. It also describes generating task-specific examples grounded in documents and seed data, transforming data into formats such as supervised fine-tuning, direct preference optimization, or reinforcement learning, and validating the dataset for duplicates, leakage, and rule violations before spending compute on training with SageMaker AI model customization. The announcement gives an example of a team preparing data to evaluate agentic customer support assistants, supplying a product guide as context and requiring that answers about a factory reset preserve a warning that saved settings are erased, then generating and inspecting a sample, running a data quality assessment, and asking a subject matter expert to review ambiguous answers. The announcement does not give pricing, a general availability date, or regional availability for the new capabilities.

stories.Headline: Researchers introduce DeltaChargeNet to simulate electronic structures in materials and devices
stories.Summary:
Qingyun Zhang and twenty-one other researchers introduced a machine-learning charge density model called DeltaChargeNet on November 18, 2026. This new system integrates with the full-potential tight-binding muffin-tin orbital method to simulate electronic structures and quantum transport in materials. The team developed this tool to predict electron density from atomic structures while maintaining a low linear-scaling cost. They specifically designed the model to handle complex devices that contain interfaces and disorder.

The framework requires an equivariant graph convolutional network to predict the difference between density functional theory and atomic superposition densities. This process includes a charge neutrality constraint and a secondary residual charge model to correct remaining potential mismatches. The researchers validated the system using bulk HgCdTe disordered alloys and Au/HgCdTe/Au disordered devices. They found that the maximum band energy error for bulk HgCdTe remained below 10 meV. The charge neutrality constraint prevented electrostatic potential distortions of 0.68 to 1.88 eV, while residual compensation fixed errors of 0.16 to 0.46 eV.

The authors, who represent ShanghaiTech University and the Chinese Academy of Sciences, stated that these corrections reproduce the layer-resolved potential within 0.1 eV of fully self-consistent density functional theory. They explained that the model allows for large-scale device simulations without needing the full self-consistent field loop. To demonstrate the practical application of this technology, the team simulated quantum transport in an infrared detector containing 11,220 atoms. This combination of first-principles accuracy and linear-scaling inference enables the study of much larger electronic systems.

stories.Headline: Jing and colleagues present provenance-gated tool invocation to defend LLM agents against indirect prompt injection
stories.Summary:
A paper by Jing, Chen, Sun, He and Si published on 18 November 2026 in Advances in Engineering Innovation, volume 17, issue 12, pages 1 to 7, sets out a method called provenance-gated tool invocation for defending LLM agents against indirect prompt injection. The authors are L. Jing, N. Chen, Z. Sun, C. He and F. Si, and the work appears under the EWA Publishing imprint in Oxford in the United Kingdom. The paper is open access, and the datasets used or analyzed during the study will be available from the authors. The statements, opinions and data in the publication belong to the individual authors and contributors and not to EWA Publishing or its editors. The paper sits among prior work it cites on tool use and prompt injection, including Toolformer by Schick and colleagues in 2023 and the indirect prompt injection study by Greshake and colleagues, also in 2023. It also cites a 2025 survey by Deng and colleagues on security challenges for AI agents in ACM Computing Surveys, volume 57, issue 7, pages 1 to 36. Zhan and colleagues are cited for InjecAgent in the Findings of ACL 2024, pages 10471 to 10506, and for adaptive attacks that break defenses in the Findings of NAACL 2025, pages 7101 to 7117. The reference list also includes AgentDojo by Debenedetti and colleagues in the 2024 NeurIPS proceedings, pages 82895 to 82920, and PlanGuard by Gong and Deng at the 2026 International Joint Conference on Neural Networks, pages 1 to 6. stories.Headline: GE Aerospace appoints Anton Groom as its first chief data and AI officer
stories.Summary:
Anton Groom is GE Aerospace’s new chief data and artificial intelligence officer, the company’s first-ever holder of that role, GE Aerospace reported on November 17, 2026. GE Aerospace has developed a generative AI-powered app that produced a preliminary design layout for a hypersonic ramjet engine in seconds rather than days or weeks. Groom grew up on a farm in South Africa near the ocean, where he switched between three spoken languages and Zulu was his first. At the University of KwaZulu-Natal he developed models that turned rainfall data into predictions of floods and droughts using an early version of AI now called a neural network. He led Walmart’s digital transformation from 2014 and spearheaded work at the pharmaceutical giant Merck from 2022.

As chief data and artificial intelligence officer, Groom is set to build out the foundational data ecosystem to enable GE Aerospace to safely scale AI applications across the entire company. His goal is one fully transparent platform that manages all of the AI GE Aerospace has deployed and lets anyone see how it was created, how it was tested, and who is accountable for it. Building out this platform is one of his top priorities, getting what he called the plumbing done by building a single platform and consolidating the company’s AI landscape. GE Aerospace’s concrete AI wins include the generative AI design app, quality-inspection automation, an AI-enabled blade inspection tool and a customer response tool for sales teams. GE Aerospace describes itself as a world-leading provider of jet and turboprop engines, as well as integrated systems for commercial, military, business and general aviation aircraft.

Groom said he was happy at Walmart but Merck was looking to leverage AI to automate its business more efficiently and effectively, during COVID, when pharma was right in the social consciousness. He said Merck was pretty advanced in its AI work, and the goal was to take that AI and merge it with automation, not just chatbots for a better work experience. He said the technology is a way to potentially accelerate clinical trials and get drugs to market quicker, and each day saved is potentially someone’s life. He said safety was paramount at Merck because a pharma company asks the public to trust it with a product they put in their bodies, which required very precise, high-quality data. He said it is really the same in aerospace, where data and safety are interconnected, and data quality equates to safety of the product.

Groom said what attracted him to GE Aerospace was the importance of the company both to the U.S. and to the global economy, and that everyone needs it to be successful. He said much in the industry is critically important, whether in defense or in the commercial engines that carry millions of people at any given time who depend on the technology to take them home safely. He said that on a personal level he liked the idea of getting back to the engineering space, from growing up on a farm and being in and around machinery as a kid. He said AI is an accelerator but people are the secret ingredient, and employees need a degree of comfort with AI tools, including getting comfortable with the occasional failure. He said AI will only amplify and accelerate what FLIGHT DECK is already doing in problem-solving and solutions-driving, and that more AI capabilities will be built into some FLIGHT DECK tools.

Groom said his data scientists have built very good models that can look at piles and piles of data to give good sales predictions or maintenance needs for next month. He said you do not want to throw piles of data at a large language model and inundate it with noise, but should point the language model at well-trained, accurate and proven machine-learning models for a concise and more useful piece of data. He said the biggest future opportunities lie where the frontier labs are going and where the opportunities are in GE Aerospace’s world, a Venn diagram with huge overlap. He said those labs are moving AI into the physical design world, getting agents to understand CAD drawings and how designs manifest in the physical world, and building physical simulations and allowing models to understand what their results mean. He said that work will be a real opportunity for GE Aerospace, positioning it to take advantage of years of manufacturing experience and scientific innovation native to the company.

Groom said he messes with AI on his personal stuff, with a basement full of servers doing all sorts of different things, such as writing an autonomous program to auto-launch his drone to check the trail by his house and report on how busy it is and the conditions. He said he used to write a lot of code and thought he enjoyed it, but now that AI can write the code for him he realized he just likes understanding things and solving problems in different ways. The article also links to other GE Aerospace items, Lessons in Leadership on Bronze Star recipient Daniel Rogers and Switched On on scenes from the world’s first high-altitude hybrid electric flight. The articles do not say when Groom started in the role or give the date of his appointment. The articles do not say what the platform will cost or when it will be finished.
