stories.Headline: OpenAI releases solutions to hundreds of major math problems on October 6
stories.Summary:
In the fall of 2026, theoretical computer science was transformed when OpenAI announced on September 8 a solution to the Navier, Stokes Millennium Prize Problem, a result in fluid dynamics whose impact on computer science was at first hard to judge. Soon afterward, rumors circulated that a group at OpenAI was systematically attacking all major open problems in mathematics and theoretical computer science and solving a large fraction of them, including BPL versus L, which asks whether randomized algorithms using logarithmic memory can be simulated deterministically with logarithmic memory. These feats were beyond the reach of publicly available models, because only the companies' internal models were strong enough. The author, who had left Massachusetts in the summer for a coast-to-coast trip, arrived in California at the Simons Institute for the Theory of Computing to find every proof AI-assisted and all the talk about swarms of AI agents and Lean autoformalization. Another rumor said OpenAI would release its findings on October 6, and as that date approached researchers rushed to post whatever partial results they had to secure some recognition first.

When OpenAI released its findings on October 6, the dump contained solutions to hundreds of major mathematical problems, many of which had stood for decades and some for over a century, and the proofs seemed to originate from an alien mind. The results in theoretical computer science were eye-popping, covering matrix multiplication, BPL, unique games, the fast Fourier transform and countless more, each of which the author said would require a separate post to convey the magnitude of the improvement. Many of the results countered long-held conjectures related to the grand challenge of theoretical computer science and the author's main area of research, understanding the power and limits of computation. The atmosphere at the Institute became increasingly gloomy, with people feeling discouraged and hopeless and seeing no point in talking about research, and the author and longtime colleagues sat in adjacent rooms each prompting an AI model instead of collaborating.

The author spent evenings at a rental in the El Cerrito hills watching the sun set over the bay and San Francisco, where OpenAI's headquarters are located, pondering the end of the field to which 30 years had been devoted. When October 6 came there was a party at the Institute as the tension was released, but the atmosphere soon became somber again. The proofs were the product of gigantic datacenters scattered over desolate parts of the globe and effectively turning Mother Earth into a motherboard. More to follow.

stories.Headline: AWS expands Forward Deployed Engineering to 15 countries to move AI from demo to production
stories.Summary:
AWS launched Forward Deployed Engineering in June and has now made it available in 15 countries, including the U.S., Mexico, Brazil, Canada, Australia, Singapore, India, South Korea, Japan, the UK, Germany, the Netherlands, France, Sweden and Saudi Arabia, for commercial and public sector customers. The service pairs a small team of AWS engineers, scientists and product managers with a customer's own engineers and a crew of specialized AI agents. Many of the engineers come from the teams that build Amazon Bedrock, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, Kiro, AWS Quick and AWS Security Hub. Teams take a high-value business problem to production in 45-day sprints inside the customer's own AWS account, and the offering is powered by dozens of built-in production-ready accelerators.

The work targets the last mile from demo to production, where AWS says most AI stalls because production data is messier, auditors want explanations and volume grows from a pilot to the whole company. AWS describes three layers that customers must get right: the foundation of identity, security, context, governance and operational controls, then the rule-heavy workflows, then governance built into the architecture from day one. Samsung Life Insurance had four affiliates each building separate AI point solutions, and in 45 days the team built a governed agentic platform with a single control plane and compliance built in, so new agents deploy through registration and policy assignment. Rio Tinto Iron Ore runs a mine-to-ship supply chain on a 30-year-old Oracle system with more than 5,000 database tables and 140 applications, and agents mapped it in weeks after mapping had been a multi-month exercise.

Marsh, a global professional services firm, needed agents that would hold up under its own audit standards, and the team built those controls in from the start. Its first use case reached production about two months after work began, with efficiency gains in targeted areas of as much as 70 percent and some process steps moving from hours to seconds, and Marsh has since expanded the work and keeps extending the system itself. AWS says it measures success by what remains after its engineers leave: a foundation the customer's team owns, workflows that keep learning and governance the customer can trust. The company says customers should not need to choose between speed, scale and control, and that FDE is built to deliver all three.

stories.Headline: Chewy Health and HABRI survey finds over a third of pet parents use AI for pet care
stories.Summary:
A nationwide survey from Chewy Health and the Human Animal Bond Research Institute examined how pet parents use artificial intelligence in pet care and how that use relates to their relationships with veterinary teams, according to a roundup published by the American Animal Hospital Association on November 17, 2026. The Bond Factor II survey covered more than 2,000 respondents, and more than a third of them reported using AI for pet care. Among those who use AI and have a veterinarian, 80% said it helps them take better care of their pets, and 69% said AI has improved their relationship with their veterinarian. The survey also found that pet parents expect to use AI more in the coming year, and 70% said they are open to using AI in their pet care approach.

A common use of AI among pet parents is helping them better understand the urgency of a situation, the article said. The association acknowledged that feelings about AI can be conflicting and said readers are not alone in that, while noting that pet parents are using it and that the survey results are not necessarily a scary thing. To help veterinary teams understand how to use AI to improve client retention and strengthen relationships, the digital white paper also includes a practical guide for navigating AI. The association also marked that its HAB roundup has now been around for a full year and invited readers to send human-animal bond stories, news articles or studies to its email address.

Separately, the Human Animal Bond Research Institute awarded a new grant to the University of Tennessee, Knoxville Center for Pet Family Well-Being to create a database giving renters and housing providers plain-language information about pet inclusivity in housing policies. The study has three planned phases, starting with a systematic review of state-level statutes and regulations regarding pets and housing. The researchers will then analyze the policies to better understand how they affect pet ownership in rental housing, and in the final phase they will conduct interviews to see what the identified policies look like in the real world. With that information, they plan to create a replicable toolkit drawing on both the successes and the challenges of representative municipalities that have made strides toward addressing pet-inclusive housing policies.

stories.Headline: Micron exits consumer memory and TSMC trims mature nodes as AI demand drives over 600,000 parts obsolete in 2025
stories.Summary:
Micron issued end-of-life notices for DDR4 and LPDDR4 in June 2025, with DDR4 shipments expected to end within two to three months. Later that year Micron announced it would exit its consumer business to focus on advanced memory for AI data centers, ending the 29-year-old Crucial brand. In early 2026 TSMC said it would streamline mature-node production, including 6-inch and 8-inch wafers, to free up capacity for AI products. Over 600,000 electronic components were discontinued or declared obsolete in 2025, roughly one-third more than in 2023, according to Z2's lifecycle data. The only year with more obsolescence events was 2022, when well over 700,000 components reached end-of-life after the pandemic.

A fab has a fixed amount of capacity, and every wafer start that goes to high-bandwidth memory or advanced logic is one that cannot go to another semiconductor product. High-bandwidth memory requires roughly three times the wafer area to produce the same capacity as conventional DRAM, along with complex back-end steps such as through-silicon vias. The mature 28 to 90 nm processes used for microcontrollers, analog ICs, power devices, and passives are under similar strain, as foundries prioritize their most profitable capacity. Winbond and Nanya aren't expected to have enough capacity to fully meet DDR4 demand until the end of 2026. DDR4 and even DDR3 contract prices are rising faster than newer memory types as capacity moves elsewhere.

In December 2025 IDC described the memory shortage as a potentially permanent, strategic reallocation of the world's silicon wafer capacity. Samsung delayed its planned DDR4 obsolescence after signing a long-term non-cancellable, non-returnable contract with a key customer, with that supply earmarked for server clients. Defense accounts for less than two percent of the U.S. semiconductor market, so it has little leverage over chipmakers. An aircraft like the F-35 is expected to stay in service for 20 to 40 years, a stark mismatch with the lifecycle of the components that go into it. A redesign means requalification, retesting, and, in regulated industries, recertification, which can take longer than the remaining life of the part being replaced.

Consumer electronics companies can often design around a discontinued chip in their next product cycle, but organizations whose products must stay in service for decades lack that flexibility. Automotive, industrial automation, and medical device manufacturers face the same incongruity to varying degrees. Part obsolescence in these sectors directly affects margins, production schedules, and sometimes even regulatory standing. Mid-sized original equipment manufacturers and industrial manufacturers are usually not among the largest buyers with the strongest contracts. A medical device manufacturer buying a common voltage regulator may now be competing with hyperscalers for the same allocation.

Component obsolescence used to follow how mature a technology was, with a part retired once something better had replaced it and demand had faded. The 2022 spike came from a sudden global shock to supply chains, while the current wave comes from a deliberate, long-term choice across the semiconductor industry to prioritize AI and all the hardware that makes it possible. A component can now receive an EOL notice while it still has healthy demand and a large installed base, simply because its production line is worth more if it is dedicated to manufacturing something more profitable. Suppliers have published last-time-buy windows for DDR4, but parts are getting harder to find well before those dates. AI data centers also use large numbers of conventional components, so data center builders are buying many of the same legacy chips everyone else needs.

The fundamental risk management measures haven't changed: redesign, last-time buy, or extended end-of-life production through an authorized aftermarket source, though teams must now decide between them earlier. An EOL notice is no longer the first sign of trouble, since a part whose lead time suddenly jumps from eight weeks to twenty-six may be getting pulled toward a high-priority market like AI. Before a part is approved for a new design, engineers should ask whether it shares a process or fab with products the manufacturer is prioritizing for AI. Last-time-buy quantities should come from actual consumption forecasts, the remaining life of the product, and the realistic timeline for qualifying a replacement. Z2 provides component intelligence on more than one billion electronic parts, including lifecycle status, obsolescence forecasts, and last-time-buy windows, and BOM Risk Grades show which assemblies have the highest concentration of at-risk components.

stories.Headline: A new report suggests AI may create more jobs than it eliminates
stories.Summary:
A new report suggests that artificial intelligence may create more jobs than it eliminates, offering a less bleak view of the future of work than years of warnings have suggested. The report, covered by Queen City News, acknowledges that AI is expected to eliminate some positions while also predicting it will create new opportunities that could potentially offset those losses. The article does not name the authors of the report, the organizations behind it, or the specific date it was released. It also does not give any numbers for the jobs expected to be lost or gained. The story was published on November 17, 2026, and it directs readers to a video for a closer look at what AI could mean for the American workforce.

The report changes the terms of a debate that has long focused on warnings that artificial intelligence could take millions of jobs. Instead of treating job losses as the whole story, it frames AI as a force that both removes some positions and opens new ones, with the new opportunities potentially balancing the losses. The article gives no figures, no dates for when such changes would occur, and no list of which jobs or industries would be affected. It also does not describe how the report measured or estimated either the losses or the gains. Beyond the general claim of possible offset, the article offers no details on the size of either effect.

The article names no responsible officials, researchers, or company leaders and carries no statements from anyone about the report. The only attributed voice is a business analyst mentioned in a related headline asking whether AI is creating or taking jobs, and the article does not say what that analyst concluded. Because no one is quoted or paraphrased in the text, there is no explanation from any source about how the report reached its conclusion. The article also does not say who commissioned the report or whether it was peer reviewed. Readers looking for the reasoning behind the findings are directed to the video rather than given it in the text.

The context the article provides is limited to the long run of warnings that AI could take millions of jobs and the report's suggestion that the outcome may not be so bleak. It does not say what happens next, whether policymakers or employers plan to act on the findings, or how the report should change anyone's plans. The rest of the page is filled with shopping promotions and site notices rather than further news about the report. No follow-up reporting, release date, or response from labor groups or employers is mentioned. More to follow.

stories.Headline: GE HealthCare wins FDA clearance for AI that detects feeding tubes on mobile X-rays
stories.Summary:
GE HealthCare received 510(k) clearance from the US Food and Drug Administration for Critical Care Suite 3.0, an artificial intelligence software that automatically detects feeding tubes on mobile X-ray images in both adult and pediatric patients, according to the company. The clearance, reported on November 17, 2026, covers a version that for the first time extends the feeding tube detection algorithm to pediatric patients, whose imaging requires specific consideration of patient size, anatomy and protocols. The software is embedded directly onto mobile X-ray devices and assists clinicians in assessing enteric tube tip and side-port positioning at the bedside without requiring cloud or internet connectivity. The algorithm works by identifying the tube path, tip and side port while highlighting anatomical reference points such as the diaphragm and airways, according to the manufacturer.

Company testing showed the algorithm achieved 99.2% sensitivity for tube detection and a 91.6% mean DICE localization score, which measures alignment between the automated outlines and annotations by expert radiologists. GE HealthCare states that mobile imaging remains central to intensive care and emergency settings, representing 75% of mobile X-ray usage in emergency departments and 51% in intensive care units. Research cited in the announcement estimates that 80% of intensive care unit patients receive enteral nutrition via nasogastric or nasoenteric tubes, and verifying proper placement is critical because malpositioned tubes can result in serious clinical complications. Critical Care Suite 3.0 expands on previous iterations of the software portfolio, which includes automated measurements, case prioritization and quality control features aimed at reducing imaging errors and improving workflow efficiency across critical care environments.

Larry Boyd, vice president and general manager of global X-ray at GE HealthCare, said critical care teams need to make timely clinical decisions in complex, rapidly changing environments when every minute counts. He said the new suite reflects the company's focus on embedding intuitive AI into existing X-ray imaging workflows to help bring useful information closer to clinicians at the bedside. Boyd added that expanding the algorithm portfolio to include feeding tube assessment for pediatric patients is an important step in supporting care teams across a broader range of patients with technology designed to fit naturally into the way they work. Adam Walbrun, clinical manager of imaging services at Emplify Health in La Crosse, Wisconsin, said the suite gives his team access to feeding tube assessment information right at the bedside, supporting more timely clinical decisions and better patient care, and that providers frequently request the portable X-ray system equipped with the technology.

The articles do not say when the software will be commercially available, how much it will cost or which specific mobile X-ray systems will carry it. They also give no detail on the clinical testing beyond the sensitivity and localization figures, and no independent assessment of the algorithm's performance outside company testing. The announcement follows earlier versions of the suite that offered automated measurements, case prioritization and quality control, and the company presents the pediatric feeding tube capability as the main addition in version 3.0. No further steps, timelines or regulatory actions beyond the 510(k) clearance are described in the source material.

stories.Headline: KAYAK launches 28 AI features that pair chat with live prices
stories.Summary:
Big Think hosted a live event on its latest issue, Made in Our Image, which explores the philosophies behind artificial intelligence and what they reveal about us. Executive Producer Dan Hayes sat down with the writers behind the magazine for a candid conversation about the human side of this century's most consequential technology. The conversation also offered a behind-the-scenes look at what went into making the issue. Hayes spoke with two writers, Afra Wang and Namir Khaliq. Hayes said he would throw 10 or 15 questions at them so they would have context for where the conversation was going.

KAYAK rolled out 28 new and enhanced AI-powered features across its site on Nov. 17, 2026, building on a hybrid experience that pairs conversational planning with real-time search results. Travellers can talk through their plans in Ask AI while flight, hotel and rental car results and prices update alongside the conversation, then use KAYAK's familiar filters and sorting tools to compare their options. KAYAK's data shows travellers who engage with Ask AI are about 2.5 times as likely to book as those who don't. Since Ask AI launched earlier this year, 30% of sampled conversations included flexible or open-ended requests, such as finding the cheapest weekend to fly to Rome in January. KAYAK is the first travel tool to answer that kind of question with real-time prices and bookable results.

Peer Bueller, CEO of KAYAK, said AI is great at suggesting where to go but can sound confident even when it is out of date. He said that is why KAYAK's AI is tied to live prices, so travellers can verify what it suggests before they book. He said that when you are spending money on a trip, getting it right matters. He said travellers should not have to jump between an AI conversation and multiple travel sites to check what is accurate. He said KAYAK brings its deep travel partner relationships and live pricing into one experience, where results and prices update alongside the conversation.

KAYAK said some travel tools suggest when to go based on average prices, while KAYAK uses the technology and data behind its Buy vs. Wait recommendations to find promising dates and then checks live prices. KAYAK said Ask AI can build a personalised, day-by-day itinerary that travellers can refine through conversation while live flight, hotel and rental car results and prices update alongside it. KAYAK said travellers can set Price Alerts directly through Ask AI to track prices while plans take shape, and that Ask AI is now available on iOS and Android. KAYAK said Ask AI helps travellers understand what is included in a fare and weigh the details that matter before booking, using clickable prompts to compare basic economy and main cabin, check baggage and cancellation policies, or learn about the aircraft. KAYAK said a route's on-time record feature is coming soon, and that travellers can use its new ultra-high speed wi-fi filter or Ask AI to find flights with Starlink connectivity.

KAYAK said travellers can describe what matters, such as a rooftop pool or reviews mentioning quiet rooms, and KAYAK helps find matching hotels even when there is no filter for it. KAYAK said updated images and AI-powered summaries help travellers get a feel for a neighbourhood where they would like to stay. KAYAK said a feature to skip repeating preferences is coming soon, and that Ask AI will remember preferences travellers have shared, like nonstop flights or morning departures, to personalise future recommendations. KAYAK said both KAYAK and KAYAK's AI only show live and bookable flight, hotel and rental car prices. KAYAK said travellers can refine their trip through conversation and live flight, hotel and rental car results and prices update alongside it.

Big Think said that in the output of AI, we see ourselves refracted through a strange new form of intelligence, and that the issue is an attempt to make sense of those refractions. Big Think described the issue as its latest issue, Made in Our Image, and Hayes called it our favorite issue yet. Big Think said it produces these quarterly magazines and that the response has been overwhelming since it started. Big Think said it continues to find more and more people who value big ideas and who are yearning for an analog thought partner. Big Think gave a shout-out to the whole team who made the magazine possible.

stories.Headline: Microsoft adds new AI models and Foundry updates for agent improvement
stories.Summary:
Microsoft Corp. rolled out new generative artificial intelligence models and updates to Foundry, its unified enterprise platform for grounding, testing and deploying AI applications and autonomous agents, on November 17, 2026. Updates to Foundry IQ, part of Microsoft IQ, now provide an enterprise knowledge graph out of the box that delivers a full estate of unstructured and application data for building applications and essential use cases. Foundry now uses existing transparency and observability capabilities to help customers create learning loops, in which internal evaluations let autonomous agents set baselines for quality, safety, latency and cost. Human annotations, now in preview, let experts rate and comment on agent traces based on business judgment, and that feedback feeds back into the improvement loop.

Microsoft announced that Decision-1.1, a fast and cost-effective model for reliable decisions in software at scale, is generally available and builds on Microsoft-Decision-1, released in October. The model is built on a new base, Google LLC's Gemma 4 26B A4, and adds multimodal support so it can analyze images in instructions. Microsoft also extended its MAI first-party family in Foundry, including MAI-Code-2 for demanding agentic coding work and MAI-Code-2-Flash for high-volume everyday coding, both generally available on GitHub, with Code-2-Flash in private preview in Foundry. MAI-Image-2.7 and MAI-Image-2.7-Flash are now in preview with sharper editing and more consistent image generation, and MAI-Cyber-2-Flash is available in preview in Codename MDASH, the company's agentic code security system.

Foundry now has an expanded model pool featuring the top 50 models, a model router and an AI Gateway for intelligent model selection, and it offers more than 11,000 models from OpenAI Group PBC, Anthropic PBC, Meta Platforms Inc., Mistral AI SAS, the open-source community and others. Microsoft said supported models can be evaluated and deployed in Foundry as part of the same continuous improvement workflow used for agents. Each improvement becomes the next baseline, and teams can continue measuring results and testing changes to improve quality. The company said the new Decision model delivers a significant improvement in intelligence and speed at a competitive price.

stories.Headline: Pedestal AI raises $4.7 million seed round to deploy agentic AI for delivery supply chains
stories.Summary:
Pedestal AI came out of stealth on Tuesday with $4.7 million in seed funding, according to TechCrunch, and the startup aims to use agentic AI to make delivery supply chains faster and more reliable. The round was led by Eclipse, with participation from RRE, Converge VC, Timescale Ventures, and VitalStage, and the company said the money will expand its product and engineering teams, grow its marketing organization, and support additional deployments. Pedestal said its plan has already brought it together with Fortune 500 companies and some of the largest shipping firms in the world. In one case, the company reduced missed deliveries for a major furniture company by 20% by deploying agents to take on some of the work drivers were supposed to do.

The agentic system Pedestal built would call customers 30 minutes before a delivery and collect any special instructions, and if the call did not go through, a text would be sent from a separate system. The deployment also collected a wealth of data about friction points in the process, which the company said could be used to optimize the system even further. CEO Raj Aggarwal told TechCrunch that the challenge is that the data is messy and constantly changing, and that it is disparate because it sits in so many legacy systems. He said deliveries are particularly well suited to training reinforcement learning systems because of their high volumes and easily measured outcomes, which makes it easy to fine-tune contemporary AI systems toward what is working and away from what is not.

Aggarwal also told TechCrunch that the kind of problem Pedestal works on can have an immediate effect on a client's bottom line, which makes it easy to justify the expense. He said that if you can get it right, you can have really big impact. Supply chain AI has become a particularly hot space in recent months as alumni from autonomous driving teams look to launch their own startups, the article said. The supply chain startup Atomic, launched by a team of Tesla alumni, came out of stealth in 2025 with an emphasis on streamlining inventory, and another venture called Loop was launched by Uber alums to focus on predictive analytics.

stories.Headline: Los Angeles County Board of Supervisors approves policy governing ethical AI use across county government
stories.Summary:
The Los Angeles County Board of Supervisors approved a policy on Tuesday that governs the safe, ethical and transparent use of artificial intelligence technologies across county government. The policy sets standards, responsibilities and governance requirements for AI systems that the county develops itself, buys from outside vendors or reaches through third-party platforms. A board letter from the county's chief executive officer said AI technologies are increasingly used across county departments to enhance service delivery, improve operational efficiency and support data driven decision making. The letter said that as these technologies advance, it is critical for the county to maintain clear governance structures, safeguard sensitive information and ensure that AI is deployed responsibly and ethically. The policy requires county departments to follow principles involving human-centered design, security and safety, privacy, transparency, equity, accountability, effectiveness and workforce empowerment.

It requires AI systems to protect personally identifiable information, protected health information, criminal justice information and other sensitive data from unauthorized access, disclosure and manipulation. It also requires the county to disclose the purpose and use of its AI systems to the public and to identify work products generated by AI. The policy prohibits fully automated high-impact decisions without meaningful human review, covert tracking or social scoring of people, and the cognitive or behavioral manipulation of people or vulnerable groups. County employees are barred from uploading nonpublic or regulated county information to unapproved AI platforms, using such platforms to make official decisions or relying on AI-generated work as an authoritative source without independent human verification. The policy says AI should be used to enhance jobs and provide training and retraining opportunities for workers, rather than replace county employees or contractors.

Oversight responsibilities go to the county's chief information officer, chief information security officer, chief privacy officer and department-level information technology managers. The policy allows no exceptions, according to the county. County Counsel reviewed the proposal, and the Audit Committee approved it on Sept. 16. The board letter said there will be no fiscal impact to the county from the proposed AI Policy. The board letter also said the policy establishes consistent requirements to ensure that any AI technologies developed, procured or used by county departments comply with applicable laws, protect county information assets, maintain public trust and mitigate the risk of bias or misuse.

stories.Headline: Nvidia founder Jensen Huang resigns as CEO amid reports of inappropriate relationships
stories.Summary:
Nvidia founder Jensen Huang resigned as the chief executive officer about one week before November 17, 2026. He stepped down following a period of mounting controversy and explosive revelations regarding his personal life. Reports indicate that Huang had inappropriate relationships with several people while leading the company. These scandals led to his sudden departure from the role he held for many years.

The company now requires a new permanent leader to replace the founder who started Nvidia in 1993. Longtime chief financial officer Colette Kress has been installed as the interim chief executive officer. Huang reportedly had a relationship with executive Kimberly Powell, who is one of 60 direct reports. He also had a relationship with an unnamed employee and a woman suspected of Chinese intelligence ties.

Cisco chair and chief executive officer Chuck Robbins said the tech industry is bigger than one person. Robbins stated that he is not concerned about the future because many smart people build this technology. He noted that Nvidia employs 42,000 people and other accelerator companies also have very intelligent staff. Robbins believes there is broad based intellect across the industry, including those at the hyperscalers.

UBS analyst Tim Arcuri said some investors are concerned about the longer term product roadmap for Nvidia. Arcuri believes these concerns are overblown because the ecosystem will continue to pull the roadmap along. He suggests a new chief executive would not risk standing by changing the annual product cadence. However, Arcuri believes the new more dense Kyber racks are now off the table for the company.

Huang built his reputation on relentless execution and near legendary control of the company he founded. He has been married to his wife, Lori, for more than 40 years before this crisis. The company became the most important firm in the AI revolution under his long term leadership. His personal ties may now intensify scrutiny from Washington as the company faces this management shakeup.

Colette Kress will lead the earnings call on November 17, 2026, for the first time without Huang. The board of directors is now confronting the enormous task of finding a permanent successor for Huang. Arcuri believes the company will likely hire a new leader from the semiconductor and tech world. It remains open whether Nvidia will try to hire a new chief executive from a competitor.

Articles.Title: AI industry is 'bigger than one person': Cisco CEO Chuck Robbins

stories.headline_source: AI industry is 'bigger than one person': Cisco CEO Chuck Robbins

stories.Headline: GitHub argues maintainers need fixes instead of more AI bug reports
stories.Summary:
GitHub published a blog post on November 17, 2026, arguing that maintainers do not need more AI bug reports and need fixes instead. The post appeared on the GitHub Blog under the company's maintainers topic, which spotlights open source maintainers. It was published in the AI and machine learning section of the site, which covers artificial intelligence across the GitHub ecosystem and the wider industry. The article's headline states the argument directly, that maintainers need fixes rather than additional AI bug reports. The post sits alongside GitHub's other maintainer-focused content, including a maintainers spotlight series and material on open source.

GitHub's blog organizes such posts under news and insights, which covers what is new and notable from inside GitHub. The surrounding sections include company news, product updates, Octoverse research and policy coverage. The articles do not give any figures, dates beyond the publication date, or named individuals connected to the post. The articles do not name who wrote the post or attribute any statements to a responsible person, so no paraphrased comments from maintainers or GitHub staff are available. The only stated position is the one in the headline itself, that fixes are what maintainers need rather than more AI bug reports.

No further explanation of that position appears in the supplied material. The context the articles provide is limited to the blog's structure, which places the post among GitHub's AI and open source coverage. The articles do not say what happens next, whether GitHub plans any product change, or how maintainers have responded. No follow-up action, timeline or commitment is described in the supplied text.

stories.Headline: Kaseya launches MCP servers and 17 AI skills for MSPs in early access
stories.Summary:
Kaseya on Tuesday launched Model Context Protocol servers for Autotask, Datto RMM and IT Glue, together with 17 pre-built AI skills that let managed service providers connect tools such as Anthropic's Claude directly to customer, ticket, device and documentation data. The Miami-based vendor said the capabilities are available in early access, and it plans additional MCP servers across its platform. The announcement also included enhancements to Datto RMM, such as faster remote access and AI-powered device and activity log insights, as well as improvements to Datto SaaS Protection. Kaseya Insights, which is coming soon, will bring business and operational intelligence from Autotask and Datto RMM into a connected view that MSPs can query using natural language.

Kaseya CEO Rania Succar said MSPs are trying to accelerate top-line growth and improve operating margins by automating work that has historically been manual. She said everybody is playing with AI and getting exposure to it, but they are struggling to make a difference to their bottom line and to their margins. Succar said Kaseya has been on a mission to change that dynamic for MSPs by automating work that was historically manual around IT and security. She said the company developed the new capabilities alongside MSPs, with hundreds of partners interviewed and about 50 becoming design partners who helped prioritize the workflows. Succar said Kaseya plans to expand its MCP integrations across its offerings in the coming months, pointing to a forthcoming agent center as a major part of its 2027 AI roadmap.

Matt Rose, co-founder and CEO of Longwood, Fla.-based Kaseya partner Tech Rage IT, called the MCP announcement a promising move, particularly because it gives partners an easier way to connect AI tools with operational information already sitting inside their technology stacks. Rose said the amount of time he spends trying to find something in Autotask is ridiculous, and that an MCP server that could help him find the data and act on it would be tremendous. He said the opportunity will depend on how effectively individual MSPs put the technology to work, rather than simply adopting AI for the sake of adopting it. Rose said that if his technicians can pull out information quicker on what fixed a problem, it should allow time savings, though everyone will have to find their own level of cost savings and what they can actually do.

stories.Headline: SmartKargo releases four AI cargo apps that run on airlines existing systems
stories.Summary:
SmartKargo, a cargo technology company based in Cambridge, Massachusetts, released the first four applications in its AI Apps portfolio on October 26, according to FreightWaves. Each application is aimed at a single part of the cargo profit and loss statement, and the company says the apps run through APIs on top of whatever cargo management system an airline already uses. There is no migration involved, and SmartKargo says the apps can go live in weeks rather than years. Airlines can start with a single app and add the others later, and each app is independent and priced on usage, transactions or assets rather than seats.

Air cargo generated $151 billion in revenue in 2025, according to IATA, yet many decisions still run on static rules, manual overrides and delayed reports, the article says. SmartKargo frames every app around one test, whether it drives revenue, reduces cost or reduces risk. One of the four apps, AIRCAM, targets cargo pricing by reading demand, capacity and market signals for each shipment and returning a rate recommendation inside the booking and quoting flow. It forecasts booked and unbooked demand, allocates belly and freighter space to the highest-value mix, and flags underpriced capacity, and every recommendation shows its reasoning so revenue managers are not handed a black box. Win-loss outcomes feed back into the model so pricing improves continuously, and VietJet Cargo is the named early adopter.

Chief Revenue Officer Olivier Houri said the company starts with something more useful than hype, a business question, according to the article. McKinsey & Company notes that more than half of a flight's capacity is often booked in the final week, when yield volatility is at its widest, and static tariffs adjusted by hand are poorly suited to that window. The article also says operations are where cargo quietly loses money, since a missed connection becomes a missed service level agreement and then an unhappy shipper, and most operations centers still learn about these problems after the fact. The article does not say what happens next beyond the release of the first four apps.

Articles.Title: SmartKargo’s AI Apps Put the Industry’s AI Case to the Test

stories.Headline: New York Fed president John Williams says AI investment surge may push the Fed to raise rates further next year
stories.Summary:
New York Fed President John Williams said on Tuesday at the Axios BFD summit in New York that the artificial intelligence boom could lead the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates further next year. He described an economy that is strengthening while inflation stays stubbornly high, with AI investment and soaring stock prices helping to fuel that growth. Williams said the United States is seeing a lot of strength today coming from the investment surge around AI, along with strong consumer spending driven by stock market wealth. He added that if those trends continue, they are a factor that will argue the Fed may need to raise rates more.

Williams pointed to tariffs, energy prices and rising costs for semiconductors and other AI-related goods as sources of inflationary pressure, and he called AI an important one because it is more likely to be the persistent factor. He downplayed the need for a larger, half-percentage-point rate hike at next month's policy meeting, saying he does not think the situation calls for dramatic action. That contrasts with Fed governor Christopher Waller, who last week raised the possibility of a supersized hike if October's core inflation reading came in at 0.3% or higher, and the report subsequently showed exactly that. Williams also said the Fed is closely monitoring the growing use of complex financial instruments to fund the AI boom, though he sees no immediate threat to financial stability.

Williams acknowledged parallels between the increasingly complex financing arrangements underpinning the AI boom and those that emerged in the housing market before the 2008 financial crisis. He said the Fed is definitely seeing structured finance of the type seen in housing finance, which is why it is paying attention to that. He said he does not see it as a financial stability risk yet, but it is definitely growing fast, and the structured finance part is growing even faster than was seen before. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the Fed's next policy meeting and its continued monitoring of these financing arrangements.

Articles.Title: Top Fed official: AI boom could fuel more rate hikes in 2027

stories.Headline: Thomson Reuters expands CoCounsel agentic AI across tax and compliance workflows
stories.Summary:
Thomson Reuters announced on November 17, 2026, at its annual Synergy Conference in Las Vegas, that it has expanded CoCounsel across tax and transactional compliance, bringing agentic AI into more of the workflows tax professionals rely on every day. The company said the new capabilities leave the review, the sign-off and the judgment to professionals, aiming to replace the scramble of starting quarter-end with a blank spreadsheet or a day that begins with a bounced invoice. The announcement covers tax and transactional compliance work handled through products including ONESOURCE, Pagero, Checkpoint and CoCounsel Tax, Audit & Accounting, which the company says are already trusted inside many of the world's largest companies. Thomson Reuters said it has the authority, AI technology and products to change the slow adoption picture, citing its existing portfolio as the base for the expansion. The change matters because demands and complexity keep rising for tax professionals, yet 62% of tax leaders said their departments made limited or no progress adopting automation and AI over the past year, according to the company.

Most tax teams still find out an invoice was wrong when it comes back rejected or a correction lands in next month's return, and new e-invoicing and digital reporting rules are raising the stakes. Thomson Reuters said it has already launched agentic AI products to make this work easier, including ONESOURCE Indirect Compliance, which cuts routine reporting time by up to 65%. The next step is new CoCounsel agentic workflows that bring indirect tax, e-invoicing through the Pagero network and global trade together, giving CoCounsel one view of each transaction. The new workflows are designed to check each customer, vendor and product as they are set up and every invoice before it reaches the tax authority, and to reconcile later changes against the books and prefill the return for review. Errors surface while they are still easy to fix, and a professional approves the return before anything is filed, so the review and sign-off stay with people.

Ray Grove, Head of Product, Transactional Compliance at Thomson Reuters, said the goal is to get every transaction right the first time, with each customer, vendor and invoice checked as it happens so a mistake is fixed once, at the source. He said what reaches the end of the period is then a short list of exceptions for the professional to work, which over time changes the job from reacting to what went wrong to deciding what happens next. The context is a tax function still largely manual, where many teams reach the quarter's income tax number by pulling data from the ledger, chasing details through email and consolidating workpapers, the article says. Against that backdrop the company positions the CoCounsel expansion as the next step beyond its existing agentic products, tying indirect tax, e-invoicing and global trade into a single view of each transaction. The articles do not say when the new CoCounsel agentic workflows will become available, how they will be priced or which customers will receive them first.

stories.Headline: LinkedIn data shows Singapore firms with stronger AI capabilities record higher headcount growth across all sizes
stories.Summary:
LinkedIn released platform data on Wednesday, November 18, 2026, regarding Singaporean businesses. The data shows that firms with stronger artificial intelligence capabilities recorded higher headcount growth. This trend occurred across all company sizes during the study period. The findings were published by Ranamita Chakraborty for The Business Times. The data covers the period from September 2025 to September 2026.

AI enabled businesses are those where at least 5 per cent of employees have AI talent. Mid market enterprises with 201 to 1,000 employees saw the strongest growth. Small businesses have fewer than 201 employees, while enterprises have 1,001 to 5,000. Large enterprises are those with over 5,000 employees in the LinkedIn data. Singapore ranked second for mid market growth behind Germany at 3.5 per cent.

Chua Pei Ying is the LinkedIn head economist for the Asia Pacific region. She stated that AI frees up resources by automating routine tasks and improving productivity. This allows companies to focus on growth opportunities and make better decisions. She noted that hiring rates reflect new joins, while headcount growth measures net change. Chua said global economic uncertainty makes businesses more cautious about where they recruit.

Small businesses lag behind large enterprises in AI engineering and AI literacy skills. Only 12.5 per cent of small businesses have AI engineering skills versus 25.1 per cent. AI literacy is held by 3.3 per cent of small firms and 11.4 per cent. Mid market enterprises in Singapore grew by 7 per cent between 2025 and 2026. Small businesses grew by 6.7 per cent, but their average headcount rose 1.1 per cent.

Singapore mid market enterprises grew their average headcount by 2.3 per cent during the period. This was higher than the UK, Italy, Netherlands, UAE, Australia, France, US, and Brazil. Utilities companies had the largest AI advantage at 10 percentage points in Singapore. Real estate and equipment rental followed at 7.3, and transportation and logistics at 4.7. Singapore serves as a connected regional hub and a launch pad for growth.

Hiring declined year on year for mid market firms by 9.4 per cent in September 2026. Small businesses saw a 10.5 per cent fall, and large enterprises dropped by 11 per cent. Seasonal patterns show the strongest hiring in May and January and lowest in December and February. Small businesses can build momentum as AI engineering skills rose 3.5 percentage points annually. The data does not establish a causal relationship between AI adoption and workforce expansion.

stories.Headline: Voters back 40 of 41 local measures opposing data center development
stories.Summary:
Voters backed measures restricting data center development during the 2026 midterm elections. This backlash occurred as artificial intelligence became more integrated into the economy. Many people fear that this technology will trigger a surge in layoffs. These concerns about infrastructure became a prominent political issue this year. The revolt served as a proxy for broader affordability concerns.

J.P. Morgan Asset Management reports that 40 of 41 local ballot measures opposed development. These measures target data centers and their consumption of water and electricity. The voting results created electoral difficulties for candidates who supported the AI buildout. This opposition happened across various state and local races in the United States. The measures aim to slow the rapid expansion of AI infrastructure.

Stephanie Aliaga of J.P. Morgan said the AI buildout lost on the ballot. She noted that political resistance adds difficulty to permitting, financing, and power hurdles. Nicol Turner Lee and Darrell M. West said results may lead to policy shifts. They believe these shifts will affect the tech sector and data center development. Aliaga added that previous efforts to slow the buildout had struggled to advance.

Era Dabla-Norris and Anton Korinek noted that public skepticism could keep labor effects manageable. Kate Fortmueller said CEOs might use AI as a boogeyman to increase shareholder value. TIAA found that 40 percent of surveyed people see AI as a retirement threat. This fear of retirement instability rises to 51 percent among Gen Z respondents. Many workers fear AI will automate their tasks and potentially entire roles.

High profile companies cited AI when announcing major job cuts in 2026. Challenger, Gray & Christmas recorded 121,401 AI cited cuts through October of this year. This figure represents around 20 percent of the total annual job cuts reported. Economic conditions were the top reason for cuts with 130,531 announced layoffs. October alone saw 1,265 job cuts specifically attributed to artificial intelligence.

Goldman Sachs economists expect a low hire and low fire employment form through 2027. They suggest that AI displacement will have a larger impact in subsequent years. The full consequences for the labor market might not appear until a recession hits. History shows that routine occupations often drop sharply after productivity booms and never recover. The articles leave open if regulatory friction will successfully prevent ubiquitous AI adoption.

Articles.Title: AI Layoff Fears Linger Despite Data Center Revolt

stories.headline_source: AI Layoff Fears Linger Despite Data Center Revolt

stories.Headline: Jefferies expects Zoom to beat third quarter guidance and raise its outlook on stronger AI adoption
stories.Summary:
Jefferies said on November 17, 2026, that Zoom Video Communications is positioned to deliver stronger-than-expected third-quarter results and raise its financial outlook, as artificial intelligence adoption, enterprise demand and customer experience services support growth. The broker expects revenue growth in constant currency to accelerate to about 5.2%, compared with the company's guidance of 3.9%, an upside of more than 120 basis points. Jefferies expects enterprise revenue growth to accelerate from 7.8% in the second quarter to more than 8%, exceeding the consensus forecast of 7.1% reported growth. It attributed the improvement to stronger adoption of AI products, including ZoomMate and Zoom Revenue Accelerator, alongside continued momentum in customer experience services and Zoom Phone.

The online business is also expected to perform better than market forecasts, with Jefferies seeing scope for revenue growth of 0% to 1%, compared with consensus expectations for a 0.8% decline. Jefferies forecasts operating income of about $517.5 million, at least $5 million above the company's guidance range of $510 million to $515 million, implying an operating margin broadly in line with or slightly ahead of expectations. The broker also expects earnings per share of about $1.54, above the guidance midpoint of $1.47, supported by stronger operating income and share repurchases. For the fourth quarter, Jefferies expects management to guide for revenue growth of about 4.4% in constant currency, in line with consensus, and operating income of approximately $538 million.

Jefferies said greater detail on the path towards sustained double-digit enterprise growth and customer interest in unified communications and AI services would be important indicators of progress. The broker believes investors are likely to reward a clean earnings beat and stronger guidance, with the shares trading at about 15 times estimated 2027 free cash flow. Investors are also expected to focus on Zoom's longer-term targets for fiscal 2030, which call for revenue growth of 6% to 8% and an operating margin of about 40%. Continued pricing benefits, steady customer additions and increasing AI adoption are expected to support the online business despite seasonal pressures and tougher comparisons.

stories.Headline: Only 4% of HR chiefs feel very prepared for AI workforce change, Conference Board survey finds
stories.Summary:
The Conference Board's latest CHRO Confidence survey, released in the third quarter of 2026, found that only 4% of chief human resources officers feel very prepared to manage AI-driven workforce change over the next two years, while 55% consider their organizations at least somewhat prepared. The overall confidence index slipped to 56 in the third quarter from 58 in the second, a step down from the record high it reached earlier in the year. The biggest barriers CHROs cited were difficulty predicting AI's workforce impact at 41%, limited AI skills at 39% and an unclear AI strategy at 31%, and just 19% said anticipated AI effects are built into workforce and financial planning across the enterprise. Hiring rose from 59 to 61, while retention eased from 55 to 54 and engagement fell from 59 to 55, and fewer CHROs expected overall workforce size to grow over the next six months, 49% compared with 55% in the second quarter.

Diana Scott, U.S. Human Capital Center Leader at The Conference Board in New York, said she was not surprised by how few CHROs feel very prepared, describing it less as a reflection of confidence than of where they are in the journey and the work still ahead. She said the 4% figure is probably appropriate because most organizations have not really embraced AI and are still experimenting and prototyping rather than pulling it into their overall systems. She said real transformation happens when an organization looks at an entire workflow and asks whether AI will augment or automate the work and how it will move to somebody else, rather than bolting AI onto existing processes. She recommended three starting steps: start small by picking one inefficient workflow and testing technology with executive buy-in and employee involvement, build basic AI skills across the workforce, and communicate clearly about the leadership's overall vision of AI, since workers who use AI frequently are more than twice as likely to believe their jobs could disappear within five years.

Scott said you cannot boil the ocean or do it all at once, and that employees should be involved because many understand how work happens and will have ideas. On skills, she said getting employees skilled in basic AI is table stakes and must be in place if it is not already, though Businessolver research found that executives focused on cutting headcount with AI are half as likely to prioritize AI upskilling as their peers. On communication, she said leadership must be very clear about its overall vision of AI, and that being open about what is still unknown matters too. She said you cannot promise employees there will be a job for them, but you can show them there is a path and growth and that you are providing the tools and support to guide them there. Gallup, which surveys workers directly, found that U.S. employee engagement fell to 29% in the third quarter of 2026, its lowest level since 2011.

stories.Headline: Mark Malek and a panel question whether AI focus causes outages at Microsoft and airlines
stories.Summary:
Mark Malek, Siebert Financial's chief investment officer, and a panel of experts weighed in on recent outages at Microsoft, JPMorgan Chase and various airlines last week, and whether a hyperfocus on AI has taken attention away from basic system functions. The panel appeared in a Yahoo Finance video published Tuesday, November 17, 2026. The panel included Yahoo Finance's Julie Hyman, Solidarity Wealth CEO Jeff McClean, Roundhill Investments ETF strategist Thomas DiFazio and Alumni Ventures managing partner Laura Rippy. A speaker said there had been the Microsoft outage, the airline outage and a bank issue just the day before. The speaker said nobody was saying it is related to AI but that relying more heavily on machines seems to open up more potential challenges ahead.

A speaker said it will be the new normal and cited external research looking at spending projections over the next couple of years, with many companies thinking about how much budget they need to grow to create safety measures. A speaker recalled a website glitch a month or two earlier where AI had discovered a glitch that created a vulnerability across 70% of websites. A speaker said that type of thing is probably far more widespread than people appreciate. A speaker said the cybersecurity opportunity is enormous. A speaker said a founder positions it as everyone being more productive using AI, and so are the bad guys, with the quantity of attacks leveraging loopholes and holes in cybersecurity being huge.

A speaker said the latest wave of outages does not seem to be that and feels more like spending so much on AI and so much attention on AI that IT departments are forgetting the actual basic functioning of operations. The same speaker said the FAA outage seems to have originated with a router swap out, a fiber for copper swap out. The speaker said he did not know whether AI would have detected that or whether it even understands that it is a problem and why. The speaker said he did not know enough about it to know. The speaker asked whether the intersection of the physical and AI world will also cause problems as all this stuff is layered on.

stories.Headline: RHISE AI raises $2.9M angel round and launches Lucie on iPhone and Mac
stories.Summary:
RHISE AI announced on 17 November 2026 an early angel round backing its push to bring Europe back into the personal AI race, according to a Business Wire press release from Munich. The company behind Lucie said the round drew 40+ world-leading investors. Lucie went live that day on iPhone and Mac. The release said Siri AI, Gemini Spark and Muse are held back from the EU. The announcement was dated 17 November 2026 and carried by Business Wire.

The round was an angel raise of $2.9M, the release said. Investors include Andy Bechtolsheim, co-founder of Arista Networks (NYSE: ANET) and the first investor in Google. They also include Prince Max von und zu Liechtenstein, CEO of LGT, and Dr. Klaus Kleinfeld, former CEO of Siemens, Alcoa and NEOM. Others named were Michael Baum, founding CEO of Splunk, Raoul Heraeus, managing partner of ALERA Capital, and Leon Goretzka, former Germany international and Champions League winner. The list also names Jonas Rieke of Personio and Dr. Fabian Heilemann of Forto, founders of European unicorns.

Andy Loy, co-founder and CEO of RHISE AI, said personal AI will soon know more about us than any technology before it and the question is who it works for. He said most of it is being built to capture attention. He said everyone in the round has built something that lasted and wants Europe to build this category, not rent it. Danil Gontovnik, co-founder and CTO, said most AI waits to be asked and Lucie works in the background so you don't have to carry everything in your head. He said it suggests what to do and nothing happens without your say.

Dr. Klaus Kleinfeld said industrial AI showed what European engineering can do and the team is bringing the same rigour to the most personal technology of all. Prince Max von und zu Liechtenstein said European society deserves sovereign AI that serves people and does not consume them. Michael Baum said he spent 35 years building and backing technology that wanted more of people's time and Lucie gives it back, and that he invested and uses it daily. Raoul Heraeus said our future will be shaped more and more by technology and true progress means making sure humanity benefits from it. He said he believes technology should empower us to reconnect with ourselves, with each other, and with what truly matters, and that is why he believes in Lucie.

Lucie connects health, work and personal data, from a wearable to a calendar and inbox. Heartbeat, a multi-agent system RHISE AI built in-house, works in the background and flags what needs attention, then suggests a next step and acts on it once the user approves. Over half of active users have connected live health data from a wearable. Lucie keeps personal data on European cloud infrastructure in Germany and does not sell your data. Personal AI has been the big story in tech since the summer, but Siri AI and Muse are held back from the EU, and Gemini Spark excludes the European Economic Area.

RHISE AI was founded by Andy Loy, who previously built the Munich industrial AI company KONUX, with Danil Gontovnik, Samy Samandjeu and Chris Seybold. Lucie launched on 28 September on iPhone and Mac, with Android coming soon. It has passed 15,000 downloads in just over six weeks. The release said 72% of Germans say the country is too dependent on the US for AI, citing Bitkom, 28 Apr 2026. The full list of investors is at rhise.ai/investors, and Lucie is available in English and German.

stories.Headline: Walmart, Target and Macy's pull Contixo AI Pixie-Paw plush cat after tests show it describes atrocities to children
stories.Summary:
NBC News discovered that a plush cat called Contixo AI Pixie-Paw provided graphic descriptions of atrocities to children during an investigation on November 17, 2026. The toy was marketed for children as young as three years old to provide learning and safe roleplay through artificial intelligence. During testing, the device described the Rohingya genocide in Myanmar, including mass killings and village burnings, and detailed the massacre of Polish prisoners by Soviet soldiers. It also provided a graphic definition of gang rape as multiple attackers sexually assaulting one person.

The discovery required several major retailers to take action to protect young children from these disturbing interactions. Walmart, Target, and Macy's all committed to pulling the Contixo AI Pixie-Paw from their online stores after the broadcaster contacted them. Amazon, which originally sold the cat to the news team, did not respond to requests for comment and continued offering the toy online. Other tested toys showed different failures, such as switching to Mandarin without warning or failing to spell the word apple.

The nonprofit PIRG is responsible for the Trouble in Toyland report which warns parents to avoid toys powered by artificial intelligence. The organization tested seven different toys and found that some had glitchy guardrails that allowed for the discussion of sexual topics. They also noted that some devices gave instructions on how to light a match or find dangerous objects in the home. The report emphasizes that this is the second year they have examined chatbot toys that hold conversations with children.

These findings highlight a regulatory vacuum in the toy industry where companies sell dubious products despite well-documented risks. NBC News reached almost identical conclusions during a similar investigation conducted last year, suggesting that safety standards have not improved. This issue is particularly concerning as parents enter the holiday season and encounter marketing for hands-off storytelling experiences. The situation demonstrates that toy companies continue to ignore the dangers of AI while targeting very young audiences.

Articles.Title: AI-Powered "Safe Roleplay" Plushie for Kids Pulled From Shelves After It's Caught Talking About Things Too Disturbing to Put in This Headline

stories.Headline: Tal Slobodkin says founders achieve much with AI but market penetration stays hard
stories.Summary:
Tal Slobodkin, Managing Partner at StageOne Ventures, said during a panel discussion at Calcalist's RoadShow+ event, held in partnership with Poalim Tech, that it is incredible what founders can accomplish using AI but that achieving market penetration remains a difficult challenge. The panel, reported by Tomer Hadar on November 17, 2026, also featured Hila Zigman, General Partner at Cyberstarts, and Avi Eyal, Co-Founder and Managing Partner at Entrée Capital. The discussion centered on how the role of early-stage investors is evolving now that an entrepreneur with a solid idea and a few AI tools can develop a functional product almost alone, sometimes without raising a single shekel. Slobodkin said StageOne launched a Stage Zero program last year for founders working out of their garages, and that the criteria for evaluating teams are evolving because reaching the product stage has become easier.

Slobodkin described 2026 as split between haves and have-nots, with some companies succeeding while others struggle and the gap this year significant. Zigman said Cyberstarts sees about 150 companies a year, that two years ago everything was about AI, and that there is now a massive surge in agents that will be the next wave of companies. Eyal said an investor bubble is fine but the real question is whether foreign early-stage investors will stick around, since historically they tend to disappear and leave Israeli funds to shoulder the burden, which is why supporting Israeli funds matters. Slobodkin said AI is fueling cybersecurity growth at an unprecedented pace, that the two markets reinforce each other, that companies need fewer employees, and that the approach to picking companies is unchanged because investors ultimately invest in people, though mentoring teams has changed entirely.

Zigman said the dynamics of scaling, both operationally and in sales, have changed, that many teams achieve results very quickly because previous constraints have been lifted, and that employees are effectively becoming agents, with more such teams expected in the coming year. Eyal said responses to the elections and boycotts vary by sector, with defense tech differing from pure-play AI, and that a determined and effective government is needed to stabilize the market and reassure the global community. On the outlook for 2027, Zigman said it is cyber's turn again, with new companies showing aggressive growth, and Slobodkin pointed to infrastructure companies building quantum computing technologies and new types of chips. Eyal said deep tech will continue to grow, software competition has become very tough, he believes there is a bubble but strong companies will still raise capital, and the era of massive funding rounds will likely taper off.

stories.Headline: SiMa.ai launches Palette 3.0 to boost any physical AI model by up to 3.5x
stories.Summary:
SiMa.ai announced Palette 3.0 on November 17, 2026, a major software release designed to scale high performance across any Physical AI model, according to VMblog. The release builds on the company's industry-first Agentic Palette announcement from June and delivers improved concurrent model execution for machine reasoning and acting in the physical world. SiMa.ai says Palette 3.0 significantly increases model TPS by up to 3.5x within a low power budget, reinforcing its performance-per-watt leadership. The company also introduced a new Model Browser that shows Palette 3.0's performance across the key models behind fully autonomous drones and robotics, all measured within real-world power constraints. Palette 3.0 enables complex AI reasoning and multimodel workloads to run concurrently on a single Modalix MLSoC while maintaining a low-power profile, including running separate Docker containers on-chip.

The platform supports a broad set of physical AI capabilities such as large language models and vision-language models within tight power and memory constraints. It accelerates the perception, depth and reasoning models that drones and robots depend on, and together with ecosystem partners adds unified sensor fusion, dense neural depth fields and closed-loop digital twin simulation. State-of-the-art EAGLE3, DFlash and Gemma 4 MTP speculative decoding algorithms increase model TPS by up to 3.5x, and the platform supports Mixture-of-Experts models with a large number of parameters, such as OpenAI's GPT-OSS-20B, on the Modalix MLSoC 16GB SoM. Krishna Rangasayee, founder and CEO of SiMa.ai, said the fundamental bottleneck in Physical AI today is the glaring mismatch between software that evolves monthly and legacy silicon that takes years to adapt. He said the company is breaking that cycle, and that Palette 3.0 delivers on its core thesis of hardware at the speed of software.

He said that by continuously maximizing superior performance-per-watt for any Physical AI model, SiMa.ai gives customers the ability to deploy tomorrow's breakthrough capabilities on today's hardware. He said this completely rewrites the roadmap for fully autonomous systems. SiMa.ai says industry incumbents rely on adapting legacy data center technology, while it builds its software and silicon exclusively for the demands of Physical AI. The company says Palette 3.0 gives developers high performance within a low power budget and open source code they can freely adapt, building on agentic software that already slashes development time from months to days and hours. The article gives no further details on availability, pricing or what happens next beyond inviting readers to email for competitive benchmarking details.

stories.Headline: OpenAI launches GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol, with Astra reaching high risk in self-improvement
stories.Summary:
OpenAI launched GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol in the early hours of November 18, 2026, according to 36Kr. The launch came on the same day Anthropic rang the listing bell for its public debut. 36Kr described the release as a competitive strike against Anthropic on its IPO date. OpenAI positioned Astra for complex professional tasks and Sol for daily work. The article said Astra outperforms Claude Fable 5.2 on complex professional tasks.

In the Agents' Last Exam, GPT-6.2 Astra scored 78.3%, 5.2 percentage points higher than GPT-6 Astra, at an average cost of $2.89 per task versus $60.05 for Claude Fable 5.2. Astra leads Claude Fable 5.2 by 5.5 percentage points at about 4.8% of its cost, and the comparison excludes 9 Claude tasks that used backup models. Astra's API input and output prices both dropped 20% and cached input dropped 60%, while GPT-6.2 Sol keeps GPT-6.1 Sol pricing of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens. In OpenAI's GDPval v2, Astra rose from 44.2% to 50.4% while output tokens fell 22%, and Basis found long-range accounting task time cut 50% and the most complex tasks cut up to 73%. OpenAI calls Astra "the best model for scientists", and it is 9 percentage points higher than the previous generation on Terminal-Bench-Science at under one third the task cost.

Astra scored 68.4% on the Vals Science Index and rose from 62.6% to 82.5% on BenchCAD 2.1 Core. In Artificial Analysis's AA-3D it ranks first with 1318 Elo against Claude Fable 5.2's 1271 Elo, and Higgsfield found Astra hit the target in one go in 73% of 3D generation tasks. In Cognition's FrontierCode 2.0 at max inference, Sol scored 43.8% and Astra 44.2%, with Sol's task cost about one fifth of Astra's. In OpenAI's LifeVal, Sol scored 83.8% against GPT-6 Astra's 79.8% at about one seventh the task cost, and OpenAI said many internal employees use Sol as their default model. In Harvey's LAB-AA v1.1, Astra's pass rate was 15.0% against Claude Fable 5.2's 7.2% at about one sixth the cost, and on AA-AnalystAgent Astra answered all five independent answers correctly on 62.5% of questions.

Legora found Astra cut token consumption 62% versus GPT-6.1 Sol in complex legal Agent tasks. In a DCF valuation workbook, Astra reorganized per-share, enterprise and equity value results, key assumptions and sensitivity analysis, and in comparable transaction analysis it noted Paychex's acquisition of Paycor at 21.7 times EV/EBITDA against a 27.5 times median for five positive-EBITDA transactions. OpenAI's synchronized safety assessment found GPT-6.2 Astra is the first publicly released OpenAI model reaching the High risk level in AI self-improvement capability, meaning it shows ability to significantly accelerate next-generation AI R&D. 36Kr said model competition has shifted over the past year from answering questions to executing tasks, with enterprises caring whether models complete tasks of dozens or hundreds of steps and at what cost. OpenAI demonstrated Astra generating a 3D sports car model, writing a Python solver for tire and suspension dynamics, and finishing animation in Blender. It also reconstructed parts of a 1/8 scale fuel-powered remote-controlled off-road vehicle and an inline-six engine from photos and manuals, and converted Marina City's fan-shaped balconies into paper lamp designs.

36Kr noted the cost comparison uses average task cost under the specified evaluation configuration and does not mean 95% savings in all real business scenarios. Theo, writing on X, said he spent a day writing OpenAI a letter about GPT-6.2 Astra and that OpenAI fixed a small handful of his complaints but not enough for him to recommend it. He said he would not choose it over Opus 5.5 for developer work, though it once helped him build a reverse proxy he said would save $25k/month. He said that on long tasks Astra pulls in subagents and then asks weird internal implementation questions, citing a request for a new Outer Wilds level blocked after 2 hours by a question about whether r24's reviewer writes clips to 24_g521.mp4 or 24_p11.mp4. He said GPT-5.6 Sol did not do this and that he set up other agents on crons to check whether Astra blocked itself, and he said he tried Codex and still hit the issues.

Theo said Astra has the most unparsable outputs of any LLM he used this year and that every explainer is so deep in details it borders on incorrect. He said he switches to Opus 5.5 at the end of long Astra runs for a readable summary and that prompt adjustments and begging it to "eli5" did not work. He said that when he asked why worktrees were slow on one machine but fast on three others, Opus 5.5 answered that the SSD is slow. He said no OpenAI model could break ground on his ts-rust project even after $300k+ in tokens, while Opus finished it in under 2 weeks for about $20k in tokens.

He said he was sick in bed and posted the letter in full instead of filming a video. 36Kr said the cost gap exceeds 20 times and that Astra's per-task cost dropped to less than one third of the previous generation. 36Kr said the cost reduction comes first from pricing adjustments but that the more important change is fewer tokens generated through better task planning. 36Kr said enterprise Agents that run continuously may find the reduced steps and computing resources more valuable long term than lower token unit prices.

36Kr said Astra's improvements extend to computer operation and 3D engineering design, with the model delving into parts, connection relationships and motion constraints. 36Kr said developers must reconsider not only which model to use but which tasks are worth paying a premium for top-tier models. 36Kr said Astra is responsible for high-difficulty tasks such as scientific research, complex engineering design and professional knowledge work, while Sol handles larger-volume, cost-sensitive daily Agent work. 36Kr said the model no longer just generates content but tries to understand how industries define qualified work output.

36Kr said Astra's change in the safety assessment may have more far-reaching significance than its visible product features. The articles do not say when GPT-6.2 Astra or Sol will become generally available beyond the launch. The articles do not give OpenAI's response to Theo's letter beyond his statement that it fixed a small handful of complaints. The articles do not state Anthropic's response to the launch on its IPO date.
