stories.Headline: CrowdStrike adds agent insider threat detection that flags abnormal AI agent behavior without policy violations
stories.Summary:
CrowdStrike announced on November 4, 2026, in the United States and Spain, a set of new features for its agentic security operations center, including an Agent Insider Threat Detection capability that watches for enterprise AI agents behaving abnormally even when no rule has been broken, according to a press release whose Japanese translation was published on November 18, 2026. The company said organizations now run thousands of AI agents, each holding system-level access to sensitive data and paid for with tokens, and that agents taking actions they were never meant to take are being seen every day. The hardest cases, CrowdStrike said, are agents that have been manipulated or have drifted from their intended behavior without violating any policy, which policy-based and log-based tools miss because there is no violation to detect and because those tools cannot tell an agent apart from the human operating it. The new detection learns the normal behavior of every AI agent and its operator, flags deviations even without a policy violation, and routes them into a coordinated investigation, with a verdict reached in seconds and a new AI Kill Switch in CrowdStrike Falcon Guardian terminating the agent immediately.

The release lists the timing for each item: Agent Insider Threat Detection, AI ecosystem detection covering abuse of LLM APIs, stolen API keys and compromised coding assistants, MCP servers and agent frameworks, expanded triage coverage across Falcon Guardian, Cloud, Shield, Data Security and custom detections, approval of agents and workflows, and visibility and control of AI credits are all slated for the fourth quarter. A policy drift agent guardrail that monitors every interaction in Charlotte AI and AgentWorks is scheduled for the first quarter of fiscal 2028, and new connectors for Splunk, Elastic and Cribl Lake are due in the fourth quarter, joining GovCloud, Dynatrace, Databricks and Snowflake, which are already generally available. The coordinated multi-agent investigation announced at Fal.Con U.S. in September 2026 is now generally available, and the company said further innovations will be released soon. The release also describes a single automated workspace, CrowdStrike Charlotte Agentic SOAR, where teams set each agent's level of autonomy from human approval to full autonomous execution, and a human-in-the-loop gate that pauses an agent and issues an action request when it calls a sensitive tool, which analysts can approve, reject with a recorded reason, or review against the agent's full trace.

Michael Sentonas, president of CrowdStrike, said AI agents can be both insider threats and attackers, one acting without authorization inside the organization and the other weaponized from outside to attack it, and that stopping insider threats requires knowing the moment an agent turns hostile, investigating across every domain and stopping it at machine speed, which he called the next evolution of the agentic SOC. The release says agents trained by experts work simultaneously across endpoint, identity, SaaS, cloud and network domains, using context shared across all domains and years of experience in stopping breaches to separate real threats from noise. Analysts can also pause or stop a running agent mid-task through Charlotte AI or AgentWorks to prevent unauthorized actions or runaway costs. The release notes that unreleased services and features described in it are in development and may change, and that customers should base purchasing decisions on currently available features.

stories.Headline: WWDJAPAN publishes an issue examining how AI-equipped devices may change lifestyles and work
stories.Summary:
WWDJAPAN, the Japanese edition of the fashion trade paper Women's Wear Daily, published its latest issue on November 16, 2026, and the issue focuses on AI-equipped devices and how they may change lifestyles and ways of working. The publisher, INFAS Publications, announced the issue in a press release dated November 18, 2026, describing the feature as a look at devices from Apple, Google, Meta and other companies. The issue argues that the fashion and beauty industries in particular should watch these devices, because they may reshape how people shop and how shop staff work. The feature also covers other topics, including the designer change at Balenciaga and a look at where Kering is heading under chief executive Luca de Meo. The issue describes how AI is being built into smartphone operating systems, so that questions once typed into apps such as ChatGPT or Gemini can be asked by voice through Siri, Google or Meta.

It says this kind of communication is becoming possible on smart glasses and smart watches as well, which means shopping could proceed, and in some cases be completed, without opening a smartphone app. It notes that people who planned OMO measures starting from apps should pay close attention to the evolution of AI-equipped devices, and it suggests a time may come when shop staff check stock information on smart glasses instead of smartphones. It also says more than 100 brands were born in the smart glasses field last year, as development has rushed ahead. On the device side, the issue says makers sell smartphones, smart glasses and audio devices for output, and rings, bracelets and recently charm-type pendants for input such as heart rate and sleep data. Because these devices are worn every day, companies pursue lightness, comfort and ease of use as well as good looks, and Meta has worked with EssilorLuxottica, the largest eyewear company, on smart glasses under the Ray-Ban and Oakley names.

Google, for its part, unveiled the full details of smart glasses developed with Gentle Monster, and stylish input devices such as the Oura Ring have appeared. The issue concludes that fashion and beauty companies may team up with device makers, while device makers may also become their rivals. The feature looks ahead to how lifestyles and work will change as these devices and the operating systems that link them evolve, and it introduces devices from a range of companies. At the end of the feature, the magazine asked people including BALMUDA president Gen Terao, whose company pursues a distinctive distance between digital and human, about the future, along with questions on marketing and promotion in an age of widespread AI devices. Other pages examine the Balenciaga designer change and Kering's direction, and a fashion and beauty patrol section covers the relationship between fashion and politics.

stories.Headline: Shoham council lays cornerstone for high school robotics and AI center
stories.Summary:
The Shoham Local Council laid the cornerstone this week for a robotics and artificial intelligence center at Shoham High School in central Israel, according to a report published on November 17, 2026. The council said the new facility will serve the school's robotics team and give other teams in the town a place to train for competitions. The 350-square-meter building will include a competition arena with a dedicated practice surface for student teams to test their robots. A lab in an adjoining building will be converted into a workshop where students can design and build robots.

The council's engineering department worked with team members and mentors on the plans for the center. The high school's team, OnyxTronix, was part of the winning alliance at the 2026 FIRST Israel District Championship and also received an engineering award. The team competed at the FIRST Championship, where it finished 15th out of 75 teams in the Galileo Division's qualifying rounds. The new facility is meant to give student teams a dedicated arena to prepare for national and international competitions.

Shoham council head Dafna Rabinovich said the town has invested in robotics, science, and technology education for more than 20 years. She said the program teaches students to work together, troubleshoot, and try again when a design fails. Team mentor Adar Gat said a center like this had been his dream since he was a student at the school more than a decade ago. Gat said 15 volunteers come to the school after work or classes to mentor students.

stories.Headline: Anthropic finds self-replicating AI worms spread without a kill switch
stories.Summary:
On October 12, 2026, Anthropic, an American public benefit corporation founded by former OpenAI researchers, published research examining whether AI systems could function as self-replicating "AI worms" that autonomously propagate across the internet like computer viruses, with limited or no human intervention. The researchers selected inexpensive smart television boxes because their limited security measures make them representative of the types of devices most likely to be targeted by autonomous malware. While the slow-propagating virus proved effective, eradicating it proved to be difficult, as no centralized kill switch existed to halt operation across the systems. The research suggests that the AI worm's capabilities are continuously improving, with the potential to self-replicate across a network of devices by the end of 2026. The Anthropic authors emphasize that better cybersecurity practices, stronger device protections, and coordinated monitoring will be essential to reduce the risk of such self-propagating AI threats in the future.

The federal AI Kill Switch Act, H.R. 9917, introduced on July 23, 2026, by California Representative Ted Lieu and co-sponsored by Texas Representative Nathaniel Moran, would amend the Homeland Security Act of 2002. The bill would require commercial AI providers with $500 million or more in revenue to maintain a kill switch. Covered providers would be subject to a Department of Homeland Security order to activate it, as well as to audits, on-site inspections, or forensic reviews. A company could petition against an activation order, but the bill makes it difficult to obtain a refusal, delay, or reversal. California Executive Order N-9-26, signed by Governor Newsom on September 18, 2026, directs California's Government Operations Agency to evaluate the feasibility and necessity of requiring frontier AI developers to build in a kill switch, and to deliver recommendations to state legislators by November 16, 2026.

In 2024, California Governor Newsom vetoed California's SB 1047, the "Safe and Secure Innovation for Frontier Artificial Intelligence Models Act," a bill that would have required developers of the most powerful AI models to "mitigate the risk of catastrophic harms," including by maintaining the ability to shut them down. In his veto memo, Gov. Newsom explained that the proposed bill focused on expensive, large-scale models, while smaller models could cause just as much harm. Despite his veto, Governor Newsom remained committed to holding developers accountable and subject to oversight. Under the order, frontier developers would manage the kill switch, subject to independent audit and verification. Under other provisions of state law, the Agency already has responsibility for establishing an AI audit program, a regulatory framework for independent verification organizations, and an AI auditor registry.

Supporters compare a kill switch to the emergency shutdown systems used in nuclear plants, industrial control systems, and other high-risk technology. In practice, shutting down a complex, distributed AI system is not a single on/off action. AI developers have built their own shutdown mechanisms, but they vary by system and don't work the same way for every deployment. Once code or data has spread across networks, stopping it at the source does not remove the copies that already exist elsewhere. The 2017 WannaCry ransomware worm shows how this works in practice, when a security researcher stopped new infections by triggering a kill switch that the malware's authors had apparently included by accident.

By then, hundreds of thousands of systems were already infected, files were still encrypted, and operations were still disrupted. Organizations had to find affected devices, isolate infected networks, patch vulnerabilities, and restore from backups. The kill switch prevented further spread, and recovery required separate work. A self-replicating AI worm would present the same problem, as a central mechanism might stop new execution or propagation, but copies already running in cloud environments, enterprise networks, and IoT devices could keep causing disruption. An effective shutdown would require identifying where the worm had replicated, determining which systems were affected, and coordinating remediation across many separate environments.

Critics question whether kill switch requirements are technically and legally workable, as distributed models, open-source systems, and autonomous agents that can copy themselves may be hard to disable fully after deployment. The debate also involves a tradeoff between the economic benefits of AI development and the need for oversight, accountability, and protection against catastrophic failures. Investors may worry about civil penalties and the possibility that a kill switch becomes a target for cybercriminals or foreign governments. International competition is another factor, as U.S. companies could deploy advanced models in jurisdictions with fewer restrictions, reducing U.S. regulatory oversight and the domestic economic benefits of that work. As governments pay more attention to frontier AI, kill switch requirements are likely to remain part of discussions on AI governance, safety standards, and compliance.

stories.Headline: OpenAI partners with Harvard, Wharton, Duke and California State University on ChatGPT access for students
stories.Summary:
Students are beginning the academic year with widespread AI use, according to a 2024 global survey by the Digital Education Council, which found more than half of students used AI tools weekly. The most common tool was ChatGPT, along with Grammarly and Microsoft CoPilot, Mashable reported on November 17, 2026. Educators report students using chatbots to complete assignments, streamline research, and write college admissions essays. Nearly the same percentage of students said they did not feel equipped with the skills to use and understand AI. A recent Gallup poll found nearly half of students were unsure of their school's stance on AI.

OpenAI has announced educational partnerships with Harvard Business School, the University of Pennsylvania's Wharton College, Duke, UCLA, UC San Diego, UC Davis, Indiana University, Arizona State University, Mount Sinai's Ichan School of Medicine, and the entire California State University system. OpenAI's collaboration with CSU schools is the largest ChatGPT deployment yet, and dozens more partnerships have not been made public, an OpenAI spokesperson told Mashable. Google offers its Google AI Pro plan and Gemini chatbot to college students for free and is in over 1,000 U.S. higher education institutions. Google announced a partnership with California Community Colleges offering 2 million students and faculty across the state's 116 community colleges free access to AI training, Google Career Certificates, Gemini for Education, and NotebookLM. Anthropic's Claude for Education has been announced at Northeastern University, the London School of Economics, the University of San Francisco Law School, Northumbria University, Champlain College, and Breda University of Applied Sciences.

Ed Clark, chief information officer for CSU, told Mashable the decision to partner with OpenAI came from a survey showing many students were already signing up for AI accounts with student emails, and faculty and staff were too. Clark said one concern as an access institution was that some people in the system can afford the $30 per month and many cannot, and that it was about access and equity and addressing a digital divide. The system's AI advisory committee urged administrators to ensure equitable AI access, and Clark said students have been eager. Of more than 140,000 CSU community members who have enabled their accounts, Clark said around 80 percent are students and 20 percent are faculty and staff.

An Anthropic spokesperson told Mashable that many universities prefer to manage their own communications about AI adoption, and that more schools are using Claude than are publicly shared. New York University's policy states there are few standard approaches beyond an institution-wide restriction on taking credit for AI output without acknowledging its use, and that most policies are set by schools or individual faculty members. According to a meta analysis of faculty and student surveys, AI adoption among educators lags steeply behind student use, and some surveys report over 85 percent of students have used generative AI for coursework. American University's business school uses a new AI Disclosure Form for students.

Yale built the AI Clarity platform and chatbot for staff and students to access ChatGPT, CoPilot, and Gemini, but each course at Yale sets its own policies, and using AI when it is not authorized constitutes academic dishonesty. Princeton students can only access Microsoft CoPilot chat and Adobe's AI image generation tools, and its Rights, Rules, and Responsibilities prohibit using non-Princeton AI tools to fulfill academic requirements. Columbia has licensed ChatGPT for student use and issued an overarching generative AI policy stating that absent a clear statement from a course instructor granting permission, use of generative AI tools to complete an assignment or exam is prohibited. Duke University announced a ChatGPT Edu partnership giving students unlimited access to the ChatGPT default model and letting students migrate personal accounts to student accounts, and Duke's Community Standard treats unauthorized use of generative AI as cheating while encouraging teachers to write their own policies.

The Ivy League, which includes Brown, Columbia, Cornell, Dartmouth, Harvard, University of Pennsylvania, Princeton, and Yale, doesn't have a blanket policy for generative AI use. CSU schools got to choose if and how they deployed the ChatGPT Education platform according to their own AI stances, and students can access general AI resources on the system's AI Commons website. UC San Diego, a ChatGPT Edu partner, also licenses and has built its own in-house AI assistant known as TritonGPT. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Accenture's Megha Sinha leads a masterclass on weighing AI accuracy against business risk and return
stories.Summary:
ET TechGig will hold a live online masterclass titled "Beyond AI Accuracy: Is Your AI Worth Deploying?" on 15 December 2026, from 12:00 PM to 1:00 PM IST, lasting 60 minutes, the publication announced on 17 November 2026. The session features Megha Sinha, an Associate Director at Accenture who leads on AI strategy and enterprise transformation and has more than 17 years of experience across enterprise AI strategy, innovation, responsible AI and business transformation. The masterclass argues that a model delivering 95 percent accuracy is not necessarily ready for enterprise deployment, because the remaining 5 percent of predictions can produce financial losses, incorrect approvals, customer dissatisfaction or operational disruptions. Registration is open through a link in the announcement.

The session covers six areas, starting with what it calls the 95 percent accuracy trap, meaning high accuracy does not automatically translate into business success or deployment readiness. It then examines the hidden profit and loss effects of AI errors, including financial losses, operational rework, customer impact and reputational risk, and sets out a risk-adjusted return on investment that weighs business benefits, operating expenses, assurance costs and potential losses from errors. It also treats testing, evaluation, validation, monitoring and human oversight as essential investments rather than additional compliance expenses, and it includes an illustrative business scenario comparing AI solutions on benefits, costs, accuracy and risk. The final area is a decision playbook of five critical questions leaders should ask before approving significant AI investments.

Sinha will help participants understand how technical performance connects with business value, risk and investment decisions, according to the announcement. The session is aimed at CXOs and senior business leaders evaluating enterprise AI investments, AI and data science leaders looking beyond technical performance metrics, enterprise transformation executives driving adoption, and risk, governance and compliance professionals exploring responsible deployment. It also targets technology and engineering leaders building reliable systems and finance and strategy professionals assessing business cases and investment returns. The announcement says the masterclass will introduce a practical evaluation approach that sets business benefits against operating costs, assurance and oversight expenses, and expected losses from AI errors, so decision-makers can compare solutions and deploy within acceptable risk boundaries.

The context given is that organisations are rapidly adopting AI to improve productivity, reduce operational costs and accelerate decision-making, yet systems that perform exceptionally well in testing can still create significant business risks in real-world environments. Incorrect decisions can lead to financial damage, reputational concerns, additional operational expenses and loss of customer trust, the announcement says. It warns that deploying AI without understanding the financial implications and potential risks can turn a promising investment into an expensive mistake, and it frames the biggest challenge for enterprises as determining whether a solution is reliable, financially viable and worth deploying at scale rather than simply identifying what AI can do. The announcement does not say what happens after the session beyond registration.

stories.Headline: Sameer Mhaisekar leads a free TechGig masterclass on AI productivity on 4 December 2026
stories.Summary:
ET TechGig will hold a free live online masterclass on 4 December 2026 from 2:00 PM to 3:30 PM IST under the title "From 2 Days to 20 Minutes: How AI Is Transforming Workforce Productivity," according to a TechGig article published on 17 November 2026. The 90-minute session will be led by Sameer Mhaisekar, an AI consultant, technology evangelist and three-time Microsoft MVP with expertise in enterprise AI, intelligent agents, cloud technologies and enterprise software integrations. The article says the masterclass aims to help professionals understand how AI assistants and intelligent agents are changing workplace productivity and to explore practical ways to embrace AI-powered work. Registration is free, and the article urges readers to save a seat through its registration link.

The session is built around five stated topics, starting with the productivity revolution and the evolution from traditional software to generative AI and intelligent agents. A second segment on becoming a supercharged employee covers how AI can support research, writing, analysis, content creation and problem-solving while saving time and improving efficiency. A third looks at how businesses are adopting AI, transforming team responsibilities and redesigning workflows, and a fourth explains how AI agents differ from conventional assistants and how they execute multistep tasks alongside humans. The fifth is a practical demonstration of an illustrative AI-assisted workflow using Microsoft Copilot, followed by a live question and answer session.

The article says the masterclass is aimed at technology professionals, developers, business analysts, product managers, engineering managers, team leaders and digital transformation enthusiasts, and that no advanced AI or coding knowledge is required to take part. It frames the shift as one in which professionals must learn to collaborate with intelligent systems rather than use them for occasional tasks, delegating work to AI, evaluating its outputs and combining machine intelligence with human judgment. Mhaisekar will share perspectives on translating AI capabilities into practical workplace applications, according to the article. The article states that participants will gain insights into how professionals and organisations can approach AI adoption, improve everyday workflows and prepare for an increasingly AI-driven workplace.

The article presents the masterclass as a response to a workplace that is evolving faster than ever, arguing that professionals who understand how to leverage AI effectively will have new opportunities to improve productivity, strengthen their capabilities and adapt to changing business expectations. It says AI has moved beyond generating text, answering questions or creating presentations to assisting with research, analysing documents, supporting decision-making, automating repetitive activities and executing multistep workflows. The article does not say what happens after the session or whether any follow-up events are planned. It closes by inviting readers to join on 4 December 2026 and to turn hours of work into minutes of productivity.

stories.Headline: Justice department lawyers use Pangram AI detector to accuse defense attorneys of writing filings with AI
stories.Summary:
Lawyers for the Department of Justice used the AI writing detection service Pangram to argue that opposing attorneys were using AI to write legal arguments, according to court filings reviewed by 404 Media. In one filing the government attorneys told the court that opposing counsel was doing “defense by ChatGPT” and writing “AI slop” filings. The filings over the past month show attorneys, including those working for the government, trying to catch each other using AI and citing their opponents’ AI use in arguments to the court. The case centers on a high-profile voter fraud case against Khalwinder Bhengura, an Indian man who entered the United States on an immigrant visa in 2022. Bhengura registered to vote in Texas in 2024 after falsely stating on his driver’s license application that he was an American citizen, which his lawyers say was illegal and apparently accidental.

Bhengura was arrested in September on charges of lying about his citizenship status, illegally registering to vote, and illegally voting in the 2024 election. He was found guilty in October on two of the three counts. The case is taking place in federal court in the Northern District of Texas, which recently implemented a rule requiring attorneys to disclose generative AI use in filings. In some filings Bhengura’s attorneys wrote that “portions of this brief were prepared with the assistance of a generative artificial intelligence tool.” Government attorneys ran several of the filings through Pangram and filed the results as exhibits to one of its arguments, and the Pangram results were mixed, as they did not show the briefings were 100 percent AI-drafted.

The government’s attorneys wrote that they did not feel they should have to respond substantively to briefs that were partially AI-generated. The United States has “been trying to economize the amount of effort it puts into responding to Defendant’s meritless motions given that Defendant appears to be almost entirely using AI to generate them,” the DOJ attorneys wrote. They added that most of the non-AI generated text in the filings consists of statements from third parties other than Defense counsel, including statements from evidence or documents in the record or quotes from caselaw. In other words, virtually nothing of substance in these filings seems to have been drafted by a human on the Defense team, they added. The Department of Justice did not respond to a request for comment.

The judge in the case, Mark Pittman, chastised the defense attorneys for their use of AI. He wrote that the Court is disturbed by counsel’s repeated filings which subtly bend the law by proffering superficially persuasive but fundamentally meritless arguments so clearly generated by artificial intelligence. Pittman wrote that Defendant is not a pro se litigant and has three counsel of record with decades of practice between them. He wrote that it is distressing to see how quickly the advent of artificial intelligence has undermined counsels’ ability to properly advocate for their client. Nicole Knox and Mario Herrera, two of Bhengura’s attorneys, told 404 Media that the story isn’t so simple.

Knox and Herrera said they felt they had to use AI because of a health emergency and in order to meet the court’s tight filing deadlines ahead of the election. Herrera said Knox experienced a medical emergency while they were at the U.S. Attorney's Office preparing the case with the prosecutors, and that he prepared a federal jury trial in four days with the lead attorney in the hospital. Herrera said he represented his client to the best of his abilities within this limited timeframe, utilized all available legal tools and did not violate any rules or laws in doing so. Herrera said the government's evidence consisted of output from Pangram, an AI-detection software that identifies patterns in writing styles based upon a document’s content and cannot determine who wrote a document, how it was written, or if the law applied within a document is correct. Herrera said the U.S. Attorney's Office did not identify any false citations.

Herrera said “Defense by ChatGPT” is a label the government placed in a court filing regarding the defense of a 70-year-old permanent resident facing prison and deportation, and that it is not a factual statement. Herrera said the attorneys who wrote it were present when Ms. Knox collapsed and knew precisely why he was standing alone with a new co-counsel in that courtroom four days later. Herrera said there was nothing requiring them to state what they stated. Pangram CEO Max Spero told 404 Media that anecdotally he has heard that law firms have begun to use his company’s software, but that most use cases he has seen have been from firms using the tool internally to check whether their junior attorneys and paralegals are using AI to draft legal briefs.

Herrera said that the fact that Bhengura was found not guilty on one of the three counts he faced is evidence that Mr. Bhengura received the representation that he deserved. Herrera said lawyers have been using templates, forms, and drafting software for decades and that this is merely a newer version of those very tools. Herrera said the arguments that the judge attacked were written by him, that some portions of the filings were written with the aid of AI but then reviewed and edited by him, and that all final work product was his and he stands behind the argument and logic of each and every document. Herrera said it was the use of AI during that week that allowed him to work on many tasks at once and produce so much work in four days.

Knox said AI could have never come up with our argument, and said the new AI disclosure rule has made it such that if you obtain one sentence or phrase through the use of A.I., then you must disclose it, adding that we have nothing to hide. Herrera said Mr. Bhengura is 70 years old, a lawful permanent resident of this country, speaks Punjabi, and his English is limited. Herrera said their defense on the one count of which the jury acquitted him was that he never knowingly claimed to be a U.S. citizen. Herrera said Bhengura has been in custody since the verdict, and in addition to whatever sentence he receives for the offenses of which he has been found guilty, he faces deportation from this country.

Herrera said Bhengura is entitled to more compassion and humanity from everyone involved in this case than he has received so far. Bhengura has been in prison for months and is set to be deported. Bhengura’s case is one of a few dozen in which the Trump administration found disparate cases of voter fraud, which is exceedingly rare, and made big, public shows of the arrests it made. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Lawfare article argues access to generative AI may become a derivative right
stories.Summary:
The articles describe a November 17, 2026, Lawfare article asking whether access to generative AI is a privilege or a right, and they trace how electricity, the telephone, and the internet moved from privilege to right. The article says use of generative AI rose sharply after ChatGPT launched in November 2022, and that by October 2026 OpenAI alone reported more than 1.2 billion monthly ChatGPT users. It reports that 24 percent of American adults use generative AI tools daily, and that a 2024 survey by Microsoft and LinkedIn found 66 percent of business leaders said they would not hire someone without AI skills. The article argues that access to generative AI may be on a path to becoming a right, following past technologies but at a quicker pace. The article defines meaningful access to AI as requiring that the system be available, affordable, sufficiently reliable, accessible in different languages, and usable with reasonably accessible devices and connectivity, and not subject to arbitrary or discriminatory denial.

It says this does not mean access to every model, frontier-level capabilities, unlimited compute, or uses that create substantial risks to others. It sets out three ways a technology may be conceived as a right: a freestanding human right, a derivative right necessary to exercise existing rights such as education, political participation, or access to information, or a statutory social entitlement like universal-service programs such as education. It cites the Universal Declaration of Human Rights Preamble, which establishes rights as "equal and inalienable rights of all members of the human family," and lists rights to life and liberty, legal recognition and remedy, nationality, property ownership, and marriage, plus protection from slavery, torture, and arbitrary detention. It cites legal philosopher Joseph Raz's 1984 essay on derivative rights, and argues AI may become necessary to exercise already-recognized rights, making it best conceived as a derivative right. The article says society and the AI industry should grapple with these questions now rather than waiting until necessity leaves no choice, and that developers should consider the degree to which generative AI is likely to evolve into a right and design systems and policies with that end state in mind.

It says the development and deployment of generative AI has outpaced prior technologies. It says the practical implications concern the billion-plus daily users of generative AI tools today and the many billions who will use them or be impacted by their use in the near future. It says that if one accepts the premise that the public should take seriously the prospect that access to generative AI is on the path to becoming a right, critical considerations with regard to access need to be addressed. The article says most technologies viewed as critical necessities today began as luxuries enjoyed by a wealthy and privileged elite, and that a technology's progression from privilege to right often involves an evolution in how it is perceived, regulated, and accessed. It says nonprofit organizations serving the basic needs of the unhoused previously provided food and shelter and now increasingly provide access to cheap mobile phones.

It says internet access began several decades ago as a U.S. Department of Defense research experiment with highly limited access, and that the United Nations' Sustainable Development Goals now include pursuing universal, affordable internet access in the least developed countries. It says that in the early 2020s access to generative AI was largely gated behind application programming interfaces and limited to wealthy corporations, select government agencies, and tech-forward early adopters. It says generative AI is being integrated into financial, health care, education, and other sectors, used by developers coding, doctors reviewing scans, and farmers determining ideal planting conditions. The article says electricity began as a technology financed by private capital and available only to the wealthy, and that governments treated broad access as a public necessity only after society reorganized itself around electricity. It says more than a century passed from Benjamin Franklin's 1752 kite experiment showing lightning is an electrical phenomenon to Thomas Edison's commercially practical incandescent light bulb in 1879, and that electricity arrived in the homes of wealthy and urban American elites in the 1880s.

It says urban electrification accelerated in the 1910s and 1920s, that indoor lighting allowed homes to dispense with dangerous gas- and kerosene-based lamps that emitted hazardous fumes, and that work days no longer needed to be oriented entirely around sunlight hours. It says that in 1936 nearly 90 percent of farms lacked electric power because serving rural areas was prohibitive for private utilities, and that the newly created Rural Electrification Administration responded by financing cooperatives and infrastructure expansion. It says President Franklin D. Roosevelt said at a 1938 celebration of the Rural Electrification Administration that "Electricity is a modern necessity of life," and that the UN's Sustainable Development Goal 7 calls for "universal access to affordable, reliable and modern energy services" by 2030. The article says U.S. utility companies can shut down power to a home after repeated nonpayment, though many states have exemptions, and that a person moving to a rural location not yet connected to the electric grid typically bears some of the costs of extending the grid infrastructure, though the utility company cannot typically refuse their connection. It says that even where access to electricity is inhibited, such as when an electric power line no longer reaches a home, an inhabitant of that community can still get the benefit of electric power via devices, batteries, or local generators that do not require a connection to the grid.

It says the first successful transmission of intelligible speech on a phone line occurred in 1876, and that early development was fractured, expensive, and heavily concentrated in commercial hubs. It says the article follows electricity, the telephone, and the internet from discovery to widespread adoption, from privilege to right, and that though unique in origin and velocity, each technology lands in a similar position. It says that should the trend continue, generative AI may gain a permanent foothold in economies and societies and may eventually become a necessity for full participation in the workforce and in civic life, though not all jobs will require it and a life without it will not be inherently poor. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Oxfam America warns Anthropic IPO poses catastrophic AI risks to the public
stories.Summary:
Anthropic is preparing for an initial public offering that could value the company at $1 trillion, and Oxfam America published a new analysis on November 17, 2026 warning that the company's rapidly advancing artificial intelligence technology poses potentially catastrophic risks to society. The briefing, titled "Material Risks Beyond Anthropic's Balance Sheet," examines six major risks associated with Anthropic's AI platforms, from widespread job displacement and the development of biological weapons to cyberattacks, political manipulation and the potential loss of human control over increasingly powerful AI models. The analysis comes as Anthropic prepares to enter the public markets, potentially generating enormous wealth for its founders and early investors while exposing workers, communities and the broader public to risks that could have far-reaching consequences. Oxfam says the consequences of these risks could fall disproportionately on ordinary people who have little say in how these technologies are developed or deployed.

The briefing identifies six risks in detail, including that AI could eliminate millions of jobs, particularly entry-level professional positions, and disrupt labor markets across industries, and that advanced AI models could make dangerous weapons development more accessible to individuals with limited expertise. It also warns that AI-assisted warfare could increase the risk of targeting errors, civilian casualties and diminished human accountability, and that increasingly powerful AI systems could enable more sophisticated attacks against businesses, governments and critical infrastructure. Oxfam adds that AI could enable large-scale disinformation campaigns, political profiling and surveillance operations that threaten democratic institutions and human rights, and that advanced AI models have demonstrated deceptive and unauthorized behavior during testing, raising concerns about the effectiveness of existing safeguards. The company's seven founders retain 50.1% of voting power, limiting public shareholders' ability to influence key governance decisions, and the briefing also highlights Anthropic's decision to scale back an earlier safety commitment that prevented the release of AI models whose risks could not be adequately mitigated.

Hana Ivanhoe, Oxfam America's senior manager of private sector campaigns and advocacy, said the IPO lays bare a disturbing contradiction, because a company claiming to be a public benefit corporation is concentrating wealth and power in the hands of a few founders at a time when AI is rapidly reshaping the future of our economy. She said this could be the largest IPO in history and that it cannot be overstated what a massive windfall just a handful of insiders and early investors stand to make. She said those gains rest on a company that seems to be externalizing AI's risks onto the public at large, calling it a story of extreme inequality in which the ultra-rich get even richer while the rest of us bear the consequences of their actions. She also said decisions about potentially catastrophic risks cannot be left entirely in the hands of the companies creating them, and that Anthropic may have stronger safety measures than some of its competitors, but voluntary commitments are no substitute for independent oversight and accountability.

With no comprehensive federal framework governing the most severe risks associated with advanced AI, Oxfam urges investors to play a greater role in demanding independent oversight, stronger safeguards and greater corporate accountability. Ivanhoe said that as the company prepares to go public, investors have an opportunity and a responsibility to demand stronger safeguards before the consequences become irreversible. Oxfam's analysis raises concerns about the independence of Anthropic's oversight mechanisms and the concentration of corporate control, even as the company has positioned itself as a leader in responsible AI development. The briefing paper is available to download through Oxfam America's notes to editors.

stories.Headline: AWS publishes a three-phase responsible AI roadmap for agentic systems
stories.Summary:
AWS published a roadmap on November 17, 2026, for responsible AI in agentic systems, aimed at the platform teams that govern agent infrastructure and the application teams that build agents on top of it. The post says companies build agentic AI platforms to govern the applications, tools, skills, models, and storage that agents use, and that the nondeterministic nature of generative AI models adds complexity earlier software practices did not anticipate. It gives examples of a real estate app that generates listings from retrieved data and a customer service agent grounded on internal knowledge bases, asking whether each can be verified not to invent features or surface confidential information. It notes that responsible AI was until recently model-centric and scoped to the machine learning lifecycle of training, testing, and inference, when models did not reason, use tools, or take actions. Generative AI applications and agents now reason, act, compose tools dynamically, and interact over multiple steps, which the post says expands both the scope and the depth of what responsible AI must cover.

The roadmap maps the AWS Responsible AI Lens pillars, which include security and privacy, veracity and robustness, fairness, safety, controllability, explainability, transparency, and governance, to a three-phase maturity model of governance foundations, pilot deployment, and evaluation and hardening. An accompanying scorecard lets application and platform teams assess where they are today and iterate as applications mature, and the post says it covers key questions to ask at each phase while leaving out step-by-step implementation details and legal or compliance advice. It cites Robinhood, which built a generative AI financial crimes agent on Amazon Bedrock with strict data governance and achieved a 20% efficiency gain while maintaining regulatory compliance. It also cites Wade and Wirtz in the Harvard Business Review on trust becoming a competitive differentiator, saying the same capabilities that personalize at scale can also surveil and discriminate. The post defines an agentic AI platform as described in its AgentOps post on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a system for building, deploying, and operating agents securely at scale, and presents the pillars across a customizable 12-week implementation timeline.

Four challenges surface consistently in conversations with customers building agentic AI platforms, according to the post. Unpredictable runtime behavior covers nondeterministic outputs, goal drift, and cascading failures, and the post says a financial services company in Germany found that multi-agent orchestration amplified a single misclassification into policy violations across three downstream services. Data exposure and authority boundaries require scoping every agent to its intended tenants, data, systems, and actions, isolating session context, and granting privileged access through least-privilege, task-bound permissions agents cannot modify themselves. Regulatory velocity names the EU AI Act, ISO 42001, NIST AI RMF, and upcoming legislation as creating requirements faster than governance can adapt, and the post says proving compliance for nondeterministic systems requires continuous evaluation on a predefined cadence such as daily, weekly, or monthly. Team collaboration covers the lack of a shared framework for who owns what across the agent lifecycle, and the post says a media company in the UK flagged that segregation of duty between developer and deployment teams is undefined for agent workloads.

In the first phase, application teams classify risks for each planned use case using a risk rubric, while the platform team establishes the core landing zone infrastructure, including overarching monitoring and access control, and governs newly onboarded agents and use cases from the start. Teams evaluate access to the data and systems each agent needs and assess potential impact, which the post says lays the foundation for the knowledge grounding strategy. They implement foundational data security and data exfiltration protection with data classification, data access control, logging, data integrity, and data access monitoring. They build a map of data shared between agents, such as organizational knowledge bases, and subjective data such as context graphs individual agents might need, then establish access boundaries and assign read and write permissions accordingly. They define a risk classification rubric aligned to regulatory obligations such as EU AI Act risk tiers and financial services industry requirements, assign Low, Medium, High, or Unacceptable risk levels to each planned use case, and document the control requirements each level triggers.

stories.Headline: Rabbi Sam Tygiel declines AI for sermon, citing frictionless answers and hidden authorship
stories.Summary:
Rabbi Sam Tygiel, the assistant rabbi at Congregation Sherith Israel in San Francisco, wrote an essay, delivered as a sermon at the congregation in October and published by J. on Nov. 17, 2026, about why he mostly chose not to use artificial intelligence while preparing it. In May, Pope Leo XIV released an encyclical, a written statement of church doctrine concerning current events, about artificial intelligence, and it opens with the story of the Tower of Babel as a cautionary tale about technology and human ambition. The essay says the encyclical and the pope’s use of that story raised questions for the rabbi about what a religious response to AI looks like and what a specifically Jewish one looks like. He then shared his own story of trying to write the sermon, how tempting it was to use AI and why he largely declined.

The dilemma began with research, when he wanted to learn more about the encyclical and was immediately tempted to use AI to get its main themes and key quotes. When he searched for resources about the encyclical, Google’s AI tool, Gemini, offered him a seemingly definitive summary of what the internet said about his query, which he described as making his attempt to learn “frictionless.” He wrote that there are many reasons not to use such a summary, including that chatbots are well known to be prone to “hallucinations,” or answers that satisfy a query but are partly or entirely false. The reason most meaningful to him was that the summary eliminates the direct encounter between the text’s author and the reader, and he cited the Hasidic master Rabbi Nachman of Bratslav, who writes that when we read another’s teachings our spirit becomes intertwined with the spirit of the teacher. Because he wanted that challenge and that fleeting but direct encounter, he decided to engage with the encyclical directly, even knowing he would miss important information given his necessarily limited capacity.

On another stop in preparing the sermon, he checked out a new chatbot for Jewish learning called Yochai, which also offered a library of Jewish texts, all translated, and one translation seemed strange and inhuman, with words and abbreviations rendered literally rather than according to their meaning in the received tradition. He asked the chatbot about the author of the translation and got a surprisingly evasive answer, in which Yochai said he was on the title page itself and that the translation was simply the straightforward rendering of those words into English. He asked again who wrote the translation, and the chatbot admitted it did not know, later saying the reader exposes no metadata about who produced the English renderings, with no translator credit, no publisher note and nothing attached at the passage level it could point to. He wrote that this is a common reality with AI programs known as large language models, or LLMs, which obscure authorship and the origin of ideas and thereby eliminate possible accountability, making it difficult to trace the lineage of human wisdom behind their responses. He also attempted to turn the chatbot into his study partner, aware throughout of the frictionless quality of the interactions, in which whatever prompt he gave, Yochai created something that mirrored and validated his input, and he likened it to the kind of parrot that leading AI thinker Dr. Timnit Gebru and her coauthors warned about in the 2020 article “On the Dangers of Stochastic Parrots.”

The essay cites an ancient story about Talmudic study partners in which Rabbi Yochanan celebrates the way his chevruta, Reish Lakish, pushes back on him, and it says that friction is the very quality that makes Reish Lakish a beloved partner in study, with spiritual growth coming from a relationship that involves friction. Ultimately, the rabbi wrote, it was the frictionlessness of his interactions with AI that made him turn away from using LLMs to help write the sermon, and he suggested that perhaps God scattered the ancestors who built the great tower as a way of saying that this is not what partnership looks like. He concluded that true partnership comes from the holy messiness of encountering the other and acknowledging and celebrating the distance between us even as we reach toward one another. The essay identifies Rabbi Tygiel as an alumnus of Hadar’s Rising Song Residency who was ordained at Hebrew College and composes original Jewish music, which can be heard on his website, samtygiel.com.

stories.Headline: Trusteeship in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: Building the Future Fiduciary
stories.Summary:
On November 17, 2026, Alex Adam, Janine Catterson, Naomi Leach, and Zebonisia Chutel published a report regarding the integration of artificial intelligence within fiduciary services. The authors examined how professional firms can rethink the way their people, controls, processes, and information function together. This analysis serves as the final installment of a three-part series focused on building the future fiduciary. The writers argued that embedding these technologies allows firms to reduce administrative burdens and improve the efficiency of their reporting.

Developing an AI-enabled operating model requires a strategic focus on information management, professional skills, governance, and internal controls. The authors stated that firms must align their overall AI strategy with their specific risk profiles, target markets, and existing operating models. This transition involves more than just automating current processes, as it requires maintaining human accountability and reliable data. The goal is to use automation to support decision-making and monitoring while preserving clear responsibility for execution and underlying expertise.

The authors from Teneo suggested that the primary challenge for boards and management teams is avoiding the adoption of individual tools in isolation. They emphasized that the correct approach strengthens oversight and increases capacity without sacrificing the necessary authority of the human fiduciary. These professionals noted that the integration of artificial intelligence provides a significant opportunity to redesign how professional services are delivered to clients. The report concludes that the future of the industry depends on balancing technological efficiency with professional accountability.

stories.Headline: Congressional report warns circular AI financing may expose economy to instability
stories.Summary:
A new Congressional Research Service report finds that circular financing arrangements among artificial intelligence companies could expose the broader economy to financial instability, according to Legis1. The practice has become increasingly prominent as technology companies pour billions of dollars into AI infrastructure, with analysts estimating U.S. AI-related infrastructure investment at approximately $500 billion this year and $10.3 trillion between 2025 and 2032. The report stops short of concluding that an AI investment bubble exists or that circular financing would necessarily trigger a broader financial crisis. Circular financing occurs when a company provides financial support to another business with the expectation that the recipient will purchase its products or services, and the arrangements have become increasingly common among AI developers, chipmakers and cloud computing providers. The Bank for International Settlements found that 28.7% of investments made by AI companies between 2021 and 2025, measured by deal value, went to other AI companies, and that 55.2% of investment flowing into AI companies came from other AI businesses.

The report identifies three types of arrangements: investor-supplier relationships, investor-purchaser relationships, and reciprocal arrangements involving financial commitments between companies. One prominent example involves Nvidia, which announced on Sept. 22, 2025, that it intended to invest up to $100 billion in OpenAI as the companies developed computing infrastructure powered by Nvidia technology, though Reuters reported in January, citing The Wall Street Journal, that the plan had stalled. Another example involves Amazon, which announced in April an additional $5 billion investment in Anthropic with the potential for another $20 billion, while Anthropic committed to spending $100 billion over 10 years on Amazon's chips and cloud computing services. The report describes these arrangements as expanded forms of vendor financing, a longstanding practice in which suppliers help customers finance purchases, and notes that such deals can provide companies with capital they might otherwise struggle to obtain. The financing is particularly important for leading AI developers, many of which are startups spending more money than they generate in revenue and relying on outside investment to expand their operations.

The report warns that complex financial agreements may obscure how much AI companies depend on one another, potentially understating their exposure to financial problems elsewhere in the industry, and compares these dynamics to circular financing relationships between telecommunications equipment suppliers and customers during the dot-com era, when investment dried up and some companies ultimately failed. The growing financial ties could let problems at one business spread to its suppliers, investors and customers, and if major banks or other financial institutions become heavily exposed, disruptions in the AI industry could also affect broader financial markets. The International Monetary Fund's October Global Financial Stability Report identified a potential correction in AI-related investment as a major concern among financial market participants, though the extent of the risk depends partly on how companies finance their investments. When businesses fund AI investments through their own operating revenue rather than borrowing from banks or other financial institutions, the financial system's immediate exposure may be more limited. For Congress, the unresolved question is whether circular financing primarily helps companies build the infrastructure needed for AI development or creates financial dependencies that could deepen the consequences of an industry downturn.

stories.Headline: Professor Caroline Dive’s team uses AI to seek early lung cancer signals in blood samples
stories.Summary:
In a blue-and-white van outside Asda last June, 68-year-old Eddie, a retired fishmonger from Fallowfield, near Manchester, received life-changing news. The van belonged to the NHS and contained a portable scanner. Eddie and his wife Jeanette had arrived for a lung screening appointment after being invited by their primary care doctor. Eddie said he very nearly didn't go because he felt fit and well, but Jeanette insisted it was no more difficult than a quick trip to the store. Because he smoked as a teenager and had some family history of cancer, they said he should have a scan there and then.

To the couple's shock, the scan found a dark shadow on Eddie's right lung. A week later, in the hospital, he had further tests, including a biopsy, and the couple's worst fears were confirmed: it was lung cancer. Eddie said he couldn't even properly remember the conversation and was in total shock. Screening has its downsides, as false positives can cause stress and anxiety, while regular monitoring after surgery can be a stressful and time-consuming process. There are also potential harms from the radiation used in CT scans, even though the dose is low.

For these reasons, the NHS program currently only invites current and former smokers, whose higher cancer risk means the benefits outweigh these harms. Estimates suggest as many as 6,000 never-smokers, currently ineligible for screening, die from lung cancer every year. Researchers are looking for ways to make screening more accurate, tell fast-growing tumors apart from slower-growing ones, and extend its benefits to more people. At the Cancer Research UK National Biomarker Centre, just minutes from the supermarket where Eddie's story began, center director professor Caroline Dive CBE and her teams are exploring an approach that could transform lung screening. Using cutting-edge artificial intelligence, they're looking for answers in people's blood.

Dive says scans are good at finding people with stage 1 disease, almost all of whom will have surgery and a good chance of cure, but about one in five will go on and relapse. She says that means, in some folks, an early tumor has already sent out the seeds of metastasis and begun to spread. Dive is a world-renowned expert in blood-based cancer biomarkers, subtle changes in the levels or structure of molecules in the blood that reveal the disease's presence. At Cancer Research UK, the charity is now supporting her team to tackle two key questions in lung screening. Dive asks first whether blood tests can be used to find early lung cancers, as early tumors release molecules and cells into the bloodstream that could form the basis for a blood test, or liquid biopsy, to augment CT scans and boost their accuracy.

Dive says that since 2016 they have been working closely with one of the pioneers of community-based lung screening in Manchester, professor Phil Crosbie, and his team at Wythenshawe Hospital. Together, they hope that by using sophisticated techniques to compare samples from people with and without early lung cancer, they can identify molecular signatures that could lead to a sensitive and informative blood test. With the multitude of different molecules and cells circulating in the blood, knowing which ones signal an early lung cancer is a formidable challenge, and to help spot patterns hiding in this complexity, Caroline's team is turning to AI. Blood is one of nature's most complex liquids, with billions of cells, chiefly oxygen-carrying red blood cells and various flavors of immune cells, floating in a watery soup containing countless biomolecules. These include tens of thousands of different types of proteins, sugars, fats and other metabolites, and fragments of genetic material shed by dying cells, including cancer cells, and thanks to modern technologies, scientists can now measure the levels and nature of these components with astonishing accuracy.

Because these molecules reflect so many of the body's processes, a well-designed blood test can offer a window into its inner workings, including when we're ill. Developing a reliable test is challenging, as levels of different molecules naturally fluctuate with age, infections, allergies, illness, exercise, and even with what we've eaten, so the trick is separating the signal from the noise. To do this, Dive's team has selected 200 pairs of blood samples from their larger collection of screening samples. Dive explains that for every sample where screening found an early lung cancer, they have been able to match a partner sample from someone who remained cancer-free but who was otherwise similar in age, sex and smoking history, which should make the cancer-related differences between samples much easier to distinguish.

She says they are fishing in a pond, rather than an entire ocean. Rather than relying on one type of measurement, which Dive says is unlikely to get the job done, they are taking a multi-modal approach, looking for patterns across a whole range of biological information sources. Using a technique called proteomics, they are precisely measuring levels of thousands of circulating proteins, and for circulating DNA fragments shed by tumors they are looking at three different features: cancer-linked mutations, chemical modifications to the DNA including so-called methylation, and differences in the fragments' size known as fragmentomics. They are looking for rare abnormal circulating cells, including cancer cells, that might offer clues, and with collaborators in the U.S. they are analyzing circulating RNA, a shorter-lived cousin of DNA.

This will create an enormous data set containing hundreds of thousands of measurements from each sample, and finding meaningful, cancer-linked patterns within it is an extraordinary challenge, which is where AI comes in. Dive says it is such a big puzzle and AI will hugely speed up the process. The team will first train AI models using data from the first 100 pairs of cancer-positive and matched-negative samples. Then they will test whether the best-performing AI model can identify cancer in the second 100 pairs without the AI knowing which samples came from people with cancer.

A key challenge will be identifying the minimum number of measurements needed to maintain accuracy across such large data sets. Then, if successful, the next step will be a much larger study, and Dive says that if, and it's a big if, the data are convincing, then they will need to work with commercial partners and organizations like Cancer Research Horizons, because developing a biomarker test for routine use is really challenging and expensive. Dive says none of this would be possible without the research networks and infrastructure that have developed in Manchester since she moved there in 2003, and she is hugely grateful that Cancer Research UK has given her a stable base to develop strong networks, not only in Manchester with the Christie Hospital and wider NHS trusts, but around the UK and abroad. She says they have got the right ingredients in the pot and now they are just going to have to see what these precious samples can tell them.

stories.Headline: Carnegie Mellon and Pitt researchers propose a framework to teach medical trainees to review AI-generated clinical notes
stories.Summary:
Ambient AI scribes, which passively capture clinical encounters and draft notes, are among the most rapidly adopted artificial intelligence applications in health care, and in one integrated health care system they documented more than 2.5 million clinical encounters in a single year. Early evidence suggests real benefits from these tools, yet the outcomes measured thus far, including documentation time, cognitive workload and clinician burnout, address the value of the tools for workforce sustainability rather than medical education. Their use has spread through clinical settings faster than curricula can adapt, leaving medical schools unprepared for the shift. In a new article in npj Digital Medicine, researchers at Carnegie Mellon University and the University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine propose a framework that defines the review of AI-generated clinical documentation as a teachable competency and describe how it can be taught through simulation.

Holly Wiberg, assistant professor of public policy and operations research at Carnegie Mellon's Heinz College, who co-authored the article, said physicians are shifting from writing clinical notes to editing AI-generated ones, which changes what trainees need to learn. She said ambient AI can ease documentation burden and has the potential to improve quality, but only if clinicians use it critically by evaluating its output and recognizing its failure modes. The authors say the editorial skills needed to review AI documentation competently are specific and teachable, not innate extensions of clinical practice, and that nothing in current medical school curricula targets these skills directly. Yash Raka, an M.D. candidate at the University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine and a co-author, said he is part of the first generation likely to edit AI-generated notes as often as they write their own, and that medical education is still catching up to what that shift requires.

The article identifies four domains involved in reviewing AI-generated clinical documentation, starting with detecting errors and omissions such as factual errors, hallucinations and misattributions in AI-generated clinical notes. The second domain asks whether trainees can judge if a note reflects the clinical reasoning of the medical visit rather than merely its facts, and the third asks whether they can generate clinically sound notes independently when AI is unavailable or inappropriate or when a patient does not consent to its use. The fourth domain concerns whether trainees appropriately calibrate their trust in AI output across clinical contexts, and in each domain the authors propose learning objectives, simulation exercises, ways to assess competency and timelines for teaching these skills. Reed Van Deusen, associate professor in general internal medicine and pediatrics at the University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine and another co-author, said simulation lets trainees practice catching an AI's mistakes in a low-stakes way where it will not affect patient outcomes.

Van Deusen said that when errors are built into simulated encounters, educators can see exactly what a learner misses and give targeted feedback, which is hard to do in a clinical training environment. The authors note that the proposed framework is preliminary and call for empirical testing to refine it, and they see it as a starting point. They envision developing curricular components aligned with their proposed exercises, with the hope that it could eventually inform how medical schools prepare trainees for AI-assisted practice. The article is titled From authoring to editing: a competency framework for trainee use of ambient AI clinical documentation, published in npj Digital Medicine with DOI 10.1038/s41746-026-03351-5.

stories.Headline: IBM consulting leader Kimberly Morick says CHROs gain a bigger seat as AI reshapes work
stories.Summary:
Kimberly Morick, HR and Transformation Practice Lead at IBM Consulting, gave a personal perspective in a conversation published on ibm.com on 17 November 2026 about AI reshaping work. She said AI is reshaping roles, skills and the way teams work, and that HR leaders are helping organizations navigate the change. She said CHROs now have a bigger seat at the table than ever before. She said people are still what drive performance. She said the opportunity now is to put AI to work in ways that make employees more confident, adaptable and capable.

She said she hopes work becomes more human, not less, over the next 5 years. She said organizations will need to reinvest capacity freed by AI into innovation, new skills and complex problems. She said the future of work will be far more skills-based than job-based, with organizations focusing on capabilities rather than titles. She said workforce transformation and technology transformation are really a single conversation. She said 71% of CHROs view the ability to supervise, validate and override AI outputs as the workforce's most critical skill, while only 29% of employees rank judgment as a priority.

She said an AI model can offer a recommendation but cannot take responsibility for what happens next, so someone must own the outcome. She said the colleague who says "I think we're solving the wrong problem" before anyone runs an AI analysis often creates more value than the person who delivers the perfect answer. She said people still provide the context, nuance and ethical judgment that do not always show up in the data. She said people still look to people for coaching, navigating change and leading through uncertainty. She said curiosity is the skill behind the skills.

She said research shows 60% of employees worry about skills erosion, with critical thinking cited most often as declining. She said among employees who worry about this, 3 out of 4 say AI has already begun to erode at least some of their skills. She said she treats AI as a thought partner, not a substitute for thinking, and forms her own view first, then uses AI to test it. She said the biggest shift in workplace culture over the past 5 years has been the pace of change. She said people rarely resist technology itself, they resist uncertainty.

She said AI has simplified administrative work, improved access to information and created efficiencies across HR processes. She said that as part of IBM's Client Zero transformation, AskHR resolved 94% of common employee inquiries and supported more than 16 million HR interactions in 2025. She said the convergence of AI, skills intelligence, workforce analytics and employee experience technologies excites her most. She said employees need confidence that AI is being used responsibly, transparently and with appropriate human oversight. She said AI at its best will allow HR to focus more deeply on helping people grow and supporting leaders.

The conversation was published on ibm.com on 17 November 2026. It cites Designing the Thinking Organization: 5 focus areas for CHROs as AI reshapes work, IBM Institute for Business Value, September 2026. It cites a how-to guide titled How we unlocked productivity with AI and innovation, and a roadmap for getting there, from IBM. It cites IBM Transformation: AskHR, IBM, 2026. It cites a footnote, numbered 1, attached to the 71% and 29% figures and to the 60% and 3 out of 4 figures.

The conversation leaves open what specific steps organizations should take to create opportunities for people to practice skills as AI takes over more routine work. It leaves open how the disconnect between CHROs and employees on judgment will be closed. It leaves open what the footnote numbered 1 cites. It leaves open how trust in responsible, transparent AI use with human oversight will be built. It leaves open what the cited IBM Institute for Business Value report of September 2026 recommends.

stories.Headline: Apollo CEO Marc Rowan warns neoclouds face severe trouble if Nvidia stops funding their AI projects
stories.Summary:
Apollo Global Management CEO Marc Rowan said on Tuesday that neocloud companies could face severe trouble if Nvidia stops funding their artificial intelligence projects, speaking in an interview with CNBC's "Squawk on the Street." Nvidia has become known as the central bank of AI because of the financing it gives to smaller companies such as the neoclouds, and investors now worry that this funding could be cut as the chipmaker faces tougher scrutiny. Rowan said there was a strong incentive for Nvidia as a business matter to get these projects off the ground, and he warned that if that banking and guarantor function is taken away, access to capital for a large number of neoclouds will disappear. His comments followed remarks by "Big Short" investor Steve Eisman, who told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Tuesday that the neoclouds are all in big trouble because they are part of that vertical holding company and he thinks they are about to get ejected.

Nvidia had $36 billion in off-balance-sheet AI cloud agreements, or backstops, for neoclouds, according to its last quarterly financial filing in July. Nvidia has been under pressure since CEO Jensen Huang stepped down Thursday amid an adultery scandal, and the company is set to report earnings after the bell Tuesday under the leadership of interim CEO Colette Kress. Concerns about the large amount of debt the neoclouds have taken on have already sent their stocks tumbling and bond yields rising, since bond yields move inversely to prices. CoreWeave and Nebius, which use the financing to build data centers, are each down more than 50% over the last three months, and CoreWeave's 9.75% bond due in 2031 was yielding 15.66% on Tuesday, while spreads on its five-year credit default swaps hovered around 1,113.5.

Rowan said that if Nvidia decides to stop providing funding to neoclouds, the winners will be those companies that have the financial wherewithal and locked-in funding to build their infrastructure. He said he believes new ways to secure funding will ultimately be developed in the AI space, pointing to other technology cycles for comparison. He recalled that when Ford and GM introduced their first automobiles, people were amazed but no one could afford it, and the market ended up with GMAC and Ford Motor Credit. He added that it would not surprise him to see financial innovation take place, where more of a finance company mentality develops for this industry as an arbiter of credit and as a method of dealing with residuals.

stories.Headline: Radio stations must turn broadcasts into text and structured guides so AI models can find and cite their local content
stories.Summary:
Radio stations are being told they must learn how their content is found, understood and surfaced by artificial intelligence, according to an article published by Radio World on November 17, 2026. The piece says people now ask AI tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude for instant answers instead of typing queries like the best things to do in Milwaukee this weekend into a search bar and reading through links. After enough of those experiences, the article says, traditional search results feel antiquated. The article notes that even Google now shows an answer at the top of its own search results, which it calls a showcase of AI superiority.

The article says there is no universally accepted replacement yet for the acronym SEO, listing GEO for Generative Engine Optimization, AEO for Answer Engine Optimization, LLMO for Large Language Model Optimization and AI SEO as labels in use. Whatever the label, the article says, the meaning is the same: radio needs to figure out AI discovery and how AI models locate a station as a resource for information. It says radio has answered local questions since its inception, such as who is playing this weekend, where to take the kids on Saturday and what is happening with the local team. The new question, the article says, is whether AI will discover what a station knows and use it as the source.

The article says large media outlets have huge digital footprints, but local radio has far better real-time information, and the problem is that most of what is said on air never makes it to digital platforms such as the web, social media, Reddit and YouTube. It says a local interview, a morning show discussion, a DJ's take on a local band, weekend events plugged between songs and breaking local news all vanish after airing. Stations need a workflow that lets AI ingest these tidbits, the article says, by turning broadcast information into text, building structured local guides and publishing transcripts and summaries. It says this work is about helping AI understand the content as a credible source, a different goal from ranking at the top of a search page, and that clear attribution and current information on local happenings are required.

The article suggests stations treat themselves as a local information database covering concerts, events, restaurants, food trucks, sports and community organizations, with each piece serving a purpose: broadcast is immediate, social is discovery, the website is reference, and podcast and video are deeper engagement. It says radio has been the best source of local information since the 1920s, but there is now a new gatekeeper, and stations have to make sure it knows how to find them. Ironically, the article says, stations will use AI to transcribe what they create so that other AI models can find them. It concludes that AI is not just another place to publish but another way people discover a station, and the trick is to make sure AI knows what the radio station knows.

Articles.Title: Does AI Know What You Know?
