stories.Headline: Microsoft 365 outage technical; phishing campaign exploited it
stories.Summary:
Microsoft confirmed that its November 12 Microsoft 365 outage was caused by a technical issue and not by a cyberattack, according to a SecurityWeek report. The disruption blocked access to Exchange Online mailboxes and Outlook, and it may also have affected Teams, SharePoint Online, and Microsoft 365 Copilot. The company traced the failure to an earlier network capacity upgrade that a later network change exposed. Microsoft said it had fixed the underlying problem and was restoring services in stages to keep things stable.

Microsoft Threat Intelligence found that attackers used the disruption to run a phishing campaign against users. The fake emails posed as Microsoft 365 service health notices and referred to the real incident identifier EX1550543. Some messages falsely warned that emails held during the outage would be deleted within 24 hours unless the recipient clicked a link to restore them. Subject lines began with the word Outage followed by a six-character code, and sender display names combined organisation-specific wording with Outage Notification or Service Health. Microsoft named moments-notice[.]com, planetmaison[.]com, and newbooker[.]com as the domains used to send these emails, and it said recipient-specific SendGrid tracking links redirected to reallifeaccounting[.]com.

Microsoft advised security teams to examine suspicious emails and links, to investigate any user clicks, and to review their Safe Links policies. The company also confirmed that its security products were blocking the campaign. The report did not say how many users received the phishing emails or whether anyone clicked the links before the messages were blocked. It also gave no details on when the phishing messages were first seen or how long the campaign lasted.

Articles.Title: Microsoft 365 outage technical; phishing campaign exploited it

stories.Headline: Investment experts advise diversification as AI stocks decline and Nvidia shares drop
stories.Summary:
Investors are currently feeling uneasy because shares of Nvidia have dropped 35 percent since October 6. This decline followed the resignation of co-founder Jensen Huang as CEO after reports of his romantic ties to a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. Technology companies within the S&P 500 have fallen nearly 17 percent from their peaks in early October. These events have led many market participants to wonder if the artificial intelligence bubble is finally popping.

The current market structure requires a careful look at diversification because the ten largest S&P 500 companies command 37 percent of the index. As of November 17, technology stocks also represent 37 percent of the benchmark weighting. This concentration exists even before the initial public offering of Anthropic, which targets a valuation that would make it the tenth largest public firm in the United States. Experts suggest that nervous investors should evaluate their exposure and consider equal weight indexes or international stocks.

Dan Lefkovitz of Morningstar Indexes says that exiting the market is an extreme option that could cause investors to miss tremendous gains. Anthony Saglimbene from Ameriprise notes that market capitalization weighted funds do not work well when technology stocks experience a sell off. Jamie Cox of Harris Financial Group believes younger investors should focus on long term opportunities rather than short term volatility. Ryan Detrick from Carson Group explains that broad market pullbacks of 5 percent or more happen more than three times per year on average.

The broader context involves a persistent demand for data centers and microchips that may benefit megacap firms like Microsoft and Alphabet. While short term drawdowns are possible, the historical trend of the United States stock market has generally moved upward. Investors are encouraged to talk with financial advisors before making wholesale changes to their portfolios. The goal is to participate in the market without being overly reliant on a single theme or the top end of the market.

stories.Headline: Cardinal Czerny says humans must stay accountable for violence unleashed by AI
stories.Summary:
Cardinal Michael Czerny, the Prefect Emeritus of the Dicastery for Promoting Integral Human Development, spoke in Sofia on November 17, 2026, at a gathering co-hosted by the Bulgarian Academy of Sciences and the Apostolic Nunciature in Bulgaria. He was there to present Magnifica humanitas, Pope Leo XIV's first encyclical, with a particular focus on war and peace. In his remarks, the Cardinal said that humans must remain directly responsible for any violence and destruction which their technologies unleash. He also said that decisions about lethal force must remain in human hands and that it must always be possible to identify the people who made them.

Cardinal Czerny drew on two biblical building projects, Babel and the rebuilding of the walls of Jerusalem after the exile, to show that the difference between them lies in the desire that guides the act of building. He applied the same question to artificial intelligence, asking what kind of world and what kind of civilization these tools help to build. He warned that the term "just war" is often used loosely to justify aggression, even as weapons have become more destructive. He said Pope Leo upheld the right to self-defense in the strictest sense while declaring that the just war theory is outdated, pointing instead to dialogue, diplomacy and forgiveness as ways to resolve conflicts.

The Cardinal set out three criteria from the encyclical, the first being that the chain of responsibility must be identifiable and verifiable, from those who design and train a system to those who authorize and use it. The second is that those deciding whether to use lethal force must have time to exercise judgment, because speed and efficiency cannot determine an irreversible decision. The third is that civilians must be distinguished from combatants and protected, along with the infrastructure they need to survive. He also recalled the encyclical's warning that a culture of power pushes the suffering of people at war into the background as governments pursue strategic interests, and that this outlook takes hold when societies regard war as inevitable and dismiss those who seek peace through dialogue as unrealistic.

For Cardinal Czerny, that responsibility also has a personal dimension, since Pope Leo's call for the disarmament of heart, mind and life reaches into ordinary encounters where the words and images people choose can themselves do harm. As the Cardinal put it, the roots of both war and peace are within, and everyone needs to pacify the belligerence at work in each one's heart.

stories.Headline: IBM chief Arvind Krishna urges India to scale chip and AI ecosystems
stories.Summary:
IBM Chairman and CEO Arvind Krishna said in New Delhi on November 16 that India must scale its semiconductor and artificial intelligence deployment ecosystems to become a global player. He identified chip design and assembly as India's strengths because of its skilled workforce, existing infrastructure and technical capabilities. He noted that India's contribution to the trillion-dollar global semiconductor manufacturing industry is only about $3 billion, which shows a significant gap. Krishna also said that while India has a strong position in software exports, its role in other technology value chain segments is limited.

Krishna advised the Indian government to focus on scaling these initiatives, and he pointed to AI deployment for global companies as another opportunity India can capture. Estimates suggest that AI could add around $500 billion to India's gross domestic product growth by the end of the decade, but India needs to accelerate AI adoption to realise this potential. An IBM survey found that more than 75 per cent of organisations have made little progress in AI adoption, even though more than 90 per cent acknowledge its usefulness. Integrating AI at scale requires preparing enterprise data and re-engineering business processes, according to the report.

IBM is expanding hiring in design, software, testing, site reliability engineering and AI skills, the article says. The report does not say what the Indian government plans to do in response to Krishna's advice, and it gives no timeline for any policy changes. It also does not say whether IBM's hiring expansion is tied to India specifically or spread across its operations. The article ends by inviting readers to share their thoughts, and it provides no further details on next steps.

stories.Headline: VAST Data reports $10B in commitments from 14 customers
stories.Summary:
VAST Data reported ten billion dollars in commitments from fourteen customers during the first three quarters of its fiscal year. This spending covers VAST software and supporting hardware for customers from a base of more than one thousand. Four of these customers committed more than one billion dollars each to the storage infrastructure. The company has also secured agreements for over two hundred exabytes of flash capacity through 2029.

The company uses a Disaggregated Shared Everything architecture to share storage resources across large computing environments. Its AI Operating System brings data management and processing into one platform to support nine of the top ten frontier AI labs. VAST raised one billion dollars this year at a thirty billion dollar valuation, up from nine point one billion in 2023. It has a reported one point one seven billion dollar contract with CoreWeave and reports of deals with Microsoft and Google Cloud.

VAST co-founder Jeff Denworth said the company secured supply deals to ensure smaller cloud providers can still get storage. He noted that the biggest AI players are placing enormous orders for flash capacity. The company believes its technology solves the problem of GPUs needing a constant supply of data to avoid wasting computing power. VAST states that storage is becoming a much bigger part of the investment for cloud providers and AI labs.

Rival company VDURA reported that the price of thirty terabyte SSDs rose between the second quarter of 2025 and the first quarter of 2026. VDURA first claimed a price increase of two hundred fifty seven percent, but later revised this figure to four hundred seventy two percent in April. Hard drive prices also increased by thirty five percent according to the same company. Other rivals seeking a share of AI spending include NetApp, which bought PEAK:AIO, as well as DDN and WEKA.

The articles state that most attention on AI infrastructure has gone to GPUs, but storage is essential for keeping massive systems running. VAST Data has not named its customers or stated when the ten billion dollars in promised spending will actually happen. The company has not disclosed how much of the committed spending goes directly into its own pocket. It is also unknown which supply chain partners provided the flash capacity or how much capacity is expected each year.

The industry must now see how much of the promised ten billion dollars in spending actually materializes. VAST Data continues to compete with VDURA, which pitches a mix of flash and hard drives as a cheaper route. The market remains volatile as flash prices for solid state drives fluctuate significantly. Future reports may reveal the identities of the four buyers planning to spend over four billion dollars. More to follow.

stories.Headline: New AI method generates anatomically accurate foot x-ray images
stories.Summary:
Researchers at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology in Ålesund have developed an artificial intelligence model that generates x-ray-like images of the foot while preserving the actual skeletal structure, according to Di Wu, an associate professor at the university's Department of ICT and Natural Sciences. The method is called a skeletal-constrained conditional diffusion model, and it is designed specifically to produce anatomically accurate images of hallux valgus, the misalignment of the big toe commonly known as bunions. Wu and her colleagues also created two measurement methods to check whether the generated images are anatomically accurate, and they tested the approach against other methods used to generate new digital images. The work lies at the intersection of medical imaging and artificial intelligence, and the technology is similar to that used by many AI tools that generate images.

The method could in the long term mean that patients avoid some x-ray examinations and that diagnostic imaging becomes more accessible where equipment is unavailable or unaffordable, since images of hallux valgus must be taken while the patient is standing and bearing weight. Wu said the results also suggest that an ordinary photograph of the foot could serve as an additional source of information for AI-assisted screening, medical assessment and treatment planning, and some doctors have suggested the approach could be used for early-stage screening rather than clinical diagnosis. The technology remains at the research stage, and the AI-generated images are not intended to replace actual x-rays or clinical assessments, at least not yet. Wu said more work involving larger and more diverse patient groups will be needed before that can happen.

Wu is responsible for the research and described the method as a machine-learning approach that makes it possible to preserve the actual skeletal structure of the foot when the model creates an x-ray-like image. She said tests showed the method produced both better image quality and a more accurate representation of the foot skeleton than other methods used to generate new digital images. She also pointed to a 2023 meta-analysis based on studies involving more than 186 million people, which estimated that 19 per cent of people worldwide have hallux valgus, with 24 per cent among women and 11 per cent among men. Among people aged 20 to 60, 12 per cent have the condition, compared with 23 per cent of those over 60, and Wu said various studies suggest it may be under-researched in many regions.

Hallux valgus has a long history, with one of the earliest anatomical descriptions provided by the physician Galen of Pergamon, who lived from AD 129 to 200, and the first book on the condition published in 1781 by Nicholas-Laurent Laforest, personal chiropodist to King Louis XVI and Queen Marie Antoinette. Archaeologists in England found an unusually high number of misaligned big toes in skeletons from the 14th and 15th centuries, when tight, almost carrot-shaped shoes were fashionable, and among 177 skeletons the highest prevalence was at an Augustinian friary, where as many as 43 per cent of those buried had the condition. By 1463, shoes had become so pointed that King Edward IV introduced a law prohibiting anyone below the rank of lord from wearing shoes with toes extending more than two inches beyond the foot. Toes that point inwards can range from a cosmetic issue to causing considerable pain, problems with footwear and changes in the way people walk, which can place uneven strain on the knees, hips and back, and surgery can correct the deformity.

stories.Headline: CoinShares CEO Jean-Marie Mognetti says AI is pulling every marginal dollar away from crypto
stories.Summary:
CoinShares CEO Jean-Marie Mognetti said on CNBC's Squawk on the Street that artificial intelligence is pulling every marginal dollar away from crypto, and he made the remark during a discussion of the AI trade and the Bitcoin sell-off. The interview aired on November 18, 2026, in a segment that ran about two minutes and fifty-eight seconds. The clip was posted on CNBC's website under the headline carrying his remark about AI and crypto. The same page lists CoinShares under the ticker CSHR and Bitcoin under BRRR and BCH.CM.

The remark ties the Bitcoin sell-off to competition from AI for investor money, with Mognetti saying AI is taking the marginal dollar that might otherwise go to crypto. The segment covered the artificial intelligence trade alongside the Bitcoin sell-off, and the page gives no further figures on prices or flows. The page also lists other CNBC videos, including one on succession weighing on Nvidia's report and one on Democrats nominating Hakeem Jeffries for Speaker of the House. It also lists a House Energy and Commerce Committee request for a briefing from Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress and remarks by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman on a public listing and on Jensen Huang.

Mognetti is the chief executive of CoinShares, and the view is his own as stated in the interview. The page does not say whether CoinShares holds a position on the AI trade or on Bitcoin. It also does not give any response from crypto exchanges or other executives to his remark. The surrounding videos on the page are separate CNBC segments and carry no comment from Mognetti on those topics.

The articles give no further context on the size of the Bitcoin sell-off or on how much money has moved from crypto into AI. They also do not say what CoinShares plans to do or what happens next for the company or the market. The page offers only the short interview clip and the list of other videos. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Körber study finds AI adoption outpaces execution as 77% of US respondents report deeper AI involvement in decisions
stories.Summary:
A new Körber study, reported by Marina Mayer on November 18, 2026, finds that AI adoption is accelerating faster than organizations can execute on it across the United States and Germany. Companies piloting AI and companies running it enterprise-wide are investing in AI-powered decision support at virtually the same rate, 59% versus 59.4%. Yet the enterprise-wide group shows significantly stronger reported performance and confidence in its future readiness than the piloting group. Among U.S. respondents specifically, 77% say AI has become increasingly involved in decision-making, while 78% say decision-making has become more complex.

The findings point to execution challenges such as information delays, data friction, disconnected systems, and reluctance to give technology final authority, all coexisting with increased decision complexity. Organizations operating globally report higher use of AI in decisions and stronger transformation results overall, but scale also multiplies the coordination challenge through more systems, more sites, more partners, more data sources, and more people who need clear decision rights. Supply chain leaders report the deepest AI involvement at 92% but face execution pressure around variability and exceptions handling at 36% and systems integration at 24%. Life sciences leaders report slower adoption at 60% along with challenges in systems integration at 48% and workforce skills at 46%.

The study identifies four conditions that distinguish organizations converting AI investment into measurable results, including timely and trustworthy data reaching the point of decision instead of after the fact. It also names clear accountability for who makes the final call and when, defined exception handling for the cases AI cannot or should not resolve alone, and the right balance of automation and human oversight calibrated by decision rather than applied uniformly. The study finds this plays out differently by market and industry, with distinct patterns across the United States and Germany and across sectors such as supply chain and life sciences. The article does not say what happens next beyond the study's findings.

Articles.Title: AI Adoption Accelerates: Why Leaders Face Complex Decisions

stories.Headline: National security and AI leaders urge Justice Department to probe Nvidia over chip smuggling to China
stories.Summary:
Fifteen national security and AI leaders urged the Justice Department to investigate Nvidia on Tuesday, November 18, 2026. They want to know if the chipmaker knew about illegal transfers of advanced AI chips to China. The group asks if Nvidia continued selling to customers after evidence of illegal diversion emerged. They also question if the company deliberately blinded itself to export control violations. This request follows growing scrutiny and calls from Congress to investigate the company.

The letter was addressed to Attorney General Todd Blanche and mentions a March 2026 case. In that case, three people were charged for routing 510 million dollars of chips to China. The total value of servers in that specific Southeast Asian intermediary scheme was 2.5 billion dollars. The Justice Department also investigated Megaspeed, a Singaporean company tied to suspected Chinese asset Alice Huang. Megaspeed reportedly acquired billions of dollars in chips and is suspected of smuggling them to China.

Brad Carson, president of Americans for Responsible Innovation, organized the letter and said chips are highly desired. Other signatories include former CIA inspector general David Buckley, retired Army general Randy Manner, and former official Chris McGuire. A Justice Department spokesperson stated that any investigation is based on evidence and facts. Nvidia did not respond to requests for comment but will establish a compliance committee. A source said Nvidia is not currently the target of any national security investigation.

Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said new rules disrupt global supply chains and infringe on Chinese rights. Some lawmakers want stricter export rules and better chip tracking to keep hardware out of China. Chinese AI companies reportedly lease chips from data centers in Malaysia, Singapore, and other Southeast Asian countries. Smuggled chips may equal at least 25 percent of those obtained by Chinese firms through legal routes. Tech titans Alibaba and Tencent are among the companies that have reportedly leased these chips.

Commerce opened an investigation into Megaspeed in 2024 and requested Nvidia sales records in May 2025. Nvidia placed Megaspeed on a no-sell list in June 2025 after a facility inspection in Singapore. Former CEO Jensen Huang allegedly had an affair with Megaspeed's Alice Huang. Current rules allow Nvidia to sell H200 family chips to China if the White House takes 25 percent. The Justice Department created the Super Intelligence Task Force in early November to fight AI crime.

Jensen Huang will be interviewed by House committees on December 1 regarding a potential national security breach. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick announced new regulations to stop foreign data centers from renting chips to China. These rules create new requirements for chip customers in five Southeast Asian countries, including Malaysia and Singapore. The Justice and Commerce departments will continue working together to pursue any criminal conduct. The articles leave open whether the Justice Department will formally probe Nvidia's corporate knowledge.

Articles.Title: National security and AI figures urge DOJ to probe what Nvidia knew about chip smuggling

stories.Headline: Ford Philanthropy president Mary Culler says skilled trades still need human workers present
stories.Summary:
Speaking at the Fortune 500 Innovation Summit on Tuesday, Mary Culler, president of Ford Philanthropy, said that nothing is future-proof, but that many skilled trades are jobs that will always require a human present. She said auto technicians, who are in short supply, could increasingly use AI to help diagnose vehicle problems, but a person is still needed to do the actual manual labor. Carhartt CEO Linda Hubbard, interviewed on stage by Fortune's Kristin Stoller, agreed that AI-driven efficiency will change how trades workers do their jobs, but said labor needs fueled by the data center boom and broader infrastructure investments will keep outpacing any productivity gains from the technology. Hubbard said that no matter how good the industry gets at encouraging people, it will always be challenged to bring enough workers into the trades to rebuild the country's infrastructure.

Employers are expected to fill approximately 1.7 million skilled trades openings annually between now and 2034, while roughly a quarter of the industry's existing 18 million workers are over 55 and nearing retirement, according to the article. Maria Flynn, CEO of Jobs for the Future, said pushback over the cost of college and what jobs really require degrees is growing, but that decades of trade policies and other economic shifts have left some communities with fewer skilled trades opportunities than before. She said the industry has to rebuild trust and awareness and help parents, young people and school counselors understand what the 124 different skilled trades occupations offer and what the paths into those roles are. A report released earlier this year by the Alliance for America's Skilled Trades found that while 95% of counselors agree trade school is a valuable and credible post-high school option, just 54% say they often recommend vocational or trade school and only 28% often recommend an apprenticeship.

The Alliance's September report found that among every 100 people who start an apprenticeship, just 48 complete the program, and only 29 enter a skilled trade occupation within five years of leaving it. The numbers are similarly challenging for related postsecondary programs, where of every 100 entrants, 48 complete their programs and just 34 go on to work in a skilled trade. Flynn described the problem as pipeline leakiness, which can often come down to a lack of support for workers navigating training programs, including barriers like transportation and childcare. Culler said the perception of the trades needs to change and guidance counselors need to start talking about the opportunities, and Flynn said the industry really needs to be working on this together.

stories.Headline: Michael Anello shows how Drupal developers cut AI token costs with browser models and metering
stories.Summary:
Sessions at NEDCamp 2026 explored how developers can manage the costs and keep control of AI features built into Drupal sites, and speakers said cost and control should be treated as design inputs from the very start of a project. Michael Anello, in a session on Drupal AI modules worth knowing about, said Chrome's built-in model can be reached through developer settings and used by Drupal through the AI Browser Provider module, which cuts token costs for everyday summarising and drafting. He also demonstrated AI Metering, a tool that tracks token usage, estimates costs and enforces per-user monthly quotas. That module allows a local fallback provider such as Ollama when limits are reached, which offers an alternative to blocking editor requests, and the choice between blocking and falling back has a significant impact on the user experience.

Jacob Rockowitz, in a talk titled AI ate my Work, and I'm okay with that, discussed optimising coding agents by giving them small and predictable toolsets. He uses Git worktrees and custom DDEV commands as isolated playgrounds for agents, an approach that avoids hardcoded paths and reduces token spending by keeping agent context light. Jim Birch presented a company-wide AI governance system in his session on guardrails, governance and proof that a team still owns the work. His agency uses a PREP framework, meaning purpose, risk, evidence and person, to scope each AI use case, and the system includes a harness for tools, approved tools that do not train on company data, and managed settings. Birch also introduced ownership, where each AI-assisted piece of work receives a delivery record, a YAML file detailing the producer, reviewer, approvals and model used, which answers client questions about verification.

Fredric Mitchell, in a session on defending budgets, addressed budget defence in an AI-driven landscape and noted that AI overviews are eroding organic search traffic, which makes it harder to justify platform budgets based on traffic metrics. He proposed the Web Operations Maturity Model, a rubric that scores platform health across six areas, as an alternative. Ethan Marcotte's keynote, The Work We Want, explored the broader societal impact of AI and framed it within Ursula Franklin's stages of technology. Marcotte argued that AI is institutionalising control with a few firms, likening it to the historical trajectory of the sewing machine, and he suggested that AI limits function best when editors help set them, which gives those editors more control over their work.

stories.Headline: CERT-In flags low severity emBridge flaw and eMudhra removes file browsing functions to fix it
stories.Summary:
CERT-In issued a vulnerability note on November 13 about eMudhra's emBridge digital signature utility, a client-side application that lets web portals communicate with digital signature certificates and hardware tokens installed on a user's computer. The agency said the flaw could let unauthorised entities on the same local area network access file and directory names on an affected device, and it classified the threat as low severity. Cybersecurity expert Karan Saini reported the vulnerability to CERT-In. CERT-In stated that file-browsing functions within the interface did not verify whether requests came from an authorised source, and that these functions operate with the highest system privileges on Windows.

An attacker on the same local network could use a malicious webpage to send requests to emBridge and map out file and folder names on the targeted machine. The affected versions are 5.9.1.x to 5.9.3.x on Windows, 3.2.4.x to 3.2.6.x on macOS, and 3.2.0.x to 3.3.0.x on Ubuntu and Red Hat Linux. CERT-In advised users to upgrade to version 5.9.4.x or later on Windows, 3.2.7.x or later on macOS, and 3.3.1.x or later on Linux. Several government portals, including the Ministry of Corporate Affairs' MCA V3 portal, the Directorate General of Foreign Trade and the National Single Window System, rely on emBridge for DSC-based signing, and the Income Tax Department also recommends it for managing DSCs.

The agency confirmed that the flaw does not provide access to file contents, permit changes or deletions, allow code execution, or expose cryptographic keys or token PINs. eMudhra published its own advisory on the CVE and said it fixed the issue on November 11, two days before CERT-In's note, by removing the file-browsing functions from emBridge entirely. The company said that with these endpoints removed the file enumeration capability is no longer available through emBridge, and it rated the flaw's impact and risk as low. An attack would also require several conditions at once, including an affected emBridge version, a malicious webpage on the same local network, the user opening it, and a browser without Local Network Access restrictions.

The company added that its firewall and local-only request handling block direct access from other machines. Saini posted on X that while the bug was trivial, eMudhra's own advisory had further downplayed it. eMudhra told Inc42 that every digital signature certificate requires the user to enter a token PIN before use, and it pointed out that CERT-In's note confirmed keys and token PINs had not been exposed. A company spokesperson said identifying and fixing vulnerabilities is a routine part of responsible software development, and added that large global vendors like Microsoft, Oracle, Google and Adobe addressed thousands of vulnerabilities every month. The incident follows a major cybersecurity event in October where weak private keys for eMudhra's intermediate certificate authority certificates were reported.

Articles.Title: CERT-In flags eMudhra emBridge vulnerability, users urged to upgrade

stories.Headline: Google Cloud opens applications for a 15-week sovereign AI accelerator for European and Israeli startups
stories.Summary:
Google Cloud announced on November 17, 2026 an open call for applications to its Google for Startups Accelerator: Sovereign AI, which is available in Europe and Israel and supports startups building AI solutions for European regulatory environments. The announcement was made by Giorgia Abeltino, Head of Government Affairs and Public Policy for Google Cloud Europe, Middle East and Africa. The program is described as equity-free and runs for 15 weeks in a hybrid format with virtual and in-person sessions. Applications close on January 15, 2027, and founders can apply on the Google for Startups Accelerator page.

The accelerator is aimed at a small, high-touch cohort of late-seed to post Series A startups headquartered across Europe and Israel with strong traction that use AI for sensitive, regulated workloads. Target areas include government and public service technologies such as sovereign document processing and citizen service portals, with defense applications excluded, as well as healthcare and life sciences, regulated finance, and cybersecurity and data trust. Selected startups receive architectural mentorship, one-to-one pairing with Google Cloud engineers, and advisory support to prepare for EU AI Act Regulatory Sandboxes. Participants also get support to deploy across Google Cloud's tiered sovereign portfolio, from regional data controls and external key management to partner-operated clouds such as S3NS in France and Thales in Germany and fully air-gapped Google Distributed Cloud environments.

Abeltino wrote that artificial intelligence represents an estimated €1.2 trillion economic opportunity for Europe, and that enterprises and public institutions need advanced AI while meeting data governance requirements including the EU AI Act, NIS2, DORA, and national frameworks such as SecNumCloud and BSI's cloud security and sovereignty principles. She said the program wants founders to build in Europe with solutions made in Europe, and that digital sovereignty for startups should not mean settling for second-rate tools or lock-in to a single rigid stack. She described co-engineering with Europe's tech ecosystem so founders can scale on their own terms from day one, for instance by combining Gemini models, open-weight models like Gemma and Mistral, and verifiable data residency and cryptographic controls delivered with local European sovereign partners. Past participants, quoted in the post, said access to Google Cloud engineers who understand sovereign and regulated constraints saves young companies time and that the program helps build compliance answers into architecture from day one.

stories.Headline: Philippines residents protest planned US led AI and manufacturing hub
stories.Summary:
Local residents in the Philippines held protests on Monday against the upcoming visit of President Trump to Manila. These demonstrations center on a planned artificial intelligence and manufacturing hub located just north of the capital city. The project serves as the first major action for Pax Silica, which is an international initiative led by the U.S. State Department. This effort aims to secure high-tech manufacturing supply chains that do not rely on China.

The proposed industrial hub will cover more than 4,000 acres of land in the Philippines. This project follows the December 2025 announcement of Pax Silica, which has since attracted over 25 participating countries including India, Japan, Israel, and the United Kingdom. The Philippines officially joined this initiative in April, leading to the current plans for the manufacturing center. The Marcos administration claims this development could create between 100,000 and 130,000 new jobs for the local population.

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. expressed great excitement in October, calling the hub a grand opportunity to move the country up the value chain. Conversely, advocate Maninging Vilog argued that the project only benefits the United States while grabbing local lands. Protester Kaiser Cortina questioned why farmers and bus drivers should care about artificial intelligence. Representative Antonio Tinio noted that opposition to AI data centers is a global issue seen across Southeast Asia, including Indonesia and Malaysia.

The U.S. government is pursuing this strategy because of long-standing concerns regarding Chinese access to advanced chips and hardware. Recent attention increased following reports that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. Participants in Pax Silica signed a declaration on Sunday regarding the protection of critical infrastructure and sensitive technologies. President Trump is expected to meet with President Marcos on Wednesday during the ASEAN summit before he flies to China.

Articles.Title: Protests flare in Philippines over Trump's visit and planned AI hub

stories.Headline: Academic librarians expect AI to drive change and want to lead AI literacy, Elsevier study finds
stories.Summary:
A global study from Elsevier found that 83 percent of academic librarians surveyed expect artificial intelligence to be the biggest driver of change in academic research, while 81 percent also named the misuse of AI as the greatest threat to the integrity of the scholarly record. The findings come from the Librarian of the Future report, which draws on responses from 1,100 academic librarians across 88 countries, alongside interviews with researchers and academic leaders. The research highlights the increasingly strategic role librarians could play within universities as institutions respond to technological change, evolving research needs and growing concerns around research integrity. Almost all respondents, 95 percent, expect demand for AI support to increase over the next five years.

The report says 82 percent of respondents believe librarians should lead AI literacy initiatives for researchers, and 76 percent believe librarians should contribute to AI governance. Despite these expectations, only 30 percent report that their institution has implemented an AI policy, which suggests a significant gap between the adoption of AI technologies and the development of institutional frameworks to manage their use. More than three-quarters of respondents, 76 percent, anticipate greater collaboration between libraries and other university departments over the next five years. The findings also point to the growing importance of leadership, influencing skills and the ability to navigate complex institutional decisions as librarians take on broader responsibilities.

Ann Gabriel, Senior Vice President, Global Strategic Networks at Elsevier, said librarians have always been essential to research, but the study shows an opportunity for their expertise to play an even more strategic role. She said that as AI transforms how research is discovered, conducted and evaluated, librarians bring a unique combination of technical expertise, ethical judgement and trusted relationships across their institutions. She added that ensuring they have the skills, support and visibility to contribute fully will be important as universities navigate this next phase of change. Jim O'Donnell, University Librarian and Professor at Arizona State University, said librarians long thought they were in the book business, or perhaps the information business, and that the survey shows the community now broadly recognises it is in the research business.

The report suggests that librarians are increasingly positioning themselves as partners in the wider research process, rather than solely as providers of information resources. Alongside AI literacy and governance, demand is expected to grow for library expertise in open access, research data management and research integrity. The report identifies responsible AI adoption, trusted information and research integrity as areas in which librarians could play a more prominent role in supporting researchers and institutional leadership. Elsevier says it will continue working with the global library community to explore how the profession can respond to these changing demands, and the full report is available at Librarian of the Future.

Articles.Title: Academic librarians "see artificial intelligence as biggest driver of change"

stories.Headline: Pearl engineering leader urges CIOs to measure cycle time and rework to gauge AI productivity
stories.Summary:
Nazar Yaremchuk, senior director of engineering at Pearl, wrote in CIO on Nov 17, 2026 that AI can write code in seconds but that is only the first stage of software development. He said AI-generated output can introduce errors, miss internal requirements or require extensive rework, so the time saved upfront can quickly disappear. Accenture reports that 82% of C-suite leaders are increasing AI investments, signaling continued confidence in the technology. Yaremchuk said that if you talk to tech leaders, the returns aren't so clear-cut. A report from Bain & Co found AI coding tools help developers complete roughly 21% more tasks, but time spent reviewing outputs rose 91%.

Yaremchuk said CIOs need to look at the entire process, from the initial idea to software in production, to understand whether AI is improving productivity. He said AI adoption metrics such as token usage and developer participation show how much a company is using AI, but not necessarily whether it is becoming more productive. He said a more useful approach is to track engineering cycle time, end-to-end lead time, review and rework time, and software quality. He said these measures are most useful when considered holistically, and leaders should assess whether quality is consistent or improving and whether review and rework are consuming too much time. He said establishing a baseline before expanding AI use, then tracking these measures over time, can help CIOs distinguish genuine improvements from shifts in where work happens.

At Pearl, Yaremchuk said, the team asked AI to help create pipeline automation, but it generated GitHub Actions workflows for an engineering environment that uses Azure DevOps and Jenkins. He said astute engineers caught the mismatch during review and had to rewrite the integration, and the code was plausible but didn't account for Pearl's actual infrastructure. He said Pearl has a quality-control process that combines AI-assisted review with human oversight based on risk, with lower-risk changes such as unit tests often reviewed primarily by AI while critical production-facing code still receives human review. He said Pearl's AI reviews identify an average of 16 errors per 10 pull requests, including security and architectural issues. He said the goal is not to remove humans from the review process but to use automation to catch issues efficiently and reserve human judgment for decisions where risk and complexity warrant it.

Yaremchuk said Pearl tracks engineering cycle time and has seen it decline month over month in 2026 as its use of AI-generated code has increased. He said that in September 2026, the average pull request Pearl released to production was 75% AI-generated, and 45% of all pull requests were written entirely by AI, with no line edited by a person before commit. He said savvy organizations have taken advantage of AI to automate repetitive tasks so that engineers can focus more on architecture, complex problem-solving and validating results. He said enterprises introducing AI agents that can execute multistep tasks and work together will need to rethink how they assign, supervise and evaluate that work, with clear permissions, defined responsibilities and appropriate oversight. He said of critical importance is determining where human judgment remains essential and how teams should adapt as more work becomes automated.

Yaremchuk said the priority for CIOs should be to redesign engineering workflows around the capabilities of AI, rather than simply adding AI tools to existing processes. He said this starts with establishing a baseline for development speed and software quality, then measuring how both change as AI adoption increases. He said it also means using the results to adjust workflows, review requirements and the allocation of engineering time. He said AI investments should be held accountable to the same business outcomes as any other technology investment, and more code, more tokens and broader adoption can indicate progress but can be misleading. He said the real measure of AI productivity is whether an organization can deliver better software faster, with quality and security intact.

Yaremchuk has nearly 20 years in software delivery and over a decade leading engineering organizations, and he oversees architecture, DevOps, security and AI adoption across a 280-person engineering organization at Pearl. He led a transformation that increased production releases from one to approximately 400 per week and now champions AI-native software delivery. He is completing an Executive MBA at Oxford Saïd Business School. The article was published Nov 17, 2026 and runs 5 minutes.

Articles.Title: The illusion of AI productivity in software development and what to measure instead

stories.Headline: An advisor urges accounting firms to agree AI data access and review rules with each client before use
stories.Summary:
A firm that brings artificial intelligence into bookkeeping, write-up or the monthly close usually does most of its preparation internally, with partners choosing a tool, staff being trained and someone writing an internal policy, but the conversation most often skipped is the one with the client, according to a November 18, 2026 article in CPA Practice Advisor written by an author who says he has spent more than a decade building custom AI systems, much of it for the finance function. The client owns the ledger, and their bank feeds, vendor list, payroll data and customer records are what the AI will read and in some cases change, so if the firm and client have not agreed in advance what the AI may touch, who checks its work and what happens when it gets something wrong, the firm carries a risk nobody has priced and nobody has signed for. The article says the technical problems are usually solvable, while the problems that cause real trouble tend to be about expectations that were never written down.

The article recommends starting with access, because many AI tools connect through the same integrations the firm already uses and can inherit far broader access than the task needs, so a tool that categorizes bank transactions does not need to read payroll and a tool that drafts monthly commentary does not need the ability to post journals. It says the firm should agree in writing with the client which data sources the AI will connect to, keep that list as short as the work allows, and ask whether any data is off limits, since some clients will be relaxed about vendor invoices but uneasy about employee pay or customer details. It also says this sits on top of obligations firms already have, because tax professionals are expected to keep a written information security plan and the IRS guidance in Publication 4557, Safeguarding Taxpayer Data, is a sensible baseline, so a new AI connection not reflected in that plan leaves the plan out of date. The article adds that reading data and changing data are different levels of trust, and it describes three modes for clients: suggest, where the AI proposes a categorization, match or draft and a person accepts or rejects it; act with review, where the AI posts the entry and a person reviews a sample or an exception report before the period is closed; and act alone, where the AI posts and nobody looks unless something breaks.

The article presents these points as the author's recommendations drawn from his experience building AI systems, and it does not name any firm, client or regulator action behind them. It says a firm that can explain plainly what its AI does, what it does not do and who stands behind the numbers offers clients confidence that faster does not mean less careful. The article does not say what happens next beyond urging firms to reach these agreements with each client before AI goes anywhere near their books.

Articles.Title: Trust in the Numbers: What a Firm Should Agree With Each Client Before AI Touches Their Ledger

stories.Headline: Stephen Ferrara launches AI + Nurse Academy to give nurse practitioners a foundation in AI
stories.Summary:
Stephen Ferrara, a doctor of nursing practice and family nurse practitioner, was named Medscape's Nurse Practitioner of the Month in a feature published on November 17, 2026, recognizing his work helping nurses navigate artificial intelligence. He is the chief executive officer and founder of AI + Nurse Academy, an educational platform that gives nurse practitioners a foundation in AI, which he launched in October 2025. Ferrara said his motivation comes down to trying to fix a system he feels is not working as intended for the people it is designed for. Early in his clinical career, he realized state law did not allow him to do things he had been educated and prepared to do, such as performing licensing physicals for people pursuing a barber career, and he turned his attention to overcoming barriers such as full practice authority laws.

The academy currently offers nurse practitioners and registered nurses a 60-minute continuing medical education module, and upon completion users receive a certificate of completion and one accredited hour of continuing education. Participants can also join a community of peers to ask questions, share concerns and exchange experiences, with responsible use as the company's guiding principle. Ferrara said the main goal is to expose every nurse to what generative AI is, what it means for their practice, and to prompt them to consider how they will integrate it thoughtfully into clinical practice. He explained that he wants nurses to understand where AI makes mistakes and how it can affect patient outcomes, stressing that keeping a human or clinician in the loop means AI does not make any decisions without a human or clinician reviewing it.

Ferrara said that in nursing school he was taught that at the end of the day it is your license to lose, and that if you adopt a tool it is your clinical judgment on the line regardless of whether you choose it or are told by administrators to use it. He pointed to flaws in the research large language models rely on, such as the lack of robust cultural, socioeconomic and ethnic studies in certain patient populations, and said he wants the human between AI and the patient to be able to discern whether a recommendation is pertinent. He said it is his core belief that AI can potentially make him a better clinician through rapid access to information and the ability to personalize it to patients, but that it is not magic. He said clinicians are ingrained to do no harm and asked how AI can be made to better anticipate things and patients rather than spewing things that are not necessarily helpful.

Before retiring from his Columbia appointments earlier this year, Ferrara served as inaugural associate dean of AI, spearheading strategy and programs to ensure nurses gained foundational AI literacy, and he moved from assistant to full professor of nursing at Columbia University in New York City. As associate dean of clinical affairs and chief clinical officer for the ColumbiaDoctors Nurse Practitioner Group, he expanded services to include house calls and integrated mental health services, achieving Patient-Centered Medical Home recognition. As president and immediate past president of the American Association of Nurse Practitioners, he advocated for the Improving Care and Access to Nurses Act so nurse practitioners can practice to the top of their license and education. Ferrara reported receiving profits from AI + Nurse Academy, and the article says the path starts with a basic framework and AI literacy and ideally ends with improved patient outcomes, with nurse practitioners determining what happens in between.

stories.Headline: The Hacker News publishes a 15 question checklist for choosing AI pentesting vendors
stories.Summary:
The Hacker News published a guide on November 18, 2026, regarding the selection of artificial intelligence penetration testing vendors for web applications. This advice follows reports from Mandiant M-Trends 2026 showing that exploitation often begins before patches are available, and VulnCheck noting that 23 percent of vulnerabilities in the first half of 2026 were hit on or before disclosure. Additionally, the Google Threat Intelligence Group identified a threat actor using an AI developed zero-day exploit to bypass two-factor authentication through a logic flaw.

The guide provides a checklist of 15 questions, red flags, and a scorecard to help companies evaluate if a vendor can actually reach logged-in workflows and validate findings. It suggests a structured bake-off where multiple vendors test the same application, accounts, and scope within the same week to compare results. This process requires logging three specific timestamps for when access was granted, when discovery finished, and when the first test occurred. The evaluation focuses on context, reach, validated findings, guardrails, and the ability to perform retests.

The authors argue that standard demos are often misleading because they run on the vendor's own targets rather than the client's actual application. They explain that agentic pentesting can close security gaps, which is why 87 percent of surveyed United States security leaders are currently piloting or using the technology. The text notes that manual pentests take between 63 and 95 hours, with 20 to 30 of those hours spent on reconnaissance and analysis. They emphasize that a true pentest must provide verifiable evidence of exploitation rather than just a list of suspected patterns.

The context for these recommendations includes a case study where an AI agent discovered a flaw in a major insurer's website that allowed login codes to be sent to any email address. This vulnerability existed despite the insurer having conducted a manual pentest approximately six months earlier. Another example mentions a researcher who found an unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerability, identified as CVE-2026-68982, in Apache Airflow by testing how deployment parts trust each other. The guide concludes that the best agent is one that proves its findings and runs safely on a production application.

Articles.Title: AI Pentesting Checklist for Web Apps: 15 Questions to Ask Before Choosing a Vendor

stories.headline_source: AI Pentesting Checklist for Web Apps: 15 Questions to Ask Before Choosing a Vendor

stories.Headline: Dr Alliende-Ferrada leads study showing routine ultrasound AI predicts preterm birth risk
stories.Summary:
A peer-reviewed study led by Dr. Rodrigo Alliende-Ferrada tested whether routine ultrasound images alone can predict when a baby will be born, and the work was published in npj Digital Medicine with the DOI 10.1038/s41746-026-03453-0. The investigators ran Ultrasound AI's technology, unchanged, on past scans from 2,550 pregnancies at four public hospitals in Chile, and about a third of the mothers were migrants. For babies who came early, the AI's predicted delivery date was within two weeks 71% of the time and off by about 11 days on average. When the researchers took two pregnancies at the routine 23-week scan, one that went on to deliver early and one that did not, the AI picked the one headed for early birth 86% of the time using only the images, while a coin flip gets 50%.

The warning showed up both for natural early labor and for early deliveries that doctors scheduled for medical reasons, and across all pregnancies the predicted date was within two weeks of the actual birth more than 9 times in 10. The results held up for women who did not have an early scan, often the mothers with the least access to care, and accuracy was similar for Chilean and migrant mothers. The study was a look back at past pregnancies, and no patient's care was based on the AI, with the investigators describing the early-birth results as exploratory and calling for a forward-looking study as the next step. In the United States, Delivery Date AI is not intended to predict preterm birth.

Dr. Alliende-Ferrada said that ten years ago he started working on a simple question of whether an ultrasound image holds more than the few measurements taken from it, and that this study, led by doctors at four public hospitals in Chile, suggests it does. He said that knowing when a baby may come early could give mothers and their care teams time to prepare, and he serves as a strategic advisor to Ultrasound AI, which gave the investigators access to its web platform to upload de-identified images. The article notes that complications of preterm birth are the leading cause of death among children under five worldwide, according to the World Health Organization, and that every pregnancy gets a due date even though a due date assumes every baby arrives at 40 weeks. Blood tests can flag a higher risk of preterm birth, but they report a risk rather than a date, which is the gap the researchers set out to address.

Articles.Title: Routine ultrasound AI accurately predicts risk of preterm birth

stories.Headline: Pulumi launches Pulumi Delivery and Pulumi Agents to let AI agents release and fix software
stories.Summary:
Pulumi, a Seattle cloud-infrastructure startup led by co-founder and CEO Joe Duffy, announced two new products called Pulumi Delivery and Pulumi Agents on Wednesday, November 18, 2026, which let AI agents take over more of the work of releasing software and fixing it when something breaks. The company calls its current fiscal year, which began in July, "the year of absurd ambition," and these are the first results of that push. Duffy said the ceiling on what the company can accomplish is no longer limited by how fast it can build software but by how ambitious it is willing to be. The company was started in 2017 by Duffy and Eric Rudder, both Microsoft veterans, to let engineers manage cloud infrastructure such as servers, networks and permissions by writing code in everyday languages like Python and TypeScript.

Pulumi Delivery lets engineers and AI agents write the steps for releasing software, from testing to sign-off to rollout, as code, and an AI reviewer can judge how risky each change is and either send it live or hand it to a person. Pulumi Agents are AI agents for jobs such as investigating outages, cutting cloud costs and fixing security problems, and each one has limits on what it can touch, with every change it makes showing up as proposed code the team can review. To decide whether a change is safe to ship, Pulumi Delivery can use Jev, an AI model from TypeSafe AI that estimates the odds of specific risks the team asks about in a planned change, and if a risk is higher than the threshold the team sets, the release stops. Both products are available now in public preview, and some features, including Jev decision gates and setting up agents, require Pulumi's paid Pro or Enterprise plans.

Duffy said he first noticed TypeSafe in May when it signed up as a Pulumi customer, because he liked the name, and a few months later Jev took off and TypeSafe used Pulumi to expand worldwide. Daniel Gafni, a member of the technical staff at TypeSafe AI, said in the Pulumi announcement that now even the call on whether a change ships can be made by a model, which he said is exactly the kind of decision Jev was built to make. Duffy said he wishes he could say he predicted 10 years ago that Pulumi's founding bet on everyday programming languages would suit AI agents, but it turns out that what is good for humans is also good for agents. AI agents now handle 40% of the operations on the Pulumi platform that people used to do, up from 15% in April and none in January, and agents such as Claude Code, Codex and Pulumi's own Neo are making infrastructure changes on their own.

Duffy said many companies building AI coding tools stop once the code is written and reviewed, and that for them life stops at the merge, while the new products cover the steps after that, from testing through release. He pointed to Harness, which calls it the "agentic SDLC," and GitHub, which pitched "agentic software delivery" at its Universe conference last month, and said Cursor aspires to solve the problem and Anthropic built its own internal system. The new products could replace some of the work now done by tools such as Argo CD and GitHub Actions, along with lots of homegrown scripts, he said. Pulumi has about 100 employees, down from about 130 last year, and Duffy said there were no layoffs and that AI has changed people's roles and made the company more efficient, with annual recurring revenue per employee more than doubling over the past year; the company isn't profitable yet but has had a few months of positive cash flow this year, and it hasn't raised money since 2023, when it landed a $41 million round led by Madrona, bringing its total to about $99 million over its lifetime.

Articles.Title: ‘Absurd ambition’: Pulumi expands into software delivery with AI agents that ship and fix code

stories.Headline: Psycho-oncology society hosts webinar with Bires leading AI discussion
stories.Summary:
The International Psycho-Oncology Society is promoting a live webinar titled The New Voice in the Room: AI and the Future of Psychosocial Oncology, according to an announcement published by OncoDaily on November 18, 2026. The session will feature Jennifer Bires, Executive Director of Inova Peterson Life with Cancer, as the lead speaker. Adrian Pogacian, Founder of the INCKA Psycho-oncology Center and a clinical psychologist, will moderate the discussion. The announcement frames the event around a simple question, asking what the rapid changes in artificial intelligence mean for the future of psychosocial oncology.

The webinar is built around several questions that the organizers say the field now faces, including whether AI can improve access to psychosocial support. It will also examine how professionals should respond when patients turn to AI for guidance on their own. The discussion will cover emerging applications of AI in psychosocial oncology research, clinical practice and patient self-directed use. Organizers list the potential benefits and risks for access, equity, trust and the therapeutic relationship, along with practical strategies for discussing AI with patients. The session also addresses how to integrate AI thoughtfully while preserving clinical judgment, ethical safeguards and human connection.

Pogacian said in the announcement that he invites people to join what he called a tremendous webinar and topic. He confirmed that he will moderate the session and that Bires will lead the discussion. The announcement states that being part of the conversation is essential as AI continues to reshape healthcare. It directs interested participants to register for the live webinar and to check their local time using a time zone converter. The article does not give a date or time for the session beyond the registration and time zone links.

The announcement places the webinar in the context of artificial intelligence creating new possibilities in cancer care while also raising important questions. It says the topic matters because AI is changing healthcare and the field must decide how to respond. The article also links to a related IPOS announcement about a webinar on fear of cancer recurrence in caregivers. Beyond the registration link and the time zone converter, the article gives no further details on what happens after the session.

stories.Headline: ILO study finds AI and streaming reshape pay and working conditions in media and culture
stories.Summary:
The International Labour Organization published a study on 17 November 2026 examining how streaming and artificial intelligence are reshaping pay and working conditions in the media and culture sector. The report, titled Trends in remuneration and working time: Recorded media and live performance, looks at how creative workers are paid, how their working time is counted, and how digitalization and AI are changing both. Streaming has moved recorded media from physical sales and downloads toward subscription and advertising-funded services, and in recorded music streaming accounted for about 70 per cent of global industry revenue in 2024. AI adds a further layer because voices, images and performances can now be replicated, translated and reworked in new ways, which raises questions of consent, control and remuneration.

The study identifies three main ways AI can affect pay and work. First, AI systems can use existing works and performances as input, as when a recorded voice-over artist's voice is used to generate new dialogue, which raises issues of licensing, attribution and payment. Second, AI can generate or modify content, helping small production firms cut costs through tools such as subtitling and translation, but it may also reduce demand for some types of work or increase competition from AI-generated content. Third, AI can change job tasks, as when an editor spends less time on an initial cut and more on reviewing and correcting AI-generated material, and the question is whether those new tasks are reflected in pay, working time and skills. The report also cites a United Kingdom survey in which 61 per cent of screen directors said they had not fully understood the rights they were granting when signing their contracts.

Workers' organizations emphasize transparency and the need for creative workers to share in the value of later uses of their work, while employers and producers stress upfront investment, uncertain commercial returns and clear rights to finance and distribute the work. Collective agreements can clarify how such uses are permitted and paid, and the report points to the 2023 United States TV/Theatrical Agreement and a 2025 German film industry agreement, which include negotiated provisions on consent and remuneration for some uses of performers' digital replicas. The ILO's human-centred approach emphasizes transparency, human oversight and social dialogue, and the report says social dialogue can support a negotiated transition that promotes adequate remuneration, human creativity and viable enterprises. The report also notes that the ability to benefit from AI is highly uneven, since smaller enterprises and workers in less connected markets are likely to have less access to finance, skills, technology and the systems to manage rights and payments.

Articles.Title: Who shares the value? AI, streaming and decent work in media and culture

stories.Headline: TrustYou adds SummaryAI, Ask TrustYou and Report Builder to its Customer Experience Platform
stories.Summary:
TrustYou, a hospitality technology company headquartered in Munich, Germany, announced on 17 November 2026 that its Customer Experience Platform now opens on three conversational entry points built around jobs hotel teams do every day. The first, SummaryAI, has already read every new review across all sources so each property starts the day with its priorities set. The second, Ask TrustYou, answers any question about guest feedback and lets users follow up and dig deeper within the same conversation. The third, Report Builder, is new today and handles reporting for hotel teams.

A team describes a report once, including the KPIs, the properties and the comparison periods, and CXP then builds it, keeps it on schedule and delivers it as a PDF or Excel file in each recipient's language. That delivery reaches owners and boards who never log in to the system. All three tools work on one principle, which is that a user describes the outcome and CXP delivers it, so hotel teams act on guest issues sooner and guest insight reaches every role without training or analyst support. Multi-property groups get back the days each month they now spend consolidating reports across dozens or hundreds of properties, where quality and operations teams produce reports for general managers, owners, boards and regional leadership, and each audience expects its own KPIs, format and language.

Benjamin Jost, Founder and CEO of TrustYou, said hospitality is becoming conversational on both sides of the front desk, with guests already talking to AI to plan and book their stays. He said that on the guest side the company already closes the loop, because its Customer Data Platform sends every message and its agents answer every reply. He said staff should be able to work the same way with every system a hotel runs, so that you say what you need and it gets done. He described SummaryAI, Ask TrustYou and Report Builder as CXP's biggest step yet toward that vision, where opening it means the reviews are read, asking gives the answer and describing the report means the board has it every month.

SummaryAI, Ask TrustYou and Report Builder are live for all CXP customers, according to the announcement. TrustYou describes itself as hospitality's memory, a platform that unifies what guests feel, what they do and what they ask in a single system, and it says more than 100,000 hospitality businesses have used it since 2008. The company says its AI Review Summaries turn guest reviews from all relevant sources into structured, benchmarked insight for over 2 million properties worldwide, and that the same verified insight reaches travel platforms, booking engines and AI assistants via API and MCP. TrustYou is headquartered in Munich, Germany, and serves hospitality brands in over 165 countries.

stories.Headline: National Insurance Crime Bureau reports AI mentions in questionable claims rise over 1,400%
stories.Summary:
The National Insurance Crime Bureau, a nonprofit based in Oak Brook, Illinois, published its 2026 threat assessment on November 16, 2026, reporting that mentions of AI in questionable claims rose by more than 1,400% from 2025 to mid-2026 across auto, liability, cargo and workers' compensation lines. The report identifies three converging threats: AI-enabled identity schemes, organized crime networks that mix digital and physical tactics, and professional networks of attorneys, medical providers and auto repair firms working together to inflate claims. Fraudsters are using widely available tools to generate fabricated medical records, synthetic identities and doctored accident photographs at a volume that existing claims workflows were not built to handle. A separate Verisk study published in March 2026, based on surveys of 1,000 US consumers and 300 claims professionals, found that 36% of consumers would consider digitally altering a claim image or document even if it broke insurer rules, rising to 55% among Generation Z. On the insurer side, 76% of claims professionals said manipulated media submissions had grown more sophisticated over the past year, while only 32% were confident their organization could identify a deepfake. The report also found more than 1,600 transnational, interstate and state-level organized crime rings operating in 2025, running schemes that span staged accidents, vehicle theft and complex multi-party fraud.

The NICB describes predatory legal and medical networks as systematically exploiting the litigation system, turning low-severity incidents into mass litigation and driving settlement values well beyond the underlying loss, and it has focused legislative efforts on fraud in litigation funding. The FBI estimates non-health insurance fraud costs the US at least $40 billion annually, and fraud losses inflate loss ratios, which in turn drive premiums. In commercial cargo, total supply chain crime incidents across the US and Canada held roughly steady in 2025 at 3,594 events against 3,607 in 2024, but estimated losses reached nearly $725 million, a 60% year-on-year increase, according to Verisk CargoNet's January 2026 annual analysis. The average value per theft rose 36% to $273,990, confirmed cargo theft cases rose 18% year-over-year, and California, Texas and Illinois accounted for just over half of all incidents, while New Jersey, Indiana and Pennsylvania each recorded significant increases. Pranay Mittal, vice president of Travelers Investigative Services, said in a statement issued alongside the NICB report that shared insight is the industry's strongest defense because every insurer holds a piece of the picture, and that working with NICB and other fraud-fighting partners helps investigators spot patterns sooner and focus investigations with greater precision as new threats emerge.

Aimee Stidham, president of the International Association of Special Investigation Units, a global nonprofit headquartered in Albany, New York, and claims SIU manager at Hiscox USA, said in a statement issued alongside the report that the fight against insurance fraud is no longer undertaken by any single organization, and that today's most effective anti-fraud initiatives are driven by collaboration, intelligence sharing and a shared commitment to protecting policyholders. The NICB is integrating business intelligence across its member companies, authenticating digital evidence and building infrastructure to flag emerging fraud patterns earlier, while its field agents work alongside law enforcement to disrupt cargo theft operations directly. For brokers placing cargo or logistics cover, the articles say policies underwritten against 2023 or 2024 loss assumptions may no longer reflect current exposure, and carriers are tightening terms, adding exclusions and demanding stronger chain-of-custody controls from clients, conversations that now fall to brokers to initiate. Policyholders and industry professionals can report suspected fraud to NICB at reportinsurancefraud.org.

Articles.Title: Insurance fraud AI tools surge across US claims and cargo
